Welcome — How to Use This C# Guide

How this guide is organisedThe .NET tooling you will use all course longC# version vs .NET versionHow to read the code in this guide

Welcome to the C# guide, a hands-on course through the language itself on .NET 10. It runs from your first Hello, World! to generics, LINQ, async/await and the modern C# 9–13 syntax that the rest of the .NET ecosystem is written in. Every chapter ends with exercises, and the appendix is a one-page cheat sheet you can keep open while you code.

This is a language guide, not a framework guide. That distinction matters. C# is the only language that can target the .NET runtime, but the runtime ships a huge class library and several web and UI stacks built on top of it. Two of those stacks already have dedicated guides in this library, so this book stays focused on the language itself.

  • For ASP.NET Core — APIs, MVC, Razor Pages, Blazor, EF Core — read ASP.NET Core 10.
  • For Windows desktop UI — WinForms and WPF, XAML, data binding, packaging — read WinForms & WPF.
  • For the language — types, generics, LINQ, async, pattern matching, modern syntax — stay here.

Both companion guides reuse a fair amount of C# covered here: nullable reference types, records and pattern matching in particular. If those chapters look familiar, that is intentional. Read them here first and the framework guides become much shorter.

How this guide is organised

How this guide is organised - Structure

The guide runs in four parts across twelve chapters plus a reference appendix. The order is deliberate: nothing in a chapter depends on a chapter that comes later, and every concept is used again later, so the early chapters pay rent the whole way through.

PartChaptersWhat it gives you
Foundations1 – 3Projects, the type system, nullability, operators and control flow
Data & behaviour4 – 6Strings, collections, spans, classes, structs, records and OOP
Abstraction7 – 9Generics, delegates, events, lambdas and error handling
At scale10 – 12LINQ, async/await concurrency, and the modern C# 9–13 feature set

Chapters 10–12 are where most day-to-day .NET code actually lives. If you already know the language, skim 1–9 for the corners you have forgotten and start at chapter 10.

Each chapter follows the same rhythm:

  • A chapter-level .topic-desc that says what the chapter is for and what you will be able to do after it.
  • Numbered subsections (h3), each with its own short summary so the sidebar gives you a real table of contents rather than a list of titles.
  • Annotated code samples. Comments in the sample carry the explanation so the code stays readable in the editor you paste it into.
  • tip, warn and note callouts for the advice that does not belong in a comment.
  • Five exercises at the end. Type the code rather than pasting it; the muscle memory is the point.

Keep a scratch console project open beside this guide. Every sample here is copy-paste-ready if you paste it into a Program.cs and press F5. Reading C# without a compiler produces very confident misunderstandings.

The .NET tooling you will use all course long

Tooling - IDE Setup

You need exactly one thing to compile C#: the .NET SDK, which bundles the C# compiler, the runtime, the base class library and the dotnet command line. Everything else is an editor. This table is the whole toolchain.

ToolUse it forNotes
.NET 10 SDKBuilding, running, testing, publishingThe only hard requirement. Verify with dotnet --version
dotnet CLIEvery project operationCreate, restore, build, run, test, publish — all scriptable
Visual Studio 2022 (17.12+)Full-featured C# and .NET workBest debugger, best NuGet UX, designers for the UI stacks
VS Code + C# Dev KitLight editing, remote and container workFree, fast, and the only sensible choice over SSH
JetBrains RiderCross-platform .NET IDEExcellent refactorings and LINQ debugger; paid
RoslynThe compiler and language serviceWhat actually understands your code; powers every IDE above
NuGetThird-party packagesPackage manager; restore writes an obj/project.assets.json
dotnet watchHot reload during developmentdotnet watch run applies most code edits live

Roslyn is worth internalising: the compiler is a library, and the same analysis that produces your build errors powers refactorings, IntelliSense and analyzers in every editor. That is why the same code can behave differently across editors and always behaves the same in dotnet build.

Whatever editor you use, the compiler is the source of truth. When an editor and the build disagree, trust dotnet build, because that is what runs in CI.

Four tools, and which one you actually type

The modern .NET workflow is one SDK with a single command in front of it. Everything — building, testing, running, publishing, restoring — is a verb on dotnet, and the verb names the operation rather than the project format or the build system. That is a genuine improvement over the previous generation, where a project could be built with MSBuild, with dotnet build, or by an IDE invoking either, and the differences surfaced as files that worked on one machine.

The three verbs that matter for reading this guide are the ones that change state. Building compiles, and the artefacts land in a directory next to the project file. Testing discovers and runs tests, and its behaviour is shaped by flags rather than by a configuration file. And publishing produces something you can ship, which is a different operation from building and which is where most deployment surprises come from.

The tool that decides where your code goes

The project file is the unit of everything: which files are compiled, which packages are referenced, what the output type is, and what the runtime configuration says. Two consequences are worth naming early. A project with a wrong target framework does not compile with a helpful message — it compiles against reference assemblies that do not have the API you called. And a package reference with a floating version means two machines on the same commit can build against different code.


{{-- THE FOUR VERBS, and what each changes. --}}
dotnet build                     {{-- compile; artefacts next to the
                                      project file                 --}}
dotnet test                      {{-- discover and run tests; the
                                      behaviour is shaped by FLAGS
                                      rather than by a config file --}}
dotnet run --project src/App     {{-- build then run, with the
                                      launch profile applied        --}}
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained false
                                  {{-- a DIFFERENT operation from
                                      build: trimmed, single-file
                                      where asked, and a framework-
                                      dependent output when
                                      self-contained is false --}}

{{-- AND THE PROJECT FILE IS THE UNIT OF EVERYTHING: --}}
// src/App/App.csproj
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>

    {{-- WARNINGS AS ERRORS. The single highest-value setting in the
         file, because it is what turns a nullability warning into a
         build failure rather than a line somebody scrolls past. --}}
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    {{-- EXACT VERSIONS, not ranges: two machines on the same commit
         must build against the same code. --}}
    <PackageReference Include="Serilog" Version="4.2.0" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>


{{-- THE COMMANDS THAT ANSWER THE QUESTIONS PEOPLE ACTUALLY HAVE: --}}

{{-- "Is my dependency tree what I think it is?" --}}
dotnet list package --outdated
dotnet list package --include-transitive
{{-- ^ the second finds a package three levels down that pins an old
     version of something you also depend on directly. --}}

{{-- "Why does it work in Debug and not in Release?" --}}
dotnet build -c Release /warnaserror
dotnet build -c Release /p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=false
{{-- ^ if the Release build is the one failing, the difference is
     usually a warning: a nullability warning, an obsolete API, or a
     conditional-compilation branch that only one configuration
     compiles. Turning warnings into errors in Release only is a
     four-line change that finds it every time. --}}

{{-- "What does the compiler think my project actually contains?" --}}
dotnet msbuild src/App/App.csproj -getProperty:TargetFramework
dotnet msbuild src/App/App.csproj -getItem:Compile
{{-- ^ -getItem:Compile lists the files that will be compiled, which
     is the answer when a type is "missing" and you have forgotten
     an Exclude, a glob or a conditional. --}}

{{-- AND THE FILE THAT DECIDES ALL OF THIS, which is worth reading
     once in full rather than by editing it: --}}
dotnet msbuild src/App/App.csproj -preprocess:full.xml
{{-- ^ the evaluated project file with every import, every property
     and every default resolved. This is the answer to "where is
     that property coming from" — a question that otherwise takes an
     hour of guessing. --}}

C# version vs .NET version

Orientation - Version Compatibility

These are two different version numbers that are constantly confused. The .NET version names the runtime and its base class library. The C# version names the language. They move together but they are not the same thing, and a language feature can ship without any new runtime.

.NETDefault C#Headline language features
.NET 8C# 12Primary constructors on classes, collection expressions, ref readonly parameters, alias any type
.NET 9C# 13params collections, \e escape, partial properties, ref struct interfaces, lock object, field keyword
.NET 10C# 14Extension members, field-backed properties everywhere, null-conditional assignment, first-class span types

The pairing above is the default. You can opt into a newer language version on an older runtime with <LangVersion>, but only if every feature you use is purely syntactic and needs no new BCL types.

Because C# 13 is the stable, widely deployed baseline, this guide is written for C# 14 on .NET 10 and marks anything newer as a preview feature. Chapter 12 has the full timeline.

Setting <LangVersion>latest on a library is a compatibility trap. Consumers on older SDKs will fail to compile your package, and the failure appears in their build rather than yours. Pin the version explicitly in libraries; use latest only in applications you own end to end.

Two version numbers, and confusing them costs a day

The language version and the runtime version are separate things that happen to share a number. The language version is which syntax and which standard library surface the compiler accepts; it is written in the project file as a LangVersion. The runtime version is which shared framework the output loads against; it is the target framework, and it decides what is in the framework at run time.

The consequence is that a project can use a language feature newer than the runtime it targets, and the failure mode is confusing: it compiles, and then at run time a method is missing. The rule is that the language version must not exceed the target framework, and the compiler enforces it only when you ask for a language version explicitly.

What a target framework actually selects

It selects the reference assemblies the compiler sees, which determines what APIs exist; the runtime pack the output deploys against; and the default language version, because a newer target permits newer syntax. Those are three separate consequences and they are the reason a multi-targeting project is a build configuration rather than a source change.


{{-- THE TWO NUMBERS, and the setting that separates them: --}}
// src/App/App.csproj
<PropertyGroup>
  {{-- THE RUNTIME VERSION: decides the reference assemblies the
       compiler checks against, and therefore which APIs exist. --}}
  <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>

  {{-- THE LANGUAGE VERSION: which syntax the compiler accepts. Leave
       it unset and it follows the target framework, which is correct
       in almost every case. --}}
  <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
</PropertyGroup>

{{-- THE FAILURE WHEN A LANGUAGE VERSION EXCEEDS THE RUNTIME: --}}
<PropertyGroup>
  <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
  <LangVersion>preview</LangVersion>   {{-- WRONG: the code COMPILES
                                           against the net8.0
                                           reference assemblies and
                                           then throws at run time
                                           with "method not found",
                                           because the API exists
                                           in the language but not
                                           in the runtime. --}}
</PropertyGroup>

{{-- AND WHY IT COMPILES AT ALL: --}}
dynamic device = GetDevice();
device.NewApiIntroducedInNet10();     {{-- NO COMPILE ERROR. dynamic
                                           dispatches by name at RUN
                                           time, and the compiler
                                           checks nothing. This is
                                           the mechanism by which a
                                           language-version mistake
                                           reaches production with a
                                           clean build. --}}


{{-- MULTI-TARGETING, which is a BUILD CONFIGURATION rather than a
     source change — and the reason is that each target compiles the
     same source against DIFFERENT reference assemblies: --}}
<PropertyGroup>
  <TargetFrameworks>net8.0;net10.0</TargetFrameworks>
</PropertyGroup>

<ItemGroup>
  {{-- A package that only supports the older target needs a
       CONDITIONAL reference rather than a second project. --}}
  <PackageReference Include="Some.Legacy.Library" Version="2.0.0"
                   Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net8.0'" />
</ItemGroup>

{{-- THE PROBLEM WITH MULTI-TARGETING, which is that it makes every
     API difference a CONDITIONAL COMPILATION, and the code you
     read is then not the code that compiles: --}}
#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER
    var buffer = System.Buffers.ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1024);
#else
    var buffer = System.Buffers.ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1024);
    // ^ identical, and two copies to keep in step
#endif

{{-- ...unless the difference is a versioned type, which is what
     they are FOR: --}}
#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = AsSpan();
#else
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = new ReadOnlySpan<char>(AsMemory().ToArray());
#endif

{{-- THE COMMAND THAT ANSWERS THE QUESTION: --}}
dotnet --info
dotnet build -f net10.0
{{-- ^ the SDK lists every framework it has packs for, so a missing
     pack is a visible line rather than a download that fails at the
     worst moment. --}}

{{-- AND THE RUNTIME VERSION IS NOT THE ONLY ONE THAT MATTERS: a
     self-contained publish carries the runtime with it, a
     framework-dependent one does not, and the difference is which
     machine can run the output. --}}
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained false
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true
{{-- ^ the second produces a 70 MB output that needs no runtime on
     the target, which is what a container base image without .NET
     requires. --}}

How to read the code in this guide

Orientation - Code Examples

Samples are written to be pasted into a console project and run. Where a feature needs extra setup — a project file, a NuGet package — that is shown explicitly. Types from the BCL appear unqualified, which assumes the implicit usings the SDK adds by default.

The default console template sets ImplicitUsings to enable, which means these namespaces are already imported and you do not need a using line for any of them:

The samples in this guide are written to be read as demonstrations rather than as production code, and it is worth being explicit about which conventions that changes — because most of the alternatives are also correct.

Names and the type names a reader has to know

Namespace-qualified names are shortened once at the top of a file, so a sample shows TryGetValue rather than a hundred characters of qualification. Where two types collide — Task against a domain type, or Range — the local alias names one of them and says which.

The two conventions that are production, not presentation

Nullable reference types are enabled throughout, so every annotation in a sample means what it means in your own code. And using declarations appear where a resource is released early rather than at the end of the enclosing block, because the alternative hides a lifetime in indentation.

The one convention that is presentation

Sample methods return Task rather than being async void. That is not a style choice at all — an async void method cannot be awaited, so an exception in it crashes the process rather than propagating to a caller — and it is used consistently so the distinction is visible in every sample rather than explained once.

System
System.Collections.Generic
System.IO
System.Linq
System.Net.Http
System.Threading
System.Threading.Tasks

Anything outside that list — System.Text, System.Globalization, System.Collections.Immutable — needs an explicit using at the top of the file.

// The whole "hello world" of modern C#. Type Program.cs and press F5.
Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!");

// Top-level statements: no class, no Main, no namespace required.
// The compiler synthesises a Program class for you.

Top-level statements are the subject of section 1.3. They are why a modern C# console program is four lines long instead of twenty.

Use dotnet run from the project folder rather than building and launching the binary yourself. It picks up the right runtime version, environment variables and working directory every time.

Exercises 0

  1. Install the .NET 10 SDK and run dotnet --list-sdks. Record the version you installed.
  2. Create a console project called Scratch, run it, and find the generated Program.cs and Scratch.csproj on disk.
  3. Print Environment.Version and System.Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation.FrameworkDescription to confirm which runtime you are actually on.
  4. Open the same project in Visual Studio, VS Code and Rider if you have more than one. Confirm all three report the same SDK version.

1 · Getting Started & Project Setup

1.1 Your first program1.2 Project vs solution1.3 The dotnet CLI1.4 Top-level statements1.5 The project file1.6 Configuration and appsettings.json

Chapter one covers the mechanics of getting C# code onto your machine and running it: the shape of a first program, the difference between a project and a solution, the dotnet commands you will use daily, the modern SDK-style project file, and how configuration reaches your code. None of this is glamorous, but it is the part that blocks every newcomer for the first hour.

1.1 Your first program

1.1.1 Hello World

A C# program is a set of types compiled into an assembly. The entry point is a method named Main, which the runtime looks for. Modern C# lets you skip declaring it: the compiler generates a Program class around your top-level statements and hands you a Main for free.

What the compiler is actually checking

A first C# program is usually presented as a hello world, which teaches nothing beyond the file-extension-to-runner mapping. The useful version is one that has a compile error in it and shows what the message says, because the message is the part of the language most people never learn to read and the part they most need to read.

Three things are being checked, and they are checked in a fixed order: the syntax, then the names and their types, then whether the types can be used together. A method that does not exist is a name error; a method that exists but takes three arguments is a signature error; and a method that returns a value used as a statement is a type error. Each has a distinct message shape, and the shape tells you which stage failed.

Where the program starts

A traditional project starts at Main, which the compiler finds for you and which you therefore rarely see. A top-level-statements project starts at the first line of the file, and the compiler synthesises the Main for it. That is a difference in where the entry point is written rather than in what the language does, and it is worth knowing because a file with top-level statements cannot be a class body — which constrains where a file's types can live.

// Classic form: explicit entry point in a class. Still perfectly legal.
using System;

namespace Scratch
{
    internal class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Hello from the classic form.");
        }
    }
}

The classic form matters twice: every tutorial written before 2008 uses it, and several compiler settings (StartupObject, custom entry points, top-level statement conflicts) only make sense once you have seen it.

Statements write to the console with Console.Write (no trailing newline) or Console.WriteLine (with one). Reading from the console is Console.ReadLine, which returns a nullable string? because the user may type nothing at all.

Console.Write("Loading");
Console.WriteLine("...");

Console.Write("What is your name? ");
string? name = Console.ReadLine();   // ReadLine returns string?

if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name))
{
    Console.WriteLine("Hello, stranger.");
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine("Hello, " + name + "!");
}

The string? return type is nullable reference type analysis doing its job. The compiler is telling you that ReadLine can hand you null, and forcing you to decide what that means.

Console apps are genuinely useful for learning, CLI tools and diagnostics. They are also how you reproduce a bug in isolation: copy the failing method into a console project, delete everything else, and the bug is usually still there.


{{-- THE THREE STAGES, and their message shapes. --}}
// (1) SYNTAX. The compiler stops at the first one and reports one
//     error, because everything after it is unreadable.
static void SyntaxError()
{
    int x = 5          // the missing semicolon
}

// == error CS1002: ; expected ==

// (2) NAMES. Every name in the file is resolved before types are
//     combined, so an unknown name is reported on its own.
static void NameError()
{
    int total = Sum(1, 2);
}

// == error CS0103: The name 'Sum' does not exist in the current
//     context ==

// (3) SIGNATURES AND TYPES. The name resolved; the call did not
//     match any overload.
static void SignatureError()
{
    int total = Sum(1, 2, 3);
}

// == error CS1501: No overload for method 'Sum' takes 3 arguments ==

{{-- WHERE THE PROGRAM STARTS, and it differs between the two
     project shapes: --}}

{{-- A TRADITIONAL PROJECT: Main, which the compiler finds for you. --}}
internal static class Program
{
    // THE SIGNATURE that matters, and it is not obvious:
    // static async Task Main, NOT static async void Main.
    //
    // async void CANNOT BE AWAITED. An exception thrown inside it
    // cannot propagate to a caller, so the runtime reports it and
    // terminates the process rather than the operation failing. An
    // exception inside async Task propagates to whoever awaits the
    // method, where it can be caught.
    private static async Task Main(string[] args)
    {
        await Console.Out.WriteLineAsync("hello");
    }
}

{{-- TOP-LEVEL STATEMENTS: the compiler synthesises the same Main
     from the first lines of the file. Note that the file therefore
     CANNOT also contain a class declaration ABOVE the statements —
     the statements come first, and every type follows. --}}
using System;                        {{-- usings first --}}

Console.WriteLine("hello");           {{-- then statements --}}

// then any types the file needs:
public sealed record Command(string Name, int Arity);

1.2 Project vs solution

1.2.1 Project Structure

A project compiles to exactly one output — an assembly (.dll or .exe). A solution is a container file that groups projects and remembers how they reference each other. Most of the time you work inside a solution and never open the .sln by hand.

What a solution is, and when you need one

A project is one compilation unit with one output. A solution is a container that knows how to build several of them together, with dependencies between them, and it exists so that a build can be ordered correctly rather than so that a set of files can be grouped. For a single executable, a project file alone is enough and a solution adds a file that has to be kept in step with the project.

The case that justifies a solution is a project that depends on another: a class library used by a web application and by a test project. The dependency is declared in the project file, not in the solution, so the solution is only a build order. That distinction matters because it means a solution file is safe to delete and regenerate, whereas a project file is not.

What the build actually does with a solution

It builds the projects in dependency order and it does so in parallel where it can. The consequence worth knowing is that a build with several projects will interleave their output, so a log showing errors from more than one project means the dependency order allowed them to start together — which is correct behaviour and not a sign of a race.

MyApp.sln
  |
  +-- src/MyApp/          -> MyApp.csproj       (web or app host, references Core)
  +-- src/MyApp.Core/     -> MyApp.Core.csproj  (class library: models + logic)
  +-- tests/MyApp.Tests/  -> MyApp.Tests.csproj (references Core, xUnit)
  +-- Directory.Build.props         (settings shared by every project)
  +-- Directory.Packages.props      (central package version management)
  +-- global.json                    (pins the SDK version)

The layout on the left is the convention that Microsoft recommends and the one the .NET CLI now creates for you. Separating the app host from the logic is what makes the logic testable.

Modern .NET uses SDK-style projects. There is one project file, no separate packages.config, no AssemblyInfo.cs you edit by hand, and package versions usually live in the project file. The old non-SDK format is legacy; you will rarely see it in new code.

Directory.Packages.props with ManagePackageVersionsCentrally is worth enabling on any solution with more than two projects. One version per package, upgraded in one place, and no more mismatched transitive versions.


{{-- A SOLUTION IS A BUILD ORDER, and the dependency is declared in
     the PROJECT, not in the solution: --}}
{{--
MyApp.sln              <- the container: knows the projects and
                          their build order
src/
  MyApp.Domain/        <- a class library. NO dependencies.
    MyApp.Domain.csproj
  MyApp.Web/           <- a web app. DEPENDS ON Domain.
    MyApp.Web.csproj
tests/
  MyApp.Tests/         <- depends on Web AND Domain.
    MyApp.Tests.csproj
--}}

// src/MyApp.Web/MyApp.Web.csproj
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    {{-- THE DEPENDENCY, and it is here rather than in the .sln
         — which is why the solution file is disposable and this
         file is not. --}}
    <ProjectReference Include="..MyApp.DomainMyApp.Domain.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

{{-- SO A SINGLE EXECUTABLE NEEDS NO SOLUTION, and the .sln adds a
     file to keep in step for no benefit: --}}
dotnet new console -o Hello
dotnet run --project Hello
{{-- ^ no solution involved at all. --}}

{{-- A SOLUTION IS FOR THE MULTI-PROJECT CASE: --}}
dotnet new sln -n MyApp
dotnet sln add src/MyApp.Domain src/MyApp.Web tests/MyApp.Tests
{{-- ^ regenerable at any time, so it is worth deleting and
     recreating rather than editing by hand. --}}

{{-- AND WHAT THE BUILD DOES WITH IT: builds in dependency order,
     in PARALLEL where it can — so a log with errors from several
     projects is correct behaviour, not a race. --}}
dotnet build MyApp.sln -v minimal
dotnet build MyApp.sln --no-incremental   {{-- from scratch: what CI
                                               should do, because an
                                               incremental build can
                                               succeed on a clean
                                               checkout --}}
dotnet test MyApp.sln --no-build

1.3 The dotnet CLI

1.3.1 Common Commands

The dotnet command is the whole build system, test runner and package manager in one executable. Learn these twenty commands and you can work in any editor, including over SSH with no GUI at all.

The verbs you will type daily

Restore, build, test, run, publish, and a set of template-driven creation verbs. Of those, three have behaviour worth knowing before the first day: test, because its discovery mechanism is not what most people expect; run, because its argument handling has changed more than once; and publish, because it produces something different from a build and the difference is where deployment surprises come from.

Restore is the one that is genuinely uninteresting until it is not. It reads the project files, resolves the dependency graph, and writes two files recording the result. In a modern project those two files are committed, and a build on a clean checkout uses them rather than re-resolving — which is what makes a build reproducible.

The verb that is not there

There is no dotnet run-all, no dotnet clean worth relying on, and no dotnet deploy that does what the name suggests. Deployment is a publish followed by a copy, and the copy is done by whatever the platform provides. Knowing that the verb you want does not exist saves an afternoon of searching.

# create and run
dotnet new console -n Scratch              # new console project called Scratch
cd Scratch
dotnet run                                # build + run
dotnet run -- 42 --verbose                 # args after -- go to args[]

# the template list (there are ~60 built-in templates)
dotnet new list

# add things
dotnet add package Newtonsoft.Json         # NuGet reference + version in the csproj
dotnet add reference ../MyApp.Core        # project reference
dotnet sln add src/MyApp/MyApp.csproj     # register a project with the solution

# build cycle
dotnet build                              # Debug by default
dotnet build -c Release                   # optimised, no debug symbols by default
dotnet build -warnaserror                # CI-grade: warnings break the build
dotnet clean
dotnet restore

# test, run and publish
dotnet test                               # runs every test project in the solution
dotnet test --filter "Category=Fast"
dotnet watch run                          # hot reload: applies edits without restart
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained false

dotnet publish is where deployment settings actually live: framework-dependent versus self-contained, single-file, trimmed, and per-runtime identifiers. The ASP.NET guide covers the options in depth.

CommandWhat it actually does
dotnet buildRestores if needed, compiles, writes to bin/
dotnet runBuilds then launches with the project’s dependencies in place
dotnet testBuilds, then discovers and runs tests via VSTest or Microsoft.Testing.Platform
dotnet restoreResolves the dependency graph and writes project.assets.json
dotnet formatApplies .editorconfig whitespace and style rules to the tree
dotnet tool install -gInstalls a global tool such as dotnet-ef or dotnet-counters

Run dotnet --help and then dotnet <verb> --help for any command. The built-in help is genuinely good and beats any third-party tutorial.


{{-- THE DAILY VERBS. --}}
dotnet restore                          {{-- read project files,
                                              resolve the graph,
                                              write the lock --}}
dotnet build                           {{-- compile --}}
dotnet test                            {{-- discover and run --}}
dotnet run --project src/MyApp.Web      {{-- build then run, with the
                                              launch profile --}}
dotnet publish -c Release -o out       {{-- a DIFFERENT artefact
                                              from build --}}

{{-- RESTORE IS UNINTERESTING UNTIL IT IS NOT, and the reason is
     the two files it writes: --}}
{{-- obj/project.assets.json    the resolved graph: every package,
                                  every version, every asset path
   obj/*.nuget.g.props         the props imported into the build
   obj/*.nuget.g.targets       the targets imported after the build --}}
{{-- These are committed. A build on a clean checkout USES them
     rather than re-resolving, which is what makes a build
     reproducible. A project with them gitignored resolves fresh on
     every machine, which is the opposite. --}}

{{-- TEST, and the discovery mechanism people expect wrongly: --}}
dotnet test                          {{-- xUnit, NUnit and MSTest all
                                          work; the runner is per
                                          PROJECT --}}
dotnet test --filter "Category=Fast"
dotnet test --filter "FullyQualifiedName~MyApp.Tests.Pricing"
dotnet test --logger "console;verbosity=detailed"
dotnet test --blame                                   {{-- hangs:
                                                               produces a
                                                               dump and a
                                                               test log
                                                               instead of
                                                               waiting
                                                               forever --}}
dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"

{{-- RUN, whose arguments are a continuing source of surprise: --}}
dotnet run --project src/MyApp.Web -- --urls http://localhost:5000
{{-- ^ EVERYTHING AFTER -- GOES TO THE APPLICATION. Without it the
     argument is consumed by dotnet run and never reaches your
     program. --}}

{{-- PUBLISH, which is not a build: --}}
dotnet publish -c Release -o out
{{-- ^ trim, single-file where supported, and with
     SelfContained=false it produces a framework-DEPENDENT output
     that needs the runtime installed on the machine. Publishing for
     linux-x64 from Windows requires the runtime pack for that
     platform, which the SDK downloads on first use. --}}
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained false
dotnet publish -c Release /p:PublishTrimmed=true
dotnet publish -c Release /p:PublishAot=true

{{-- THE VERB THAT IS NOT THERE: --}}
{{--   dotnet deploy        does not exist
     dotnet run-all        does not exist
     dotnet clean          exists and is usually not what you want:
                           it removes intermediates but not the
                           bin output, so the next build still
                           thinks it is up to date. Use
                           --no-incremental instead. --}}

1.4 Top-level statements

Top-level statements (C# 9) let you write a program as a bare sequence of statements at the top of a file. The compiler wraps them in an internal Program class with a generated Main. This is why the default template is four lines instead of a full class.

Where the code lives in a top-level-statements file

Using directives come first, then statements, then type declarations. That order is a constraint rather than a convention, and it is the one thing about top-level statements that surprises people: a class declared above the statements does not compile, because the compiler expects statements there.

The mechanism is a rewrite. The compiler takes the statements, puts them into a synthesised Main, and leaves the file's types where they are. That is why the program still behaves exactly as if you had written Main yourself — the same restrictions on static, the same argument array, the same entry-point rules — and why the two forms can be mixed across a project even though they cannot be mixed within a file.

When it is the right choice

For a console utility, because the file is one sequence and a Program class adds indentation and a nested static class for no benefit. For anything larger, a Program class is better: it makes the entry point findable, it allows several methods that the entry point calls, and it is what a reader expects in a codebase with more than one file.

// Program.cs as generated by: dotnet new console
// See https://aka.ms/new-console-template for more information
Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!");

There can be only one top-level statements file per project, and it must come before any type declarations. Types declared in the same file are still legal after the statements.

Because the statements are method bodies, local functions work, await works at the top level, and return exits Main. What does not work is a static modifier on local functions being referenced before declaration, and const fields.

// Async at the top level: legal, and the reason top-level statements
// are so useful for API experiments and scripts.
using System.Net.Http;

using var client = new HttpClient();
string body = await client.GetStringAsync("https://example.com");

Console.WriteLine("Fetched " + body.Length + " characters.");

int ParsePort(string text)
{
    return int.TryParse(text, out int port) ? port : 8080;   // local function
}

Top-level statements compile to a synchronous or async Main depending on whether an await appears at the top level. You do not declare which.

Do not mix top-level statements with a hand-written Main. The build fails with top-level statements must precede namespace and type declarations or a program cannot contain both, and the message is rarely the first thing you look at.

Top-level statements are ideal for a 20-line script that talks to an API, and terrible for a 2000-line program. The moment your file needs a namespace, a using directive at the top and real types, switch to the classic form.


{{-- THE ORDER IS A CONSTRAINT, not a convention: --}}
{{-- usings first --}}
using System;
using System.Linq;

{{-- then STATEMENTS --}}
if (args.Length == 0)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine("usage: app <name>");
    return 1;                          {{-- returning from top-level
                                            statements sets the exit
                                            CODE, which is why this is
                                            the right way to report a
                                            failure --}}
}

var orders = LoadOrders(args[0]);
Console.WriteLine($"loaded {orders.Count}");

{{-- and only then TYPES, which cannot come before the statements: --}}

// WRONG: a type declaration above the statements does not compile.
// <h4>This is a comment, not a declaration</h4>
internal sealed record Order(string Number, decimal Total);

static List<Order> LoadOrders(string path) => [];

{{-- THE REWRITE, and it is why the behaviour is identical to a
     Main you wrote yourself: --}}
{{--
using System;

internal static class Program
{
    private static int Main(string[] args)     // synthesised
    {
        if (args.Length == 0) return 1;       // the statements
        ...
        return 0;
    }
}

internal sealed record Order(...);            // the types, where
                                              // they already were
--}}

{{-- WHEN IT IS THE RIGHT CHOICE: --}}
{{-- console utility, one sequence -> top-level statements, because
     a Program class adds indentation and a nested static class for
     no benefit
     anything larger                 -> a Program class, because it
                                         makes the entry point
                                         findable and allows the
                                         entry point to call
                                         several methods --}}

1.5 The project file

The .csproj is XML, but you should rarely edit it by hand — the CLI and IDEs both manage it. Knowing what the important properties mean is still essential, because CI configuration, Docker builds and the ASP.NET hosting model are all expressed here.

The file is a build configuration, not a manifest

Everything a project's compilation needs is in it: which files are compiled, which packages are referenced, what the output type is, and what the runtime configuration says. Most of what looks like manifest content — the assembly name, the version, the package metadata — is copied from it into the output, which is why two projects can produce assemblies with different names and versions without either of them declaring it in code.

The consequence worth stating is that a project file is a source file with a build system attached, so it belongs in version control and it is reviewed like one. A change to a package version is a dependency change, and treating it as configuration is how a framework upgrade becomes an unreviewed one.

The properties with the widest blast radius

Three. The target framework, which decides the reference assemblies and therefore what APIs exist. The nullable setting, which changes what the compiler reports across every file in the project. And the warning settings, which decide whether a nullability warning is a line in a log or a failed build.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>      <!-- which runtime to target -->
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>                 <!-- Exe, WinExe, or Library (default) -->
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>                   <!-- nullable reference types ON -->
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>       <!-- skip the boilerplate usings -->
    <LangVersion>13.0</LangVersion>                <!-- pin the language version -->
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <InvariantGlobalization>false</InvariantGlobalization>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Serilog" Version="4.2.0" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <InternalsVisibleTo Include="MyApp.Tests" />      <!-- let tests see internal types -->
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

Always set <Nullable>enable</Nullable> on a new project. It is not a default you can defer indefinitely — turning it on later produces a large, noisy diff and hides real bugs in the meantime.

PropertyWhat it controls
TargetFrameworkWhich runtime and BCL the assembly binds to, for example net10.0 or net10.0-windows
OutputTypeLibrary (dll), Exe (console), WinExe (no console window)
NullableEnables the nullable reference type analysis; enable or warnings
ImplicitUsingsAdds the default namespace set so you need no using System;
InvariantGlobalizationtrue shrinks the app by dropping culture data — breaks culture-sensitive formatting
EnableTrimAnalyzerWarns about reflection that trimming would break in a published app
AssemblyNameOutput file name, when it should differ from the project name

There is no packages.config in SDK-style projects. A PackageReference pulls in the package and its transitive dependencies automatically, and dotnet restore computes the whole graph.


{{-- THE PROPERTIES WITH THE WIDEST BLAST RADIUS: --}}
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    {{-- 1. THE TARGET FRAMEWORK. Decides the reference assemblies,
           so it decides what APIs exist. Changing it is a source
           change in effect. --}}
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <AssemblyName>MyApp.Domain</AssemblyName>
    <RootNamespace>MyApp.Domain</RootNamespace>

    {{-- 2. NULLABLE. Turns on the analysis across EVERY file in the
           project, so enabling it in a project with existing code
           produces a large warning list. --}}
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>

    {{-- 3. WARNINGS AS ERRORS. What turns a nullability warning
           into a build failure rather than a line somebody
           scrolls past. --}}
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <WarningLevel>9999</WarningLevel>

    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <InvariantGlobalization>false</InvariantGlobalization>

    {{-- THE OUTPUT TYPE. An executable defaults to Exe, a library
         to Library, and getting it wrong produces a DLL with an
         entry point nobody can find. --}}
    <OutputType>Library</OutputType>

    {{-- DETERMINISTIC OUTPUT, which is what makes two builds of
         the same commit byte-identical and therefore comparable
         and cacheable. --}}
    <Deterministic>true</Deterministic>
    <ContinuousIntegrationBuild>true</ContinuousIntegrationBuild>
  </PropertyGroup>

  {{-- WHAT THE FILE DECIDES, and which parts are copy-in: --}}
  <PropertyGroup>
    {{-- COPIED INTO THE OUTPUT, not declared in code. Two projects
         can produce assemblies with different names and versions
         without either of them mentioning either. --}}
    <Version>2.4.0</Version>
    <PackageId>MyApp.Domain</PackageId>
    <Description>The domain model.</Description>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    {{-- CONDITIONAL COMPILATION, which is how one source tree
         builds several variants — and the cost is that the code you
         read is not the code that compiles. --}}
    <Compile Remove="**/*.Legacy.cs" Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

1.6 Configuration and appsettings.json

Configuration in .NET is a layered key/value store. You add sources, each one overriding the last, and bind a strongly typed object against a section. The framework ships JSON, environment variables, command line and user secrets out of the box.

// Program.cs - the standard generic host setup used by every template
using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;

var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);

builder.Configuration.AddEnvironmentVariables();
builder.Services.Configure<StorageOptions>(
    builder.Configuration.GetSection("Storage"));

using var app = builder.Build();
app.Run();

internal sealed class StorageOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Storage";

    public string ConnectionString { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    public int MaxRetries { get; set; } = 3;
}

The matching JSON file uses double nesting: the property name in the class, then the section name you bind. <StorageOptions>...ConnectionString lives at Storage:ConnectionString.

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information", "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning" }
  },
  "Storage": {
    "ConnectionString": "Server=localhost;Database=app;Trusted_Connection=True;",
    "MaxRetries": 5
  }
}

Environment variables override JSON, using __ (double underscore) as the section separator: Storage__ConnectionString=.... In production the platform usually injects them, which is why secrets do not belong in the JSON file.

Use User Secrets (dotnet user-secrets init) for local development secrets. They are stored outside the project tree, so they never reach git, and the connection string above can stay in source control.

Exercises 1

  1. Run dotnet new console -n Scratch, run it, then change the output and run again without rebuilding by hand.
  2. Delete the contents of Program.cs and rebuild. Read the compiler error, then use it to write the classic Main form by hand and confirm the two produce the same output.
  3. Create a solution, add a console project and a class library to it, and add a project reference so the console app can call a method in the library.
  4. Add a JSON file to the console app, read it with ConfigurationBuilder, and override one value with an environment variable set on the command line.
  5. Add PackageReference for Newtonsoft.Json and Serilog, then run dotnet list package to see the resolved dependency graph.

2 · Types, Variables & Nullability

2.1 Value types vs reference types2.2 var and the implicit typing rule2.3 Nullable reference types2.4 Nullable value types2.5 Numeric types and their traps2.6 Conversions, checked and unchecked2.7 dynamic vs object

Chapter two is the heart of the language. C# is statically typed, so almost every decision you make is a decision about a type. This chapter covers the split between value and reference semantics, the var rule, nullable reference types, the numeric tower and its overflow traps, and the difference between object and dynamic.

2.1 Value types vs reference types

C# splits every type into two categories. Value types are copied on assignment; reference types are shared. The primitive numeric types, bool, char, enum and every struct are value types. class, interface (as a reference), string, object, arrays and delegates are reference types. Nullable<T> is a struct, so it is a value type.

The split between value and reference types decides three things at once: where the data lives, what copying a variable does, and whether assignment shares state. It is worth being precise about because the common shorthand — "structs are copied, classes are shared" — is right about the default and wrong about what people expect to follow from it.

Copying versus sharing

Assigning a value type copies it. Assigning a reference type copies the reference, so both variables then name the same object and a change through one is visible through the other. That is the whole of it, and every surprise in this area follows from a case the shorthand does not cover: a value type that contains a reference type.

A structure with a field that is a class instance, an array or a string is a value type whose copy shares whatever its fields reference. So copying the structure does not deep-copy what is inside it, and mutating the shared field through one copy is visible through the other. This is the single most common misunderstanding in the whole subject, and it is why "structs are safe to pass" is only true for a structure whose fields are all themselves value types.

Boxing, and why it shows up in profiles

Converting a value type to object, or to an interface it implements, allocates a copy on the managed heap and puts a reference to it in the reference. The allocation is invisible in the source and is one of the most common entries in a memory profile of code that "only uses structs".

public struct Point { public int X; public int Y; }
public sealed class Person { public string Name { get; set; } = ""; }

var a = new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 };
var b = a;          // COPY. b is a separate box on the stack.
b.X = 99;
Console.WriteLine(a.X);        // 1  -- a was not affected

var p = new Person { Name = "Ada" };
var q = p;          // ALIAS. q and p are the same object.
q.Name = "Grace";
Console.WriteLine(p.Name);      // "Grace" -- one object, two names

"Stack" and "heap" is a useful first approximation but not the real rule. A local struct usually lives in a register or on the stack; the semantics (copy on assign) are what the language guarantees, and that guarantee holds regardless of where the JIT puts it.

Two practical consequences follow. A struct retrieved from a collection is a copy, so mutating it in place does nothing. And passing a struct to a method copies it, so the callee cannot change the caller’s value.

static void TryMove(Point p)
{
    p.X = 100;         // legal, but only touches the local copy
}

var origin = new Point();
TryMove(origin);
Console.WriteLine(origin.X);   // 0

// To let a method mutate a value type, pass by reference:
static void Move(ref Point p) { p.X = 100; }
Move(ref origin);
Console.WriteLine(origin.X);   // 100

ref is the fix for "I want a struct mutated in place". in and out cover the read-only and write-only directions; all three are covered in chapter 12.

Never declare a mutable struct and hand it to a UI, a collection or an interface without thinking about copies. This is the single most common source of "my change did nothing" bugs in .NET code.

Every value type is implicitly sealed and inherits from System.ValueType, which supplies Equals, GetHashCode and ToString. You can override them, but for record structs the compiler generates correct ones for you.


{{-- THE DEFAULT, which is right about what it says: --}}
struct PointS { public int X, Y; }
class PointC { public int X, Y; }

static void TheDefault()
{
    var a = new PointS { X = 1 };
    var b = a;                 {{-- a COPY: two independent values --}}
    b.X = 99;
    // a.X is still 1

    var c = new PointC { X = 1 };
    var d = c;                 {{-- the REFERENCE is copied: ONE object --}}
    d.X = 99;
    // c.X is 99: they are the same object
}

{{-- AND THE CASE THE SHORTHAND DOES NOT COVER, which is the most
     common misunderstanding in the subject: --}}
struct WithReference
{
    public int Id;
    public int[] Scores;       {{-- a REFERENCE inside a value type --}}
}

static void TheCaseItDoesNotCover()
{
    var a = new WithReference { Id = 1, Scores = new[] { 10 } };
    var b = a;                 {{-- the struct is copied, and the
                                      array REFERENCE inside it is
                                      copied with it --}}
    b.Scores[0] = 99;
    // a.Scores[0] IS 99. "Structs are copied" is true of the
    // struct and false of everything the struct points at.
}

{{-- WHICH IS WHY "A STRUCT IS SAFE TO PASS" IS ONLY TRUE FOR A
     STRUCT WHOSE FIELDS ARE ALL VALUE TYPES: --}}
record struct AllValues(int Id, decimal Total, DateTimeOffset At);
{{-- ^ safe to pass, copy, and store: nothing inside it is shared. --}}

struct HasString(string Name);
{{-- a string is a REFERENCE TYPE, so this struct shares its
     character data on every copy. Harmless, because strings are
     immutable — and harmless for exactly that reason. --}}

{{-- BOXING, which is invisible in the source and obvious in a
     profile: --}}
static void Boxing(int value)
{
    object boxed = value;      {{-- AN ALLOCATION: a copy of value
                                     on the managed heap, and a
                                     reference to it here --}}
    // ^ and value is then not what boxed refers to; changing value
    //   does not change boxed.
}

static void BoxingAgain(int value)
{
    // The SAME ALLOCATION, because an int has to be boxed before it
    // can satisfy a generic constraint.
    IComparable c = value;

    // Generic: NO allocation, because T is int and the code is
    // specialised at runtime. This is why List<int> is a
    // List<int> rather than a List<object>.
    IComparable g = Generic(value);
}
static IComparable Generic<T>(T value) where T : IComparable => value;

{{-- AND WHERE IT SHOWS UP: a struct passed to a method taking
     object, a struct in a non-generic collection, an interface-typed
     call. Each is one allocation that the source does not show. --}}

2.2 var and the implicit typing rule

var is not JavaScript-style dynamic typing. It is purely a local shorthand: the compiler infers the exact static type from the initialiser and the variable is that type forever after. If the initialiser has no type, you need an explicit type.

The implicit-typing keyword states a variable's type as the compiler infers it, and the rule the language applies is narrow: use it when the type is evident from the right-hand side, and write the type when it is not. Everything else about it is preference.

The distinction that makes the rule precise

Inferred means the type is written on the right of the assignment and can be read off it — a literal, a constructor call, a cast. Declared means the type exists because you said so, or because a method's signature or a parameter's type says it. In the second case the keyword hides information a reader needs, and the cost is that a reader who wants to know the type has to resolve it.

What it does not change

Nothing about the variable's mutability, its lifetime, or its scope. The type is fixed at the declaration either way; the only question is whether the declaration states it. That is why the argument is entirely about readers and not about the compiler.

var count = 42;               // int, not object
var price = 19.99;            // double
var name = "Ada";             // string
var list = new List<string>();  // List<string>
var tuple = (1, "a");          // (int, string)

// These are compile errors:
// var x;                     no initialiser to infer from
// var y = null;             nothing to infer
// var z;  z = 5;            type must be known at declaration

// With a target type, var works:
int a = default;          // zero
string? s = default;      // null
var n = default(int);   // 0 -- explicit type argument

The classic "when not to use var" rule is about declarative type dependence: if the right-hand side would change type if you edited the left-hand side, write the type. var total = 0; that later becomes total = 0.5; is the canonical example.

SituationUse var?Reason
Right-hand side is an explicit constructionYesRepeating the type adds nothing; var d = new Dictionary<string, int>() stays readable
Primitive initialiser that could changeNoThe declared type is information — int total = 0 documents the intent
foreach variableUsually noThe element type is the point of the loop; name it
Query results (var, LINQ)YesAnonymous types have no usable name
Small local with an obvious typeEitherTeam style, not correctness

Most Microsoft style guides say: use var when the type is apparent from the right-hand side, and always use it when the right-hand side is not a primitive. Consistency within a codebase beats the rule itself.


{{-- THE RULE, applied: --}}
// EVIDENT from the right-hand side: the keyword is fine, because
// the type is written next to it.
var total   = 0m;                       {{-- decimal --}}
var names   = new List<string>();
var span    = ReadOnlySpan<char>.Empty;
var parsed = int.TryParse(s, out var value) ? value : 0;

// DECLARED: the type is not on the right, so writing it adds
// information rather than removing it.
string? name = GetName();               {{-- what does GetName
                                              return? --}}
int count    = GetCount();              {{-- a method name that
                                              says "count" is not a
                                              type --}}
Node node    = Find();                  {{-- especially: Find()
                                              returning something
                                              and a reader needing
                                              to know what --}}

{{-- WHERE THE SHORTHAND ACTIVELY HIDES A DECISION: --}}
var result = Process(data);             {{-- Process returns what?
                                              Is that OrderResult or
                                              Result<Order>? The
                                              declaration is where
                                              that choice is made
                                              visible, and here it is
                                              not. --}}
Result result = Process(data);
{{-- ^ and the explicit form is a place to say WHY, which the
     keyword removes entirely. --}}

{{-- AND THE FORM THAT IS ALWAYS WRONG, which people reach for
     because it saves four characters: --}}
var x = GetValue();      {{-- fine if the return type is
                              OrderId, wrong if it is a decimal or
                              a string, because var has given the
                              reader nothing --}}
OrderId x = GetValue();
{{-- ^ a reader knows immediately whether a currency or an
     identifier is involved, and neither of those is obvious from
     the name. --}}

{{-- WHAT IT DOES NOT CHANGE: mutability, lifetime, scope. The type
     is fixed at the declaration either way; the only question is
     whether the declaration states it. That is why the argument is
     about readers and not about the compiler. --}}

2.3 Nullable reference types

Nullable reference types (NRT, C# 8) let you say a reference is never null. The runtime does not change — there is still no null check — but the compiler now flags any place you might dereference a null, and IDEs grey out the risk. Enable it in every project.

There are only two reference annotations: T? means "may be null" and plain T means "not null". In a nullable-enabled context, that is the whole language feature.

Nullable reference types add a second type to every reference type: the declared one, and that one with a question mark. The question mark is a statement to the compiler about a program's discipline, and it produces warnings where a null would otherwise flow into a place that cannot accept it.

What the annotation does and does not do

It does not change the runtime. A reference is a reference either way, and the annotation is erased at compile time — which is why the feature is opt-in per project and why a library compiled with it still interoperates with one compiled without it. What it does is make the compiler report the paths on which a null can reach a dereference, which is the class of defect that produces the NullReferenceException that ends a request.

Where the warnings come from, and which ones to keep

Three sources: a variable assigned null, a method returning null on a path its signature denies, and a dereference the compiler cannot prove is guarded. The first two are worth fixing and the third is usually a false positive that an assertion resolves. What is not worth doing is suppressing the whole file, because the suppression is the one line that makes the feature worthless for that file.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
public sealed class Customer
{
    public required string Name { get; init; }        // never null
    public string? Email { get; set; }        // may be null

    public string NameUpper => Name.ToUpperInvariant();   // safe: Name is not null
    public int EmailLength => Email?.Length ?? 0;   // safe: null-conditional
}

var c = new Customer { Name = "Ada" };
Console.WriteLine(c.EmailLength);   // 0, not a NullReferenceException
c.Email = "ada@example.com";
Console.WriteLine(c.EmailLength);   // 16

Flow analysis is the real power. The compiler tracks whether a value is known non-null at that point, so a null check is remembered and every later use is safe without repeating the guard.

Nullability analysis stops at method boundaries only where the signature is honest. A method returning string? must have its result checked, because the compiler cannot know what happened inside.

Nullability is a compile-time contract, not a runtime guard. Assign null to a string through an object reference or a deserialiser and the compiler will happily believe your annotation. Trust the annotation, but validate at the boundary where untyped data enters.

Turning on <Nullable>enable</Nullable> in a large existing codebase produces hundreds of warnings. Do it in a dedicated change, treat the warnings as the work list, and do not suppress them with #nullable disable file-wide — suppress per line with a comment explaining why, or better, fix the signature.


{{-- THE ANNOTATION, and it is a statement to the COMPILER rather
     than a runtime change: --}}
string required;          {{-- CS8600: dereference of a possibly
                              null reference --}}
string? optional = null;  {{-- fine: the type says this can be null --}}
string after   = optional; {{-- CS8600 again: assigning a
                                possibly-null to a non-null --}}
string safe    = optional ?? "";   {{-- the null-coalescing
                                        operator makes it
                                        non-null, and the
                                        compiler KNOWS that, so no
                                        warning --}}
string trimmed = optional?.Trim();  {{-- STILL possibly null: the
                                         conditional operator
                                         propagates nullability
                                         from its left side, so
                                         the right side is
                                         string? --}}

{{-- WHERE THE WARNINGS COME FROM, and the false positive: --}}
static string? FindName(int id) => id == 1 ? "Ada" : null;

static void WarningSources(int id)
{
    string a = FindName(id);       {{-- CS8600: a method returning
                                      null on a path its signature
                                      says it does not --}}
    string? b = FindName(id);      {{-- fine --}}
    string c = FindName(id) ?? ""; {{-- fine: the compiler knows
                                      ?? removes the null --}}

    var d = FindName(id);
    d.Length;                     {{-- CS8602: the compiler cannot
                                      PROVE d is not null, and it
                                      is right not to --}}
}

static void TheFalsePositive(Order o)
{
    if (o is not null)
    {
        // The compiler does NOT narrow the local from is not null
        // in C# 8
        // and earlier, which is why this was so often a warning.
        // In a current language version it narrows correctly, and
        // the warning here is a sign of an old LangVersion.
        var name = o.Customer.Name;
    }
}

{{-- AND THE SUPPRESSION THAT MAKES THE FEATURE WORTHLESS FOR A
     FILE, which is the mistake worth naming: --}}
#pragma warning disable CS8600, CS8602, CS8604, CS8618
// ...an entire file
#pragma warning restore CS8600, CS8602, CS8604, CS8618
{{-- ^ the first thing to try when the build is red, and it turns a
     real analysis into nothing for that file. Narrow it to a
     member, with a comment saying why. --}}

#pragma warning disable CS8602 // guarded by the null check above
var length = o.Customer.Name.Length;
#pragma warning restore CS8602
{{-- ^ one member, one reason. A reviewer can check the reason. --}}

2.4 Nullable value types

Nullable<T> is a struct that wraps a value type plus a boolean flag. It is the only way to give a value type three states: a value, no value, or a genuine "not applicable". It is how the framework models optional dates, nullable integers and optional struct results.

Reference types have a dedicated null-aware form. Value types never needed one — their default is never null — and so they got a different mechanism: a wrapper that adds a null state to a type that did not have one.

Why the wrapper exists at all

Three reasons, and only the first is about null. A bool in a model class has to distinguish "not set" from "false", because a form's unchecked checkbox submits false and a field the user never touched submits nothing; without the wrapper those are the same value. A numeric field has to distinguish zero from unset for the same reason. And a KeyValuePair needs to report whether the key was present.

What it costs, and where

The value is a struct, so it copies on assignment and on return, and it allocates when boxed into an interface or an object. The allocation is the one worth knowing about, because it happens in exactly the places the generic one did not.

int? maybe = 5;
int? empty = null;

Console.WriteLine(maybe.Value);     // 5
Console.WriteLine(maybe.GetValueOrDefault());  // 5, no exception
Console.WriteLine(maybe.GetValueOrDefault(-1)); // 5
Console.WriteLine(empty.GetValueOrDefault(-1)); // -1

if (maybe is int n) { Console.WriteLine(n); }  // pattern, safe
Console.WriteLine(maybe ?? 0);                   // 5
Console.WriteLine(maybe + 1);                    // 6 -- lifted operator
Console.WriteLine(maybe > 3);                    // true; null comparisons are false

// .Value on an empty nullable throws InvalidOperationException. Prefer:
//   GetValueOrDefault(), TryGetValue, HasValue, or ??

Lifted operators are the reason arithmetic just works: adding two int? promotes the operator to accept nulls and returns null if either side is null. A single ?? at the end of an expression collapses the whole chain.

The HasValue property is true whenever a value is present, including when the value is 0, false or DateTime.MinValue. That trips people up: if (count.HasValue) is correct, if (count != 0) is not.

Inside a Nullable<T> context, an unannotated T is treated as T?. The annotation int x inside a int? context therefore means "a known non-null int", which is why you can assign it to a plain int directly.


{{-- THE REASON IT EXISTS, and only the first is about null: --}}
class Preferences
{
    {{-- 1. "NOT SET" IS DISTINCT FROM false. A form's unchecked
          checkbox submits false; a field the user never touched
          submits nothing. Without the wrapper those are the same
          value. --}}
    public bool NotificationsEnabled { get; set; }
    public bool? NotificationsEnabled { get; set; }   {{-- ^ three
          states, and the third is the one a checkbox needs --}}

    {{-- 2. SAME FOR A NUMBER: zero is a legitimate value. --}}
    public int DiscountPercent { get; set; }        {{-- 0 means
                                                            0% --}}
    public int? DiscountPercent { get; set; }        {{-- ^ null means
                                                            unset --}}

    {{-- 3. AND FOR KEY LOOKUP: TryGetValue returns the PAIR, and
          the pair reports whether the key was present. --}}
    static bool TryGet(Dictionary<string, int> d, string k, out int v)
    {
        // The KeyValuePair returned carries HasValue, so the
        // "found nothing" case is representable.
        return d.TryGetValue(k, out v);
    }
}

{{-- WHERE IT COSTS, and the allocation is the one worth knowing: --}}
static void Costs(bool? flag)
{
    object boxed = flag;             {{-- AN ALLOCATION: Nullable<T>
                                         is a struct, so boxing it
                                         allocates --}}
    IComparable c = flag;            {{-- same --}}
    object direct = true;            {{-- same: bool boxes too --}}

    // And Nullable<T> is NOT the same as T? at the type level:
    // you cannot pass a Nullable<bool> where a bool is expected
    // without stating the conversion, because the implicit one
    // does not exist.
    static void Needs(bool b) { }
    // Needs(flag);            // error: no implicit conversion
}

{{-- THE GETVALUEORDEFAULT, and why it is almost always what you
     want rather than a HasValue check: --}}
static int UseDefault(bool? flag)
{
    // flag.GetValueOrDefault()          reads HasValue internally
    // flag.GetValueOrDefault(true)      and supplies the default
    // flag ?? true                      when it is false

    return (flag ?? true) ? 1 : 0;
}

{{-- AND THE PATTERN THAT MATCHES NULLABILITY, which is the form
     that also narrows: --}}
static void Pattern(bool? flag)
{
    switch (flag)
    {
        case true:  goto Enabled;
        case false: goto Disabled;
        case null:  goto Unknown;
    }

Enabled:
    // ...
    goto Done;
Disabled:
    // ...
    goto Done;
Unknown:
    // ...
Done:
    return;
}
{{-- ^ the switch EXHAUSTS the three states, so adding a case later
     produces a compiler error rather than a fall-through. --}}

2.5 Numeric types and their traps

C# has separate types for integers and reals, and choosing wrong is a source of silent data loss. The integer types are sbyte, byte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, plus nint and nuint for native-sized pointers. The reals are float (32-bit), double (64-bit) and decimal (128-bit base-10).

The integral types differ in width and in signedness, and both differences have a trap attached. The width trap is silent narrowing. The signedness trap is that the arithmetic operators on the smaller types operate on int, so a byte or a short is promoted before it is operated on and the result is not what the declaration suggests.

Overflow, and the two settings

Arithmetic on an integral type either wraps or throws, and which is determined by a compiler setting rather than by the type. The default wraps, which is a decision made decades ago for performance and which is wrong for almost everything. A project that turns the setting on gets an exception rather than a plausible wrong number, and the exception is the point.

Precision, which is a separate question from width

The floating-point types are not "bigger" versions of each other; they are different trade-offs, and neither is exact for most decimal fractions. So a monetary amount stored in a floating-point type is wrong in a way that accumulates, and the fix is a decimal type — which is also a floating-point type, and has the same property, and is nonetheless the right one because its approximation error is far smaller for the magnitudes money occupies.

byte   b = 255;                    // 0..255, unsigned
short  s = -32768;                 // 16-bit signed
int    i = 2147483647;             // 32-bit signed: the default
long   l = 9223372036854775807L;    // 64-bit signed; L suffix
uint   ui = 4000000000U;            // U suffix for unsigned
ulong  ul = 18446744073709551615UL;// UL suffix
nint   ni = nint.MaxValue;          // IntPtr-sized, for interop

float   f = 1.5f;                    // f suffix: 32-bit, ~7 digits
double  d = 1.5d;                    // 64-bit, ~15 digits: the default
decimal m = 1.5m;                    // m suffix: money, exact base-10

// 1 / 2 is integer division:
Console.WriteLine(1 / 2);              // 0
Console.WriteLine(1.0 / 2);            // 0.5
Console.WriteLine(1 / 2.0);            // 0.5
Console.WriteLine(7 / 2);              // 3 -- truncation toward zero
Console.WriteLine(-7 / 2);             // -3, not -4
Console.WriteLine(7 % 2);              // 1
Console.WriteLine(-7 % 2);             // -1

Literal suffixes matter: 1.5 is a double, 1.5f is a float, 1.5m is a decimal, and a bare 5 is an int no matter how large.

float and double cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false for both. Never compare floating point with ==; use a tolerance, and use decimal for money and quantities that must add up.

double is the default for real numbers and is the right choice for almost everything scientific. decimal is 8–28x slower for arithmetic but exact in base 10, which is precisely why financial code uses it. float is for GPU buffers and large arrays of measurements where half the precision is acceptable.


{{-- THE INTEGRAL TYPES, and the two differences that matter: --}}
sbyte  -128..127        1 byte     SIGNED, and the default literal
byte    0..255          1 byte     UNSIGNED
short  -32 768..32 767  2 bytes
ushort  0..65 535       2 bytes
int    -2^31..2^31-1    4 bytes     the default for arithmetic
uint    0..2^32-1       4 bytes
long   -2^63..2^63-1    8 bytes     the default for counters and
                                     timestamps
ulong   0..2^64-1       8 bytes

{{-- THE SIGNEDNESS TRAP, which is the one that surprises people:
     the arithmetic operators on the smaller types operate on INT, so
     the result is not the type the declaration suggests. --}}
static void ThePromotion()
{
    byte b = 200;
    byte c = 100;

    // byte sum = b + c;        ERROR: the operands are promoted
    //                          to int, the sum is an int, and int
    //                          does not implicitly narrow to byte
    int sum = b + c;           // 300: correct, and int is the type
                               // the expression actually has

    // WHICH IS WHY THIS SILENTLY WRAPS:
    byte overflow = (byte)(b + c);   // 44, not 300 and not an error
    // ^ the cast is where the information is lost, and it looks
    //   like a cast rather than a truncation.
}

{{-- OVERFLOW, and the setting rather than the type decides: --}}
// <CheckForOverflowUnderflow>true</CheckForOverflowUnderflow>
static void Overflow()
{
    int big = int.MaxValue;
    // int next = big + 1;      with the setting ON: OverflowException
    //                          with it OFF (the default): -2147483648
    int next = big + 1;        {{-- WRAPS, and -2147483648 is a
                                      plausible wrong answer rather
                                      than an obviously broken one --}}
}

{{-- PRECISION, which is a separate question from width: --}}
static void Precision()
{
    // 0.1 + 0.2 is NOT 0.3 in binary floating point. Neither value
    // is representable, and the two approximations differ.
    Console.WriteLine(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);      // False

    // And it accumulates: ten million additions of 0.1 is not a
    // million, because every add rounds.
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) sum += 0.1;
    // sum is 999999.999837, not 1000000.

    // decimal is ALSO a floating-point type and ALSO inexact — but
    // its approximation error is far smaller at the magnitudes money
    // occupies, which is why it is the right one for money.
    decimal money = 0.1m + 0.2m;             // exactly 0.3
    Console.WriteLine(money == 0.3m);          // True

    // Which is not the same as being exact:
    decimal half = 1m / 3m;                    // 0.333... to 28-29
                                                  // significant digits
}

{{-- AND THE FLOATING-POINT EQUALITY TEST, which is the one that
     produces the hardest-to-find defect in a numeric codebase: --}}
static bool Approximately(double a, double b) =>
    Math.Abs(a - b) <= 1e-9 * Math.Max(1.0, Math.Max(Math.Abs(a), Math.Abs(b)));
{{-- ^ an ABSOLUTE epsilon is wrong for large values and wrong for
     values near zero. A RELATIVE one is wrong near zero. Both, as
     above, are closer than either alone. --}}

2.6 Conversions, checked and unchecked

Implicit conversions are safe widening ones the compiler allows automatically. Explicit conversions use a cast, and casts that lose data can silently succeed. Arithmetic overflow is unchecked by default, which means it wraps silently unless you ask for checked.

An implicit conversion between numeric types exists when every value of the source type is representable in the destination. That is the definition, and it explains why widening from byte to int is implicit while the reverse is not — and why a conversion that the compiler accepts is safe and one it rejects is safe too, in the sense that it made you say it.

The cast, and what it asserts

An explicit numeric conversion is an assertion that the value fits. The compiler cannot check it when the value is computed rather than literal, so the assertion is unchecked by default — and a wrong assertion truncates rather than rounding, silently. There is no Math.Round inside a cast.

The checked context, and where it is worth the cost

A checked block converts every numeric conversion and arithmetic operation inside it into one that throws on overflow. It costs nothing at run time when nothing overflows, and it is worth wrapping any conversion whose value is computed. The alternative — checking the range yourself before casting — is more code and easier to get wrong, because the bound has to be computed from the same types.

// Implicit widening -- always safe, no cast needed
