int i = 42;
long l = i;          // int -> long, fine
double d = i;       // int -> double, fine
decimal m = i;      // int -> decimal, fine

// Explicit narrowing -- you asked for it, you get it
int narrowed = (int)3.99;      // 3, truncated
byte small = (byte)300;       // 44, silently wrong
// byte s = 300;            // compile error: constant out of range

// Overflow: unchecked by default
int big = int.MaxValue;
big = big + 1;          // wraps to int.MinValue, no error

// checked makes it throw
int safe = checked(int.MaxValue + 1);  // OverflowException

// Or make it the project-wide default:
// <CheckForOverflowUnderflow>true</CheckForOverflowUnderflow>

// Parsing returns false rather than throwing
bool ok = int.TryParse("42", out int parsed);
Console.WriteLine(ok + " " + parsed);        // "True 42"

There is no implicit conversion between numeric types of the same size category — int to uint or float to decimal both require an explicit cast, because both can lose data.

For strings, use Parse or TryParse for numbers and the Convert class when the input is loosely typed. Convert.ToInt32("3.7") rounds to 4; int.Parse("3.7") throws.

checked applies to a block, not just an expression: checked { ... } turns on overflow checking for every operation inside. This is cheap insurance in arithmetic-heavy code and free insurance in code that parses user input.


{{-- THE IMPLICIT CONVERSIONS, and the rule that defines them:
     every value of the SOURCE must be representable in the
     DESTINATION. --}}
static void Implicit(byte b, int i, long l, float f, double d)
{
    int    fromByte = b;   {{-- fine: every byte fits in an int --}}
    long   fromInt  = i;   {{-- fine --}}
    double fromInt2 = i;   {{-- fine: int is exactly
                                 representable as a double, which
                                 is NOT true of every long --}}
    // long fromLong = l;   NOT implicit: not every long fits in a
    //                     long... but a DOUBLE can lose precision,
    //                     so long -> double is explicit for the
    //                     same reason
}

{{-- THE CAST, and what it asserts: --}}
static void TheCast()
{
    double d = 3.7;
    int truncated = (int)d;        // 3: a cast TRUNCATES
    int rounded   = (int)Math.Round(d);   // 4

    // Which is the harder-to-find defect in a numeric codebase: a
    // quantity that should be a price is a count, so the cast
    // silently drops a fraction.
    decimal price = 19.99m;
    int pence = (int)(price * 100);        // 1999: correct only
                                            // because the
                                            // multiplication
                                            // happened in
                                            // decimal. In double
                                            // it would be 1998
                                            // or 1999 depending on
                                            // the representation.
}

{{-- THE CHECKED CONTEXT, which is worth the (zero) cost: --}}
static void Checked(long value)
{
    // WITHOUT checked: a silent truncation.
    int small = (int)value;   {{-- if value is 5_000_000_000 this is
                                    1410065408, which is a plausible
                                    wrong answer --}}

    checked
    {
        int safe = (int)value;   // OverflowException instead, and
                                 // the exception is the correct
                                 // answer
    }
}

checked (int bad = (int)value) { }   {{-- per-expression, and
                                           usable in a single
                                           initialiser --}}
unchecked { /* fast, and the default */ }

{{-- WHY "CHECK IT YOURSELF" IS WORSE: --}}
static int CheckItYourself(long value)
{
    if (value > int.MaxValue) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException();
    return (int)value;
    {{-- ^ correct here and WRONG the moment somebody changes the
         source type to ulong, because the bound is now the wrong
         one and the compiler does not say so. checked uses the
         types it is given. --}}
}

{{-- AND THE NARROWING IN AN ARRAY INITIALISER, which is the
     implicit version of the same trap: --}}
static void ArrayNarrowing()
{
    // byte[] small = { 200, 100 };   ERROR: array initialisers use
    //                              the same conversion rules
    int[] values = { 200, 100 };      // fine
    var bytes = new byte[] { 200, 100 };   // fine: each literal
                                          // fits
}

2.7 dynamic vs object

object is the type every value converts to and from which every reference type converts. dynamic is object plus a compiler instruction to defer member lookup to runtime. The difference is entirely about when type errors are discovered.

A value of the static type object is inspected at run time when a member is called on it. A value of the static type dynamic is inspected at run time for the call itself, and the result type of that call is whatever the runtime says it is. The difference sounds small and is the difference between a cast that can fail and a call that can fail somewhere you did not write.

The three practical consequences

A call on a dynamic value is not checked by the compiler, so a missing member is a run-time exception rather than a build failure — and it binds late, which means a class member can change between the call site and the call. Overload resolution happens at run time. And a dynamic expression produces a dynamic result, so the static type information is lost downstream and propagates.

Where it is the right answer

Interoperating with a COM object, with an object whose members are decided at run time by a plugin system, and with a scripting language host. Those are the three cases where the member genuinely does not exist at compile time. Everywhere else, dynamic trades a build-time guarantee for a run-time cost and a lost diagnostic.

object boxed = 42;
// boxed.Missing();   // COMPILE ERROR: object has no such member

dynamic loose = 42;
// loose.Missing();    // COMPILES, throws RuntimeBinderException at run time

object json = "{ \"Name\": \"Ada\" }";
dynamic dyn = System.Text.Json.JsonDocument.Parse((string)json).RootElement;
Console.WriteLine(dyn.Name.GetString());   // works, resolved at run time

// Everything from Microsoft C# spec section on dynamic:
dynamic d = "hello";
Console.WriteLine(d.Length);        // 5
d = 5;
Console.WriteLine(d);               // 5 -- the variable can hold anything

A dynamic member lookup goes through the DLR (Dynamic Language Runtime), which caches the binding result. After the first call the cost is close to a virtual call — but you have traded compile-time safety for it.

dynamic earns its place at exactly two boundaries: talking to COM or a late-bound COM-ish API from PowerShell, and reading loosely shaped data where a Dictionary<string, object> or JsonElement would be better typed. Everywhere else, object plus a cast, or generics, wins.

Do not sprinkle dynamic through application code to "make it compile". Every use disables IntelliSense, breaks rename refactoring, and converts a build error into a production crash.

Exercises 2

  1. Declare a struct and a class, assign each to a second variable, mutate the second, and print which original changed. Add a comment explaining why.
  2. Write a method that takes a Point by value and one that takes it by ref. Call both and show the difference.
  3. Enable <Nullable>enable on a scratch project and deliberately assign null to a string property. Read the warning, then fix it properly.
  4. Compute 1 / 3 as int, double and decimal, and explain in a comment why the three results differ.
  5. Write an unchecked overflow and a checked one, catch the OverflowException, and print both results.
  6. Take a JsonElement and read three nested fields once with dynamic and once with pattern matching. Note which one the compiler helped with.

{{-- object: the CAST fails. dynamic: the CALL fails. --}}
static void Difference(object o)
{
    // object: the member access is checked against OBJECT, which has
    // no Count, so this does not compile — correctly.
    // o.Count();

    // dynamic: the member access is deferred, and the result TYPE
    // is whatever the runtime says it is.
    dynamic d = o;
    int n = d.Count();      {{-- COMPILES. Binds at RUN TIME. If o
                                   is a List<int>, n is 3. If o is a
                                   string, it throws
                                   RuntimeBinderException at THIS
                                   line, not at the assignment. --}}
}

{{-- AND THE LOST STATIC TYPE PROPAGATES, which is the part people
     do not expect: --}}
static void Propagation(object o)
{
    dynamic d = o;
    var n = d.Count();       {{-- n is DYNAMIC, not int: the result
                                   of a dynamic call is dynamic,
                                   so every downstream expression
                                   is also unchecked --}}
    // int m = n + 1;         no compile error, whatever n is
}

{{-- CONVERSION TO dynamic IS ALWAYS AVAILABLE, in both directions,
     which is what makes it usable for interop and easy to misuse
     for it: --}}
static void Always(object o)
{
    dynamic d = o;
    int i = d;                {{-- fine: int converts to dynamic
                                  implicitly --}}
    object back = i;          {{-- fine: dynamic converts to
                                  object implicitly --}}
}

{{-- WHERE IT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER, and there are exactly three: --}}
// 1. COM interop, where the type library is decided at run time.
dynamic excel = Activator.CreateInstance(Type.GetTypeFromProgID("Excel.Application"));
excel.Workbooks.Add();

// 2. A plugin system whose members are decided at run time.
dynamic plugin = LoadPlugin("Acme.Exporter");
plugin.Export(report, format: "csv");

// 3. Embedding a scripting host.
public sealed class ScriptHost
{
    public void Run(string source, params object[] args)
    {
        // 3. A scripting language host.
        dynamic script = new Microsoft.CSharp.Scripting.ScriptEngine();
        script.Execute(source, args);
    }
}

{{-- AND WHAT IT COSTS, restated, because the cost is a BUILD-TIME
     guarantee: --}}
{{--   a missing member      -> a compile error, becomes a
                                 RuntimeBinderException at the
                                 call
     overload resolution     -> at RUN TIME
     a ref/out argument      -> the ref/out restrictions are
                                 NOT applied, so a call can
                                 silently pass a value where a
                                 reference was required
     result type             -> dynamic, and it propagates, so
                                 every downstream expression
                                 becomes unchecked too --}}

3 · Operators, Expressions & Control Flow

3.1 Arithmetic and assignment3.2 Comparison and logical operators3.3 Bitwise and shift operators3.4 Null-conditional and null-coalescing3.5 switch statements and expressions3.6 Loops, foreach and iteration3.7 Labels, goto and loops with break values

Chapter three covers the expression language of C#: how operators combine, how the null-aware operators shorten the most common defensive code, how pattern matching has largely replaced switch sprawl, and how the loop forms differ in allocation cost. The compiler understands operator precedence and associativity the same way any C-family language does, so the surprises are all in the details.

3.1 Arithmetic and assignment

The arithmetic operators are + - * / %. They work on numeric types, on enum values and on DateTime via subtraction (which yields a TimeSpan). Assignment has a compound form, and there is the C# 8 "target-typed compound assignment" that lets a property of a shorter numeric type receive the result.

C# has the arithmetic operators every language has, and three properties of them cause most of the defects. Integer division truncates rather than rounding, and the result type follows a promotion rule that the smaller types do not follow. Compound assignment is shorthand for a read-modify-write that involves an implicit narrowing. And the compound assignment operators on floating-point types behave differently from the two-step form in a checked context.

Compound assignment narrows silently

A compound assignment is defined as a conversion of the result back to the left-hand side's type, so it can overflow without complaint where the two-step form throws under checked. That asymmetry is worth knowing, because the natural refactoring from two statements to one changes the overflow behaviour.

Order of evaluation

The order in which the two operands of a binary operator are evaluated is not specified, so a call with two side-effecting arguments may run in either order — and an optimiser may choose differently at different optimisation levels. The rule is the same as in most languages: sequence side effects into named variables before passing them to an expression.

int a = 10, b = 3;
Console.WriteLine(a + b);     // 13
Console.WriteLine(a - b);     // 7
Console.WriteLine(a * b);     // 30
Console.WriteLine(a / b);     // 3  (integer division)
Console.WriteLine(a % b);     // 1  (remainder)

// Compound assignment
a += 5;   // 15
a -= 3;   // 12
a *= 2;   // 24
a /= 4;   // 6
a %= 4;   // 2
a <<= 1;  // 4

// Prefix vs postfix increment matters when it is the whole expression
int i = 5;
Console.WriteLine(i++);       // prints 5, then i becomes 6
Console.WriteLine(++i);       // prints 7
Console.WriteLine(i);         // 7

// Enums support arithmetic on the underlying type
var start = DayOfWeek.Monday;
int offset = (int)start + 3;
Console.WriteLine((DayOfWeek)offset);      // Thursday

Operators bind tighter than comparison, which binds tighter than &&, which binds tighter than ||. A compound assignment such as x *= 2 + 3 evaluates the right side fully first, so the result is x * 5.

The ??= operator (C# 8) assigns only when the left side is null: _cache ??= Compute(); is the one-line lazy-initialise pattern, and it is exactly as thread-unsafe as if (_cache == null) _cache = Compute();.


{{-- THE ARITHMETIC, and the three properties that cause most of the
     defects: --}}
static void Arithmetic()
{
    // 1. INTEGER DIVISION TRUNCATES, it does not round.
    int   a = 7 / 2;    // 3, not 4
    int   b = 7 % 2;    // 1: the remainder keeps the sign of the
                        // LEFT operand, so -7 % 2 is -1
    decimal c = 7m / 2m;   // 3.5: decimal does NOT truncate
    double  d = 7.0 / 2;    // 3.5

    // 2. THE OPERANDS ARE PROMOTED, and the result type follows the
    //    PROMOTED operands, not the declared variable.
    byte p = 200, q = 100;
    var   sum = p + q;    // sum is INT: 300
    // byte small = p + q;  error, because int does not narrow to byte
    byte narrow = (byte)(p + q);   // 44: silent

    // 3. COMPOUND ASSIGNMENT NARROWS SILENTLY, and that is the one
    //    that changes behaviour under a checked context.
}

{{-- COMPOUND ASSIGNMENT, defined as a narrowing conversion of the
     result: --}}
static void Compound()
{
    unchecked
    {
        int count = int.MaxValue;
        count++;                 {{-- -2147483648: a WRAP, with no
                                      diagnostic --}}
    }

    checked
    {
        int safe = int.MaxValue;
        // safe++;               OverflowException

        // THE ASYMMETRY, which is worth knowing because the natural
        // refactoring from two statements to one changes the
        // behaviour:
        int two = int.MaxValue;
        two = two + 1;           // OverflowException
        // two++;                 ALSO an exception here
        // ...but under 'unchecked':
    }

    unchecked
    {
        int u = int.MaxValue;
        u = u + 1;               // wraps: -2147483648
        u++;                     // ALSO wraps: -2147483647
        // ^ the same in both forms when unchecked. The asymmetry is
        //   only in the CHECKED context, and only because the
        //   compound form does not perform a checked conversion of
        //   its result.
    }

    // FLOATING POINT IS DIFFERENT AGAIN, because a compound
    // assignment on a float is FUSED in some contexts and not in
    // others, which is why 'a += b' and 'a = a + b' can differ in
    // the last bit.
    float x = 0.1f, y = 0.2f;
    x += y;                      // fused
    x = x + y;                   // not fused
    // ^ and neither is wrong; they are just different numbers, which
    //   is the documented behaviour rather than a defect.
}

{{-- ORDER OF EVALUATION, which is not specified: --}}
static int First()  { Console.WriteLine("first");  return 1; }
static int Second() { Console.WriteLine("second"); return 2; }

static void Unspecified()
{
    Console.WriteLine(First() + Second());
    // ^ may print "first second" or "second first", and an
    //   OPTIMISER MAY CHOOSE DIFFERENTLY AT DIFFERENT OPTIMISATION
    //   LEVELS — so this can change between Debug and Release,
    //   which is the worst possible time for it to change.
}

static void Sequenced()
{
    int a = First();
    int b = Second();
    Console.WriteLine(a + b);    // "first second": the order is now
                                 // the source's
}

3.2 Comparison and logical operators

Comparison is == != < > <= >=. Equality is value equality for value types and, unless you override it, reference equality for classes. Logical operators are && || !, plus the non-short-circuiting & and | for booleans.

The comparison operators have a property that surprises people arriving from C: a boolean expression cannot be assigned to or stored in an int. C allows it and C# deliberately does not, which removes a defect class in one line of the language design.

String comparison is the trap in this area

The equality operators on string compare content, which is correct and is not the same as comparing references. What is easy to get wrong is that the relational operators — less than, greater than — are not defined for strings at all, so an alphabetical sort cannot be written with them. Ordering requires a comparer that specifies a culture, and choosing one is a decision rather than a default.

Short-circuit evaluation, and the case that is not short-circuit

&& and || do not evaluate the right-hand operand when the left determines the result, which is what makes null checks before dereferences safe. The non-short-circuit forms exist and are the only correct choice when both sides must be evaluated for their effect — which is rare enough that their use is worth a comment.

int x = 5;
Console.WriteLine(x == 5);      // True
Console.WriteLine(x != 5);      // False
Console.WriteLine(x > 3 && x < 10);   // True
Console.WriteLine(x < 3 || x > 10);   // False
Console.WriteLine(!(x > 3));      // False

// && and || short-circuit: the right side is skipped
bool ok = true && IsPositive(3);
static bool IsPositive(int v) { Console.WriteLine("checked"); return v > 0; }

bool r1 = false && IsPositive(1);   // "checked" NOT printed
bool r2 = true || IsPositive(1);   // "checked" NOT printed

// The non-short-circuiting forms always evaluate both sides
bool r3 = false & IsPositive(1);    // "checked" printed
bool r4 = true | IsPositive(1);    // "checked" printed

// is and as for type tests
object o = "text";
Console.WriteLine(o is string);          // True
Console.WriteLine(o is not int);         // True
Console.WriteLine(o as string);          // "text"
Console.WriteLine((string?)o);       // null-safe cast

as returns null on failure and therefore only works with reference types and nullable value types. For value types use a pattern (o is int n), which is both faster and clearer.

Overriding == without also overriding Equals and GetHashCode is a classic bug: the operator will behave correctly while List.Contains, Distinct and Dictionary keys quietly do not, because they all call Equals. Either override all three, or use record, which does it for you.


{{-- COMPARISON, and the C feature C# deliberately REMOVED: --}}
static void Removed()
{
    // int ok = a < b;        C: legal, and a classic defect
    // bool ok = a < b;       C#: a COMPARISON IS A BOOL and cannot
    //                        be used as an integer, which removes
    //                        the whole class of defect in one
    //                        language decision
}

{{-- STRING COMPARISON: == compares CONTENT, which is correct --}}
static bool StringEquality(string a, string b) => a == b;

static void NotWhatItLooksLike()
{
    var s = new string(new[] { 'a', 'b' });
    var t = "ab";
    // s == t                 true: string == is CONTENT comparison
    // ReferenceEquals(s, t)  false: different objects

    string? nullOne = null, nullTwo = null;
    // nullOne == nullTwo      true
    // string.Equals(a, b)     true when both are null, which is the
    //                         reason the static form is preferred:
    //                         nullOne.Equals(nullTwo) THROWS
}

{{-- THE RELATIONAL OPERATORS ARE NOT DEFINED FOR STRINGS, so an
     alphabetical sort cannot be written with them: --}}
// "apple" < "banana"        ERROR: no operator <
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var names = new List<string> { "banana", "apple", "Cherry" };

// THE COMPARER, and choosing one is a DECISION:
//   Ordinal               binary comparison; correct for ASCII keys,
//                         identifiers, machine-readable strings
//   InvariantCulture      linguistic, stable across machines
//   CurrentCulture        linguistic, and DIFFERENT ON EACH MACHINE,
//                         so a sort can differ between a developer's
//                         laptop and a production server
names.Sort(StringComparer.Ordinal);

static readonly StringComparer KeyComparer =
    StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase;
{{-- ^ the version worth reaching for by default: it is explicit
     about the culture, it is stable, and it says whether case is
     significant. The parameterless string.Compare is none of those. --}}

{{-- SHORT-CIRCUIT, which is what makes a null check safe: --}}
static int LengthOf(string? s) => s?.Length ?? 0;

static void ShortCircuit()
{
    if (x != null && x.Value > 0)   {{-- the right side is not
                                         evaluated when x is null,
                                         so no dereference --}}
    if (x?.Value > 0)              {{-- WRONG: null-conditional
                                         PRODUCES A bool?, and
                                         lifting bool? to bool is
                                         not defined. Write
                                         x?.Value > 0 and this
                                         does not compile. --}}
    if (x is > 0)                  {{-- the PATTERN form, which
                                         narrows and so is correct
                                         because x is a
                                         nullable int --}}
}

{{-- THE NON-SHORT-CIRCUIT FORMS, which exist and should be rare: --}}
bool both = IsReady() & RunCheck();   // RunCheck ALWAYS runs
bool either = IsReady() | RunCheck(); // RunCheck ALWAYS runs
{{-- ^ correct only when both sides must be evaluated for their
     EFFECT — which is almost always a sign that something should
     be sequenced before the expression rather than inside it. --}}

3.3 Bitwise and shift operators

Bitwise operators work on the underlying bits of integral types: & AND, | OR, ^ XOR, ~ NOT. The shift operators are << and >> (unsigned right shift) and >>> (arithmetic, sign-extending). They are also the compact way to multiply and divide by powers of two.

The bitwise operators operate on the integer types and, unusually, on bool as well — which makes & and | on two booleans mean non-short-circuiting and rather than something new. The bit operators themselves are unremarkable; what is worth covering carefully is the shift family, because the right operand's meaning and the left operand's type both determine the result in ways that are easy to get wrong.

Shift counts and result types

A shift count is masked rather than rejected in some situations and rejected in others, which is a platform detail rather than something to rely on. The result type is the promoted type of the left operand, so shifting a byte produces an int — and shifting a byte left by eight is not the same as shifting a short, because the promotion happened first.

The shift that is arithmetic and the one that is not

A right shift on a signed type is an arithmetic shift: it replicates the sign bit, so a negative number stays negative. A right shift on an unsigned type is a logical shift, filling with zeroes. That asymmetry is what makes masking a flag set of signed integers a bug that produces a negative number rather than a wrong bit pattern.

int a = 0b1100;        // binary literals, C# 7
int b = 0b1010;

Console.WriteLine(a & b);            // 0b1000  = 8
Console.WriteLine(a | b);            // 0b1110  = 14
Console.WriteLine(a ^ b);            // 0b0110  = 6  (XOR)
Console.WriteLine(~a);               // -13    (NOT, two's complement)

// Powers of two by shifting
int n = 100;
Console.WriteLine(n << 2);          // 400
Console.WriteLine(n >> 2);          // 25

// Classic: test a single bit for a flags enum
[Flags]
enum Access { None = 0, Read = 1, Write = 2, Exec = 4 }

var perms = Access.Read | Access.Write;
Console.WriteLine(perms.HasFlag(Access.Read));   // True
Console.WriteLine(perms.HasFlag(Access.Exec));   // False

// Faster and allocation-free than HasFlag:
Console.WriteLine((perms & Access.Read) != 0);  // True
perms |= Access.Exec;                              // add a flag
perms &= ~Access.Write;                          // remove a flag

Always put [Flags] on an enum used as a bit field, and always give the first member the value 0 (None). The attribute makes ToString produce "Read, Write" instead of the raw number, which matters enormously in logs.

Bit flags are ideal for permission systems and state machines, and a poor choice for a growing set of independent booleans. Past about five independent flags, an enum member per combination or a HashSet of strings reads better.


{{-- THE OPERATORS, and the one that surprises people: --}}
static void TheBoolOperators()
{
    bool a = true, b = false;
    a & b     // false: NON-SHORT-CIRCUIT and
    a | b     // true:  NON-SHORT-CIRCUIT or
    a && b    // false: short-circuits
    a || b    // true:  short-circuits
    // ^ && and || on bool are the same as & and | with short-
    //   circuiting, so there is nothing new here — but the & and |
    //   forms are what the pattern-matching operators resemble, and
    //   knowing they are the bitwise ones is useful.
}

{{-- THE SHIFT FAMILY, and the two things that determine the
     result: --}}
static void Shifts()
{
    byte b = 0b1010_0000;

    // THE LEFT OPERAND IS PROMOTED, so the result type is int —
    // not byte, and not the width of the declared variable.
    var promoted = b << 1;     // 80 << 1 = 160, an INT
    // byte narrowed = b << 1; ERROR: int does not narrow to byte

    // ...which means a shift of a byte is NOT a shift within a byte:
    byte small = 0b0000_0001;
    var asInt  = small << 7;    // 128: promoted to int first, so
                                // this is a valid shift
    // small << 8               valid, and 256 — which then does
    //                           not fit in a byte

    // THE RIGHT OPERAND IS A COUNT, and its type is what matters:
    int count = 3;
    long wide = 1L << 40;      // fine: the left operand is long
    // 1 << 40                  valid: promoted to long, but
    //                          EXPLICITLY it is a shift of an int
    //                          count by 40, which is 0 after
    //                          promotion, so the answer is wrong
    //                          rather than an error

    int n = 1;
    n <<= 32;                  // 1, because the count is taken
                                // modulo the width — which is a
                                // PLATFORM behaviour, so do not
                                // rely on it
}

{{-- SIGNED IS ARITHMETIC, UNSIGNED IS LOGICAL — the asymmetry that
     makes masking a flag set of signed integers a bug: --}}
static void RightShift()
{
    int negative = -16;
    uint bits    = 0xFFFF_FFF0;

    negative >> 2    // -4:  an ARITHMETIC shift, replicates the
                     //      sign bit, so the value stays negative
    (int)bits >> 2   // -4  too, after the cast — which is the
                     //      trap: casting to int to make the shift
                     //      readable CHANGES THE ANSWER
    bits >> 2        // 0x3FFFFFFC: a LOGICAL shift, fills with
                     //      zeroes, so this is a large POSITIVE
                     //      number
    // ^ the same operator on the same bit pattern produces a
    //   different number depending only on the SIGNEDNESS of the
    //   type. Masking a flag set declared as int is therefore a bug
    //   that produces a negative number rather than a wrong bit.
}

{{-- WHICH IS WHY A FLAG SET IS DECLARED UNSIGNED OR INT-LITERALLY
     HEX, and the latter is worth preferring: --}}
const int None      = 0x0000;      {{-- int, and the values are
                                         written in hex so the bit
                                         positions are visible --}}
const int CanRead   = 0x0001;
const int CanWrite  = 0x0002;
const int All       = CanRead | CanWrite;

static bool Has(int value, int flag) => (value & flag) == flag;
static int  With(int value, int flag) => value | flag;
static int  Without(int value, int flag) => value & ~flag;
{{-- ^ Without needs the complement, and ~ on a signed int gives a
     negative number whose only correct use is as a mask. --}}

static uint UnsignedFlags(uint value, uint flag) => value & ~flag;
{{-- ^ the unsigned version needs no cast, because ~ of an unsigned
     is unsigned. Which is the argument for declaring flag sets
     unsigned. --}}

3.4 Null-conditional and null-coalescing

These four operators remove most defensive null-checking boilerplate. ?. short-circuits the rest of the member chain, ?? supplies a default, ??= assigns a default only when needed, and ?[] is the indexer equivalent of ?..

Four operators exist for working with a value that might be absent, and they compose. The conditional operator returns its left operand if that is not null and its right otherwise, without evaluating the right. The coalescing operator does the same but on a value type. The assignment form coalesces and assigns. And the conditional assignment short-circuits the assignment entirely when the left is already non-null.

What short-circuiting buys, and the case where it is not enough

The right-hand operand is not evaluated when the left is non-null, so a chain like a?.b?.c ?? fallback costs one null check per link and no evaluation beyond the first null. That is what makes the chain cheap as well as safe. The case it does not help is a method call with side effects on the right, where "not evaluated" is a behaviour rather than an optimisation — and there the fix is usually to move the call out.

Where the operators differ

The conditional operator works on any type and yields that type or null, so on a non-nullable reference type the result is a warning rather than an error. The coalescing operator is defined for a left operand that is a nullable value type or a reference type, and yields the left's underlying type — which is what makes it assignable to a non-nullable without a cast.

public sealed class Node
{
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public Node? Next { get; set;
}

Node? head = null;

// Without ?.
// string name = head.Next.Name;   // NullReferenceException

// With ?. the whole chain short-circuits to null
int? length = head?.Next?.Name?.Length;
Console.WriteLine(length);                 // null, no exception

// ?? gives a fallback
Console.WriteLine(head?.Next?.Name ?? "(end of list)");   // (end of list)
Console.WriteLine(head?.Next?.Name?.Length ?? 0);        // 0

// ??= lazily initialises, and is the modern GetOrAdd idiom
string? cached = null;
cached ??= "computed once";
Console.WriteLine(cached);                 // computed once

// ?. on a method call skips the call entirely
Node? n = null;
// n?.Dispose();   // safe: nothing happens

// Null-conditional on an indexer
int[,] grid = null!;
Console.WriteLine(grid?[0, 0]);        // null

A subtle rule: inside a ?. chain you cannot use the null-conditional operator to assign to a non-nullable value directly, and a?.b = c is illegal. Read through the chain into a local, then act on the local.

Do not chain ?. three or four levels deep to paper over a design problem. If you need that much defensive navigation, the intermediate links should not be nullable. Use ?. for one or two hops at a genuine boundary.


{{-- THE FOUR, and how they compose: --}}
static void TheFour(Widget? w, int? maybe)
{
    // 1. THE CONDITIONAL OPERATOR: the left if non-null, else the
    //    right. The right is NOT EVALUATED when the left is fine.
    int length = w?.Width ?? 0;
    //      ^ ?? IS ALSO THE COALESCING OPERATOR, because int? is
    //        a nullable VALUE type and ?? is defined for those

    Widget? other = w?.Next ?? w;      {{-- the ?? VERSION, for a
                                           reference type: the result
                                           type is Widget?, not
                                           Widget --}}
    Widget? third = w?.Next;           {{-- without ??: also Widget?,
                                           and the distinction is
                                           whether the result is
                                           known non-null --}}

    // 2. THE ASSIGNMENT FORMS, which read better in a property or a
    //    field and are the ones worth reaching for:
    w ??= new Widget();    // assign only if w is null
    maybe ??= 0;           // and the same for a nullable value type

    // 3. THE CONDITIONAL ASSIGNMENT is not a separate operator:
    //    ??= IS it. There is no ?:= in the language.
}

{{-- SHORT-CIRCUITING, and why the chain is CHEAP as well as safe: --}}
static void Chain(Node? root)
{
    string name = root?.Parent?.Name ?? "(root)";

    // ^ ONE null check per link, and NOTHING BEYOND THE FIRST NULL
    //   IS EVALUATED. So a ten-link chain on a null root costs one
    //   check, not ten — which is what makes long chains affordable.
}

{{-- AND WHERE IT IS NOT ENOUGH, because there the right-hand side
     has a SIDE EFFECT and "not evaluated" is a behaviour rather than
     an optimisation: --}}
static int NextId()
{
    Console.WriteLine("consuming an id");   // the point of the call
    return 42;
}

static void TheSideEffect()
{
    var list = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };
    int? cursor = 0;

    // WRONG: on the second iteration the right side is not
    // evaluated, so NO id is consumed — and the loop depends on it.
    while (cursor is not null)
    {
        var id = list.NextId() ?? throw new InvalidOperationException();
        // ^^ the ?? is not null COALESCING here, it is the ??=
        //   assign form reading a method result
        cursor = id < 3 ? null : 0;
    }

    // The point: a ?? on a method call is a control-flow operator
    // and reads like a fallback. Sequence it explicitly instead.
    static int? TakeNext(List<int> queue)
    {
        if (queue.Count == 0) return null;
        var id = queue[0];
        queue.RemoveAt(0);
        return id;
    }
}

{{-- WHERE THEY DIFFER, and it is a TYPE difference rather than a
     behavioural one: --}}
static void TheyDiffer(Widget? w)
{
    var viaTernary = w?.Next ?? w;   {{-- the ?? form: the result
                                            type is Widget?, because
                                            ?? yields the left's
                                            type --}}
    var viaElvis   = w?.Next;         {{-- no ??: also Widget?, and
                                            the difference is only
                                            whether the compiler can
                                            prove the result is
                                            non-null --}}

    int? maybe = 5;
    int plain  = maybe ?? 0;          {{-- int, NOT int?: ?? on a
                                            nullable VALUE type
                                            yields the underlying
                                            type, which is what makes
                                            it assignable without a
                                            cast --}}
}

3.5 switch statements and expressions

The modern switch is one of C#'s strongest features. A switch expression is an expression, so it can be returned or assigned directly. A switch statement supports pattern matching, relational patterns, logical patterns, list patterns and when guards. A switch expression must be exhaustive or the compiler will demand a discard arm.

A switch statement dispatches on a value by comparing it against case labels. A switch expression produces a value, and the two forms have different exhaustiveness requirements: a statement needs a default or a trailing break to compile, while an expression needs every possible value covered.

The fall-through rule, which is the opposite of C

C# case labels do not fall through, and each one is a block. That removes an entire defect class from C and it is why a missing break is not a hazard here — but it means a case that is genuinely meant to share a body has to say so explicitly, because two labels on one body is the only form that expresses it.

Switch expressions and exhaustiveness

A switch expression with no arms matching a possible value produces a runtime exception rather than a compile error, unless the arms cover a type the compiler can enumerate. That is the property worth relying on: switching over an enum with no default arm over its members is a compile error, so adding a member to the enum later produces a failed build rather than a wrong answer at run time.

static decimal Fee(Membership tier, int months) => tier switch
{
    Membership.Free    => 0m,
    Membership.Basic   => 4.99m * months,
    Membership.Pro     => months >= 12 ? 49.99m : 59.99m,
    Membership.Lifetime => 999.00m,
    _                  => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException()   // required
};

The _ discard arm is what makes the expression exhaustive. The throw is not decoration: it means adding a new enum member becomes a compile error at every switch that forgot to handle it.

static string Classify(object value) => value switch
{
    null                        => "nothing",
    int n when n < 0          => "negative int",      // type + guard
    int                    => "int",
    string { Length: 0 }    => "empty string",     // property pattern
    string { Length: > 100 } => "long string",     // relational pattern
    string                  => "string",
    int[] { Length: 2 }        => "pair",              // list pattern
    (DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday) => "weekend",      // or pattern
    _                              => "something else"
};

The switch statement form has the same patterns plus a case body and optional goto for fallthrough grouping. Prefer the expression form whenever the result is a single value; the statement form is still the right choice for multi-statement branches.

static int Score(int points)
{
    switch (points)
    {
        case < 0:
            return 0;

        case >= 90:
        case >= 80:              // fallthrough: no break
            Console.WriteLine("excellent");
            goto case default;

        default:
            return points / 10;
    }
}

goto case jumps to a label rather than falling through implicitly, which is clearer than a stack of empty case labels. It is one of the few legitimate uses of goto in modern C#.

A switch expression with no _ arm produces a compile error only if the compiler cannot prove exhaustiveness. Add the arm anyway: it is documentation and it protects the next person who adds an enum value at 5pm on a Friday.


{{-- A STATEMENT, and the fall-through rule, which is the OPPOSITE
     OF C: --}}
static void Statement(OrderStatus status)
{
    switch (status)
    {
        case OrderStatus.Pending:
            SendReminder();
            break;              {{-- not required for correctness
                                      (C# does not fall through)
                                      but required to satisfy the
                                      reachability rule when the
                                      case ends --}}
        case OrderStatus.Paid:
        case OrderStatus.Shipped:   {{-- TWO LABELS ON ONE BODY is
                                          the only form that
                                          expresses a genuine
                                          shared body --}}
            SendReceipt();
            break;
        default:
            LogUnknown(status);
            break;
    }
}

{{-- A SWITCH EXPRESSION, and what it changes: --}}
static string Describe(OrderStatus status) => status switch
{
    OrderStatus.Pending  => "Awaiting payment",
    OrderStatus.Paid     => "Paid",
    OrderStatus.Shipped  => "On its way",
    _                    => "Unknown",
};
{{-- ^ the compiler warns about the _ arm only if the enum is
     not fully covered — and if you OMIT it, adding a member to
     the enum later is a COMPILE ERROR naming the new member. That
     is the property worth relying on. --}}

static string Exhaustive(OrderStatus status) => status switch
{
    OrderStatus.Pending  => "Awaiting payment",
    OrderStatus.Paid     => "Paid",
    OrderStatus.Shipped  => "On its way",
    {{-- NO _ ARM: adding a member to OrderStatus is now a build
         failure rather than a wrong answer at run time. This is the
         version to use for a value the type guarantees is one of a
         fixed set. --}}
};

static string NotExhaustive(int day) => day switch
{
    0 => "Sunday",
    6 => "Saturday",
    {{-- NO _ ARM AND NOT EXHAUSTIVE: this COMPILES, because int has
         2^32 values, and throws at RUN TIME for every other day.
         The compiler cannot help here and never claims to. --}}
};
// -> SwitchExpressionException

{{-- WHERE A SWITCH IS NOT THE RIGHT TOOL, and it is worth knowing
     because the pattern-matching form looks like it is: --}}
static void TypeDispatch(object o)
{
    // switch on a TYPE, which is what the older C# did with types
    // declared. This is the replacement and it is exhaustive when
    // the object is non-null.
    string result = o switch
    {
        string s          => $"text: {s.Length}",
        int i             => $"number: {i}",
        null              => "nothing",
        _                 => "something else",
    };

    // ^ ORDER MATTERS, and it is the order of the arms — not
    //   specificity — so put null BEFORE the reference-type arms if
    //   you intend null to match one of them.
}

static void Relational(object o)
{
    // switch on a RELATION or a RANGE, which is not what a switch
    // is for and is the reason this exists:
    string size = o switch
    {
        int i when i < 0        => "negative",
        int i when i == 0       => "zero",
        1..9                    => "single digit",
        10..99                  => "double digit",
        >= 100                  => "large",
        null                    => "nothing",
        _                       => "not an int",
    };
    // ^ each arm is a PATTERN, and the 'when' arms are tried in
    //   order, so the range arms and the guarded arms interleave
    //   by position.
}

3.6 Loops, foreach and iteration

C# has for, while, do/while and foreach. The important modern addition is that foreach works over anything implementing IEnumerable<T>, including a compiler-generated pattern-based enumerator, and it disposes enumerators that are IDisposable for you.

Four loop forms, and the choice between them is nearly always decided by what the collection is rather than by performance. A for over an index is right when the index is meaningful; a foreach is right otherwise; and a while is right when the condition is not about a collection at all.

What foreach actually does

The compiler emits a try/finally around the enumeration so a break, a return or an exception still disposes it. That is a real cost on a hot path and it is the reason the span-based loop exists for the cases where it matters. On a collection that is not a List or an array it also boxes the enumerator, which is a per-iteration allocation.

Modifying a collection while iterating it

This throws, in every collection type, in every framework version. The exception is correct: an enumerator holds a position, and removing an element shifts every later position, so the enumerator's position no longer means anything. The two patterns that work are iterating a snapshot, or breaking out and re-entering.

// for: known count, index needed
for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++)
{
    // don't touch items.Count if the collection can change
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) Console.WriteLine(i);

// while: condition only
int n = 10;
while (n > 0) { n--; }

// do-while: runs at least once
int attempt = 0;
do { attempt++; } while (attempt < 3);

// foreach: the default choice
foreach (var item in items) Console.WriteLine(item);

// foreach with index, without allocating an enumerator yourself
int index = 0;
foreach (var item in items) { Console.WriteLine($"{index}: {item}"); index++; }

// Reverse iteration is a real LINQ operator, not a language feature
foreach (var item in items.Reverse()) { }

There is no foreach with an index and no reverse foreach in the language. The idiomatic replacements are Select((item, i) => ...) and Enumerable.Reverse. Both are in chapter 10.

Since C# 5, foreach over a struct enumerator that is readonly avoids the defensive copy the compiler would otherwise make, and the JIT can devirtualise the whole loop. This is a real, measurable optimisation, not folklore.

// Custom collection: implement IEnumerable<T> and foreach just works
public sealed class Range : IEnumerable<int>
{
    public Range(int from, int to) { From = from; To = to; }
    public int From { get; }
    public int To { get; }

    public IEnumerator<int> GetEnumerator()
    {
        for (int i = From; i <= To; i++) yield return i;
    }

    IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() => GetEnumerator();   // explicit
}

foreach (var i in new Range(1, 5)) Console.WriteLine(i);   // 1 2 3 4 5

The explicit non-generic GetEnumerator is a leftover from before generics. Modern collections can omit it if you only target .NET Core 3.0 and later, because the compiler prefers the generic form.

Inside a foreach over a List<T>, calling Add or Clear throws InvalidOperationException because the enumerator checks the version. Iterate over a snapshot with ToList() if you intend to modify the collection.


{{-- FOUR FORMS, and the choice is decided by the COLLECTION rather
     than by performance: --}}
static void Forms(List<int> items)
{
    // for: the INDEX IS MEANINGFUL — a grid coordinate, a page
    // offset, a comparison against a neighbouring element.
    for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++)
        Console.WriteLine($"{i}: {items[i]}");

    // foreach: everything else.
    foreach (int item in items)
        Console.WriteLine(item);

    // while: the condition is NOT ABOUT A COLLECTION.
    Queue<int> queue = new();
    while (queue.TryDequeue(out var next))
        Process(next);

    // do-while: exactly once, then conditionally. Used for a menu
    // and almost nowhere else.
    do { ShowMenu(); } while (wantsToContinue);
}

{{-- WHAT foreach ACTUALLY DOES, and the two costs: --}}
// The compiler emits a try/finally so that a break, a return or an
// exception still DISPOSES the enumerator.
foreach (var f in OpenFiles())
{
    if (f.IsTheOne) break;      // the finally still runs
}

// WHICH IS A REAL COST ON A HOT PATH, and the reason the span-based
// loop exists:
static int Sum(int[] values)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (int v in values) total += v;   // a try/finally per call
    return total;

    static int Fast(int[] values)
    {
        Span<int> span = values;
        int total = 0;
        foreach (int v in span) total += v;   // no try/finally:
                                                // the span is not
                                                // disposable
        return total;
    }
}

{{-- AND THE BOXING, which only happens on a collection whose
     enumerator is a STRUCT and which is not a List or an array: --}}
static void Boxing()
{
    // foreach over List<int> or int[]: no allocation
    // foreach over IEnumerable<int> holding something else: the
    // enumerator is BOXED, once, and every iteration is a virtual
    // call through the interface.
    foreach (int v in GetNumbers())
        Console.WriteLine(v);
}

{{-- MODIFYING WHILE ITERATING, which throws in every collection
     type in every version — and CORRECTLY: --}}
static void Modifying(List<int> items)
{
    foreach (int v in items)
    {
        if (v == 0)
            items.RemoveAt(0);
        // ^ InvalidOperationException: "Collection was modified"
        //   The enumerator holds a position, and removing shifts
        //   every later position, so the enumerator's position no
        //   longer means anything.
    }
}

{{-- THE TWO PATTERNS THAT WORK: --}}
static void Snapshot(List<int> items)
{
    // (a) A SNAPSHOT.
    foreach (int v in items.ToArray())     // or items.ToList()
        if (v == 0) items.Remove(v);
}

static void BreakAndReenter(List<int> items)
{
    // (b) BREAK OUT AND RE-ENTER.
    bool changed = true;
    while (changed)
    {
        changed = false;
        foreach (int v in items)
        {
            if (v != 0) continue;
            items.Remove(v);
            changed = true;
            break;                      // leave the loop, then
                                         // re-enter with a fresh
                                         // enumerator
        }
    }
}

3.7 Labels, goto and loops with break values

goto still exists and is still legal, with two restrictions: you cannot jump into a block, and you cannot jump past a variable declaration. It is useful for two things — escaping deeply nested loops, and implementing the retry pattern. C# 7 also lets a loop carry a break value.

Two features that look archaic and are not: labels and the ability to break out of a loop carrying a value. Both are in the language because they remove a nesting level in cases where the alternative is a flag variable, and the flag variable is the defect.

Labels and the double break

A labelled loop can be exited from an inner loop. The case that motivates it is a nested search where the inner loop's break is not what is wanted — the outer one is. The alternatives are a flag variable, an exception, or a helper returning a value; the flag variable is the one that produces the subtly wrong loop.

What the language restricts

A goto may not jump into a block, may not jump backwards past a variable declaration into its scope, and may not leave a finally. Those restrictions exist because each of them makes the value of a variable undefined, and the compiler rejects them rather than leaving it to a reader.

// Escaping nested loops: both loops must carry a label
bool found = false;
Search:
for (int row = 0; row < grid.Length; row++)
{
    for (int col = 0; col < grid[row].Length; col++)
    {
        if (grid[row][col] == target)
        {
            found = true;
            goto case Search;   // 'break' only leaves the inner loop
        }
    }
}

// A loop that produces a value: break WITH a value
static int? FirstEven(int[] data)
{
    foreach (int v in data)
    {
        if (v % 2 == 0) return v;   // clearer: just return
    }
    return null;
}

// The form that actually needs break-with-value:
static int? FindFirst(int[] data)
{
    foreach (int v in data)
    {
        switch (v)
        {
            case < 0: break;                     // skip negatives
            default: break;                  // skip the rest
        }
        if (v > 10) return v;
    }
    return null;
}

Modern C# rarely needs goto. The cases where it still wins: jumping out of a deeply nested loop, and a retry loop that must run the whole body again without an extra flag variable.

Language version 7 and earlier supported a labelled break (break Search;), which is the cleaner form of the same idea. It was deprecated in C# 7 and removed in favour of goto case label; — label the loop and use goto to exit it.

Exercises 3

  1. Write a program that classifies a number with a switch expression using relational patterns, then rewrite the same logic with a switch statement and a when guard.
  2. Add a new member to a two-value enum and watch every switch expression without a discard arm fail to compile. Add the arm and confirm it builds.
  3. Build a navigation-safe accessor chain three levels deep against a Node type and show the difference between ?. chaining and a null check at each level.
  4. Implement a [Flags] permission enum, set three flags, remove one, and print the ToString output at each step.
  5. Create a custom Range enumerable that produces an arithmetic sequence, and iterate it with foreach.
  6. Use a labelled goto to exit a nested double loop as soon as a target value is found, and count the iterations skipped.

{{-- LABELS AND THE DOUBLE BREAK, where the alternative is a flag
     variable — and a flag variable is the defect: --}}
static (int Row, int Col)? Find(int[,] grid, int target)
{
    for (int r = 0; r < grid.GetLength(0); r++)
    {
        for (int c = 0; c < grid.GetLength(1); c++)
        {
            if (grid[r, c] == target) return (r, c);
        }
    }
    return null;
}

{{-- WHICH DOES NOT NEED A LABEL, because a RETURN carries the value
     out. And that is the first rule: a labelled break is for a case
     a return cannot express. --}}

static int[,] FirstInvalid(IEnumerable<int> rows, int cols)
{
    int[,] grid = new int[rows.Count(), cols];
    int r = 0;

    foreach (int[] row in rows)
    {
        for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
        {
            if (row[c] >= 0) continue;

            // THE CASE A RETURN CANNOT EXPRESS: leave BOTH loops.
            // A return would need the grid allocated first, and a
            // flag variable would need a second traversal or a
            // sentinel that could be a legitimate value.
            goto Found;
        }
        r++;
    }

Found:
    // ^ the label sits AFTER the loop, so falling into it normally
    //   is also correct: nothing was invalid, and the caller checks
    //   r against the row count.
    return grid;
}

{{-- THE DOUBLE BREAK, in its canonical form: --}}
static bool TryFindBoth(int[,] grid, int a, int b, out int row)
{
    row = -1;
    outer:
    for (int r = 0; r < grid.GetLength(0); r++)
    {
        for (int c = 0; c < grid.GetLength(1); c++)
        {
            if (grid[r, c] == a) continue;
            if (grid[r, c] != b) continue;
            row = r;
            goto outerEnd;      // leave BOTH loops
        }
    }
outerEnd:
    return row >= 0;
    // ^ compared with a flag, which is the defect:
    //     bool found = false;
    //     for (...) { for (...) { ... found = true; break; } if (found) break; }
    //   ...where the flag has to be checked after the INNER loop,
    //   which is exactly the line somebody forgets.
}

{{-- AND WHAT THE LANGUAGE RESTRICTS, and why each restriction
     exists: --}}
{{--   goto INTO a block                    REJECTED: the value of a
                                              variable would be
                                              undefined at the label
     goto BACKWARDS past a declaration      REJECTED: same
     goto OUT of a finally                  REJECTED: it would skip a
                                              required release

   Each restriction makes the value of some variable undefined, and
   the compiler rejects them rather than leaving it to a reader. --}}

{{-- AND WHEN TO REACH FOR IT AT ALL, which is the version worth
     remembering: a labelled break is for a case a RETURN cannot
     express. Everywhere else it is a flag variable with better
     syntax. --}}

4 · Strings, Characters & Text

4.1 string is immutable4.2 String interpolation4.3 Literal flavours: raw, verbatim, unicode4.4 StringBuilder and the concatenation trap4.5 char, Rune and char classification4.6 Span<char> and search4.7 Formatting and culture

Chapter four covers text. Strings are immutable reference types with surprising cost characteristics, and the mistake of concatenating in a loop is the single most common performance bug in beginner C#. This chapter covers immutability, interpolation, the four literal syntaxes, StringBuilder, char and UTF-16 pitfalls, Span<char> for zero-copy work, and culture-sensitive formatting.

4.1 string is immutable

A string is a sealed reference type whose contents cannot change after construction. Every "modifying" operation actually returns a brand new string and leaves the original alone. That is why == on strings is value equality, why strings can be interned and shared freely, and why concatenation inside a loop is quadratic.

A string is immutable, and every operation that appears to change one produces a new one. That is a guarantee about the type rather than a convention, which means a string can be shared freely, used as a dictionary key, and passed across threads without a copy.

What follows from it, and what people expect instead

Because a string cannot change, no reference to it can observe a change. So a loop that appends with the plus operator is not mutating a buffer — it is allocating a new string per iteration and discarding the previous one, which is quadratic in the length and shows up in profiles as an allocation rate rather than as a loop.

The corollary is the caching the runtime does. String literals are interned, so two references to the same literal are the same object and the comparison is a reference check first. Interning is also why a computed string is not the same object as an equal literal, which matters when testing with reference equality and is a test bug rather than a language bug.

string a = "hello";
string b = a.ToUpper();
Console.WriteLine(a);            // hello  -- unchanged
Console.WriteLine(b);            // HELLO  -- a NEW string

// The quadratic trap: n iterations, n new strings, n(n+1)/2 char copies
string result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) result += "x";   // ~50M character copies

// The fix: interpolation into one builder, or just join
string fixed1 = new string('x', 10000);
string fixed2 = string.Concat(Enumerable.Repeat("x", 10000));

// Equality is by value, not reference
Console.WriteLine("abc" == new string([char'a', char'b', char'c']));  // True
Console.WriteLine("abc" is { Length: 3 });             // True

The rule of thumb: a handful of + in an expression is fine and readable. A + inside a loop is a bug. StringBuilder for loops, string.Join for collections, and interpolation for everything else.

Because strings are immutable they are inherently thread-safe for reading, and a const string in C# is a compile-time constant that the compiler can substitute directly into your code. This is also why a static readonly string is subtly different from a const: the former is a real field read at run time.


{{-- IMMUTABILITY, and what follows from it: --}}
static void Immutable()
{
    var a = "hello";
    var b = "hello";
    // a == b                   true
    // ReferenceEquals(a, b)    TRUE: string literals are interned,
    //                          so two references to the same
    //                          literal ARE the same object

    string Compute() => new string(['h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o']);
    // ReferenceEquals(Compute(), a)   FALSE: a computed string is
    //                                  not the same object as an
    //                                  equal literal. Testing with
    //                                  reference equality is a TEST
    //                                  bug, not a language one.

    // THEREFORE: shareable as a key, safe to pass, no copy on read.
    var counts = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.Ordinal);
    counts["hello"] = 1;
}

{{-- AND THE TRAP: appending with + IS NOT MUTATING A BUFFER. --}}
static void Quadratic(List<string> parts)
{
    // WRONG: O(n^2). Each iteration allocates a NEW string of the
    // running total length and discards the previous one. It shows
    // up in a profile as an ALLOCATION RATE, not as a loop.
    string result = "";
    foreach (string part in parts)
        result += part;

    // RIGHT: the builder mutates its internal buffer and only
    // materialises a string at the end.
    var sb = new System.Text.StringBuilder();
    foreach (string part in parts)
        sb.Append(part);
    string good = sb.ToString();

    // THE SINGLE-CASE FORM, which is genuinely better and worth
    // knowing because it is easy to misread as equally bad:
    string joined = string.Join(",", parts);
    // ^ ONE allocation, and the framework's separator handling is
    //   better than the loop's.
}

{{-- WHY THE PROFILE SHOWS AN ALLOCATION RATE, which is the
     diagnostic point: --}}
static void WhatTheProfileShows()
{
    // Ten thousand appends of a short string:
    string s = "";
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) s += "x";
    // Total allocated: about 50 MB, in 10,000 objects, of which
    // 9,999 are garbage IMMEDIATELY. A sampled allocation profiler
    // attributes this to the line above — which is why it is
    // reported as "the loop" rather than as "string concatenation".
}

4.2 String interpolation

Interpolated strings ($"...", C# 6) are not just prettier concatenation. The compiler rewrites them into either a string.Format, a DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler (C# 10 and later) or, in the best case, direct calls to AppendFormatted. That means they avoid boxing and can avoid allocating an intermediate string entirely.

Interpolated strings come in two forms that differ in when the work happens and in how the result is formatted. The plain form produces a string immediately, with the current culture. The handler form produces a value that the runtime formats lazily, which means it can be passed to something that expects a format item and formatted against a different culture at that point.

Alignment and format specifiers

Both forms accept an alignment and a format specifier after a colon, and both are worth knowing because they remove the string concatenation that would otherwise be written. The alignment comes first and is not optional if the specifier is present; the separator is a comma.

The trap: culture

Interpolation uses the current culture by default, which means a number formatted in a user's locale appears in a log or an invoice in that locale's separators. That is correct for display and wrong for anything machine-readable, and the fix is the invariant form.

int id = 42;
string name = "Ada";

Console.WriteLine($"User {id} is {name}");              // User 42 is Ada
Console.WriteLine($"Sum is {id + 8}");              // Sum is 50
Console.WriteLine($"{name,-10}|");               // left-aligned in 10 columns
Console.WriteLine($"{name,10}|");                // right-aligned
Console.WriteLine($"{id:X}");                       // 2A   (hex)
Console.WriteLine($"{id:D5}");                      // 00042 (padded)
Console.WriteLine($"{name.Length,3}: {name}");

// Escaping braces inside interpolation
Console.WriteLine($"{{literal braces}}");       // {literal braces}

// Multiple lines without concatenation: raw string literal + interpolation
var sql = """
    SELECT Id, Name
    FROM   Users
    WHERE  TenantId = 1
    """;

// A format specifier can be an expression or a local
string fmt = "N2";
Console.WriteLine($"{1234.5:fmt}");          // 1,234.50

// Logging should never use interpolation: the message is built eagerly.
logger.LogInformation("Loaded {Count} rows for {TenantId}", count, tenantId);  // correct
logger.LogInformation($"Loaded {count} rows");   // wasteful, do not

The logger overload matters for more than style: the message template and its arguments are stored, so a structured logging provider can index them. Interpolating destroys that and allocates a string even when the level is disabled.

C# 10+ interpolation with more than three holes uses DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler, which formats straight into a pooled char buffer. Below that threshold the compiler still calls string.Format. Either way it beats + concatenation in a loop.


{{-- THE TWO FORMS, and what differs: --}}
static void Forms(double amount, DateTime when, CultureInfo fr)
{
    // 1. PLAIN: a string IMMEDIATELY, with the CURRENT culture.
    string now = $"{amount:N2}";                 // "1 234,57" in fr-FR

    // 2. HANDLER: a VALUE, formatted LAZILY by the runtime, so it
    //    can be handed to something that formats it later —
    //    including against a different culture.
    FormattableString lazy = $"{amount:N2}";
    string later = lazy.ToString(fr);             // formatted NOW,
                                                  // against fr
}

{{-- ALIGNMENT AND SPECIFIERS, which remove the concatenation: --}}
static void Formatting()
{
    // ALIGNMENT, then a COMMA, then the specifier. The alignment is
    // not optional when the specifier is present.
    Console.WriteLine($"{"left",-10}|");
    Console.WriteLine($"{"right",10}|");
    Console.WriteLine($"{42,5:D5}");              // 00042: zero-padded

    // INTERPOLATION, not concatenation:
    // "Name: " + name + " (" + count + ")"   -- replaced by:
    var text = $"Name: {name} ({count})";

    // A VERBATIM INTERPOLATED STRING, when the braces are content:
    var path = $@"C:Users{user}Documents";

    // NESTED BRACES need doubling, and this is worth knowing because
    // it is not obvious:
    // $"{value}"        an interpolated expression
    // $"{{literal}}"    an escaped literal brace
}

{{-- THE TRAP, and it is a CORRECTNESS one rather than a style one: --}}
static void TheCultureTrap(double amount)
{
    // CURRENT CULTURE BY DEFAULT: the number appears in a log, an
    // exported file or an API response in the user's separators.
    Log.Information($"processed {amount:N2}");
    // with fr-FR, that log line contains "1 234,57" — including a
    // NON-BREAKING SPACE, which no parser expects.

    // THE INVARIANT FORM, for anything machine-readable:
    Log.Information(
        FormattableString.Invariant($"processed {amount:N2}"));
    // -> "processed 1,234.57" everywhere

    // OR, better, do not format a number into a log line at all:
    Log.Information("processed {Amount}", amount);
    // ^ the structured logging sink owns the formatting, and it
    //   formats it into the SINK's representation rather than the
    //   server's locale.
}

{{-- AND THE RENDERING PATH, which is the one to use when the
     result must be interpolated into markup: --}}
static string Markup(string name) =>
    // A DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler formats into a pooled
    // SPAN and only allocates the final string, so an interpolated
    // string inside a string.Format or a logger costs one
    // allocation rather than one per argument.
    string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, $"<span>{name}</span>");

4.3 Literal flavours: raw, verbatim, unicode

C# has four ways to write a string literal, each solving a different escaping problem. Knowing which to reach for removes most backslash noise from your source.

Three literal forms exist because three problems exist: a literal containing a backslash, a literal containing a quote, and a literal containing characters outside the basic multilingual plane. Each solves its problem and has a cost, and the costs are worth knowing because the forms are not interchangeable.

Raw string literals

The newest form removes the need to escape almost anything, by using a delimiter that must not appear in the content. It solves the awkward cases — embedded quotes, JSON, a path — and it also makes the number of quotes in a literal a deliberate choice rather than a convention, which is what lets a linter or a formatter reformat one without changing its meaning.

The cost of each

The verbatim form's cost is that a doubled quote is a quote, so a literal containing a run of quotes is unreadable. The escaped form's cost is that the escapes are evaluated at compile time and the result is what the runtime sees, so a raw literal and an escaped literal with the same apparent content are not the same if the content contains a backslash. And the Unicode form's cost is that the escape is only one unit wide, so a character outside the basic plane needs a surrogate pair written as two escapes.

// 1. Regular: backslash escapes, best for short strings
string path = "C:\\Users\\ada\\file.txt";
string nl = "line1\nline2";
string q = "He said \"hi\"";

// 2. Verbatim @"": backslashes are literal, escape a quote by doubling it
string winPath = @"C:\Users\ada\file.txt";
string quoted = @"He said ""hi""";

// 3. Raw """: no escapes at all, quotes determined by the delimiter count.
//    With three or more quotes the content may contain quotes and newlines.
string json = """
{
  "name": "Ada",
  "tags": ["a", "b"],
  "note": "has ""quotes"" inside"
}
""";

//    Interpolation works too: $ plus the same raw delimiter
int count = 3;
string report = $"""
    Report for {count} items
      generated inline
    """;

// 4. Unicode: U+XXXX escape, useful for invisible or control characters
string nul = "a\0b";
string heart = "\u2665";
// C# 11 added \e for ESC and \x41 for two hex digits.

Raw string literals (C# 11) are the biggest quality-of-life win in this list. SQL, JSON, HTML, XML and regex all read correctly now instead of being a wall of doubled quotes.

In a raw string literal the indentation of the closing delimiter is stripped from every line. If the closing """ is indented to match your code, the content is unindented too — which is exactly what you want for SQL and exactly what breaks a JSON template that needs leading spaces.


{{-- THE THREE FORMS, each solving a specific problem: --}}
static void TheThree()
{
    // 1. ESCAPED: \ is a backslash, " is a quote, 
 is a newline.
    string escaped = "C:\Users\test\file.txt";
    string withQuote = "he said "hello"";

    // 2. VERBATIM, prefixed with @: \ is ONE backslash, "" is one
    //    quote. Everything else is literal.
    string verbatim = @"C:Users	estile.txt";
    string q = @"he said ""hello""";

    // 3. RAW, no prefix, delimited by a run of quotes that must not
    //    appear in the content.
    string json = """
        { "name": "test", "path": "C:\temp" }
        """;

    // ^ NO ESCAPING AT ALL, which is the point. The quotes around
    //   name are content, and the path keeps its backslashes
    //   because there is no escape processing.

    // THE DELIMITER IS CHOSEN BY THE CONTENT:
    string triple = """He said "hello" to me.""";
    string withTriple = """"He said ""hello"" to me."""";
    // ^ the second uses FOUR opening quotes because the content
    //   contains a run of three; the count is how the parser knows
    //   where the literal ends.
}

{{-- AND THE COSTS, which are worth knowing because the forms are
     not interchangeable: --}}
static void TheCosts()
{
    // A VERBATIM literal's doubled quote makes a run of quotes
    // unreadable:
    string run = @"he said """""""" what";     // five quotes in a row

    // AN ESCAPED literal is evaluated AT COMPILE TIME, so a raw
    // literal with the same apparent content is NOT the same when
    // the content contains a backslash:
    string a = "a\nb";      // a backslash then 'n': 4 characters
    string b = """a
b""";   // a newline: 4 characters, DIFFERENT bytes
    // ^ the first has backslash-n as two characters; the second has
    //   a newline. They look the same and are not.
}

{{-- THE UNICODE FORM, and the one-unit-wide limit: --}}
static void Unicode()
{
    string basic    = "A";     // 'A': inside the BMP
    string emoji    = "U0001F600";  // the surrogate PAIR for
                                      // U+1F600, as TWO code units
    string rawEmoji = """😀""";      // ^ the character itself, and
                                      //   the source is readable
                                      //   where U0001F600 is not

    // ABOVE THE BMP the escape is a surrogate pair written as two
    // escapes in older sources:
    // "😀"   == "U0001F600"
    // ^ and this is worth knowing because the pair is two CHARs,
    //   so emoji.Length is 2 and any code assuming one char per
    //   visible glyph is wrong.
}

4.4 StringBuilder and the concatenation trap

StringBuilder is a mutable character buffer. You append to it and call ToString() once at the end. The performance rule is simple: switch to a builder when you do more than about three concatenations, or any concatenation inside a loop.

A string builder is a mutable buffer that materialises a string when asked. Its reason for existing is not performance in the abstract; it is that the string concatenation operator has no way to mutate, so a loop appending to a string is quadratic and a builder's is not.

When it is and is not worth reaching for

The rule of thumb is that a small number of concatenations in an expression is not a problem — the compiler folds adjacent literals, and a handful of + operations over short strings is cheaper than allocating a builder. The rule that actually matters is that the alternative to a builder is a loop, and a loop over a collection is where the quadratic behaviour appears.

What else belongs in it

The builder has two behaviours worth knowing. It can be given a capacity, which avoids the doubling reallocations for a result whose length is known. And it has an AppendFormat that takes arguments rather than a pre-formatted string, which matters because it can format in place rather than allocating an intermediate string per argument.

using System.Text;

// Bad: quadratic, allocates n strings
string bad = "";
foreach (var row in rows) bad += row + "\n";

// Good: linear, one buffer, one final allocation
var sb = new StringBuilder(capacity);
foreach (var row in rows)
{
    sb.Append(row.Id).Append(',').Append(row.Name).AppendLine();
}
string good = sb.ToString();

// C# 11 raw literal: append lines directly, no escapes needed
sb.AppendLine("""
    {"id": 1, "name": "Ada"}
    """);

// Interpolated strings append without allocating an intermediate
sb.Append($"User {id} scored {score:N1}%");

// Chaining and selective clearing
sb.Append("a").Append("b").Append("c");
sb.Clear();
sb.Length = 0;

// Overloads worth knowing
sb.Append(char.IsDigit);   // delegate
sb.AppendLine();
sb.Insert(0, "[header] ");
sb.Replace("old", "new");

Pass a capacity to the constructor when you know roughly how much you will append. The builder grows by doubling, so starting at zero for a 1 MB result means about twenty reallocations and copies along the way.

Use string.Create (C# 10) or a Span<char> when you want the performance of a builder without the intermediate object. Handlers that need to format into a span should implement ISpanFormattable to take part.


{{-- WHY IT EXISTS, and it is not performance in the abstract: --}}
static void Why(List<string> parts)
{
    // The + OPERATOR HAS NO WAY TO MUTATE, so this is O(n^2):
    string result = "";
    foreach (string p in parts) result += p;

    // THE BUILDER'S AMORTISED GROWTH makes it O(n): it keeps a
    // buffer and doubles it when full, so the total copying is
    // linear in the final length.
    var sb = new System.Text.StringBuilder();
    foreach (string p in parts) sb.Append(p);
    string good = sb.ToString();
}

{{-- WHEN IT IS NOT WORTH REACHING FOR, which is the rule of thumb:
     a SMALL NUMBER of concatenations in an EXPRESSION is not a
     problem. --}}
static void NotWorthIt(string a, string b, string c)
{
    // The compiler FOLDS adjacent literals at compile time, so this
    // allocates once.
    string folded = "prefix: " + a + " " + b + " " + c;

    // And a handful of + operations over short strings is cheaper
    // than allocating a builder — the builder is an OBJECT with a
    // buffer, and for three short strings the object costs more
    // than the copies.
}

{{-- THE TWO THINGS ELSE WORTH KNOWING: --}}
static void TheTwoThings()
{
    // 1. A CAPACITY, which avoids the doubling reallocations for a
    //    result whose length is known. Measuring the result first is
    //    the cheap way to get it.
    static string Join(IEnumerable<string> parts, string separator)
    {
        int length = separator.Length * (parts.Count() - 1);
        foreach (string p in parts) length += p.Length;

        var sb = new System.Text.StringBuilder(length);
        bool first = true;
        foreach (string p in parts)
        {
            if (!first) sb.Append(separator);
            sb.Append(p);
            first = false;
        }
        return sb.ToString();
    }

    // 2. AppendFormat TAKES ARGUMENTS rather than a pre-formatted
    //    string, so it can format IN PLACE rather than allocating an
    //    intermediate string per argument — which is what the + form
    //    of the same thing does.
    var report = new System.Text.StringBuilder();
    report.AppendFormat(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                        "{0}: {1:N2} of {2:N0} ({3:P1})",
                        name, amount, total, share);
    // ^ ONE allocation at the end. The alternative,
    //   sb.Append(string.Format("{0}: {1:N2}", name, amount));
    //   allocates the intermediate string for EVERY line.
}

4.5 char, Rune and char classification

char is a 16-bit unsigned integer holding a single UTF-16 code unit. That is not the same as a user-perceived character: an emoji such as a family or flag is two or four char values. For text that may contain anything outside the basic multilingual plane, work in terms of code points (Rune) or grapheme clusters.

A char is sixteen bits, which is smaller than a Unicode code point and larger than a byte. That single fact produces almost everything surprising about character handling in the language: an emoji does not fit, a surrogate pair occupies two of them, and any code that assumes one char is one visible glyph is wrong for every character above the basic multilingual plane.

Runes, and the enumerations that use them

A rune is a Unicode scalar value, which is the thing that is actually a character — and enumerating a string as runes rather than as chars is what makes the counting correct. The trap is that a range-based foreach over a string still gives char, not Rune, so the two forms have to be chosen deliberately.

Classification, and what it costs
