The classification methods on char and string are Unicode-aware rather than ASCII-only, which is correct and which costs more than the ASCII version. For a hot path that only ever sees ASCII, an explicit ASCII check is faster and the difference is worth knowing — though the correct answer is usually to avoid the per-character classification entirely.

char c = 'A';
Console.WriteLine((int)c);                  // 65
Console.WriteLine(char.IsLetter(c));              // True
Console.WriteLine(char.IsUpper(c));               // True
Console.WriteLine(char.IsDigit('7'));            // True
Console.WriteLine(char.IsWhiteSpace(' '));        // True

// Iterating a string yields char -- UTF-16 code units
string family = "\U0001F468\u200D\U0001F469\u200D\U0001F467";
Console.WriteLine(family.Length);            // 7 code units, 1 visible character

// Enumerate code points instead (System.Text)
foreach (var rune in family.EnumerateRunes())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"U+{(int)rune.Value:X4} {rune}");
}

// System.Text.StringBuilder gets a Rune-based overload too
// System.Globalization.StringInfo handles grapheme clusters for real UI

Length is measured in code units, not characters. "abc".Length is 3, and a flag emoji is 4. If you validate user input by length, validate in Runes or you will reject valid input — or accept invalid input on a system counting differently.

Do not slice a string with text[i] or text.Substring(i, 1) when the input can contain emoji or combining marks. You will cut a character in half and produce mojibake. Use System.Globalization.StringInfo for grapheme-aware slicing, or normalise first.


{{-- A CHAR IS 16 BITS, which is smaller than a Unicode code point
     and larger than a byte. That one fact produces almost
     everything surprising about character handling. --}}
static void SixteenBits()
{
    char c = 'A';                    // 1 char = 2 bytes
    string emoji = "😀";         // a surrogate PAIR
    emoji.Length                     // 2: TWO chars for one glyph
    char.ConvertToUtf32(emoji, 0)     // 0x1F600: the code point
    emoji.EnumerateRunes().Count()    // 1: ONE rune for the glyph
    // ^ the same visible character is 1 rune and 2 chars, and any
    //   code assuming one char per glyph is wrong above the BMP.
}

{{-- AND A RANGE foreach GIVES CHAR, NOT RUNE, so the two forms
     have to be chosen deliberately: --}}
static void CharsOrRunes(string s)
{
    foreach (char c in s)            // 2 iterations for "😀"
        Console.WriteLine(c);

    foreach (var rune in s.EnumerateRunes())   // 1 iteration
        Console.WriteLine(rune.Value);

    // The SPAN version, which does not allocate the enumerator:
    foreach (var rune in s.AsSpan().EnumerateRunes())
        Console.WriteLine(rune.Value);
}

{{-- CLASSIFICATION, which is Unicode-aware rather than ASCII-only:
     correct, and it costs more than the ASCII version. --}}
static void Classification(string s)
{
    char.IsDigit(c);        // Unicode digits, not just 0-9: Arabic-
                             // Indic digits are digits
    char.IsLetter(c);       // any script
    char.IsWhiteSpace(c);   // NBSP, U+2028, and others that ASCII
                            // isspace does not recognise
    char.IsAsciiDigit(c);   // the ASCII-only version, faster

    // FOR A HOT PATH THAT ONLY SEES ASCII, the explicit check is
    // measurably faster — and the better answer is usually to
    // avoid per-character classification altogether:
    static bool AllDigits(string s)
    {
        foreach (char c in s)
            if (!char.IsAsciiDigit(c)) return false;
        return s.Length > 0;
    }
}

{{-- AND THE OPERATION THAT IS ALMOST ALWAYS RIGHT, because it does
     the work once rather than per character: --}}
static bool IsDigits(string s) =>
    !string.IsNullOrEmpty(s) && s.All(char.IsAsciiDigit);
{{-- ^ LINQ over a string walks a span internally in current
     runtimes, so it is fast; the value is that it is correct without
     a per-character loop somebody has to think about. --}}

4.6 Span<char> and search

A Span<char> is a view over existing characters. It costs no allocation, and slicing it is a pointer adjustment. That makes it the right tool for parsing, trimming and searching without producing intermediate strings.

A span over characters is a view: a pointer, a length and an offset, with no reference to a string and no ability to grow. It exists so that a substring operation can be free — the index of a delimiter in a larger buffer, the argument between two markers in a line — without allocating a string for each stage.

What a span forbids, and why

A span cannot escape the method it was created in, and the compiler enforces that: a field of type Span<char> is a compile error, and so is a yield return of one. That is the whole point — a span's lifetime is bounded by the buffer it points into, and a type that could outlive that buffer would be a use-after-free waiting to be found.

Searching, and the two families

Indexing operations come in two forms: those taking a span, which search without allocating, and those taking a string, which allocate a substring when they find something. Using the span form when the result is only compared or parsed is the difference between one allocation and none.

// Stackalloc a small buffer, or slice an existing string: zero allocation
Span<char> buffer = stackalloc char[64];
int written = "hello".AsSpan().CopyTo(buffer);
Console.WriteLine(buffer.Slice(0, written).ToString());   // hello

// Slicing a span
ReadOnlySpan<char> src = "one,two,three".AsSpan();
ReadOnlySpan<char> tail = src[(src.IndexOf(',') + 1)..];
Console.WriteLine(tail.ToString());        // two,three

// Search without allocating a substring
var index = src.IndexOf("two".AsSpan(), StringComparison.Ordinal);
Console.WriteLine(index);                   // 4

// Span-based comparison rules: ALWAYS pass a StringComparison
// src.IndexOf('t')                // ordinal char, no allocation, fine
// src.Contains("two")            // culture-sensitive, allocates on some runtimes
// src.Contains("two".AsSpan(), StringComparison.Ordinal)   // best

// span is a ref struct: it cannot live in a field, be boxed, or cross an await
// A Span<T> method is therefore synchronous by necessity.

Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> are ref structs: stack-only, non-boxable, and forbidden in async methods or lambdas that are not synchronous. That restriction is the design — a span points into memory someone else owns, so it must not outlive that owner.

Implicit conversion means you rarely write new Span<char>(array). Assign the array and it becomes a span; use AsSpan() for the read-only form. The stackalloc keyword only works for Span<T>, never for a heap array.


{{-- A SPAN IS A VIEW: a pointer, a length and an offset, with no
     reference and no ability to grow. --}}
static void View()
{
    string log = "[2026-01-01] ERROR something failed";

    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = log.AsSpan();

    int open  = span.IndexOf('[');
    int close = span.IndexOf(']');

    // A SUBSTRING IS FREE as a span: no allocation, because a span
    // is a pair of pointers into the ORIGINAL string.
    ReadOnlySpan<char> date = span[(open + 1)..close];
    Console.WriteLine(date.Length);      // 10, and nothing was
                                        // allocated

    if (date.SequenceEqual("2026-01-01"))
        Console.WriteLine("matched, with no allocation");

    // WHICH IS THE POINT: the string-form search allocates a
    // substring at every step, so four searches over a 40-character
    // line is four allocations before any real work starts.
    // string date2 = log.Substring(open + 1, close - open - 1);
}

{{-- WHAT A SPAN FORBIDS, and the compiler ENFORCES it: --}}
class Field
{
    // private Span<char> _buffer;   ERROR: CS8345: cannot use
    //   Span<T> as a field, because a field outlives the buffer it
    //   points into.
}

static IEnumerable<char> Yield(ReadOnlySpan<char> span)
{
    // yield return span[0];        ERROR: a span cannot cross an
    //   iterator boundary for the same reason.
    yield break;
}
{{-- ^ the restriction is not inconvenience, it is the property
     that makes a span SAFE. A type that could outlive its buffer
     would be a use-after-free waiting to be found. --}}

{{-- SEARCHING, and the two families: --}}
static void Searching(string line)
{
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line.AsSpan();

    // THE SPAN FORMS: no allocation when they find something.
    int colon = span.IndexOf(':');
    if (colon >= 0)
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<char> value = span[(colon + 1)..];
        // use value                                    no allocation
    }

    // THE STRING FORMS: allocate a substring on every call.
    int colon2 = line.IndexOf(':');
    if (colon2 >= 0)
    {
        string value = line[(colon2 + 1)..];
        // an allocation, per call
    }

    // Use the span form when the result is only COMPARED or PARSED.
    // Use the string form when the substring is stored or returned.
    if (int.TryParse(span[(colon + 1)..], out int port))
        Connect(port);
}

{{-- AND THE CASE WHERE THE SPAN VERSION IS CORRECT AND THE STRING
     ONE IS A BUG, because the substring is only compared: --}}
static bool IsDebugLine(string line) =>
    line.AsSpan().StartsWith("[DEBUG]", StringComparison.Ordinal);
{{-- ^ one comparison, zero allocations. The string version
     allocates a substring before comparing it. --}}

4.7 Formatting and culture

Formatting a number, date or currency is culture-sensitive, and the culture comes from the thread unless you override it. On a machine set to a European locale, 1.5.ToString() prints "1,5". That is correct behaviour and also a classic source of bugs in data pipelines, where a stable machine-readable format is required.

Formatting a number, a date or a currency uses a culture, and a culture is a set of conventions rather than a language: which separators a number uses, which field order a date uses, and which calendar a date is expressed in. The default is the current culture, which is the right choice for a user interface and the wrong choice for a log line, a file, an exported report or anything a machine will read.

What invariant actually means

Invariant is not a language; it is a fixed, culture-neutral set of conventions. It is the right choice for machine-readable output, for a protocol, and for a stored value that will be parsed by something else. It is the wrong choice for anything a person reads, because a number written in invariant form on a page in a German locale looks wrong to the person reading it.

String comparison, which is a related decision

Ordering and equality of strings both take a comparison type, and the default for equality is ordinal while the default for CompareTo is current culture. That asymmetry is the source of the defect where two lists sort differently on different machines, and where a lookup that was populated under one culture misses under another.

using System.Globalization;

decimal amount = 1234.56m;

Console.WriteLine(amount.ToString());                          // current culture
Console.WriteLine(amount.ToString("C", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture));    // $1,234.56
Console.WriteLine(amount.ToString("N2", CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("de-DE")));  // 1.234,56

// Invariant culture is the correct choice for:
//   - anything parsed by a machine (files, APIs, CLI output)
//   - anything compared as text in tests
//   - anything the user never sees

// Explicit parsing with a culture
bool ok = decimal.TryParse("1.234,56",
    NumberStyles.Number, CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("de-DE"), out decimal parsed);

// Dates: always format, never rely on ToString()
DateTimeOffset now = DateTimeOffset.Now;
Console.WriteLine(now.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture));  // 2026-03-14
Console.WriteLine(now.ToString("o"));        // round-trippable ISO 8601

// Comparison: culture-aware vs ordinal
Console.WriteLine("apple".CompareTo("Apple"));                    // culture: -1
Console.WriteLine(string.CompareOrdinal("apple", "Apple"));   // 1
Console.WriteLine("a".Equals("a", StringComparison.Ordinal));  // True -- use this

// Pin the culture for a whole thread (background work, WPF/WinForms init)
CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;

The default for Equals, IndexOf and StartsWith is CurrentCulture, which is slow and surprising. Pass StringComparison.Ordinal (or OrdinalIgnoreCase) explicitly everywhere except where you genuinely want linguistic behaviour such as "cafe" matching "café".

Exercises 4

  1. Build a 5000-line report by +=, time it, then rebuild with StringBuilder and time it again. Record both numbers.
  2. Write the same SQL statement as a regular string, a verbatim string and a raw string literal. Confirm all three produce identical text.
  3. Format a decimal under InvariantCulture and de-DE, and add a comment explaining which one belongs in an API response and which belongs on screen.
  4. Print the length of a string containing a family emoji, then enumerate its runes and count the code points. Explain the difference.
  5. Parse "a,b,,c" with ReadOnlySpan<char> and Split without allocating intermediate substrings.
  6. Write a TitleCase helper that uses CultureInfo correctly and does not corrupt multi-word strings containing apostrophes.

{{-- A CULTURE IS A SET OF CONVENTIONS, not a language: which
     separators, which date field order, which calendar. --}}
static void Conventions(double amount, DateTime when)
{
    // THE DEFAULT is the current culture, which is RIGHT for a
    // display and WRONG for a log, a file or a protocol.
    string here = amount.ToString("N2");                 // 1,234.57 or
                                                          // 1.234,57
    string machine = amount.ToString("N2", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
                                                          // 1,234.57
                                                          // everywhere

    // WHY IT MATTERS: invariant FORMATTING is not the same as
    // invariant PARSING, and a value written one way and read the
    // other fails.
    string written = amount.ToString("N2", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    // Parse with a DIFFERENT culture and it fails or truncates:
    // double.TryParse("1.234,57", NumberStyles.Any, de-DE, out _)  false
}

{{-- STRING COMPARISON, and the asymmetry that causes the defect: --}}
static void TheAsymmetry()
{
    // EQUALITY defaults to ORDINAL: a byte comparison.
    bool same = a.Equals(b);                    // ordinal: correct for
                                               // identifiers

    // COMPARISON defaults to CURRENT CULTURE: linguistic.
    int order = a.CompareTo(b);                 // current culture,
                                               // and therefore
                                               // DIFFERENT ON EACH
                                               // MACHINE

    var names = new List<string> { "banana", "Apple", "cherry" };
    names.Sort();                               // WRONG: two machines
                                               // order this
                                               // differently, so a
                                               // LIMIT is applied at
                                               // a different row on
                                               // each
    names.Sort(StringComparer.Ordinal);         // RIGHT: stable,
                                               // machine-independent
    names.Sort(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
}

{{-- WHERE A LOOKUP GOES WRONG FOR THE SAME REASON: --}}
static void LookupGoesWrong()
{
    // A DICTIONARY POPULATED under one culture and QUERIED under
    // another MISSES, because the comparer is part of the key.
    var index = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.CurrentCulture);
    index["resume"] = 1;
    // index["RESUME"]     may be 1 or a KeyNotFoundException,
    //                     depending on the culture of the CURRENT
    //                     culture setting at the time of the lookup

    var stable = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    stable["resume"] = 1;
    // stable["RESUME"]    1, always
}

{{-- AND THE CALENDAR, which is the one nobody expects: --}}
DateTime.Parse("01/02/2026", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
// -> 1 February 2026: invariant interprets it as MONTH/DAY
DateTime.Parse("01/02/2026", new CultureInfo("en-GB"));
// -> 2 January 2026: en-GB interprets it as DAY/MONTH
{{-- ^ the same string is two different dates, and a date stored
     without an offset and without an explicit format is a defect
     waiting for a user in another locale. --}}

5 · Arrays, Collections & Spans

5.1 Arrays5.2 List<T>5.3 Dictionary<K,V> and lookup5.4 HashSet, Queue, Stack and PriorityQueue5.5 Immutable collections5.6 ArrayPool and renting buffers5.7 Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T>5.8 stackalloc, slices and ranges

Chapter five covers the data structures you will use every day, and the modern span-based family that removes allocation from hot paths. The rule that organises the whole chapter: know the cost of each structure, because the difference between List<T> and ImmutableList<T> is not just an API difference — it is a design difference.

5.1 Arrays

An array has a fixed length, contiguous storage and direct indexing. It is a reference type even when it holds value types, it is covariant (which is unsound for value types and only there for legacy reasons), and every element is initialised to the type default.

An array has a fixed length established at creation and a contiguous layout. Both properties produce the same set of facts: access is bounds-checked by the runtime rather than by the type, a length change means allocating and copying, and a two-dimensional array is a single flat block indexed by a computed offset rather than an array of arrays.

Bounds checking, and turning it off

An array access outside its bounds throws rather than reading adjacent memory, and that is a deliberate cost. The performance argument for removing the check is real and it is also the reason a whole category of defect becomes possible, so the trade is a decision rather than a default. Where it is removed it is removed in a leaf function whose contract is checked by the caller, and the caller is where the check moves to.

Multi-dimensional arrays

A rectangular array is one allocation, and its element access multiplies indices and adds an offset — which is correct and is also a bounds check per index rather than per access. An array of arrays is a different structure: each row is a separate allocation, rows can be different lengths, and the access is two dereferences. They are not interchangeable, and the choice is about whether the rows are genuinely ragged.

int[] numbers = new int[5];           // all zeros
string[] names = new string[3];          // all null, despite the type
int[] primes = [2, 3, 5, 7];      // collection expression, C# 12
int[] implied = [1, 2, 3];              // target-typed, also C# 12

Console.WriteLine(numbers[0]);        // 0  -- the default, not garbage
Console.WriteLine(names[0]);          // null: NRE waiting to happen
Console.WriteLine(primes.Length);    // 4

// Bounds checking happens on every access, in every build configuration
// numbers[5]  -> IndexOutOfRangeException

// Multi-dimensional: rarely what you want
int[,] grid = new int[3, 4];
grid[1, 2] = 99;            // row 1, column 2
Console.WriteLine(grid.GetLength(0));  // 3 -- rows, not total elements

// Jagged arrays: arrays of arrays, no bounds checking on the inner ones
int[][] jagged = new int[3][];
// jagged[0].Length  -> NullReferenceException until you assign

// Array operations
Array.Sort(numbers);
Array.Reverse(numbers);
int found = Array.IndexOf(numbers, 42);
int pos = Array.BinarySearch(numbers, 42);   // requires sorted input
numbers.CopyTo(other, 0);
var slice = primes[1..3];        // C# 8 range: [3, 5]

Always initialise a string[] element before use. The type system will not stop you writing names[0].Length, and the compiler’s nullable analysis cannot either because the element type is not annotated.

Prefer List<T> unless you know the exact count up front and never change it. An array is marginally faster to index and marginally worse at everything else, and the difference is dwarfed by getting the data structure right.


{{-- THE TWO PROPERTIES, and both produce the same facts: fixed
     length, contiguous layout. --}}
static void Properties()
{
    int[] a = new int[5];              // 5 zeros
    int[] b = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };      // length inferred
    int[] c = [1, 2, 3];              // the same thing

    // MULTI-DIMENSIONAL IS ONE FLAT BLOCK:
    int[,] grid = new int[3, 4];
    int[,] literal = {{ 1, 2 }, { 3, 4 }};
    Console.WriteLine(grid.GetLength(0));   // 3
    Console.WriteLine(grid.GetLength(1));   // 4
    // ^ a bounds check PER INDEX, because the access has to validate
    //   both.

    // AN ARRAY OF ARRAYS IS A DIFFERENT STRUCTURE: each row is a
    // separate allocation and rows may be different lengths.
    int[][] jagged = new int[3][];
    jagged[0] = [1, 2, 3];
    jagged[1] = [4, 5];
    // jagged[1].Length is 2: a RAGGED array, which the rectangular
    // form cannot express at all.

    // THE CHOICE: rectangular when the rows are genuinely uniform,
    // jagged when they are not. A jagged array used for uniform data
    // costs an allocation and a cache miss per row.
}

{{-- BOUNDS CHECKING, and the trade is a DECISION rather than a
     default: --}}
static void Bounds()
{
    int[] a = new int[5];
    // a[5] = 1;            IndexOutOfRangeException: the runtime
    //                        validates, which is a COST

    // And it is a cost on every access, in a loop, which is where it
    // shows up:
    long total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) total += a[i];
}

static unsafe long Unchecked(int[] a)
{
    fixed (int* p = a)
    {
        long total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) total += p[i];
        return total;
    }
    // ^ the check removed, in a LEAF FUNCTION whose contract is
    //   checked by the caller — and the caller is where the check
    //   MOVES TO. Removing it everywhere is what makes an
    //   out-of-range read a silent wrong answer.
}

{{-- AND THE LENGTH-CHANGE PROBLEM, which is why a list exists: --}}
static void LengthChange()
{
    int[] a = [1, 2, 3];
    // a[3] = 4;   impossible

    // The idiom, and what it costs:
    Array.Resize(ref a, 4);         // allocate 4, copy 3, then write
    a[3] = 4;
    // ^ fine ONCE. In a loop it is quadratic, because each resize
    //   copies everything already added. The list exists for this.
}

5.2 List<T>

List<T> is a growable array wrapper. Appending is amortised O(1) because it doubles its internal buffer, but inserting or removing at the beginning is O(n) because everything shifts. It exposes a Count and a Capacity, and both are worth thinking about in a loop.

A list wraps an array and grows it. The growth is geometric, which is what makes appending amortised constant: the internal array doubles when it fills, so the total copying across n appends is linear rather than quadratic. The capacity is not observable except through a property, and setting it when the final size is known removes the copying entirely.

The three operations that are not O(1)

Inserting or removing at an index shifts every later element, so it is O(n) even in a list. Indexing is O(1). Searching is O(n) because there is no comparison delegate, and a list of value types searched with a comparison lambda boxes nothing but delegates on every comparison.

The enumerator, and the boxing

A list's enumerator is a mutable struct, so a foreach over a list is specially handled by the compiler to avoid boxing. A foreach over an interface-typed or object-typed reference boxes it once per loop rather than once per iteration, and boxing an enumerator whose current value is a struct boxes a copy of that value with every step.

var list = new List<int>();
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) list.Add(i);

Console.WriteLine(list.Count);      // 10  -- elements
Console.WriteLine(list.Capacity);   // 16  -- buffer size after doubling

list.Capacity = 10;          // trim the buffer; may reallocate

list.Add(99);              // append: amortised O(1)
list.Insert(0, -1);            // O(n) -- shifts everything
list.RemoveAt(0);            // O(n)
list.Remove(5);             // first match, O(n)
list.RemoveAll(x => x < 0);      // C# list, handy for filtering in place
list.Clear();

// Read-only views: a live window, not a copy
var window = list.GetRange(0, 3);   // a NEW list (a copy)
var view = list.AsReadOnly();                    // a read-only VIEW

// The single most important optimisation: set the capacity
// List<int> big = new(1_000_000);   // avoids ~20 reallocations

// CollectionsMarshal and AsSpan avoid a copy when you need an array
Span<int> asSpan = CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list);
int[] asArray = [.. list];   // spread, C# 12

"Collections" in .NET means the non-generic, pre-generics types: ArrayList, Hashtable, Queue, Stack. They are still there, they still work, and you should not write new code with them — every one has a generic equivalent that is type-safe and faster.

Modifying a List<T> while enumerating it throws InvalidOperationException, and the exception message ("Collection was modified") does not tell you which collection. If you need to filter while iterating, use RemoveAll, or project into a new list first.


{{-- GEOMETRIC GROWTH is what makes appending AMORTISED constant:
     the total copying across n appends is linear, not quadratic. --}}
static void Growth()
{
    var list = new List<int>();

    // ^ WITHOUT a capacity: the internal array doubles when it
    //   fills, so 8 resizes and ~2n copies for n appends.

    var sized = new List<int>(capacity: 1024);
    // ^ WITH one: no resizing at all. Set it whenever the final
    //   size is known — which is most of the time in a mapping
    //   from a query result.
}

{{-- THE THREE OPERATIONS THAT ARE NOT O(1): --}}
static void Costs(List<int> list, List<Item> items)
{
    // INDEXING is O(1): the list is an array with a length.
    int first = list[0];

    // INSERT AND REMOVE AT AN INDEX are O(n), EVEN IN A LIST:
    // every later element shifts.
    list.Insert(0, 99);            // 1,000 items at position 0 is
                                   // 1,000 moves
    list.RemoveAt(0);              // the same

    // At the END they are amortised O(1), because there is nothing
    // to shift.
    list.Add(99);

    // SEARCH is O(n): there is NO comparison delegate, so a search
    // is either a loop or LINQ, and LINQ on a list with a lambda
    // DELEGATES on every comparison.
    var found = items.FirstOrDefault(i => i.Id == 42);   // n
                                                       // delegate
                                                       // calls
    // The version worth writing for a hot path:
    var loop = default(Item);
    foreach (var i in items) { if (i.Id == 42) { loop = i; break; } }
}

{{-- THE ENUMERATOR, and the boxing that the compiler avoids: --}}
static void Enumerator()
{
    var list = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };

    // THE COMPILER SPECIAL-CASES THIS: the enumerator is a mutable
    // struct, and foreach over the concrete List<T> does not box it.
    foreach (int v in list) { }

    // BUT THIS DOES, once per loop:
    IEnumerable<int> asInterface = list;
    foreach (int v in asInterface) { }
    // ^ boxed enumerator. And if T is a struct, the enumerator's
    //   CURRENT VALUE is boxed with every step as well.

    // WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A REAL COST AND NOT A STYLE POINT:
    static long SumViaInterface(IEnumerable<int> source)
    {
        long total = 0;
        foreach (int v in source) total += v;   // a virtual call and a
                                                // possible box per
                                                // element
        return total;
    }
    // The fix is a generic constraint, which lets the compiler
    // specialise and skip the interface dispatch entirely.
}

5.3 Dictionary<K,V> and lookup

Dictionary<TKey, TValue> is a hash table with O(1) average lookup. Choosing a bad key type is the usual reason a dictionary is slow: if GetHashCode and Equals are not implemented for your key, you are paying for reflection-free but still linear fallback behaviour.

A dictionary is a hash table with buckets and chains, and two of its behaviours follow from that. Insertion is amortised constant because the chain is short on average. And a lookup with a wrong comparer fails even though the key is present, because the comparer is part of how a key is hashed and compared — so a dictionary populated under one comparer cannot be read under another.

The comparer is not a formatting option

This is the single most common dictionary defect: an index built with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase and then queried with the default comparer, or a CaseInsensitiveDictionary queried with an ordinal lookup. The key is in the dictionary and the lookup returns false, and nothing in the code says the two comparers differ.

Enumeration order is not insertion order

A dictionary enumerates in bucket order, which depends on the hash of the keys and on resizing history. It is stable for a given set of keys and comparer in a given run and is not stable across processes. Anything that depends on the order — a display order, a "first" result — has to sort explicitly.

var scores = new Dictionary<string, int>()
{
    ["Ada"] = 100,
    ["Grace"] = 98,
    ["Alan"] = 95
};

scores["Edsger"] = 91;          // add or overwrite

if (scores.TryGetValue("Ada", out int ada)) Console.WriteLine(ada);

scores["Nobody"];               // KeyNotFoundException

// Other accessors
Console.WriteLine(scores.ContainsKey("Ada"));
scores.TryAdd("Edsger", 91);     // false: already present, no overwrite
scores.GetValueOrDefault("Nobody", -1);      // -1, no exception
scores.Remove("Alan");              // bool: was it there?
scores.Clear();

// Two dictionaries that stay in sync
var forward = new Dictionary<string, int>();
var reverse = new Dictionary<int, string>();
forward["Ada"] = 1; reverse[1] = "Ada";

// Deconstruction for TryGetValue with a tuple key
if (scores.TryGetValue("Ada", out int v)) { }

// Capacity and comparers
var big = new Dictionary<string, int>(10_000);
var ci = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
var ord = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.Ordinal);

Always pass a StringComparer when the key is a string. The default comparer is culture-aware, which means Equals and GetHashCode both go through ICU, and the dictionary is several times slower than it needs to be. Ordinal for identifiers, OrdinalIgnoreCase for user-typed input.

Modern .NET has Dictionary.GetAlternateLookup (ReadOnlySpan overloads) which lets you look up with a ReadOnlySpan<char> without allocating a string. It is the reason span-based parsing into dictionaries is now allocation-free.


{{-- A HASH TABLE WITH BUCKETS AND CHAINS, and two behaviours
     follow from that. --}}
static void Lookup()
{
    var byId = new Dictionary<int, Order>();
    byId[42] = new Order(42);

    // TryGetValue RATHER THAN ContainsKey plus indexer: ONE lookup
    // instead of two, and no risk of a race between them.
    if (byId.TryGetValue(42, out var found))
        Console.WriteLine(found);

    if (!byId.TryGetValue(99, out var missing))
        Console.WriteLine(missing is null);   // the default for a
                                             // reference type, which
                                             // is why the bool
                                             // matters

    // THE INDEXER THROWS rather than returning null, so a KeyNotFound
    // in a hot path is an exception cost:
    var order = byId[42];
}

{{-- THE COMPARER IS NOT A FORMATTING OPTION. It is part of how a
     key is HASHED and COMPARED, so a dictionary populated under one
     comparer cannot be read under another. --}}
static void ComparerIsTheKey()
{
    var index = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    index["Resume"] = 1;

    // index["resume"]                     1: the same comparer
    // var wrong = new Dictionary<string, int>();   default comparer
    // wrong["resume"]                     KeyNotFoundException:
    //                                       THE KEY IS IN THE OTHER
    //                                       DICTIONARY, and nothing
    //                                       in the code says the two
    //                                       comparers differ

    // SO THE COMPARER BELONGS ON EVERY DECLARATION AND EVERY
    // CONSTRUCTOR ARGUMENT:
    var bySlug  = new Dictionary<string, Order>(StringComparer.Ordinal);
    var byEmail = new Dictionary<string, User>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    // ^ email is matched case-insensitively; a slug is matched
    //   exactly. Both are DECISIONS, and the wrong default is
    //   silent.
}

{{-- ENUMERATION ORDER IS BUCKET ORDER, not insertion order: --}}
static void Order()
{
    var map = new Dictionary<string, int>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) map["key" + i] = i;

    foreach (var pair in map) { }
    // ^ bucket order, which depends on the HASH of the keys and on
    //   RESIZING HISTORY. Stable for a given key set and comparer in
    //   a given run; NOT stable across processes.

    // WHICH IS WHY ANYTHING DEPENDING ON ORDER SORTS EXPLICITLY:
    foreach (var pair in map.OrderBy(p => p.Key)) { }
    // ^ or SortedDictionary, which pays O(log n) per operation for a
    //   guaranteed order. That is the trade.
}

5.4 HashSet, Queue, Stack and PriorityQueue

The specialised collections each solve one shape of problem. A set deduplicates, a queue is first-in-first-out, a stack is last-in-first-out, and a priority queue orders by a comparison rather than by arrival. Picking the right one usually makes the algorithm simpler as well as faster.

Four collections that differ in one thing each: whether membership is what matters, what comes out next, or what comes out first. A set answers "is it present" and de-duplicates. A queue answers "what has been waiting longest". A stack answers "what was most recent". A priority queue answers "what is most urgent", which is not the same as "what is next" unless the priority is the insertion order.

HashSet, and the comparer problem again

A set uses the same hashing as a dictionary, so the same rule applies: the comparer is part of membership, and a set populated with one comparer cannot be queried with another. A set of user names with the default comparer is case-sensitive, which is almost never what a person means.

The priority queue's ordering

A priority queue orders by priority, and the tie-break is unspecified: two elements with equal priority come out in an order the implementation chooses and that can change between versions. Any code depending on the order of equal-priority items has a bug that appears on a runtime upgrade rather than on a deployment.

var seen = new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
seen.Add("Ada");
Console.WriteLine(seen.Add("ada"));    // False -- already present
Console.WriteLine(seen.Contains("ADA")); // True
seen.Remove("Ada");
Console.WriteLine(seen.Count);

// Set algebra
var a = new HashSet<int> { 1, 2, 3 };
var b = new HashSet<int> { 2, 3, 4 };
a.UnionWith(b);          // {1,2,3,4}   a is modified
a.IntersectWith(b);      // {2,3}
a.ExceptWith(b);         // {}
bool overlap = a.Overlaps(b);   // any common element?
bool subset = a.IsSubsetOf(b);

// Queue: FIFO
var q = new Queue<string>();
q.Enqueue("first"); q.Enqueue("second");
Console.WriteLine(q.Dequeue());    // first
Console.WriteLine(q.Peek());        // second, does not remove
q.TryDequeue(out string? next);     // bool, no exception

// Stack: LIFO
var st = new Stack<char>();
st.Push('a'); st.Push('b');
Console.WriteLine(st.Pop());     // b
Console.WriteLine(st.Peek());    // a

// PriorityQueue: Dijkstra, A*, top-N
var pq = new PriorityQueue<string, int>();
pq.Enqueue("low", 10);
pq.Enqueue("high", 1);
while (pq.TryDequeue(out string? item, out int cost)) Console.WriteLine(item);

Queue<T> is the right structure for breadth-first search, work items and buffered writes. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> (C# 11) is the right structure for anything that needs the cheapest item next, and it beats hand-rolled sorted-list schedulers in both code and performance.

Reaching for a HashSet<T> inside a loop to test "have I seen this before" is the single highest-value collection change most codebases can make. It turns an O(n²) algorithm into O(n) with one line of change.


{{-- FOUR COLLECTIONS THAT DIFFER IN ONE THING EACH: --}}
static void TheFour(IEnumerable<int> xs)
{
    // A SET: membership, and de-duplication.
    var seen = new HashSet<int>();
    foreach (int x in xs) seen.Add(x);       // seen.Count is the
                                             // DISTINCT count

    // A QUEUE: what has been waiting LONGEST. First in, first out.
    var work = new Queue<int>();
    work.Enqueue(1); work.Enqueue(2);
    work.Dequeue();                          // 1

    // A STACK: what was most RECENT. Last in, first out.
    var undo = new Stack<int>();
    undo.Push(1); undo.Push(2);
    undo.Pop();                              // 2

    // A PRIORITY QUEUE: what is most URGENT, which is NOT the same
    // as what is next unless the priority is the insertion order.
    var urgent = new PriorityQueue<string, int>();
    urgent.Enqueue("page", 1);
    urgent.Enqueue("checkout", 0);          // higher priority
    urgent.Dequeue();                        // "checkout"
    // ^ the point: priority, not order. A FIFO would have returned
    //   "page".
}

{{-- HASHSET, and the SAME comparer rule as a dictionary: --}}
static void SetComparer()
{
    // A SET OF USER NAMES WITH THE DEFAULT COMPARER is case-
    // SENSITIVE, which is almost never what a person means.
    var wrong = new HashSet<string>();
    wrong.Add("Alice");
    // wrong.Contains("alice")   FALSE

    var right = new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    right.Add("Alice");
    // right.Contains("alice")   TRUE

    // AND THE COMBINED FORM, which is the one worth knowing: a set
    // and a dictionary with the SAME comparer, so the two agree
    // about what a key is.
    var counts = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    var keys   = new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    // ^ if these two disagree about case, a lookup that succeeded
    //   in one fails in the other, and the bug is in the DECLARATION
    //   rather than in the logic.
}

{{-- AND THE TIE-BREAK, which is the one that appears on a runtime
     upgrade rather than on a deployment: --}}
static void TieBreak()
{
    var q = new PriorityQueue<string, int>();
    q.Enqueue("first",  1);
    q.Enqueue("second", 1);      // SAME priority

    q.Dequeue();                 // order is UNSPECIFIED
    q.Dequeue();
    // ^ two elements with equal priority come out in an order the
    //   implementation chooses, and that can change between runtime
    //   versions. Any code depending on the order of equal-priority
    //   items has a bug that appears on an upgrade rather than on a
    //   deployment.

    // THE FIX is an explicit tie-break in the priority itself, or a
    // composite: (priority, sequenceNumber) packed into one long.
    long key = ((long)priority << 32) | sequence;
}

5.5 Immutable collections

An immutable collection returns a new instance on every write, and shares structure with the original where it can. They live in System.Collections.Immutable, which ships in the .NET runtime rather than a NuGet package. They are the right default for value-like state, caching and anything shared across threads.

An immutable collection cannot be modified after construction, which makes sharing one safe and makes it usable as a dictionary key or a cache value — something a mutable collection cannot be, because its hash changes when it changes and its hash is the thing the dictionary stored.

What it costs, and what it buys

Every modification returns a new collection and leaves the original alone. That is expensive for repeated modification and cheap for sharing, and the pattern where it wins is a value that is built once and read many times: a lookup table, a configuration snapshot, a parsed grammar, a set of permitted values.

The version that people want is not this

The most common reason to reach for an immutable collection is thread safety, and the answer is usually a plain collection plus a convention rather than an immutable one — because an immutable list read by ten threads still allows one of them to hold a reference and read it later, which is fine, and because the allocation per modification is the wrong trade for a list being appended to in a loop.

using System.Collections.Immutable;

var a = ImmutableList<int>.Empty.Add(1).Add(2);
var b = a.Add(3);

Console.WriteLine(a.Count);   // 2  -- a is UNCHANGED
Console.WriteLine(b.Count);   // 3

// Structural sharing: b reuses a's internal array, adding one element

// The other four
ImmutableArray<int> arr = ImmutableArray.Create(1, 2, 3);
ImmutableDictionary<string, int> map = ImmutableDictionary<string, int>.Empty
    .Add("a", 1).SetItem("b", 2);
ImmutableHashSet<int> set = ImmutableHashSet.Create(1, 2, 2);   // {1,2}
ImmutableSortedDictionary<string, int> sorted = ...;   // IReadOnlyDictionary + ordered
ImmutableSortedSet<int> iset = ImmutableSortedSet.Create(3, 1, 2);  // 1,2,3

// Immutable types can be [ThreadStatic]-free shared safely
static ImmutableArray<int> Lookup = ImmutableArray.Create(0, 10, 100);

// IReadOnlyList<T> is the interface you should expose in signatures
public static int Total(in IReadOnlyList<int> values)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (int v in values) total += v;
    return total;
}

Prefer IReadOnlyList<T> or IReadOnlyCollection<T> over List<T> in a public signature. It is an interface every collection satisfies, it documents that you will not mutate the caller’s data, and it makes testing with an array trivial.

Immutable collections are not automatically fast. Every write allocates. For a local list built in a tight loop, List<T> with a capacity beats ImmutableList<T> by a wide margin. Immutability is a sharing and reasoning benefit first and a performance question second.


{{-- IMMUTABLE, so sharing is SAFE — and it can be a dictionary key or
     a cache value, which a mutable collection cannot be. --}}
static void Sharing()
{
    var permissions = ImmutableHashSet.Create("read", "write");

    // HAND IT TO EVERY COMPONENT: nobody can change it, so nobody
    // has to lock it and nobody has to trust the caller.
    var a = Check(permissions);
    var b = Check(permissions);

    // THE MUTABLE VERSION CANNOT BE A DICTIONARY KEY, and the reason
    // is the important part:
    var mutable = new HashSet<string> { "read", "write" };
    var asKey = new Dictionary<HashSet<string>, int> { [mutable] = 1 };
    mutable.Add("admin");
    // asKey[mutable]     KeyNotFoundException: the hash was computed
    //                    BEFORE the mutation, and the dictionary is
    //                    now looking in a bucket the key is not in.
    //                    A key whose hash can change is not a key.
}

{{-- WHAT IT COSTS, and what it buys: --}}
static void Trade(List<Order> orders)
{
    // MODIFICATION RETURNS A NEW COLLECTION and leaves the original
    // alone. Every one of these is a fresh allocation.
    var withTax = orders.Add(taxEntry);
    var shipped = withTax.Add(shipEntry);
    // ^ O(n) per operation, so this loop is quadratic:
    var accumulated = ImmutableList<Order>.Empty;
    foreach (var o in orders) accumulated = accumulated.Add(o);
    //   which is why AddRange exists and why a builder exists.

    // WHICH IS WHY IT WINS FOR BUILD-ONCE, READ-MANY, and loses
    // otherwise:
    var lookup = ImmutableDictionary<string, byte[]>
        .Empty
        .AddRange(from row in schema select
            KeyValuePair.Create(row.Name, LoadIcon(row)));

    // A lookup table, a configuration snapshot, a parsed grammar, a
    // set of permitted values: built once, read many times, shared
    // across threads with no lock.
}

{{-- AND THE VERSION PEOPLE ACTUALLY WANT IS USUALLY NOT THIS: --}}
static void NotThis()
{
    // THE MOST COMMON REASON to reach for immutability is thread
    // safety, and the answer is usually a plain collection plus a
    // convention:
    private static readonly string[] AllowedCountries =
        ["GB", "IE", "FR", "DE"];
    // ^ an array IS immutable by convention: nothing exposes it for
    //   writing, so a copy is made per access and the field cannot be
    //   changed. Cheaper than an immutable collection, and the
    //   convention is enforceable by not making the field mutable.
}

5.6 ArrayPool and renting buffers

ArrayPool<T> rents arrays from a per-core pool instead of allocating them. Rented arrays are not cleared, and you must return them. In practice the return is the hard part, which is why using declarations exist.

Renting a buffer from a pool means reusing arrays rather than allocating and letting the collector find them. The saving is real and it has two preconditions that are easy to violate: the buffer must be returned, and it must not still be referenced when it is returned. Both are structural rather than a matter of care.

Why the second precondition is the dangerous one

A pooled array handed out again while something still holds a reference to it produces two unrelated parts of a program writing to the same bytes. There is no exception and no diagnostic — the failure appears as data that changes between reads, usually in a test that passed yesterday. The discipline that prevents it is to clear the array on return and to return it in a finally, and to never let a reference to a pooled buffer escape the scope that owns it.

When it is worth it

Large buffers on a hot path — a megabyte or more, allocated and discarded repeatedly. Below that, the allocation is a pointer bump and the collector handles it in a gen-0 collection measured in microseconds, so a pool is a measurable win only when the buffers are large or the rate is very high.

var pool = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared;

byte[] buffer = pool.Rent(4096);      // may return 4096 or larger
try
{
    // ... write to buffer[0..actualLength] ...
}
finally
{
    pool.Return(buffer);          // ALWAYS return it
}

// C# 8 using-declaration: the finally is generated for you
using (byte[] scratch = pool.Rent(1024))
{
    // scratch is returned even if an exception escapes
}

// ClearArray option: the pool zeroes it on return, at a cost
pool.Return(buffer, clearArray: true);

// Renting beyond the pool maximum allocates a fresh array instead
// MemoryPool<T> and ArrayPool<T>.Shared. Rent are the two entry points

// Spans over pooled arrays: the modern way
var owner = new ArrayPool<byte>.Shared;
byte[] data = owner.Rent(1024);
try
{
    int read = System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("payload", data);
    return data.AsSpan(0, read);
}
finally { owner.Return(data); }   // span is dead by now

A using declaration disposes at the end of the enclosing scope, which is what you want. Be careful with it in a loop body — the dispose happens at the end of the block, so a scope smaller than the loop body is required if you want the buffer returned each iteration.

An unreturned rented array is not a memory leak you will notice immediately — the pool simply allocates a new one next time. It is a slow, invisible loss of throughput. The try/finally or using form is not optional.


{{-- TWO PRECONDITIONS, and both are structural rather than a
     matter of care. --}}
static void Renting()
{
    byte[] buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(4096);
    try
    {
        int read = socket.Receive(buffer, SocketFlags.None);
        Process(buffer.AsSpan(0, read));
    }
    finally
    {
        // RETURN IT IN A FINALLY, so an exception does not lose it:
        ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer);
    }
}

{{-- AND THE SECOND PRECONDITION, which is the dangerous one: --}}
static void TheAliasingBug()
{
    byte[] a = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64);
    byte[] b = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64);
    // a and b may be THE SAME ARRAY. The pool is free to hand out
    // the same buffer twice, and it does exactly that under load.

    ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(a);
    byte[] c = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64);
    // c MAY BE 'a'. If anything still holds a reference to a, two
    // unrelated parts of the program are now writing to the same
    // bytes. No exception, no diagnostic — the symptom is data that
    // changes between reads, usually in a test that passed
    // yesterday.
}

{{-- THE TWO DISCIPLINES THAT PREVENT IT: --}}
static void Disciplines(byte[] buffer)
{
    try
    {
        Process(buffer);
    }
    finally
    {
        // 1. RETURN IN A FINALLY, so an exception does not lose it.
        // 2. CLEAR ON RETURN, so the next renter cannot read
        //    yesterday's bytes.
        ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer, clearArray: true);
        // ^ clearArray costs a memset and removes a whole class of
        //   information leak: a pooled buffer that still holds a
        //   previous request's data.
    }
}

{{-- AND NEVER LET A REFERENCE ESCAPE THE OWNING SCOPE: --}}
// WRONG
private byte[] _buffer;
public byte[] Buffer => ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(4096);
// ^ a field or a property can outlive the return, so the buffer can
//   be returned while a caller still holds it.

// RIGHT: pass the buffer down, and return it at the end.
public void ProcessRequest(Socket socket)
{
    byte[] buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(4096);
    try
    {
        int read = socket.Receive(buffer, SocketFlags.None);
        Process(buffer.AsSpan(0, read));    // a SPAN, which cannot
                                             // be stored or returned
    }
    finally
    {
        ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer, clearArray: true);
    }
}

{{-- AND WHEN IT IS WORTH IT: LARGE buffers (a megabyte or more)
     on a hot path. Below that the allocation is a pointer bump and a
     gen-0 collection measured in microseconds, so a pool is a
     measurable win only when the buffers are large or the rate is
     very high. --}}

5.7 Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T>

A Span<T> is a view over contiguous memory plus a length. Creating one from an array, a string or stackalloc costs nothing. Slicing is a pointer offset. Writing through a span writes to the original buffer. This is how you get zero-allocation parsing and transformation code.

A span is a view over contiguous memory: a reference, an offset and a length. It exists so that a slice of an array can be passed to something without allocating a new array for the slice, and it is the mechanism that makes the parsing and formatting code in the standard library allocation-free.

What a span forbids, and why the restriction is the feature

A span cannot be a field, cannot be returned from a method, and cannot cross an iterator boundary — and the compiler enforces all three. That is not a limitation; it is the property that makes it safe. A view's lifetime is bounded by the memory it points into, and a type that could outlive that memory would be a use-after-free waiting to be found.

Stack-only, and the escape analysis that makes it work

A span typically points at the stack, because a local array's storage is not something the collector tracks. That is what makes slicing free and what makes the lifetime restrictions necessary. A span pointing at a heap array is equally safe and slightly slower to pass, because the compiler has to keep the array alive.

// Creating a span
Span<int> fromArray = stackalloc int[4];       // on the stack, no GC
Span<int> fromSlice = new int[10].AsSpan();
ReadOnlySpan<char> fromString = "hello".AsSpan();
ReadOnlySpan<byte> fromMemory = memory.Span;

// Slicing -- free, and the result views the SAME memory
Span<int> middle = fromArray.Slice(1, 2);
middle[0] = 42;                    // writes back into fromArray

// C# 8 range and index on spans
Span<int> last = fromArray[^1..];        // final element
int final = fromArray[^1];              // Index from the end

// Copying between buffers
source.CopyTo(destination);                    // same length required
source[..4].CopyTo(destination);              // slice first
destination[..source.Length].CopyFrom(source); // reverse direction form

// Clear and fill: a fast memset
destination.Clear();
destination.Fill(0);
destination[1..5].Fill(7);

// Ref structs cannot be: fields, boxed, in async methods, in lambdas,
// in iterators, or captured by a closure. By design.

The common shape for a hot method is: ReadOnlySpan<T> in, parse or transform, Span<T> out. Because spans are stack-only, the method must be synchronous — which is why high-performance parsers in .NET are all synchronous and the async part is only at the I/O boundary.

Write the API with spans and add a convenience overload without them. void Process(ReadOnlySpan<byte>) plus void Process(byte[]) that forwards via AsSpan() gives callers ergonomics and you zero allocations.


{{-- A SPAN IS A VIEW over contiguous memory: a reference, an offset
     and a length. A SLICE OF AN ARRAY passed without allocating a
     new array for the slice. --}}
static void Slicing(int[] data)
{
    Span<int> whole = data;
    Span<int> first = data.AsSpan(0, 10);     // no allocation
    Span<int> rest  = data.AsSpan(10);

    ReadOnlySpan<int> view = whole;            // the read-only form,
                                              // which is what an API
                                              // that does not mutate
                                              // should take
    static int Sum(ReadOnlySpan<int> xs)
    {
        int total = 0;
        foreach (int x in xs) total += x;
        return total;                          // NO try/finally: a
                                                // span is not
                                                // disposable, so
                                                // foreach over one
                                                // has no
                                                // enumerator to
                                                // dispose
    }
}

{{-- WHAT A SPAN FORBIDS, and the restriction IS THE FEATURE: --}}
class Field
{
    // private Span<int> _data;    ERROR: CS8345. A field outlives
    //   the method that created the span, and the memory it points
    //   into does not.
}
static ReadOnlySpan<int> Returning() => null;
static ReadOnlySpan<int> Bad()
{
    // return new byte[10];       ERROR: a span cannot point at
    //   something the collector is free to move.
    return default;
}
static IEnumerable<int> Iter()
{
    // yield return _span;        ERROR: an iterator's state
    //   machine outlives the span.
    yield break;
}

{{-- STACK-ONLY, and the escape analysis that makes it work: --}}
static unsafe void StackSpans(int n)
{
    // A SPAN TYPICALLY POINTS AT THE STACK, because a local array's
    // storage is not something the collector tracks.
    Span<int> local = stackalloc int[n];       // NO heap allocation
    local[0] = 1;

    // Which is what makes slicing free AND what makes the lifetime
    // restrictions necessary. A span pointing at a heap array is
    // equally safe and slightly slower to pass, because the
    // compiler must keep the array alive.
    Span<int> heap = new int[n];               // the array is
                                               // tracked; the
                                               // span is a view over
                                               // it
}

{{-- AND THE MEMORY OPERATIONS THAT TAKE SPANS, which is where the
     whole design pays: --}}
static void MemoryOps(ReadOnlySpan<byte> source)
{
    Span<byte> dest = stackalloc byte[256];

    int copied = source.CopyTo(dest);           // no allocation
    source.CopyTo(dest[..copied]);              // ^ the RANGE form:
                                                 //   no cast, no
                                                 //   allocation, and
                                                 //   the bounds are
                                                 //   checked

    bool eq = source.SequenceEqual(dest);       // a span comparison
    int at = source.IndexOf((byte)'=');          // a span search
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> field = source[..at];    // a span field value

    // EVERY ONE OF THESE WOULD ALLOCATE with the array or string
    // equivalents, and they are the reason the framework's parsing
    // and formatting code is allocation-free.
}

5.8 stackalloc, slices and ranges

stackalloc allocates from the stack instead of the heap, which is faster and immediately reclaimed on scope exit. It is only valid in a Span<T> initialiser and it is bounded by the stack size, so it suits small fixed buffers, not variable-length data.

Stack allocation puts a buffer in the current frame's storage rather than on the heap, and the runtime does not have to track it, so there is no allocation and nothing for the collector to find. The cost is that the size has to be known at the point of allocation and that the buffer dies when the method returns — which is why it is only ever exposed to the caller as a span, never as a reference.

The size has to be known, or bounded

A stack buffer of unbounded size is a stack overflow, and the runtime cannot prevent it. A length taken from a network packet is therefore the one thing that must never reach a stack allocation directly, because the whole point of the optimisation is that the buffer is not a heap allocation whose size the runtime can validate.

Slices and ranges

The range operators take a span and produce a span, and both allocate nothing. The two restrictions to know are that a range index must be of the same type as the span's index — which is why Range and Index use int rather than nint — and that the result is a view rather than a copy, so a slice of a slice shares the original memory.

// Small fixed buffer: the canonical use
static bool TryParseHex(in ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out int value)
{
    if (text.Length is > 8 or < 1) { value = 0; return false; }

    Span<byte> raw = stackalloc byte[8];
    return int.TryParse(text, System.Globalization.NumberStyles.HexNumber, null, out value);
}

// The span range operator covers slicing elegantly
ReadOnlySpan<char> csv = "a,b,,c,d".AsSpan();
int start = 0;
foreach (var part in SplitOn(csv, ','))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"[{part}]");          // [a] [b] [] [c] [d]
}

static IEnumerable<ReadOnlySpan<char>> SplitOn(in ReadOnlySpan<char> src, char sep)
{
    int start = 0;
    while (true)
    {
        int i = src[start..].IndexOf(sep);
        if (i < 0) { yield return src[start..]; break; }
        yield return src.Slice(start, i);
        start += i + 1;
    }
}

// memory + span: renting from MemoryPool and slicing in one line
using IMemoryOwner<byte> owner = new MemoryPool<byte>().Rent(256);
Span<byte> span = owner.Memory.Span[..256];

Note the pattern Span<byte> raw = stackalloc byte[8]; followed by not using raw in the example above — the point is the declaration form. stackalloc is not a general-purpose allocator; a stackalloc of 1 MB overflows the stack and crashes the process with no exception you can catch.

Exercises 5

  1. Write a program that takes a comma-separated line and parses it into an int[] using spans only, with no intermediate string allocations. Verify with a memory profiler.
  2. Convert a loop that does list.Add to one that pre-sizes the capacity, and time both versions for 100,000 items.
  3. Build a HashSet<int> and show the speedup over a List<int> Contains check for 50,000 duplicate-detection lookups.
  4. Show that a rented array from ArrayPool is returned, using a using declaration, and then deliberately skip the return to observe the pool allocate again.
  5. Write a span-based CSV line splitter that handles quoted fields, and compare its allocation count to a string.Split implementation.
  6. Implement a small Dijkstra shortest-path routine using PriorityQueue and confirm the ordering of visited nodes.

{{-- STACK ALLOCATION puts a buffer in the FRAME, so the collector
     has nothing to track: no allocation, nothing to find later. --}}
static int SumSmall(ReadOnlySpan<int> values)
{
    Span<int> scratch = stackalloc int[16];
    scratch.Clear();                       // CLEARED: stack memory is
                                           // whatever was there
                                           // before, so an
                                           // unwritten element is
                                           // not zero
    int total = 0;
    foreach (int v in values) total += v;
    return total;
}

{{-- AND THE SIZE HAS TO BE KNOWN, because the runtime cannot check
     it — which is the one thing that must never reach it. --}}
static unsafe int FromUntrustedLength(byte[] data, int claimedLength)
{
    // WRONG: claimedLength came from a packet. A large value is a
    // STACK OVERFLOW, and there is no allocation for the runtime to
    // reject.
    // Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[claimedLength];
    return 0;
}

static int Bounded(byte[] data, int claimedLength)
{
    const int MaxBuffer = 64 * 1024;

    byte[] rented = null;
    Span<byte> buffer = claimedLength <= MaxBuffer
        ? stackalloc byte[MaxBuffer]
        : (rented = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(MaxBuffer));

    try
    {
        return data.AsSpan(0, Math.Min(data.Length, claimedLength))
                   .CopyTo(buffer);
    }
    finally
    {
        if (rented is not null) ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(rented);
    }
    // ^ THE RULE: a stack buffer's size is a CONSTANT or a value
    //   already bounded by something above. Never a length from the
    //   wire, unvalidated.
}

{{-- SLICES AND RANGES, and both allocate nothing: --}}
static void SlicesAndRanges(byte[] data)
{
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> whole = data;
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> head  = whole[..4];      // no allocation
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> tail  = whole[4..];

    var last = whole[^1];                       // ^ the index-from-end
                                               //   operator
    var pair = whole[^2..];                    // the last two

    // THE TWO RESTRICTIONS worth knowing:
    //   1. The range index type must match the span's index type.
    //      That is why Range and Index use int rather than nint:
    //      a nint index would make a slice of a Span<byte>
    //      require a runtime check on the length.
    //   2. THE RESULT IS A VIEW, not a copy: a slice of a slice
    //      SHARES the original memory.
    var a = whole[1..5];
    var b = a[1..3];
    b[0] = 99;
    // whole[2] is 99: two views, one memory.
}

{{-- WHICH IS WHY SPAN SLICING IS THE PATTERN BEHIND THE
     FRAMEWORK'S ALLOCATION-FREE PARSING: --}}
static bool TryReadFrame(ReadOnlySpan<byte> input, out int length)
{
    if (input.Length < 4) { length = 0; return false; }

    // FOUR BYTES, NO ALLOCATION: a BinaryPrimitives call on a span
    // rather than a BitConverter call on a byte[] plus an array
    // copy.
    length = System.Buffers.Binary.BinaryPrimitives.ReadInt32BigEndian(
        input[..4]);

    return input.Length >= 4 + length;
}

6 · Classes, Structs, Records & OOP

6.1 Class vs struct6.2 Constructors and object initialisers6.3 Properties vs fields6.4 init-only and required members6.5 records and positional records6.6 Inheritance: virtual, override, new, sealed6.7 Interfaces and default members6.8 Static members and extension methods6.9 IDisposable and using

Chapter six covers how you model data and behaviour. The choice between class, struct and record is the most consequential design decision in C#, and it is mostly about mutability and identity. Then come constructors, properties, the modern initialisation features, the inheritance keywords that trip everyone up, and deterministic resource cleanup.

6.1 Class vs struct

A class is a reference type you can subclass, a struct is a value type you cannot. Structs avoid a heap allocation and are copied on assignment, which is exactly why they should be small, immutable and blittable. A large mutable struct in a hot loop is one of the worst performance mistakes available in the language.

The choice between a class and a structure is not primarily one of performance. It decides whether assignment copies, whether a variable can be null, whether it can be used as a dictionary key, and whether a method on it can be an interface implementation. Four semantics, one decision, and the performance difference is a consequence rather than the point.

The rules that follow, and they are not negotiable

A structure cannot be null, so an "absent" structure needs a wrapper. A structure cannot be a base class, so it cannot be inherited. A structure cannot be used as a type argument unless it fully supports it, which excludes fields that are reference types in older versions. And a structure's default value is a valid value, so a field of structure type is initialised to all zeroes rather than to null — which means a default structure is often a valid but wrong structure rather than an absent one.

Where the performance difference actually is

Copying is the visible cost, and it scales with the number of fields. A structure of three small fields passed in a loop is cheap and often faster than a reference, because there is no allocation and the data is in a register. A structure containing a reference field is copied on every assignment while sharing what it references, which is the worst of both: the copy cost without the value-type benefit.

// STRUCT: value semantics, no inheritance, no null (without Nullable<T>)
public readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);

// CLASS: reference semantics, inheritance, events, identity
public class Account
{
    public required string Id { get; init; }
    public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
    public event Action<Account, decimal>? Changed;

    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount <= 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(amount));
        Balance += amount;
        Changed?.Invoke(this, amount);
    }
}

// A struct CAN implement an interface, and interfaces are how you
// abstract over both kinds:
public interface IMoney { decimal Amount { get; } }

// Rule of thumb
//   struct: small (ideally <= 16 bytes), immutable, no identity, value-like
//   class : everything else, especially anything with behaviour or events

A readonly struct or a readonly record struct gets a compiler-generated Equals, GetHashCode, ToString and deconstruction, all of which a plain struct inherits a slow reflection-based version of from ValueType.

Every method on a non-readonly struct has an implicit defensive copy of this when it could modify fields, and the compiler only warns with a specific syntax. Mark your value types readonly unless you genuinely need a parameterless constructor with settable fields.


{{-- FOUR SEMANTICS, one decision, and performance is a CONSEQUENCE
     rather than the point: --}}
struct Money
{
    public long Amount;      {{-- copies on assignment --}}
    public string Currency;  {{-- and this is SHARED, so a "value
                                   type" whose field is a reference
                                   type is the worst of both: the
                                   copy cost without the
                                   value-type benefit --}}
}
class Order
{
    public long Id;          {{-- shares on assignment --}}
    public Order? Previous;  {{-- nullable --}}
}

static void Semantics()
{
    // 1. ASSIGNMENT COPIES FOR A STRUCTURE.
    var a = new Money { Amount = 100 };
    var b = a;
    b.Amount = 200;
    // a.Amount is 100

    // 2. ASSIGNMENT SHARES FOR A CLASS.
    var c = new Order { Id = 1 };
    var d = c;
    d.Id = 2;
    // c.Id is 2

    // 3. A STRUCTURE CANNOT BE NULL.
    // Money m = null;          ERROR: a structure has no null state.
    //   "Absent" needs a WRAPPER: Nullable<Money>, or a nullable
    //   field, or a class.
    Money? maybe = null;      // Nullable<T>, which is the wrapper

    // 4. AND A STRUCTURE'S DEFAULT IS A VALID VALUE, not an absent
    //    one — which is the trap in this whole area:
    struct Line
    {
        public int Quantity;
        public decimal Price;
        public string? Description;
    }
    Line blank = default;      // Quantity 0, Price 0, Description null
    // ^ VALID AND WRONG, not absent. A collection of default
    //   Lines is a collection of zero-quantity rows, and nothing
    //   distinguishes them from lines somebody added and forgot to
    //   fill in. A CLASS gives you null, which IS distinguishable.
}

{{-- AND THE PERFORMANCE CONSEQUENCE, which is a consequence: --}}
struct PointSmall { public int X, Y; }        {{-- 8 bytes: cheap to
                                                    copy, fits in a
                                                    register, and
                                                    FASTER THAN A
                                                    CLASS in a loop
                                                    because there is
                                                    no allocation --}}
class PointBig { public int X, Y; }

static double DistanceSmall(PointSmall a, PointSmall b) { /* ... */ }
static double DistanceBig(PointBig a, PointBig b) { /* ... */ }

{{-- WHERE THE SIZE DECISION GOES WRONG: --}}
struct Big { public Guid Id; public DateTimeOffset At; public string? Note; }
// 40+ bytes: copied on every assignment, every argument, every
// return. A class is ONE pointer for the same data.
{{-- ^ the threshold is not a number, it is: does the structure
     stay small enough to stay in a register, and does it contain
     only value-typed fields? --}}

6.2 Constructors and object initialisers

A constructor initialises a new instance. There is always at least one: if you write none, the compiler supplies a parameterless one. Constructors chain with the : initialiser syntax, run base constructors first, and the primary-constructor form (C# 12) collapses the boilerplate further.

Constructors come in three forms and each says something different. A primary constructor takes the initial values as parameters and is the only form that participates in the initialiser syntax. An ordinary constructor is a named overload. And a copy constructor and a static factory cover the cases a primary constructor cannot express.

Initialiser syntax, and what it can reach

An object initialiser runs after the constructor, so it can set properties and fields but not anything the constructor computed. That produces a specific defect: a constructor validating its arguments, followed by an initialiser setting a property that invalidates the validation — and the object ends up in a state the constructor would have refused.

Validation belongs in one place

The pattern that avoids it is to make the property's setter the validating one, or to make the constructor take everything and the initialiser add only what the constructor did not already constrain. What does not work is validating in the constructor and trusting that every subsequent property set is safe, because nothing enforces that.

public sealed class Person
{
    public string Name { get; }
    public int Age { get; }

    // Parameterless constructor
    public Person() { Name = "unknown"; Age = 0; }

    // Chained to the parameterless one
    public Person(string name) : this() { Name = name; }

    // The full one
    public Person(string name, int age)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)) throw new ArgumentException(nameof(name));
        if (age < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(age));
        Name = name;
        Age = age;
    }

    // Copy constructor (rare, but needed for mutating APIs)
    public Person(Person other) { Name = other.Name; Age = other.Age; }
}

// Object initialiser sets properties after the constructor returns
var p = new Person("Ada") { Age = 36 };

// Collection initialisers
var list = new List<string> { "a", "b" };
var dict = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["x"] = 1 };

// C# 12 primary constructor: parameters are in scope for the whole type
public sealed class Order(string customerId, int quantity)
{
    public string CustomerId { get; } = customerId;
    public int Quantity { get; } = quantity;
    public decimal Total => Quantity * 9.99m;
}

Initialisers run after the constructor, so they can write to properties the constructor deliberately left open. They cannot reach private setters from outside, which is exactly the encapsulation you want.

A primary constructor does not create a public CustomerId { get; } property automatically. You must declare one, and you should think about whether the captured parameter should be exposed or copied into a field. Primary constructors on types that need real validation still want a body with class Order { public Order(...) { ... } }.


{{-- THREE FORMS, each saying something different: --}}
public sealed class Order
{
    // A PRIMARY CONSTRUCTOR: takes the initial values as
    // parameters, and is the only form that participates in the
    // initialiser syntax.
    public Order(string reference, Customer customer)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(reference))
            throw new ArgumentException("A reference is required.", nameof(reference));

        Reference = reference;
        Customer  = customer ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(customer));
    }

    public string    Reference { get; }
    public Customer   Customer  { get; }
    public OrderStatus Status   { get; private set; } = OrderStatus.Pending;

    // AN ORDINARY CONSTRUCTOR: a named overload, for the shapes a
    // primary constructor does not cover.
    public Order(string reference, Customer customer, DateTimeOffset placedAt)
        : this(reference, customer)
    {
        if (placedAt > DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(placedAt));
        PlacedAt = placedAt;
    }

    public DateTimeOffset PlacedAt { get; init; } = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;

    // A STATIC FACTORY: for a constructor that cannot be a
    // constructor, because it needs to return something else or
    // take a name that would be a bad parameter name.
    public static Order PendingFor(Customer customer, string reference)
    {
        // ...a validation that spans two fields ...
        if (customer is { IsBlocked: true })
            throw new InvalidOperationException("Blocked customers cannot order.");

        return new Order(reference, customer);
    }
}

{{-- AND THE INITIALISER, which runs AFTER the constructor — which is
     where a specific defect lives: --}}
var good = new Order("ORD-1", customer);
var bad  = new Order("ORD-1", customer) { Status = OrderStatus.Paid };
{{-- ^ the constructor could not have produced this, because a
     pending order cannot be created as paid. The initialiser runs
     after, so the invariant the constructor enforced is gone, and
     nothing complains. --}}

{{-- SO VALIDATION BELONGS IN ONE PLACE, and there are two versions: --}}
public sealed class Account
{
    private decimal _balance;

    public Account(decimal opening)
    {
        // (1) VALIDATE THE PROPERTY'S SETTER, so every path
        //     through the object is checked — constructor,
        //     initialiser, method, later assignment.
        ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative(opening);
        _balance = opening;
    }

    public decimal Balance
    {
        get => _balance;
        private set
        {
            // ^ ONE PLACE. An initialiser cannot bypass a private
            //   setter it cannot reach, and an internal method that
            //   sets it goes through the same check.
            ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative(value);
            _balance = value;
        }
    }
}

{{-- (2) OR MAKE THE CONSTRUCTOR TAKE EVERYTHING, so there is
     nothing left for an initialiser to add that the constructor
     did not already constrain. --}}
public sealed class Money(decimal amount, string currency)
{
    public decimal Amount { get; } = Guard.NotNegative(amount);
    public string  Currency { get; } = Guard.NotBlank(currency);
}
// var m = new Money(-1, "GBP");   Guard throws at the initialiser,
//                                  which is as early as possible
{{-- ^ the second version is the one to prefer for a type whose
     invariants matter, because it leaves no setter for anything to
     go wrong through. --}}

6.3 Properties vs fields

A field is raw storage. A property is a pair of methods named get_ and set_ that the compiler generates from an accessor pair. Use a property for anything public, because it lets you add validation, change representation or raise a change notification later without breaking callers.

A property is a pair of accessor methods with the appearance of a field. It exists so that a value can be validated on the way in or computed on the way out, and it costs more than a field: a non-virtual property is usually inlined by the optimiser, but an expression-bodied property that does real work may not be, and a property that is also an interface implementation cannot be inlined at all.

Auto-properties, and what the compiler generates

An auto-property generates a private backing field and two trivial accessors, which after optimisation is the same as a field. A property with an initialiser generates the same plus a constructor assignment. What it does not generate is a backing field you can reach from outside — which is the point, and which is also why a property that must be set from a serialiser needs an init accessor or a constructor.

Where a property is the wrong tool

A hot-path value read millions of times should be a field if it is never computed, because a property that is never inlined is a call. And a property whose getter has a side effect is a design problem rather than a performance one: Count that increments a counter is a field with a trap in it, and the trap is that writing to it no longer looks like a mutation.

public sealed class Temperature
{
    private double _celsius;                        // backing field, private

    // Full property with backing field
    public double Celsius
    {
        get => _celsius;
        set => _celsius = value;
    }

    // Expression-bodied: a get-only computed property
    public double Fahrenheit => (_celsius * 9 / 5) + 32;

    // Set-only is legal but rare (builders, fluent configuration)
    public string Label
    {
        set => _label = value.ToUpperInvariant();
    }

    // Static and const
    public const int MaxScale = 1000;       // baked into every caller
    public static int InstanceCount;             // one copy for all

    // Nullable value type property: back it with a private nullable field
    private int? _rank;
