    public int Rank { get => _rank ?? 0; set => _rank = value; }

    // C# 13 field keyword: no backing field boilerplate
    public int Retries
    {
        get;
        set => field = value < 0 ? 0 : value;
    }

    // C# 14 partial properties: implement across multiple files
    public partial string Description { get; set; }
}

The field keyword (C# 14) is the biggest quality-of-life addition to this area: a property with a custom setter no longer needs a hand-written backing field, which removes the single most common source of copy-paste bugs in property-heavy code.

Name backing fields _camelCase and properties PascalCase. The compiler will not enforce it, but .editorconfig with the naming rules will, and it costs nothing to turn on.


{{-- A PROPERTY IS A PAIR OF ACCESSORS with the appearance of a
     field. The cost: a NON-VIRTUAL property is usually inlined, but
     one that does real work may not be, and one that implements an
     interface NEVER is. --}}
public sealed class Rectangle
{
    // AN AUTO-PROPERTY: the compiler generates a private backing
    // field and two trivial accessors, which after optimisation is
    // the same as a field.
    public int Width  { get; init; }
    public int Height { get; init; }

    // AN EXPRESSION-BODIED PROPERTY that COMPUTES: this is a
    // candidate for a field if the computation is not trivial,
    // because a property that is never inlined is a CALL.
    public int Area => Width * Height;          // inlined: two fields
                                               // and a multiply

    // THIS ONE IS NOT INLINED, because the getter has a branch and
    // a comparison, and it is read a million times in a loop.
    public double Discounted
    {
        get
        {
            if (Width > 1000) return Price * 0.9;
            return Price;
        }
        private set => Price = value;
    }

    public decimal Price { get; private set; }

    // AN INTERFACE-IMPLEMENTING PROPERTY is a virtual call and
    // cannot be inlined at all:
    public int Length => Width;                // implements
                                               // ICollection<T>
                                               // elsewhere: every
                                               // access is virtual
}

{{-- WHERE IT IS THE WRONG TOOL, which is the hot path: --}}
public sealed class Counter
{
    // A FIELD, because it is read a million times and never
    // computed. A property here would be a call per read unless the
    // optimiser inlines it, and whether it does depends on the
    // complexity of the body — which is not a property a reader can
    // check.
    private long _count;
    public long Count => _count;               // trivial: inlined

    public void Increment() => _count++;
}

{{-- THE DESIGN PROBLEM RATHER THAN THE PERFORMANCE ONE: --}}
public sealed class Temperature
{
    private int _celsius;
    // A GETTER WITH A SIDE EFFECT is a design problem: reading a
    // property looks like it cannot change anything, so a line
    // that increments a counter in the getter is invisible to
    // everyone who reads the code.
    public int Celsius
    {
        get { _reads++; return _celsius; }     // WRONG
        private set => _celsius = value;
    }
    private int _reads;
}
{{-- ^ and the consequence is that the write looks harmless while
     the read mutates: 'if (t.Celsius > 30)' now has a side
     effect, and nobody reading it can see that. --}}

6.4 init-only and required members

The init accessor allows assignment only during construction, so an object can be immutable after initialisation while still supporting object initialisers. The required modifier (C# 11) makes the compiler refuse to construct the type until the member is set. Together they give you near-immutable domain types without a builder class.

An init-only property can be assigned in a constructor, an object initialiser, or nowhere else — and nowhere else is enforced by the compiler rather than by convention. That is what makes a type with init-only properties genuinely immutable after construction, and it is the mechanism that lets a record be compared by value while still being a class.

Where init differs from readonly, and why it matters

A readonly field is assigned in the constructor and then frozen. An init-only property is assigned in the constructor or in an object initialiser, and then frozen. The difference sounds small and is the difference between a type that can only be built by its own constructor and one whose required values can be supplied from outside after construction.

Required members, and the trade

A required member must be supplied at construction and the compiler enforces it, so an object cannot exist in a half-initialised state. The cost is that the type needs a SetsRequiredMembers attribute to be deserialised by a source generator that cannot see the initialisation, and that a required member plus an init-only property is a pair of mechanisms doing the same job.

public sealed class Order
{
    public required string CustomerId { get; init; }   // must be set at construction
    public string Reference { get; init; } = "";  // optional
    public int Quantity { get; set; } = 1;          // genuinely mutable

    // required + init: a genuinely immutable, fully-initialised object
    public required DateTimeOffset PlacedAt { get; init; }
}

// The compiler enforces required members at every construction site
var good = new Order { CustomerId = "C-1", PlacedAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow };
// var bad = new Order { CustomerId = "C-1" };   // CS9035: PlacedAt required
// order.CustomerId = "C-2";                  // CS8852: init-only

// [SetsRequiredMembers] tells the compiler a method fills them in
[SetsRequiredMembers]
public static Order Draft(string customerId) =>
    new Order { CustomerId = customerId, PlacedAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow };

// Compiler recognises and audits the recognised patterns
//   - a constructor that assigns every required member
//   - an object initialiser that sets them
//   - a [SetsRequiredMembers] method or constructor

Beware the "required member escape hatches": a derived type’s constructor, a generic constraint of new(), reflection and deserialisers can all leave a required member uninitialised. If that matters, validate in a real constructor as well.

required is a compile-time obligation, not a runtime guarantee. Reflection-based deserialisers such as older System.Text.Json configurations will happily leave it null. Validate at the boundary where untrusted data enters.


{{-- INIT-ONLY can be assigned in a constructor, an object
     initialiser, or NOWHERE ELSE — and nowhere else is ENFORCED by
     the compiler rather than by convention. --}}
public sealed class Order
{
    // A REQUIRED PROPERTY: must be supplied at construction, and the
    // compiler enforces it, so an object cannot exist
    // half-initialised.
    public required string Reference { get; init; }
    public required Customer Customer  { get; init; }

    // AN INIT-ONLY property: assigned in a constructor or an
    // initialiser, then frozen.
    public OrderStatus Status { get; init; } = OrderStatus.Pending;
    public decimal       Total  { get; init; }

    // A SETTABLE property, because one field genuinely changes.
    public DateTimeOffset? PaidAt { get; private set; }

    public void MarkPaid()
    {
        Status = OrderStatus.Paid;
        PaidAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
        // ^ assignment to a private SETTER, which is not the same
        //   as assignment to an init-only property: init-only means
        //   "only during construction", not "only this class".
    }
}

static void Using()
{
    var order = new Order
    {
        Reference = "ORD-1",     {{-- required: the compiler refuses
                                         an object without it --}}
        Customer  = customer,
        Status    = OrderStatus.Paid,   {{-- init-only: allowed HERE,
                                             in the initialiser --}}
        // Status = ... after the object exists: ERROR
    };

    // new Order { Customer = c }          CS9035: required property
    //                                     'Reference' is missing
}

{{-- AND WHERE INIT DIFFERS FROM readonly, which sounds small and is
     the difference between a type only ITS constructor can build and
     one whose values can be supplied from outside: --}}
public sealed class Config
{
    public readonly string Name;     {{-- only in THIS constructor:
                                          a caller cannot supply
                                          another value --}}
    public string Name2 { get; init; }  {{-- in the constructor OR in
                                             an initialiser, so a
                                             caller CAN --}}
}

{{-- THE TRADE, and it is the one to know before reaching for
     required: a source generator that cannot see the initialisation
     needs the attribute. --}}
[SetsRequiredMembers]      {{-- DESERIALISERS AND SOURCE GENERATORS:
                                  they construct the object without
                                  running an initialiser, so the
                                  compiler cannot prove the required
                                  members are set --}}
public sealed class Payload
{
    public required string Name  { get; init; }
    public required int    Count { get; init; }
}
var payload = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Payload>(json)!;
{{-- ^ without the attribute, the DESERIALISER bypasses the
     requirement and the object exists with a null Name — so the
     compiler's guarantee holds for hand-written construction and
     not for machine-written, which is exactly where the null ends
     up. --}}

6.5 records and positional records

A record is a class (or struct) whose defining characteristic is value-based equality plus a compiler-generated ToString and deconstruction. You get Equals, GetHashCode, ==, !=, GetHashCode, deconstruction and a readable ToString without writing any of them.

A record is a class or a structure the compiler generates: value equality, a ToString that prints every property, a copy-with-one-change-differently with expression, and deconstruction. What it is not is a shorthand for a class with properties — it is a class whose equality is generated, and that changes what it can be used for.

Value equality, and what it costs

The generated equality compares every field, so it is correct by construction for a type whose identity is its data, and wrong for one whose identity is something else — an entity whose database identifier makes two loaded copies the same thing. A record used as an entity model compares two references to the same row as equal, which is usually harmless, and compares two rows with the same contents as equal, which is usually what nobody intended.

Positional records, and the properties they give up

The positional form declares properties, so they exist and are usable. What it does not give you is the ability to replace one, which is why the copy-with method exists. A positional record's property is init-only in the sense that it can be set in the initialiser and not afterwards, so a caller that needs a variant builds it with with.

// Positional record: the whole thing in one line
public record Point(int X, int Y);

// The compiler generates: a constructor, init-only properties,
// Equals, GetHashCode, ==, !=, ToString, PrintMembers and Deconstruct

var a = new Point(1, 2);
var b = new Point(1, 2);

Console.WriteLine(a == b);              // True  -- value equality
Console.WriteLine(a);                    // Point { X = 1, Y = 2 }
(int x, int y) = a;             // deconstruction

// with-expressions: non-destructive copy with overrides
var moved = a with { X = 10 };          // Point { X = 10, Y = 2 }
Console.WriteLine(a.X);                  // 1 -- a untouched

// Reference type record with mutable members and validation
public sealed record Customer
{
    public required string Name { get; init; }
    public string Email { get; set; } = "";

    // records can be inherited, and a derived record is still a record
    // public record PremiumCustomer : Customer;

    // Value-based GetHashCode makes these safe as dictionary keys
    var index = new Dictionary<Point, string> { [a] = "origin" };
    Console.WriteLine(index[b]);        // origin
}

// record struct: same semantics, value copy semantics
public readonly record struct Meters(double Value);

Records use value equality, which means a record with a List<T> member compares by reference for that member, because List.Equals is reference equality. If you need deep equality, override Equals in that member’s type too.

Do not put a record in a hot dictionary path and then mutate it. Its GetHashCode changes when a property changes, so the object becomes unreachable in the dictionary — a Dictionary or HashSet that appears to lose entries. Use a readonly record, or key the dictionary on something immutable.

Records are the best answer to "I just need a value object with a couple of properties and correct equality". Before C# 9 that meant a class with three overrides. Use them for DTOs, domain events, API contracts and test data; use classes for entities with identity and lifecycle.


{{-- A RECORD IS WHAT THE COMPILER GENERATES: value equality, a
     ToString that prints every property, a with expression, and
     deconstruction. --}}
public sealed record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);
public sealed record class Customer(int Id, string Name);
{{-- ^ 'record class' when you want a CLASS — a record's default is
     a REFERENCE type, so a record is a class unless you say
     otherwise. 'record struct' for the value-type form. --}}

static void Generated()
{
    var a = new Money(100m, "GBP");
    var b = new Money(100m, "GBP");

    Console.WriteLine(a == b);            // TRUE: field-wise equality
    Console.WriteLine(a.GetHashCode() == b.GetHashCode());   // true:
                                                            // so a
                                                            // record CAN
                                                            // be a
                                                            // dictionary
                                                            // key
    Console.WriteLine(a);                 // "Money { Amount = 100,
                                          //   Currency = GBP }"
    Console.WriteLine(a);                 // every property, by
                                          // default

    var c = a with { Amount = 200m };     // the copy-with-one-change
    // a.Amount is STILL 100: 'with' COPIES
    Console.WriteLine(ReferenceEquals(a, c));   // false

    var (amount, currency) = a;           // deconstruction
}

{{-- AND WHAT IT IS NOT: a shorthand for a class with properties. --}}
public sealed record class Order(int Id, OrderStatus Status);
public sealed class OrderRow(int Id, OrderStatus Status);

static void TheDifference()
{
    // VALUE EQUALITY IS THE POINT, so a record cannot express
    // "same row, loaded twice":
    var one = new Order(1, OrderStatus.Paid);
    var two = new Order(1, OrderStatus.Paid);
    // one == two                TRUE, and for an ENTITY MODEL that
    //                             is usually not what anybody meant:
    //                             two loaded copies of the same row
    //                             are the same row, and the
    //                             equality that is right for a value
    //                             is wrong for an identity.
    // one.ReferenceEquals(two)  FALSE: two objects.
}
{{-- ^ so an entity is a CLASS with a primary-constructor shape and
     a hand-written or id-only Equals. The record's generated
     equality is right for a value and wrong for an identity, and
     the difference is the whole reason both exist. --}}

{{-- POSITIONAL RECORDS, and what they give up: --}}
public sealed record Line(int Qty, decimal UnitPrice)
{
    // A PROPERTY, not a parameter, when it is computed:
    public decimal Total => Qty * UnitPrice;

    // A METHOD, freely — the positional form does not restrict
    // members, only properties.
    public Money AsMoney(string currency) => new(Total, currency);
}

static void Properties()
{
    // THE DECLARED PROPERTIES EXIST and are usable — what they do NOT
    // have is a way to be REPLACED. A positional property is
    // init-only, so a caller that needs a variant BUILDS it:
    var line = new Line(2, 10m);
    var more = line with { Qty = 3 };
    // line.Qty is still 2
}

6.6 Inheritance: virtual, override, new, sealed

C# methods are non-virtual by default, which is the safer choice. virtual opens a method for overriding, override replaces it, sealed override replaces it and stops further overrides, and new hides a member without any polymorphic relationship at all.

Four keywords decide whether a member is replaced, added alongside, or hidden, and they are not interchangeable. A virtual member is a promise that it may be overridden. An override replaces one. A new member hides one. A sealed member refuses both. The distinction between hiding and overriding is the one that produces the defect, because hiding satisfies the compiler's requirements without doing anything at run time.

Dispatch is decided by the static type

A call through a base-typed reference reaches the override, and a call through a derived-typed reference reaches the new member. So a derived type that hides rather than overrides produces two methods with the same name and signature, both callable, and which one runs depends on how the object was referred to. Nothing warns about it, because both declarations are legal.

Sealing, and why the destructor is the case to remember

A virtual method in a class that has no virtual destructor is the classic inheritance defect: deleting through a base pointer runs the base destructor only, and every derived field is leaked. The compiler warns about it in modern versions, and the warning is worth treating as an error rather than as noise.

public class Shape
{
    public virtual double Area() => 0;            // extensible
    public void Describe() => Console.WriteLine("a shape");   // not extensible
    public static string Kind => "shape";
}

public class Circle : Shape
{
    public double Radius { get; }

    public override double Area() => Math.PI * Radius * Radius;

    public new void Describe() => Console.WriteLine("a circle");
    // 'new' HIDES. Through a Shape reference you still get "a shape".
}

public sealed class Circle2 : Circle
{
    public sealed override void Describe() { }   // fixed forever
}

public abstract class Animal
{
    public abstract string Sound { get; }         // no body allowed
    public virtual void Speak() => Console.WriteLine(Sound);
    protected abstract void OnBorn();           // visible to derived only
    internal protected int Tag { get; set; }  // both derived and same assembly
}

// Calling base explicitly
public override void Speak()
{
    base.Speak();
    Console.WriteLine("...");
}

// Non-virtual methods are hidden by name, even without 'new' (a warning)
Shape s = new Circle { Radius = 1 };
s.Describe();        // "a shape"  -- the base method, because it is not virtual
Console.WriteLine(s.Area());   // pi  -- virtual dispatch works

Base constructors run before derived ones, always. A derived constructor cannot touch a derived field before the base constructor has run, and if the base constructor calls a virtual method, the derived override runs against uninitialised derived state. That is why constructors should be boring.

new is almost always a design smell. It creates two members with the same name and signature where only the base one is reachable through a base reference — a silent behavioural difference. If you need different behaviour, make the member virtual. The exception is new on members that are never called through the base type, such as a convenience overload.


{{-- FOUR KEYWORDS, and they are not interchangeable: --}}
public abstract class Shape
{
    // VIRTUAL: a promise that it MAY be overridden.
    public virtual double Area() => 0;

    // ABSTRACT: virtual, with no body, so a derived type MUST
    // implement it.
    public abstract string Describe();

    // SEALED on the member: refuses overriding.
    public sealed string Kind => GetType().Name;

    // SEALED on the TYPE: no further derivation, which also lets
    // the compiler devirtualise.
}
public sealed class Circle : Shape
{
    public sealed override double Area() => Math.PI * R * R;
    // ^ SEALED OVERRIDE: this member is final, which lets the
    //   compiler devirtualise the call when the static type is
    //   known.
    public override string Describe() => "circle";
    public double R { get; init; }
}

{{-- AND THE VIRTUAL DESTRUCTOR, which is the case to remember: --}}
public class Resource : IDisposable
{
    public void Dispose() { }        {{-- NOT virtual: deleting
                                            through a Resource
                                            pointer runs only this,
                                            and every derived field
                                            is LEAKED --}}
}

public class FileResource : Resource
{
    public FileResource(Stream s) { Stream = s; }
    public Stream Stream { get; }
    public override void Dispose()   {{-- ERROR: cannot override,
                                            because the base member
                                            is not virtual --}}
}
{{-- ^ the modern C# pattern-based alternative, which the compiler
     checks against the interface: --}}

public class StreamResource : IDisposable
{
    private bool _disposed;
    protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing)
    {
        if (_disposed) return;
        if (disposing) { /* release managed */ }
        _disposed = true;
    }

    public void Dispose()
    {
        Dispose(true);
        GC.SuppressFinalize(this);
    }
}

{{-- HIDE versus OVERRIDE, and the defect: --}}
public class BaseWithPrint { public virtual void Print() => Log("base"); }
public class DerivedHiding : BaseWithPrint
{
    public new void Print() => Log("derived");
    // ^ NEW HIDES. Both declarations are legal, nothing warns, and
    //   which one runs depends ONLY on the STATIC TYPE.
}
static void Dispatch()
{
    DerivedHiding d = new();
    BaseWithPrint  b = d;

    d.Print();   // "derived": the static type is DerivedHiding
    b.Print();   // "base":    the static type is BaseWithPrint,
                 //            so the virtual dispatch goes to
                 //            BaseWithPrint.Print, and the NEW
                 //            member is not reached at all.
    ((BaseWithPrint)d).Print();   // "base" again

    // ^ TWO METHODS with the same name and signature, both
    //   callable, and the only thing deciding which runs is how the
    //   variable was declared. Nothing warns, because both
    //   declarations are legal.
}

6.7 Interfaces and default members

An interface is a contract. Types implement it, callers depend on it, and neither side needs to know about the other. Interfaces can hold default implementations (C# 8) and static and abstract members, and since .NET 9 they can even be ref structs, which lets an interface describe a stack-only view without allocating.

An interface states a contract and no implementation. It can hold members with a body, which is called a default implementation and which is the feature that lets a new member be added without breaking every existing implementation — at the cost of the rule that a default implementation is invisible to a type that does not mention the interface.

The cost of the default member

A default member is not overridden in the common sense. It is shadowed by any member of the same name and signature on the implementing type, whether or not that member is an interface implementation. So a class that has a method of the right name gets its own, and a class that does not gets the default — and which happened is decided at compile time rather than at run time.

Where a marker interface earns its place and where it does not

A marker interface with no members is useful when something is going to be reflected over, dispatched on, or discovered by a container. It is not useful as documentation, because an attribute is better at that and produces a diagnostic when it is missing. The test is whether anything behaves differently based on it.

public interface IRepository<T> where T : class
{
    T? Get(string id);
    IReadOnlyList<T> All();

    // Default implementation: available to any implementer for free
    bool Exists(string id) => Get(id) is not null;

    // Static members with a generic host: a factory pattern with no class
    static abstract T Create();

    // Static non-abstract helper
    static bool IsValid(in T candidate) => candidate is not null;
}

// Implementation
public sealed class InMemoryRepository<T> : IRepository<T> where T : class, new()
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, T> _items = new();

    public T? Get(string id) => _items.GetValueOrDefault(id);
    public IReadOnlyList<T> All() => _items.Values.ToList();
    public static T Create() => new T();
}

// .NET 9: a ref struct interface describes a stack-only view
// public ref struct IBufferProvider { ReadOnlySpan<byte> GetSpan(); }

// Generic math since .NET 7 (see chapter 7)
// public interface INumber<TSelf> : IComparable<TSelf> { static abstract TSelf operator +(TSelf, TSelf); }

Prefer many small interfaces over one large one. A consumer that only reads should not have to implement writes just to satisfy a fat interface, and a narrow interface is trivially fakeable in tests. Keep interfaces on the consumer side of the fence, not the producer side.

Default interface members are ideal for adding a new member to a public interface without breaking implementers — the framework does this for IEnumerable<T> in .NET 9. They are a poor choice for core contract behaviour, because a class implementing the interface and a struct implementing it will end up with different code.


{{-- AN INTERFACE STATES A CONTRACT AND NO IMPLEMENTATION --}}
public interface INamed
{
    string Name { get; }

    // A DEFAULT IMPLEMENTATION, which is what lets a member be
    // added without breaking every existing implementation.
    string Describe() => $"a thing called {Name}";

    // ^ IT IS A FEATURE with a sharp cost, so read the next sample.
}

public class Widget : INamed
{
    public string Name { get; init; } = "";
}

public class Gadget : INamed
{
    public string Name { get; init; } = "";
    public string Describe() => "a gadget";      // overrides the
                                                // default
}

{{-- THE COST: a default member is SHADOWED, not overridden. --}}
public class HasItsOwnDescribe
{
    // This method is NOT declared as implementing INamed.Describe,
    // and it shadows the default anyway — because the name and
    // signature match.
    public string Describe() => "something else entirely";
}

static void TheCost()
{
    INamed w = new Widget();
    w.Describe();                  // "a thing called ...": the
                                   // DEFAULT, because Widget does
                                   // not declare Describe

    // ^ WHICH HAPPENED IS DECIDED AT COMPILE TIME, by whether the
    //   concrete type declares a matching member — not at run time
    //   and not by anything the interface says. A member added to
    //   the interface with a default therefore changes the behaviour
    //   of an EXISTING class silently.
}

{{-- AND A MARKER INTERFACE, which is worth having only when
     something behaves differently because of it: --}}
public interface IAuditable;        {{-- NO MEMBERS: and something
                                          DOES behave differently:
                                          an interceptor, a
                                          serialiser setting, a
                                          test helper --}}
public interface IClock             {{-- ...and something does NOT,
                                          so this is documentation,
                                          and an ATTRIBUTE would
                                          be better because it
                                          produces a diagnostic
                                          when it is missing --}}
public interface IClock2 { DateTimeOffset Now { get; } }

6.8 Static members and extension methods

Static members belong to the type, not to an instance. That makes them the right home for factory methods, constants, caches and pure functions with no natural receiver. Extension methods are static methods in a static class that the compiler rewrites as an instance call, which lets you add methods to types you do not own.

A static member belongs to the type rather than to an instance, and the type is loaded once. That makes a static field a process-wide singleton with no synchronisation, no lifetime control and no way to replace it in a test — which is a property rather than a defect, and the reason a static is the wrong choice for anything that varies.

Static initialisation, and the trap

A static field initialiser runs the first time the type is touched, and it runs under a lock. So a static constructor that blocks — on I/O, on a lock held elsewhere, on another static's initialiser — deadlocks, and the diagnostic names the type rather than the cause. The rule is that a static initialiser must be cheap and must not call out.

Extension methods

An extension method is a static method in a static class, callable with instance syntax. It cannot access private state, it is resolved statically rather than virtually, and it is invisible when someone reads the type's members — which means a call to one cannot be found by searching for the type's methods.

public static class MoneyExtensions
{
    // 'this' before the first parameter is what makes it an extension method
    public static decimal WithTax(this decimal amount, decimal rate = 0.2m)
        => amount * (1 + rate);

    public static IEnumerable<T> WhereNotNull<T>(this IEnumerable<T?> source) where T : class
        => source.Where(x => x is not null).Select(x => x!);

    // Generic extension methods are where extensions earn their keep
    public static void AddRange<T>(this ICollection<T> target, IEnumerable<T> items)
    {
        foreach (var item in items) target.Add(item);
    }
}

var total = 100.00m.WithTax();      // 120.00
list.AddRange(other);             // works on List<T>, HashSet<T>, ...

// Static fields: a per-process cache, initialised once
public static class AppCache
{
    private static readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, object> Items = new();
    public static bool IsInitialised { get; set; }
}

// Static constructors run once, before first access to any static member
static AppCache() { /* one-time setup */ }

Extension methods cannot override an existing instance method, cannot access private members, and are only found when their containing namespace is imported. If an instance method with the same name exists, the instance method wins silently.

Do not define an extension method on object. It becomes visible on every type in the solution and produces collisions with other libraries. The same warning applies to extension methods on string unless the namespace is deliberately opt-in.


{{-- A STATIC MEMBER BELONGS TO THE TYPE, and the type is loaded
     once: a process-wide singleton with no synchronisation, no
     lifetime control, and no way to replace it in a test. --}}
public sealed class Metrics
{
    // A PLAIN STATIC FIELD: one per process, and nothing makes that
    // safe under concurrency.
    private static long _requests;

    public static void Record() => Interlocked.Increment(ref _requests);
    // ^ Interlocked, because a ++ on a static long is a
    //   read-modify-write that loses updates. The static is the
    //   problem; Interlocked is the mitigation, and it is a
    //   mitigation rather than a fix.

    // A STATIC FIELD WITH AN INITIALISER runs under a lock, the
    // first time the type is touched:
    private static readonly Dictionary<string, Regex> _cache = Build();

    private static Dictionary<string, Regex> Build()
    {
        // A STATIC INITIALISER MUST BE CHEAP AND MUST NOT CALL OUT.
        // A constructor here that blocks — on I/O, on a lock held
        // elsewhere, on another static's initialiser — DEADLOCKS,
        // and the diagnostic names the type rather than the cause.
        return new(StringComparer.Ordinal);
    }
}

{{-- AND THE WRONG CHOICE FOR ANYTHING THAT VARIES, which is the
     real argument against statics: --}}
public sealed class Configuration
{
    public static string? Endpoint { get; set; }   {{-- process-wide,
                                                          so a test
                                                          that sets it
                                                          leaks into
                                                          every other
                                                          test in the
                                                          same process,
                                                          in an order
                                                          nobody
                                                          controls --}}
}
{{-- ^ the fix is an INSTANCE, passed in, resolved from the
     container. A static that a test must reset is a static that will
     be left set. --}}

{{-- EXTENSION METHODS: a static method in a static class, callable
     with instance syntax. --}}
public static class StringExtensions
{
    // IT CANNOT ACCESS PRIVATE STATE, it is RESOLVED STATICALLY
    // rather than virtually, and it is INVISIBLE when someone reads
    // the type's members — which means a call to one cannot be found
    // by searching for the type's methods.
    public static bool IsNullOrBlank(this string? s) =>
        string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s);

    public static bool Has(this string s, char c) => s.Contains(c);
}

static void ExtensionCosts()
{
    "abc".IsNullOrBlank();      // readable at the call site

    // BUT: an EXTENSION METHOD IS NOT VIRTUAL, so a derived type
    // cannot change what it does.
    class MyString { }
    // MyString.IsNullOrBlank()   ERROR: no such instance method, and
    //                           the extension does not apply
    //                           because it is a string extension
    //                           and MyString is not a string.

    // AND IT LOSES TO AN INSTANCE METHOD, silently:
    string s = "a";
    // s.IsNullOrBlank()        the extension runs, because string has
    //                           no such instance method
    // ...and if a FUTURE version of string adds one, the instance
    //   method wins and the behaviour changes without a compile
    //   error. Which is a reason to keep extensions few and to give
    //   them names that could not plausibly collide.
}

6.9 IDisposable and using

IDisposable is the framework’s deterministic cleanup contract: release unmanaged handles, sockets, file locks, buffers. C# turns a using block into a try/finally that calls Dispose, and the using declaration form (C# 8) makes it a single line.

Disposal is deterministic by default: the using statement calls the dispose method at the end of the block, including on an early return and on an exception. A type that holds an unmanaged resource has to participate, because the collector's finalizer runs at an arbitrary time and possibly not at all before the process exits.

The pattern, and the rule inside it

The disposable pattern is a protected virtual method that takes a boolean saying whether the caller is disposing or the finalizer is, and the distinction matters: managed references should be released only when disposing, because touching them from a finalizer thread is not safe. A type that follows the pattern needs a finalizer only when it holds something unmanaged, and a type that follows it and also holds nothing unmanaged does not need one at all.

Async disposal

An asynchronous disposable is a separate interface, and the language has separate syntax for it. The important consequence is that the synchronous form cannot await, so a synchronously disposed asynchronous resource produces an exception if its disposal is genuinely asynchronous — which is why the two interfaces are separate rather than one with a flag.

public sealed class FileSession : IDisposable
{
    private readonly FileStream _stream;
    private bool _disposed;

    public FileSession(string path) => _stream = new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open, FileAccess.Read);

    public void Dispose()
    {
        if (_disposed) return;      // Dispose must be idempotent
        _disposed = true;
        _stream.Dispose();
    }
}

// Block form: everything inside is covered
using (var session = new FileSession(path))
{
    // ... read the file ...
}

// Declaration form (C# 8): disposed at end of scope, exception-safe
using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
using var writer = new StreamWriter(outPath);

// Stacked declarations dispose in reverse order
using var a = new Resource("A");
using var b = new Resource("B");
// b disposed first, then a

// async: IAsyncDisposable for anything that awaits during cleanup
await using var conn = await OpenAsync(ct);   // awaits conn.DisposeAsync()

// A type with BOTH interfaces: Dispose for sync, DisposeAsync for async
public interface INeedCleanup : IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable { }

Every type that wraps a resource should implement Dispose and be sealed, or inherit a Dispose(bool disposing) pattern. Non-sealed disposable types leak the unmanaged handle if a derived type forgets to call base.Dispose().

Prefer using var declarations everywhere. They cover the whole scope rather than a block, so a later return or throw cannot skip cleanup, and the code has one fewer level of indentation.

GC.SuppressFinalize belongs in Dispose when you implement the full pattern, and GC.ReRegisterForFinalize is needed if you revive an object during finalisation. A finaliser is a last resort for a hard crash, not a cleanup strategy — it runs on the finaliser thread at an unpredictable time.

Exercises 6

  1. Write a readonly record struct for money and a record for an order line, then show their generated equality behaviour with == and GetHashCode.
  2. Create a type with a required member and try three ways to construct it without it (reflection, a derived constructor, a generic new()). Record which ones the compiler catches.
  3. Demonstrate the new versus override difference: call a hidden method through a base reference and print both results.
  4. Write an IDisposable type whose Dispose logs, call it twice, and prove it is idempotent. Then convert it to IAsyncDisposable.
  5. Add a default implementation to an interface member and call it through the interface reference from a class and a struct implementer. Note the difference.
  6. Write a generic extension method Chunk<T>(this IEnumerable<T>, int size) and use it to batch a large sequence without materialising it all.

{{-- DETERMINISTIC BY DEFAULT: using calls Dispose at the end of
     the block, including on an early return and on an exception. --}}
public static void Deterministic(string path)
{
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);   // disposed at the END
                                              // of the METHOD, not
                                              // of the block — which
                                              // keeps the scope as
                                              // small as possible
    Process(stream);
    if (stream.Length == 0) return;          // disposed on this path
    Consume(stream);                        // and on this one
}

{{-- THE PATTERN, and the rule inside it: managed references are
     released ONLY when disposing, never from a finalizer. --}}
public abstract class StreamWrapper : IDisposable
{
    private IntPtr _handle;                   // an UNMANAGED resource,
                                             // so this type DOES
                                             // need a finalizer
    private bool _disposed;

    protected IntPtr Handle
    {
        get
        {
            ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(_disposed, this);
            return _handle;
        }
    }

    // THE VIRTUAL DISPOSE, which is what makes deletion through a
    // base pointer safe:
    protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing)
    {
        if (_disposed) return;
        if (disposing)
        {
            // ^ MANAGED REFERENCES ONLY HERE. A finalizer runs on
            //   the finalizer thread, where touching managed state
            //   is not safe.
        }
        ReleaseHandle(_handle);
        _handle = IntPtr.Zero;
        _disposed = true;
    }

    protected abstract void ReleaseHandle(IntPtr handle);

    // A FINALIZER, and only because the type holds something
    // unmanaged. A type with no unmanaged resource should not have
    // one: it promotes the object to the finalizable queue, which
    // costs an extra collection and an extra promotion.
    ~StreamWrapper() => Dispose(false);

    public void Dispose()
    {
        Dispose(true);
        GC.SuppressFinalize(this);   // ^ so a Dispose is not followed
                                    //   by a finalizer run of the
                                    //   same resource
    }
}

{{-- AND ASYNCHRONOUS DISPOSAL IS A SEPARATE INTERFACE, and the
     reason it is separate is the reason it is a defect if you use
     the synchronous one: --}}
public sealed class DbConnection : IAsyncDisposable
{
    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        // An async dispose is genuinely asynchronous: it awaits a
        // network round trip that returns the connection to the
        // pool.
        await FlushAsync();
        await _connection.CloseAsync();
    }
}

static async Task Wrong()
{
    var conn = new DbConnection();

    using (conn)                {{-- WRONG: IAsyncDisposable is not
                                     IDisposable, so this does not
                                     even compile — which is the
                                     POINT of the separate
                                     interface --}}
    await UseAsync(conn);
}

static async Task Right()
{
    await using var conn = new DbConnection();
    await UseAsync(conn);
    // ^ disposed at the end of the METHOD, asynchronously, and the
    //   connection is back in the pool before the next line.
}

7 · Generics, Constraints & Variance

7.1 Generic classes and methods7.2 Constraints7.3 Type inference7.4 static abstract members and generic math7.5 Variance: in, out, contra7.6 Generics instead of reflection

Chapter seven covers generics: the feature that lets one piece of code serve every type without casting and without a code generator. The parts that matter in practice are constraints (what the compiler lets you assume about T), inference (how you avoid naming types), the static abstract members added in .NET 7 that finally made generic maths possible, and variance, which is the concept behind IEnumerable<out T>.

7.1 Generic classes and methods

A generic type or method is compiled once for all reference types (shared code) and separately for each value type (specialised code). That is why List<int> can avoid boxing in its internal loop and List<string> does not need a copy.

A generic type or method is compiled once per distinct type argument, so the code is specialised and the operations on the type argument are direct rather than through an interface. That is the whole performance story, and it has two consequences worth stating: a generic method over a reference type shares code with every reference type, while one over a value type gets a copy per value type, and a generic type nested in another multiplies.

Why it is not a substitute for designing

The common misreading is that generics make a type "flexible" in the way object is. It does not: it makes it type-safe and specialised, which is different. A generic collection is still one design with one set of invariants, and a generic method is still one algorithm. What generics remove is the need to write the type twice and the need to cast at the boundary — which is a large win and not the same thing as flexibility.

Static versus instance

A generic method with no use of its type parameter's instance state can be static, which matters because a static method is not a virtual call. And a generic method on a type that is itself generic reuses the same type parameter rather than introducing another, so a method on Repository<T> uses the T of its containing type.

// A generic class: one declaration, any type argument
public sealed class Result<T>
{
    public bool IsSuccess { get; }
    public T? Value { get; }
    public string? Error { get; }

    private Result(bool ok, T? value, string? error)
    {
        IsSuccess = ok; Value = value; Error = error;
    }

    public static Result<T> Ok(T value) => new(true, value, null);
    public static Result<T> Fail(string error) => new(false, default, error);
}

// A generic method: the type parameter belongs to the method
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>
    => a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;

// Generic with a default type argument (C# 7.1)
void Log<T>(T value, string level = "INFO") { }

// Overloads differing only by arity of type parameters are NOT allowed
// void M<T>(T x) { }  and  void M<T,U>(T x, U y) { }  -- this pair is fine (different
// parameter counts), but void N<T>(T x) { } / void N<T>(int x) { } is a signature clash.

// Generic local functions and generic lambdas
// T[] Copy<T>(T[] src) { var d = new T[src.Length]; ... }  -- local generics allowed

Type parameters are named T, TKey, TValue in the framework, and single letters elsewhere. A descriptive name for a domain type parameter (TCustomer) beats a single letter once you have three.

T? on an unconstrained type parameter is legal and means "maybe null" only for reference types; for a value type it means the compiler defers to the nullable context. where T : struct makes T? a real Nullable<T>, which changes the meaning of your code. Constrain before you use ? carelessly.


{{-- COMPILED ONCE PER DISTINCT TYPE ARGUMENT, so the operations on
     T are direct rather than through an interface. --}}
public sealed class Stack<T>
{
    private T[] _items = new T[16];
    private int _count;

    public void Push(T item)
    {
        // _items[++_count] = item;   with T = int: a direct array
        //                            write with no boxing, because
        //                            the code is SPECIALISED
        _items[_count++] = item;
    }

    public T Pop()
    {
        if (_count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("empty");
        return _items[--_count];
    }
}

static void Specialisation()
{
    var ints = new Stack<int>();
    ints.Push(1);                  // no boxing: _items is int[]

    var names = new Stack<string>();
    names.Push("a");               // no boxing: _items is string[]

    var when = new Stack<DateTimeOffset>();
    // ^ THREE SPECIALISATIONS, three copies of the same code, and
    //   each one is a direct operation on its own type.
}

{{-- BUT CODE SHARING IS NOT UNIFORM, and this is the thing people
     are surprised by: --}}
public class Node<T>          {{-- CODE SHARED across ALL reference
                                    types: one copy of Node<T>'s
                                    methods, because the operations
                                    are virtual --}}
{
    public Node<T>? Next { get; set; }
    public T Value { get; set; } = default!;
}

public struct NodeV<T>        {{-- A COPY PER VALUE TYPE: the
                                    operations are direct, so each
                                    value type needs its own code --}}
{
    public NodeV<T>? Next;
    public T Value;
}
// NodeV<int> and NodeV<double> are two types with two sets of
// method bodies; Node<object> and Node<string> share one set.
{{-- ^ which is why a generic over a value type in a HOT PATH costs
     more code size than one over a reference type, and why a
     generic over a LARGE value type is a poor trade. --}}

{{-- STATIC versus INSTANCE, and it matters because a static method
     is not a virtual call: --}}
public static class Parser
{
    // A STATIC GENERIC METHOD: nothing here touches an instance, so
    // the compiler can specialise it directly.
    public static T Parse<T>(string text) where T : IParsable<T>
        => T.Parse(text, provider: null);

    // AN INSTANCE METHOD ON A GENERIC TYPE reuses the CONTAINING
    // type's parameter rather than introducing another:
    public sealed class Repository<T> where T : Entity
    {
        // T is the Repository's T, not a new one
        public T? Find(int id) => null;
    }
}

{{-- AND WHAT GENERICS ARE NOT: --}}
{{--   generic != flexible, in the way object is.
     A generic collection is still ONE DESIGN with ONE set of
     invariants; a generic method is still ONE ALGORITHM. What
     generics remove is the need to write the type twice and the
     need to cast at the boundary — which is a large win and not
     the same thing as flexibility. --}}

7.2 Constraints

A constraint tells the compiler what operations are legal on T. Without constraints you can do almost nothing beyond == and assignment. Constraints are checked at compile time, cost nothing at run time, and are enforced at every use site including inside the type itself.

A constraint states what a type argument must provide, and the compiler uses it to check the body of the method once rather than at every call. Without a constraint the body cannot use the type argument's members at all, because it does not know what they are; with one, every call is checked when the method is compiled.

The kinds, and what each buys

A base-class constraint gives the members of that class. An interface constraint gives the interface's members, and several can be listed. A struct constraint says the argument is a value type, which is what makes default(T) meaningful and what lets a method avoid boxing. A new() constraint requires a parameterless constructor, which is what makes a generic factory able to construct. And the notnull constraint is a nullability constraint rather than a member one.

Where the check happens

Constraints are checked at the call site, once per call, not per operation inside the method. That is what makes a generic method with a constraint faster than one using reflection, and it is also why an unsatisfied constraint is a compile error at the call rather than a run-time failure inside.

// Reference type constraint: T must be a class
static T First<T>(in IReadOnlyList<T> items) where T : class
    => items[0];

// Value type constraint: T must be a struct; unlocks == and != directly
static bool Same<T>(T a, T b) where T : struct
    => a.Equals(b);

// Parameterless constructor constraint
static T Fresh<T>() where T : new() => new T();

// Interface constraint (up to five) -- grants the interface's members
static decimal Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> source) where T : IConvertible
{
    decimal total = 0m;
    foreach (var item in source) total += item.ToDecimal(null);
    return total;
}

// Base class constraint
static TBase Unwrap<T, TBase>(T item) where T : TBase => item;

// 'class?' and 'struct?' -- the "not null" and "not Nullable<T>" refinements
static T Ensure<T>(T? maybe) where T : class => maybe!;
static T NoNullable<T>(T? maybe) where T : struct
    => maybe ?? default;

// Multiple constraints, in the order the language requires: class, then base
// class, then interfaces, then new()
static T Complex<T, TBase>(in TBase item)
    where T : class, TBase, IDisposable, new()
    => new T();

// 'not' constraints (C# 8): exclude nullability
static T NotNull<T>(T value) where T : notnull { return value; }

// 'allows ref struct' (C# 14): accept Span<T> as a type argument
// static T[] ToArray<T>(scoped ReadOnlySpan<T> src) where T : allows ref struct

The where T : class constraint also means T? is a plain nullable reference, and the compiler knows == null is a reference comparison. Without it, the only comparison allowed is against null itself.

Prefer interface constraints to base class constraints. where T : MyBase forces every argument to be that class or a subclass, which is a much narrower door than where T : IMyInterface, and it prevents unrelated types from ever being used together.


{{-- A CONSTRAINT LETS THE BODY BE CHECKED ONCE, rather than at
     every call — and it is what makes a generic method's body
     legal at all. --}}
public sealed class Entity { public int Id { get; init; } }
public interface IParsable<T> { static T Parse(string s, IFormatProvider? p); }
public interface IComparable<in T> { int CompareTo(T other); }

// NO CONSTRAINT: the body cannot use T's members AT ALL, because the
// compiler does not know what they are.
static T Broken<T>(string s) => T.Parse(s, null);   // ERROR: T has
                                                    // no member Parse

{{-- THE KINDS, and what each buys: --}}
public static class Constraints
{
    // 1. BASE CLASS: gives the base's members, and forces T to be a
    //    REFERENCE type, because a struct cannot inherit.
    public static T ById<T>(IEnumerable<T> all, int id) where T : Entity
    {
        // all.First(e => e.Id == id)   e.Id is available BECAUSE of
        //                              the constraint
        foreach (var e in all) if (e.Id == id) return e;
        return default!;
    }

    // 2. INTERFACE: gives the interface's members, and SEVERAL can
    //    be listed.
    public static T Smallest<T>(IEnumerable<T> all) where T : IComparable<T>
        => all.Min();

    // 3. struct: says the argument is a VALUE TYPE, which is what
    //    makes default(T) meaningful and what avoids boxing.
    public static int SizeOf<T>() where T : struct
    {
        T zero = default;           // ^ MEANINGFUL: for a struct,
                                    //   default is a real value.
                                    //   Without the constraint
                                    //   default(T) is null and
                                    //   SizeOf would be meaningless.
        return System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.SizeOf<T>();
    }

    // 4. new(): requires a PARAMETERLESS CONSTRUCTOR, which is what
    //    makes a generic factory able to construct.
    public static T Create<T>() where T : new() => new T();
    // T Create<T>()            ERROR: the compiler cannot know
    //                           that T has a constructor at all

    // 5. notnull: a NULLABILITY constraint, and it is what makes the
    //    non-nullable generic argument analysis work at all.
    public static T Require<T>(T? maybe) where T : class, notnull
        => maybe ?? throw new ArgumentNullException();
    // ^ WITHOUT 'notnull', T is inferred as T? for a reference type
    //   and the body sees a possibly-null value.
}

{{-- WHERE THE CHECK HAPPENS, which is the performance point: --}}
public static T Parsed<T>(string s) where T : IParsable<T>
    => T.Parse(s, null);
{{-- ^ checked ONCE at the call, not per operation inside. That is
     what makes it faster than a reflection-based equivalent, and
     also why an unsatisfied constraint is a COMPILE error at the
     call rather than a run-time failure inside. --}}

7.3 Type inference

You rarely write type arguments explicitly. The compiler infers them from the arguments, the return type, or the target of an assignment. Inference works bottom-up through nested generic calls, which is why a fluent chain usually reads cleanly and a nested one does not.

Type arguments can be inferred at a call site from the arguments, from the assignment target, and in some cases from the body of a lambda. Inference works by fixing what it can from each argument in order and then checking the remainder against the constraints, so a call whose arguments fix the argument in different orders can fail to infer when the same call written the other way succeeds.

The three places inference is used

From an argument: passing a List<string> to a method taking IEnumerable<T> fixes the argument as string. From an assignment target: the target type fixes an argument that the expression alone does not determine. From a lambda body: the parameter types are fixed by the delegate type the lambda is being converted to, which is why a lambda with untyped parameters only compiles where a target type is expected.

Where inference fails, and what to do

It fails when two arguments constrain the type argument differently, when a lambda appears before any argument that fixes the type, and when the argument is null with no target type — because null fixes nothing. In every one of those cases the answer is the same: supply the type argument explicitly, which costs six characters and makes the call unambiguous.

// Argument inference: no type arguments written anywhere
var max = Max(3, 7);                  // T = int
var first = First(new[] { "a", "b" });    // T = string

// Target-typed inference: the destination decides T
IEnumerable<double> data = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };   // int[] -> IEnumerable<double> via implicit numeric
List<object> everything = [ "text", 1, 2.5 ];

// C# 9 target-typed new: no repetition of the type name
var dict = new Dictionary<string, List<int>>();
dict["nums"] = new();                        // List<int>, inferred from the indexer
var buffer = new byte[256];

// LinqPad-style: inference can be beaten by an over-broad first argument
// IEnumerable<object> mixed = GetAll();   // T inferred as object -> no conversions later
// IEnumerable<string> mixed = GetAll();   // T inferred as string  -> conversions apply

// When inference fails, name the type argument explicitly -- it is legal
// var ok = Process<string>(value);

Inference does not flow through var and then back. If the first call in a chain is generic and receives a broad type, every later operator is chosen for that broad type. Inserting an explicit type argument at the head of the chain fixes a whole class of "why is this object not callable" errors.

When a LINQ query gives a surprising result type, hover the first operator. If T is object, the fix is almost always an explicit type argument or a cast on the source, not a change to the query.


{{-- THE THREE PLACES INFERENCE IS USED: --}}
static IEnumerable<T> Filter<T>(IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> keep)
    => source.Where(keep);

// (1) FROM AN ARGUMENT.
var words = new List<string>();
var long1 = Filter(words, s => s.Length > 3);
// ^ T is string, fixed by the FIRST argument, so the lambda's
//   parameter is typed for you.

// (2) FROM AN ASSIGNMENT TARGET — which is why this compiles:
IEnumerable<int> numbers = Enumerate(1, 2, 3);
// ^ Enumerate<int>(1, 2, 3) with the argument type spelled out:
//   the target fixes T, because 1, 2 and 3 alone do not.

// (3) FROM A LAMBDA BODY, and only where a TARGET TYPE exists:
var twice = Select(numbers, n => n * 2);      // fine: n is int
// Select(numbers, n => n * 2);              ERROR if the overload
//                                            could not fix T: a
//                                            lambda with untyped
//                                            parameters needs a
//                                            target delegate type

{{-- WHERE INFERENCE FAILS, and the answer is the same in every
     case: supply the argument explicitly. --}}
static void TwoConstraints(List<string> a, IEnumerable<int> b) { }

// var bad = Filter(a, b);     ERROR: T cannot be both string and
//                              int. Supplying it does not help
//                              either — which is the point: the
//                              call is wrong, not the inference.

// (a) A NULL ARGUMENT FIXES NOTHING:
static void Untyped() { }
Untyped(null);          // T cannot be inferred: null is
                        // compatible with every reference type,
//                        // and the compiler will not guess

// THE ANSWER:
Untyped<string>(null);  // six characters, and the call is
                        // unambiguous

// (b) A LAMBDA BEFORE ANY ARGUMENT THAT FIXES THE TYPE:
static void Order<T>(Func<T, bool> predicate, IEnumerable<T> source) { }

// Order(n => n > 3, numbers)   CS0411: the type of parameter 'n'
//                               cannot be inferred, because the
//                               lambda comes FIRST and nothing has
//                               fixed T yet. Reordering the
//                               parameters fixes it; so does
//                               naming the argument.

// {{-- AND THE PRACTICAL RULE, which is worth stating because
//     inference failures are confusing rather than difficult: --}}
// {{--   the compiler fixes what it can FROM EACH ARGUMENT IN
//      ORDER, then checks the remainder against the constraints.
//      So a call whose arguments constrain T in DIFFERENT ORDERS
//      can fail to infer where the same call written the other way
//      succeeds. When inference fails, naming the type argument is
//      not a workaround — it is the correct code, and it makes the
//      call unambiguous for the next reader too. --}}

7.4 static abstract members and generic math

Until .NET 7 an interface could not have a static abstract member, so a generic algorithm had no way to say "add two T". static abstract interface members (C# 11) fill that gap, which is what makes the full generic maths hierarchy possible: INumber<T>, IAdditionOperators<T,T,T>, IMinMaxValue<T> and a dozen more.

A static abstract member is declared on an interface without a body, and an implementing type must supply one. It exists so that an operation can be expressed generically over the type rather than over an instance — which is what generic maths does, and which is otherwise only reachable through boxing or through source-generated specialisations.

What it enables

Calling a static method on a type argument: TSum<T>.Add(a, b), where the addition is chosen by the type rather than being resolved through a virtual call on an instance. That is what the numeric maths interfaces in the framework use, and it is what lets a generic vector or matrix type compute without knowing its element type at compile time.

Where it is not worth it

The cost is a compile-time cost: every distinct type argument produces its own implementation, and the compiler does not devirtualise as aggressively as with an instance call in some cases. For one or two operations on a numeric type, a static method on a non-generic helper is clearer and produces less code.

// The interface
public interface IDimension
{
    static abstract IDimension Zero { get; }
    static abstract IDimension Add(IDimension a, IDimension b);
    static abstract bool IsZero(IDimension value);
}

public readonly record struct Vec2(double X, double Y) : IDimension
{
    public static IDimension Zero { get } = new Vec2(0, 0);
    public static IDimension Add(IDimension a, IDimension b)
        => new Vec2(((Vec2)a).X + ((Vec2)b).X, ((Vec2)a).Y + ((Vec2)b).Y);
    public static bool IsZero(IDimension v) => v.X == 0 && v.Y == 0;
}

// The algorithm, written once, works for every implementer
static T Sum<T>(in T seed, IEnumerable<T> values) where T : IDimension
{
    T total = seed;
    foreach (var v in values) total = (T)T.Add(total, v);
    return total;
}

// Generic maths: the framework now has the whole algebra
// static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> xs) where T : INumber<T>
// T max = xs.Max();   double d = T.CreateChecked(1.5);   T.Parse("1.5");
// var sum = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Sum();   // T = int, correctly typed
// var sum = new[] { 1, 2, 3.0 }.Sum();  // T = double, because of best common type

Use static abstract when the algorithm is genuinely parameterised by behaviour (dimension, unit, numeric type). Do not use it for ordinary constants — static virtual with a default body is the right tool when implementers may want to override, as the .NET maths interfaces demonstrate.

Generic maths means double.E becomes T.E and int.MaxValue becomes T.MaxValue. That is not a gimmick: it lets a single generic numeric algorithm serve int, double, decimal, Half, Int128 and a user-defined fixed-point type with no boxing and no duplication.


{{-- A STATIC ABSTRACT MEMBER: declared on an interface without a
     body, implemented per type. It exists so an operation can be
     expressed over the TYPE rather than over an instance. --}}
public interface IAddition<TSelf>
    where TSelf : IAddition<TSelf>
{
    // A STATIC ABSTRACT METHOD: no body, and an implementing type
    // must supply one. This is what makes a generic vector able to
    // ADD without knowing its element type.
    static abstract TSelf Add(TSelf a, TSelf b);
    static abstract TSelf Zero { get; }
}

public readonly struct Vector2 : IAddition<Vector2>
{
    public readonly float X, Y;
    public Vector2(float x, float y) { X = x; Y = y; }

    public static Vector2 Add(Vector2 a, Vector2 b) => new(a.X + b.X, a.Y + b.Y);
    public static Vector2 Zero => new(0, 0);
}

{{-- AND THE GENERIC TYPE THAT USES IT, which is the point: --}}
public readonly struct Vector<T> : IAddition<Vector<T>>
    where T : IAddition<T>
{
    public readonly T A, B;
    public Vector(T a, T b) { A = a; B = b; }

    public static Vector<T> Add(Vector<T> a, Vector<T> b)
        => new(T.Add(a.A, b.A), T.Add(a.B, b.B));
        // ^ TSELF IS THE ELEMENT TYPE, and T.Add is resolved on the
        //   ELEMENT TYPE at compile time: no boxing, no virtual
        //   call, no reflection.
}

static void Use()
{
    var a = new Vector<Vector2>(new(1, 2), new(3, 4));
    var b = new Vector<Vector2>(new(5, 6), new(7, 8));
    var c = Vector<Vector2>.Add(a, b);
    // ^ nested generics compose: the OUTER operation is chosen by
    //   Vector<T> and the INNER by Vector2, and neither is a virtual
    //   call.
}

{{-- WHERE IT IS NOT WORTH IT, and the trade is a COMPILE-TIME one: --}}
{{--   Every distinct type argument produces its own implementation.
     For one or two operations on a numeric type, a STATIC METHOD ON
     A NON-GENERIC HELPER is clearer and produces less code:
       internal static class FloatOps
       {
           public static Vector2 Add(Vector2 a, Vector2 b) => ...;
       }
     ...which is the same code with none of the interface, and it
     does not grow with the number of element types. --}}

7.5 Variance: in, out, contra

Variance describes how a generic type behaves under subtyping. Covariant (out) means Derived can substitute for Base; contravariant (in) means the reverse. The rule is that the type parameter must appear only in the allowed position: out parameters may be return values only, in parameters may be parameter types only.

Variance declares whether a type argument's position makes the constructed type more or less specific. A covariant position accepts a more derived type argument; a contravariant position accepts a more general one. The rule for where each is legal is narrow, and the compiler enforces it: only output positions are covariant and only input positions are contravariant.

Where each is legal, and why

An interface's method parameters are inputs and its return type is an output, so an interface that returns its type argument is covariant. The same interface taking the argument as a parameter is contravariant — and the same interface cannot be both, because that would let an unrelated conversion arise from stacking them.

Why it matters more than it looks

Variance is what makes a read-only list assignable from a more derived list, and it is what makes the standard library's read-only interfaces usable without copying. Without it, every assignment from a specific collection to a general one needs a conversion or a copy, and the collection interfaces are the ones where the copy is most expensive.

// Covariant: IEnumerable<out T> -- a producer of T
IEnumerable<string> strings = new[] { "a", "b" };
IEnumerable<object> objects = strings;   // legal: string IS-A object

// Contravariant: an input parameter type
public interface IComparer<in T>
{
    int Compare(T? x, T? y);
}

public sealed class LengthComparer : IComparer<string>
{
    public int Compare(string? x, string? y) => (x?.Length ?? 0).CompareTo(y?.Length ?? 0);
}

var byLength = new List<string> { "aaa", "b" };
byLength.Sort(new LengthComparer());

// Both at once, with different positions
public interface IConverter<in TFrom, out TTo>
{
    TTo Convert(TFrom value);
}

// The framework's variance choices are worth memorising:
//   IEnumerable<out T>          covariant  -- LINQ works on a base reference
//   IReadOnlyList<out T>         covariant
//   IComparer<in T>             contravariant
//   Action<in T>               contravariant
//   Func<in T, out TResult>   contravariant input, covariant output
//   List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>  INVARIANT -- mutable, so no variance

// A practical use: a comparer that works for any subtype of the key type
// public sealed class CaseInsensitive : IEqualityComparer<string> { ... }

Variance cannot be added to a type that mutates its type argument, which is why List<T> is invariant. A List<Derived> that could be passed as a List<Base> would let you add a Base that is not a Derived, and the next read would blow up.

Marking a type parameter out when it also appears in an input position is a compile error, and the error message about "invalid variance" is genuinely hard to read. If you hit it, the fix is almost always to split the parameter into a second type parameter.


{{-- COVARIANT: out T. Legal ONLY in an OUTPUT position. --}}
public interface IReadOnlyCollection<out T> : IEnumerable<T>
{
    int Count { get; }
}

public class Animal { public string Name { get; init; } = ""; }
public class Dog : Animal { public bool Barks { get; init; }

public static void Covariant()
{
    IReadOnlyCollection<Animal> animals = new List<Dog>();
    // ^ LEGAL, and the whole reason 'out' exists: a
    //   IReadOnlyCollection<Dog> IS an IReadOnlyCollection<Animal>,
    //   because you can only read animals out of it.

    // List<Dog> dogs = animals;      ERROR: the reverse. A list of
    //                              animals might contain a cat,
    //                              and you cannot put a cat into a
    //                              List<Dog>.
}

{{-- CONTRAVARIANT: in T. Legal ONLY in an INPUT position. --}}
public interface IComparer<in T>
{
    int Compare(T? x, T? y);
}

public static void Contravariant()
{
    IComparer<Animal> animals = Comparer<Dog>.Default;
    // ^ LEGAL, and slightly surprising: a comparer that can compare
    //   DOGS can be used where a comparer that can compare ANIMALS
    //   is required, because it handles more of the domain.

    // Comparer<Animal> a = Comparer<Dog>.Default;   ERROR: the
    //                                               reverse. A dog
    //                                               comparer cannot
    //                                               compare animals.
}

{{-- AND NOT BOTH, which is the restriction worth knowing: --}}
public interface IBad<in T, out T>          {{-- CS1961: an interface
                                                    cannot be both
                                                    contravariant
                                                    and covariant
                                                    in T --}}
{ }

{{-- WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: it is what makes the
     read-only interfaces usable without a COPY, and a copy of a
     collection is the most expensive thing in this area. --}}
static IEnumerable<Animal> ReadOnly(IReadOnlyList<Dog> dogs)
    => dogs;                              {{-- no copy, no
                                              ToList(), and no
                                              allocation --}}
static List<Animal> NeedsACopy(IReadOnlyList<Dog> dogs)
    => dogs.ToList();                    {{-- a copy, and here it
                                              is unavoidable: the
                                              RESULT is mutable --}}

7.6 Generics instead of reflection

Reflection is flexible and slow. Generics are fast and fixed at compile time. The right answer for a serialiser, a mapper, an ORM or a validation library is: keep the reflection for discovery, then generate a delegate once and call that. MethodInfo.CreateDelegate and Expression<T>.Compile() both do exactly that.

Reflection is the right tool for the case where the members are genuinely unknown at compile time — a plugin scanning an assembly, a serialiser reading attributes, a test framework finding every test. It is the wrong tool for everything else, because a member accessed reflectively is not checked by the compiler and its name is a string that a rename breaks silently.

The three costs

A reflective call is a lookup followed by an invoke, and the lookup is a hash of a string — so it is orders of magnitude slower than a direct call. The name is a string, so a rename that the compiler would normally catch produces a run-time failure. And the result is object, so a value type is boxed on the way out and unboxed on the way in, with no nullability information anywhere.

The generic alternative

A generic method with a constraint is checked at the call site, specialised by the compiler, and devirtualised where possible. Where the choice is between an interface and reflection, the interface is right. Where the choice is between a delegate and a generic method, the delegate is right, because a delegate's target is a specific method that the compiler verified.

// SLOW: reflection on every call
PropertyInfo? prop = type.GetProperty(name);
object? value = prop?.GetValue(instance);

// FAST: build a delegate once, cache it, then call it
static readonly ConcurrentDictionary<(Type, string), Func<object, object?>> Cache = new();

static Func<object, object?> Getter(type type, string name) =>
    Cache.GetOrAdd((type, name), key =>
    {
        PropertyInfo p = key.Item1.GetProperty(key.Item2, BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.Instance)
            ?? throw new ArgumentException($"No property {key.Item2}");
        return (object instance) => p.GetValue(instance);
    });

// FASTEST: a compiled expression, no reflection at run time at all
static Func<object, object> FastGetter<T>(string name)
{
    ParameterExpression param = Expression.Parameter(typeof(T), "x");
    MemberExpression body = Expression.Property(param, name);
    return Expression.Lambda<Func<object, object>>(
        Expression.Convert(body, typeof(object)), param).Compile();
}

// Best of all, when the shape is known at compile time: generics
static TProperty Get<T, TProperty>(Func<T, TProperty> selector, T instance)
    => selector(instance);

// AOT and trimming: reflection breaks at publish time
// EnableTrimAnalyzer, source-generated JSON contexts, and [DynamicallyAccessedMembers]

Source generators are the modern answer. A generator emits C# at build time, so the "reflection" becomes real code with no run-time cost, no trimming warnings and no JIT-time surprises. System.Text.Json source generation, LoggerMessage and most of ASP.NET Core’s model binding all use them.

Rule of thumb: use generics where you know the types at compile time, reflection for one-time discovery or genuinely dynamic dispatch, and a source generator when you need both. Never call Invoke or GetValue on a per-item path in a loop.

Exercises 7

  1. Write a generic Cache<TKey, TValue> with an LRU eviction policy, and call it with a class and a struct key type to compare memory and speed.
  2. Implement INumber<T> for your own fixed-point money type and write a Sum<T> that works for int, decimal and your type.
  3. Write a generic cache of property getters using MethodInfo.CreateDelegate, then measure against a direct property access for one million calls.
  4. Prove variance works: assign IEnumerable<string> to an IEnumerable<object> and show that the reverse fails, and explain why.
  5. Write a generic Deserialize<T> using Expression<T>.Compile() and compare its throughput with plain JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>.
  6. Add a constraint to a generic method that only works with structs, and read the compiler error before adding the interface constraint that you actually wanted.

{{-- REFLECTION: right when the members are genuinely UNKNOWN at
     compile time, wrong for everything else. --}}
public sealed class PluginScanner
{
    // RIGHT: a plugin's handlers are not known at compile time, so
    // this is what reflection is for.
    public IReadOnlyList<object> Scan(Assembly assembly)
    {
        var handlers = new List<object>();
        foreach (Type type in assembly.GetTypes())
        {
            if (type.GetCustomAttribute<HandlerAttribute>() is null) continue;
            object? instance = Activator.CreateInstance(type);
            handlers.Add(instance!);
        }
        return handlers;
    }
}

{{-- THE THREE COSTS, and the second is the one that bites: --}}
public static void TheCosts()
{
    // 1. A LOOKUP THEN AN INVOKE: orders of magnitude slower than a
    //    direct call, on a hot path.
    var method = typeof(Calculator).GetMethod("Add")!;
    var result = method.Invoke(null, [1, 2]);      // boxes the result

    // 2. THE NAME IS A STRING, so a rename the compiler would
    //    normally catch produces a RUN-TIME failure:
    //    typeof(Calculator).GetMethod("Addd")   null, and
    //    the next line throws NullReferenceException.
    //    Nothing in the compiler's world connects the string to
    //    the method.

    // 3. THE RESULT IS object: a value type is boxed on the way out
    //    and unboxed on the way in, and there is NO NULLABILITY
    //    INFORMATION ANYWHERE.
    var name = (string?)method.Invoke(null, null);
    //    ^ the compiler knows this is string? because you said so.
    //      It has no idea what the invoke returned.
}

{{-- THE GENERIC ALTERNATIVE, which is checked at the call,
     specialised, and devirtualised: --}}
public interface ICalculator { int Add(int a, int b); }

// AN INTERFACE, where the choice is between an interface and
// reflection — and the interface is right.
static int ViaInterface(ICalculator calc, int a, int b) => calc.Add(a, b);
// ^ a virtual call, checked, with no string and no boxing.

// A DELEGATE, where the choice is between a delegate and a generic
// method — and the delegate is right, because its target is a
// SPECIFIC METHOD THE COMPILER VERIFIED.
var add = new Func<int, int, int>(calculator.Add);
var total = add(1, 2);

// A CONSTRAINT, which is what makes a generic helper checkable:
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>
    => a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
// ^ a.CompareTo is checked ONCE at compile time for T. There is no
//   string, no object, and no unboxing.

{{-- WHERE REFLECTION IS GENUINELY RIGHT, and it is a short list: --}}
{{--   a plugin scanning an assembly
