     a serialiser reading attributes
     a test framework finding every test
     a dependency-injection container resolving by registration
   Everything else is an interface, a delegate, or a generic
   constraint — all of which are checked by the compiler and all of
   which survive a rename. --}}

8 · Delegates, Events & Lambdas

8.1 Func and Action8.2 Custom delegate types8.3 Lambda expressions8.4 Closures and capture8.5 Events and accessors8.6 Multicast delegates and weak events8.7 IEquatable, equality and GetHashCode

Chapter eight covers how C# passes behaviour around. A delegate is a type-safe function pointer; a lambda is syntax for creating one; an event is a delegate with access control and invocation protection. This is the machinery behind callbacks, LINQ, async, event handlers and the observer pattern that every .NET framework leans on.

8.1 Func and Action

The BCL ships generic delegate types so you rarely declare your own. Action is a void return, Func has a return type (the last type argument), and Predicate<T> is a Func<bool> with a name that documents intent.

The delegate types exist so that a lambda can be assigned without naming a delegate type at every call site. They are ordinary delegates with names the compiler knows, and every one of them allocates unless the target is a static method with no captures.

The seventeen shapes, and which to use

There are a delegate type per arity per return kind. In practice two cover most of what is written: a function returning a value, and one returning nothing. A parameterised function needs the generic form; a void one with arguments needs the action form. Writing a custom delegate type is worth it when the signature is passed across an API boundary, because the name documents it and the parameter names survive.

Allocation, and the one case that avoids it

A lambda that captures nothing and calls a static method compiles to a cached delegate instance, so no allocation happens per call. A lambda that captures a variable becomes an instance method on a compiler-generated closure object, so the delegate allocates — and a lambda inside a loop allocates per iteration.

using System;

// Action: 0 to 16 parameters, void return
Action          a0 = () => Console.WriteLine("hi");
Action<int>         a1 = n => Console.WriteLine(n);
Action<int, string>  a2 = (n, s) => Console.WriteLine($"{n} {s}");

// Func: the LAST type argument is the return type
Func<int>              f0 = () => 1;
Func<int, int>           f1 = x => x + 1;
Func<int, int, int>    f2 = (a, b) => a * b;
Func<string, bool>       p = string.IsNullOrEmpty;

// Predicate<T>: the framework's LINQ filter type
Predicate<int> isEven = n => n % 2 == 0;
Console.WriteLine(isEven(4));                       // True

// The value of naming your own delegate: it appears in IntelliSense
// public delegate TResult Transform<T, TResult>(T value);

// Passing a delegate around: no reflection, no allocation beyond the closure
static int Count<T>(IEnumerable<T> source, Predicate<T> match)
{
    int n = 0;
    foreach (var item in source) if (match(item)) n++;
    return n;
}

Console.WriteLine(Count(new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }, isEven));   // 2

// Delegates are immutable and thread-safe to invoke concurrently
// as long as the target method is. Invoke returns the LAST subscriber's value.

A lambda with no captured variables is cached by the compiler as a static delegate, so it allocates nothing. A lambda that captures variables allocates a closure object plus a delegate. That is the entire difference between x => x * 2 and y => x * y in a hot loop.

Keep delegate parameter lists to a handful of parameters. Beyond four, consider a small input record, which is self-documenting at the call site and refactor-friendly. A delegate with eleven object parameters is unreadable and unrefactorable.


{{-- ORDINARY DELEGATES WITH NAMES THE COMPILER KNOWS, and every
     one allocates unless the target is a STATIC METHOD WITH NO
     CAPTURES. --}}
public static class Shapes
{
    public static int Zero() => 0;
    public static int One(int a) => a;
    public static int Two(int a, int b) => a + b;
    public static void Do(int a) { }
    public static void Do2(int a, int b) { }

    public static void AllTheShapes()
    {
        Func<int>                f0 = Zero;      // no args, returns
        Func<int, int>           f1 = One;       // one arg, returns
        Func<int, int, int>      f2 = Two;       // two, returns
        Action                   a0 = () => { }; // no args, void
        Action<int>              a1 = Do;        // one, void
        Action<int, int>         a2 = Do2;       // two, void

        // ^ ONE PER ARITY PER RETURN KIND. In practice two cover
        //   most of what is written: Func<T, TResult> and Action<T>.
    }
}

{{-- ALLOCATION, and the one case that avoids it: --}}
public static void NoAllocation(int x)
{
    // NO CAPTURES AND A STATIC TARGET: the compiler caches ONE
    // delegate instance and reuses it, so this line allocates
    // NOTHING per call.
    Predicate<int> p = static n => n > 0;
    Func<int, bool> f = static n => n > x;
    // ^ CARRIES x, so it becomes an instance method on a closure
    //   object, and the delegate ALLOCATES. Per call, and per
    //   iteration if it is in a loop.

    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
    {
        Action a = () => Console.WriteLine(x);
        // ^ ALLOCATES A CLOSURE PER ITERATION: 1,000 objects that
        //   die immediately, which a GC profile reports as an
        //   allocation RATE rather than as the loop.
    }

    // THE FIX for the loop case: compute outside, or use a state
    // object that is created once.
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
    {
        int captured = x;
        Action a = () => Console.WriteLine(captured);
        // ^ still allocates per iteration. The only fix is to hoist
        //   the delegate out, or to use a loop variable the
        //   compiler can prove does not change.
    }
}

{{-- AND WHEN A CUSTOM DELEGATE TYPE IS WORTH WRITING — which is
     when the signature crosses an API boundary, because the name
     documents it and the PARAMETER NAMES survive into intellisense
     and into the call site. --}}
public delegate bool OrderFilter(Order order, Customer customer);
{{-- ^ Compare(x, y) tells a reader nothing. OrderFilter(order,
     customer) does. --}}

8.2 Custom delegate types

A custom delegate declaration is worth it when the name carries meaning, when you want to constrain the parameters, or when you want to add attributes such as [InterpolatedStringHandler]. Otherwise Func and Action are fine.

A custom delegate type names a signature. It is worth writing one when the signature crosses an API boundary — a framework extension point, an event, a pipeline stage — because the name documents what the parameters are and the parameter names survive into the call site and into intellisense.

The variance a delegate gets for free

Every delegate type is contravariant in its parameter types and covariant in its return type, which is what lets a Func<object, string> be assigned where a Func<string, string> is expected. This is the property that makes the framework's delegate-heavy APIs composable, and it is why a delegate can be stored in a collection of the base delegate type.

Where a custom type is a mistake

For a signature used once, or for a signature that is a specialisation of one of the seventeen. A named delegate type for something that is only ever passed to one method adds a type to the assembly and a name to learn, and it cannot be inferred at a call site the way Func can — so every call site that uses it must name it, which is more typing rather than less.

// Declaration: return type first, then name, then parameter list
public delegate void LogHandler(string level, string message);
public delegate TResult Transform<T, TResult>(T value);
public delegate bool TryParse<T>(string text, out T result);

// Use it: a named type documents intent at every call site
LogHandler logger = (level, message) => Console.WriteLine($"[{level}] {message}");
logger("INFO", "started");

// Variance on delegates: in for inputs, out for the return
// public delegate TResult Converter<in TFrom, out TTo>(TFrom value);

// Delegates with ref/out parameters, and the TryParse pattern
TryParse<int> parser = static (text, out int result) =>
    int.TryParse(text, out result);

if (parser("42", out int n)) Console.WriteLine(n);

// Method group conversion: no lambda syntax needed
LogHandler fromMethod = Console.WriteLine;
Func<string, int> length = s => s.Length;
Func<string, int> same = string.Length;   // method group

// Invoking: () for no parameters, .Invoke() for the rest
logger.Invoke("WARN", "disk almost full");
a0();

A delegate and a lambda are interchangeable at any call site. Write the method group where the name already says what it does (list.ForEach(Console.WriteLine)) and a lambda where there is some transformation to express.

Adding static to a lambda (static (a, b) => a + b) tells the compiler it captures nothing. That is a free assertion, it prevents an accidental closure from being created during a refactor, and the C# compiler will warn you if the assertion breaks.


{{-- A CUSTOM DELEGATE TYPE NAMES A SIGNATURE, and it is worth
     writing one when the signature CROSSES AN API BOUNDARY. --}}
public delegate bool OrderFilter(Order order, Customer customer);
public delegate Task<Order> OrderFetcher(long id, CancellationToken ct);

public static class Pipeline
{
    public static IReadOnlyList<Order> Run(
        IEnumerable<Order> orders,
        OrderFilter filter)                    {{-- compare(x, y)
                                                     tells a reader
                                                     NOTHING;
                                                     OrderFilter(
                                                       order,
                                                       customer)
                                                     does --}}
    {
        return orders.Where(o => filter(o, o.Customer)).ToList();
    }
}

{{-- AND THE VARIANCE EVERY DELEGATE GETS FOR FREE, which is what
     makes the framework's delegate-heavy APIs composable: --}}
public delegate TOutput Converter<in TInput, out TOutput>(TInput input);

static void Variance()
{
    // EVERY DELEGATE IS contravariant in its parameters and
    // covariant in its return, so:
    Func<Animal, object> wide = (Dog d) => d;
    // ^ LEGAL: a delegate that handles Dogs satisfies one that must
    //   handle Animals, and a delegate returning object satisfies
    //   one declared to return Animal.

    // Func<object, Animal> narrow = (Dog d) => d;
    // ^ ERROR: a Dog-returning delegate cannot be used where
    //   something returning Animal must be guaranteed, because the
    //   CALLER may be told it is a Dog and write an Animal.
}

{{-- WHERE A CUSTOM TYPE IS A MISTAKE: --}}
public delegate int Transform1(int x);          {{-- a specialisation
                                                      of
                                                      Func<int,int>,
                                                      so the
                                                      name adds a
                                                      type and a
                                                      thing to
                                                      learn --}}

public delegate int Transform2(int x);          {{-- used ONCE, so
                                                      the same --}}

static void CostOfNaming()
{
    var doubled = Apply(new Transform1(x => x * 2));
    // ^ EVERY CALL SITE MUST NAME IT, because a custom delegate
    //   type is not inferred. With Func<int, int> the call site
    //   writes nothing, which is LESS typing rather than more.
}

{{-- THE TEST: does the signature cross an API boundary — a
     framework extension point, an event, a pipeline stage, an API
     other people call? If yes, name it. If it is used once inside
     your own code, use Func or Action and keep the type count
     down. --}}

8.3 Lambda expressions

A lambda is an anonymous function. There are two forms: the expression lambda x => x * 2, and the statement lambda x => { return x * 2; }. C# 10 added explicit parameter types and natural types, which lets a lambda participate in overload resolution when inference alone is ambiguous.

A lambda is a method with no name, and the compiler turns it into either a static method — when it captures nothing — or an instance method on a closure object. Which one it becomes determines whether the resulting delegate allocates, and that is the only performance question a lambda raises.

Statement versus expression

A statement lambda has a block and can contain control flow, local functions and multiple statements. An expression lambda is a single expression whose value becomes the result, and it can be a method call, a conditional, a switch expression or a new expression. The expression form is worth preferring where it applies because it keeps the lambda to one line and makes it obvious that nothing else happens.

Where the compiler needs a target type

A lambda's parameter types are inferred from the delegate type it is being converted to, so a lambda with untyped parameters only compiles where a target type is expected. That is why passing one to an overload set where two delegates are applicable is an error, and why naming the delegate type at the call resolves it.

// Expression lambda
Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;

// Statement lambda: multiple statements need braces
Action<int, string> report = (code, msg) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{code}: {msg}");
    if (code == 0) Environment.Exit(0);
};

// Parentheses are required for zero parameters, optional, or >1 parameter
Action          x1 = () => { };
Action<int>         x2 = n => { };
Action<int, int>  x3 = (a, b) => { };

// Discard parameters: the lambda exists only for its return value
Func<string, bool> hasText = s => s is not (null or "");
_ = new HttpClient();

// C# 10: explicit types and a natural return type
Func<int, string> describe = (int n) => $"{n} items";
Func<int> guess = static (int n) => n;   // natural type inferred

// Local functions: a named, zero-allocation alternative to a lambda
static bool IsValid(string s) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s);

Console.WriteLine(new[] { "a", "", "b" }.Count(IsValid));

// Local functions can be recursive, which lambdas cannot
int Fact(int n) => n <= 1 ? 1 : n * Fact(n - 1);
Console.WriteLine(Fact(5));   // 120

A lambda that is converted to a delegate is compiled into a method on a compiler-generated closure class, or a static method if nothing is captured. That means lambdas are not slower than methods — the only cost is the one-time allocation of the closure.

Do not write async void lambdas outside event handlers. An async void method cannot be awaited, cannot be tested, and an exception thrown inside it crashes the process rather than being observable. Use async Task and await the result.


{{-- A LAMBDA IS A METHOD WITH NO NAME, and it becomes either a
     STATIC METHOD (no captures) or an INSTANCE METHOD ON A CLOSURE
     (captures) — and which one decides whether the delegate
     allocates. --}}
public static void WhichIsWhich(int x)
{
    // NO CAPTURES: compiled to a static method, and the delegate
    // instance is CACHED, so this allocates NOTHING.
    Predicate<int> uncaptured = n => n > 0;

    // CAPTURES x: becomes an instance method on a closure object,
    // so the delegate ALLOCATES.
    Func<int, bool> captured = n => n > x;
    // ^ ONE allocation per assignment, which is why this pattern in
    //   a LOOP is the single most common avoidable allocation in
    //   C#.
}

{{-- AND THE LOOP CASE, where it becomes the dominant cost: --}}
public static void InALoop(int x)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
    {
        Action a = () => Console.WriteLine(x);
        a();
        // ^ 1,000 CLOSURE OBJECTS that die immediately. A GC
        //   profile reports this as an ALLOCATION RATE rather than
        //   as the loop, which is why it is found late.
    }

    // THE FIX for the common shape: the lambda does not need to be
    // inside the loop at all.
    Action a = () => Console.WriteLine(x);
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) a();
    // ^ ONE closure, hoisted, and 1,000 calls.
}

{{-- STATEMENT versus EXPRESSION, and the expression form is worth
     preferring where it applies: --}}
static void BothForms(int n)
{
    Func<int, int> statement = x =>
    {
        var y = x * 2;             // a block: control flow allowed
        if (y > 100) y = 100;
        return y;
    };

    Func<int, int> expression = x => x > 50 ? 100 : x * 2;
    // ^ ONE LINE, and it is obvious that nothing else happens —
    //   which is the property the expression form buys.
}

{{-- WHERE THE COMPILER NEEDS A TARGET TYPE, and the error it
     produces: --}}
static void NeedTargetType(List<int> xs)
{
    // xs.ConvertAll(n => n * 2);     fine: one applicable overload,
    //                                 so the delegate type is known

    // OverloadApply(xs, n => n);     CS0121 or CS0411: the lambda's
    //                                 PARAMETER TYPES cannot be
    //                                 inferred, because the
    //                                 argument has two applicable
    //                                 delegate overloads and the
    //                                 compiler does not choose.

    // THE FIX: name the delegate type at the call.
    OverloadApply<int>(xs, (int n) => n);
    // ^(int n) makes the lambda's parameter explicit, which
    //   resolves it without naming the method's type argument.
}

static void OverloadApply<T>(IEnumerable<T> xs, Func<T, bool> keep) { }
static void OverloadApply<T>(IEnumerable<T> xs, Predicate<T> keep) { }

8.4 Closures and capture

A lambda that references a local variable captures it. The compiler hoists that variable into a closure object, and the lambda reads it through that object. Two consequences follow: the variable outlives its scope, and it is shared by every lambda that captures it — which is a data race waiting to happen in parallel code.

A closure is the compiler-generated object a capturing lambda is compiled into. It exists because a lambda body that references a local needs somewhere to keep that local alive, and because a method with no name cannot have fields. So a captured local becomes a field on the closure, and the lambda becomes an instance method reading it.

Capture is by reference to the variable

A captured local is not copied into the closure; the closure holds a reference to the variable's storage. So a lambda that runs after the loop has finished sees the loop's final value rather than the value at the point the lambda was created — which is the reason a loop that starts tasks needs a local copy.

What that means for a loop

Starting one task per iteration and capturing the loop variable is the classic defect: every task sees the last value, so every task processes the same item. The fix is to declare a local inside the loop, which gives each iteration its own variable — and since a declaration inside a loop body is a new variable per iteration, that is enough without an explicit copy.

// Capture: the variable outlives the method that declared it
static Func<int> MakeCounter()
{
    int count = 0;
    return () => ++count;      // count is hoisted into a closure
}

var next = MakeCounter();
Console.WriteLine(next());   // 1
Console.WriteLine(next());   // 2  -- state persists

// Two lambdas capturing the same variable SHARE it
int shared = 0;
Action inc = () => shared++;
Action read = () => Console.WriteLine(shared);
inc(); inc(); read();          // 2

// Each loop iteration in a for-loop gets its OWN copy (C# 5+)
var actions = new List<Action>();
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) actions.Add(() => Console.WriteLine(i));
foreach (var a in actions) a();   // 0 1 2  -- correct since C# 5

// ...but a foreach variable is a SINGLE variable, so this is a classic bug
// foreach (var item in list) actions.Add(() => Use(item));  // all see the LAST item
// foreach (var item in list) { var copy = item; actions.Add(() => Use(copy)); }  // fixed

// Closures in LINQ: the deferred-execution trap
int threshold = 10;
var query = items.Where(i => i.Count > threshold);   // captures threshold
threshold = 100;                                  // changed AFTER the query was built
foreach (var i in query) { }                     // uses 100, not 10

// Fix: copy to a local, or pass a parameter
int limit = threshold;
var safe = items.Where(i => i.Count > limit);

The deferred-execution trap is the most important item here. A LINQ query stores a recipe, not a result. Anything the lambda captures is read at enumeration time, so changing a captured variable between building and enumerating a query changes the answer.

Captured variables shared across threads need synchronisation. A counter captured by a lambda and incremented from Parallel.ForEach needs Interlocked.Increment or a lock; the compiler gives no warning and the result is a wrong number, not an error.


{{-- A CLOSURE IS THE COMPILER-GENERATED OBJECT a capturing lambda
     is compiled into, because a lambda body referencing a local
     needs somewhere to keep it and a method cannot have fields. --}}
public static Func<int> MakeCounter()
{
    int count = 0;
    return () => ++count;
    // ^ 'count' BECOMES A FIELD on a generated closure object, and
    //   the lambda becomes an instance method reading it. Two
    //   calls to MakeCounter produce two closures with two counts.
}

static void ClosuresAreIndependent()
{
    var a = MakeCounter();
    var b = MakeCounter();
    a(); a(); a();               // 3
    b();                          // 1: a DIFFERENT closure, so b's
                                 // count started at zero
}

{{-- AND CAPTURE IS BY REFERENCE TO THE VARIABLE, not a copy of
     its value: --}}
public static Action[] MadeOutside()
{
    var actions = new Action[3];

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        actions[i] = () => Console.WriteLine(i);
    // ^ ALL THREE print 2, because they share one variable and the
    //   loop has finished by the time they run.

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
    {
        int local = i;            // ^ A DECLARATION INSIDE THE LOOP
        actions[i] = () => Console.WriteLine(local);
    }
    // ^ prints 0, 1, 2: a declaration inside a loop body is a NEW
    //   VARIABLE PER ITERATION, so each closure holds its own. The
    //   explicit copy is unnecessary in C# 5 and later — which is
    //   why an old workaround left in place is just a comment that
    //   lies.
    return actions;
}

{{-- WHICH IS THE CLASSIC DEFECT, and it is worth knowing in the
     form that appears in a real service: --}}
public static async Task StartAll(IEnumerable<Order> orders)
{
    var tasks = new List<Task>();
    foreach (var order in orders)
        tasks.Add(ProcessAsync(order));
    await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
    // ^ correct: ProcessAsync is an ordinary call, not a lambda,
    //   so each iteration captures its own 'order' parameter.

    foreach (var order in orders)
        tasks.Add(Task.Run(async () => await ProcessAsync(order)));
    // ^ ALSO correct: the loop body's 'order' is a new variable per
    //   iteration, and the lambda captures that one rather than the
    //   enumerator's. This is why the fix is one line rather than
    //   a copy.
}

8.5 Events and accessors

An event is a wrapper around a delegate with two protections: only the declaring type can raise it, and only the declaring type can assign or clear the delegate. Subscribers can only add or remove. This is why you subscribe with += and never assign an event directly.

An event is a pair of accessors over a delegate, and the compiler generates them. The difference from a delegate field is that a public event can only be invoked by its declaring type, so a subscriber cannot raise another subscriber's handler — which is the whole reason events exist.

Why not a delegate field

A public delegate field can be invoked by anyone holding a reference, so any code with the object could raise the event. An event hides the invocation behind an add-and-remove pair, and the only ways to raise it are inside the type. That is an encapsulation property rather than a style preference, and it is the reason the framework's events are events.

The subscription leak

An event is a reference from the publisher to the subscriber, which means a subscriber that subscribes and never unsubscribes keeps itself alive for as long as the publisher lives. For a short-lived publisher and a long-lived subscriber that is harmless; for a long-lived publisher — a singleton service — it is a leak that grows with every re-registration.

public sealed class Button
{
    // A plain event: the framework creates add/remove accessors for you
    public event Action? Clicked;
    public event EventHandler<string>? TextChanged;   // the standard shape

    // A field-like event with an explicit type
    public event EventHandler? Load;

    // Custom accessors: full control, needed for weak events and add/remove counting
    private EventHandler? _changed;

    public event EventHandler Changed
    {
        add    { _changed += value; this.HandlerCount++; }
        remove { _changed -= value; this.HandlerCount--; }
    }

    public int HandlerCount { get; private set; }

    // Raising: the null-conditional invoke is the idiomatic form
    public void Raise()
    {
        Clicked?.Invoke();
        TextChanged?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
        _changed?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
    }
}

// Subscribing and unsubscribing
var button = new Button();
void OnClick() => Console.WriteLine("clicked");

button.Clicked += OnClick;
button.TextChanged += (s, e) => Console.WriteLine("text");
button.Clicked -= OnClick;         // the SAME delegate instance removes it

// EventHandler<T>: convention is (object? sender, T args)
public sealed class OrderPlacedEventArgs(string orderId) : EventArgs
{
    public string OrderId { get; } = orderId;
}

A method group subscription is a different delegate instance each time, so button.Clicked -= Console.WriteLine will not unsubscribe a handler added as button.Clicked += Console.WriteLine. Store the handler in a field, or use a local function, and use the same variable for both.

An event invocation list that throws stops at the first exception and leaves the remaining subscribers un-notified. For long-lived subscriptions, either wrap each invocation in its own try/catch in the raiser, or use GetInvocationList() and invoke each handler in isolation.


{{-- AN EVENT IS A PAIR OF ACCESSORS over a delegate, and the
     compiler generates them. --}}
public sealed class OrderService
{
    // THE HANDLER TYPE first, so the event's signature documents
    // itself.
    public delegate void OrderChanged(object sender, OrderEventArgs e);

    public event OrderChanged? Changed;

    // ^ A PUBLIC EVENT can only be invoked by its declaring type.
    //   That is the whole reason events exist.

    public void Publish(Order order)
    {
        Changed?.Invoke(this, new OrderEventArgs(order));
        // ^ THE ONLY INVOCATION, and it is inside the type.
    }

    // WHICH A PUBLIC DELEGATE FIELD DOES NOT GIVE YOU:
    public OrderChanged? NotAnEvent;    {{-- ANY code holding a
                                               reference can raise
                                               it, including
                                               code that only ever
                                               meant to SUBSCRIBE --}}
}

{{-- SO THE ENCAPSULATION PROPERTY IS THE POINT: --}}
static void CannotRaiseFromOutside(OrderService service)
{
    service.NotAnEvent?.Invoke(this, new OrderEventArgs(new Order(1)));
    // ^ COMPILES, and any subscriber's handler runs. With an event,
    //   this line does not exist.
}

{{-- AND THE SUBSCRIPTION LEAK, which is a REFERENCE from the
     publisher to the subscriber: --}}
public sealed class OrderCache
{
    private readonly OrderService _service;
    public event EventHandler? Refreshed;

    public OrderCache(OrderService service)
    {
        _service = service;
        // A LONG-LIVED PUBLISHER holding a subscription from a
        // SHORT-LIVED SUBSCRIBER is harmless: the subscriber dies
        // first.
        _service.Changed += OnChanged;
    }

    private void OnChanged(object? s, OrderEventArgs e) => Refreshed?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);

    public void Dispose() => _service.Changed -= OnChanged;
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE ORDER THAT LEAKS: a LONG-LIVED publisher
     (a singleton service) holding a subscription from a
     SHORT-LIVED subscriber that re-registers on every request. Each
     re-registration adds a reference, nothing removes the old one,
     and the subscriber's previous instances stay alive for the
     lifetime of the service. --}}

8.6 Multicast delegates and weak events

A delegate can hold a list of targets. Adding with += appends, and invoking calls every subscriber in order, returning the last one’s value. Because the publisher holds a strong reference to each subscriber, a long-lived publisher with short-lived subscribers is a memory leak unless the subscription is removed.

A delegate holds an invocation list, and invoking it calls every entry in order. That is what makes an event with several subscribers work, and it is also what makes three properties surprising: the return value is the last handler's, an exception in one handler stops the rest, and removing a handler removes one instance rather than all of them.

The return value problem

Only the last handler's return value survives, so a multicast delegate used for its return value computes something nobody expected. A multicast Func is almost always a mistake, and it is worth knowing why rather than treating it as a general rule.

Exception handling, and the weak-event answer

An exception thrown by one handler propagates out of the invocation and the remaining handlers do not run — so a subscriber that throws silently disables every subscriber after it. And a strong reference from a long-lived publisher to a short-lived subscriber keeps that subscriber alive. Both are solved by the weak-event pattern, where the publisher holds the handler weakly and a dispatcher re-establishes the subscription.

// Multicast invocation: every handler runs, in subscription order
LogHandler h1 = (l, m) => Console.WriteLine("file:  " + m);
LogHandler h2 = (l, m) => Console.WriteLine("net:  " + m);
LogHandler both = h1 + h2;

both("INFO", "started");   // both run
both -= h1;                              // h2 only

// Inspecting the list
Console.WriteLine(both.Method.Name);
Console.WriteLine(both.GetInvocationList().Length);

// Invoking each handler in isolation so one failure does not stop the rest
static void RaiseAll(EventHandler? handlers, object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    if (handlers is null) return;
    foreach (EventHandler h in handlers.GetInvocationList())
    {
        try { h(sender, e); }
        catch (Exception ex) { Console.WriteLine($"handler failed: {ex.Message}"); }
    }
}

// The leak: publisher -> delegate -> subscriber keeps the subscriber alive
// Fix A: unsubscribe in the subscriber's Dispose (the IDisposable answer)
// Fix B: a weak event manager that stores a WeakReference to the target

// Fix B, sketched:
sealed class WeakEvent<T> where T : EventArgs
{
    private readonly List<WeakReference<EventHandler<T>>> _handlers = new();

    public void Add(EventHandler<T> h)
    {
        _handlers.RemoveAll(w => !w.TryGetTarget(out _));   // prune dead
        _handlers.Add(new WeakReference<EventHandler<T>>(h));
    }

    public void Raise(object sender, T e)
    {
        foreach (var w in _handlers)
            if (w.TryGetTarget(out var h)) h(sender, e);
    }
}

The WPF, WinForms and System.IO worlds all implement weak events differently. If you are building a publisher that outlives its subscribers, either expose IDisposable and require unsubscription, or use a weak-reference pattern — but decide deliberately, because the default is a leak.

ObservableCollection<T> avoids the problem entirely by making the change notification part of the collection’s contract: WPF and WinForms data binding subscribe and unsubscribe automatically. If your collection is going to be bound, make it observable from the start.


{{-- A DELEGATE HOLDS AN INVOCATION LIST, and invoking it calls
     every entry IN ORDER. --}}
public sealed class Bus
{
    public event Action<string>? Message;

    public void Send(string m) => Message?.Invoke(m);
    // ^ three subscribers, three calls, in SUBSCRIPTION order.
}

static void TheThreeSurprises()
{
    var bus = new Bus();
    bus.Message += m => Console.WriteLine("one");
    bus.Message += m => Console.WriteLine("two");

    bus.Send("hi");      // "one" then "two"

    // 1. THE RETURN VALUE IS THE LAST HANDLER'S, so a multicast
    //    Func is almost always a MISTAKE:
    var result = multicastFunc("x");
    // ^ whatever the SECOND handler returned, and the first
    //   handler's result is discarded — which is not documented
    //   anywhere and produces a wrong answer nobody can trace.

    // 2. AN EXCEPTION IN ONE HANDLER STOPS THE REST, so a subscriber
    //    that throws SILENTLY DISABLES every subscriber after it:
    bus.Message += m => throw new InvalidOperationException(m);
    bus.Message += m => Console.WriteLine("never runs");
    bus.Send("hi");
    // ^ "never runs" is not printed, and the exception escapes the
    //   whole Send call. A subscriber three weeks old that now
    //   throws has disabled everything registered after it, and
    //   nothing in the event's declaration says so.

    // 3. REMOVING A HANDLER REMOVES ONE INSTANCE:
    Handler h = m => Log(m);
    bus.Message += h;
    bus.Message += h;      // the same delegate twice
    bus.Message -= h;      // removes ONE. The second is still
                           // subscribed, and 'bus.Message' is not
                           // null.
    // ^ which is why Dispose must run the same number of times as
    //   the subscription, and why a subscribe that is not paired
    //   with an unsubscribe leaves the handler live.
}

{{-- AND THE WEAK-EVENT ANSWER to both, where the publisher is
     long-lived: --}}
public sealed class WeakEvent<TSender, TArgs>
    where TSender : class
{
    private readonly List<WeakReference<Action<object, TArgs>>> _subs = [];

    public void Subscribe(Action<object, TArgs> handler)
        => _subs.Add(new WeakReference<Action<object, TArgs>>(handler));

    public void Unsubscribe(Action<object, TArgs> handler)
        => _subs.RemoveAll(w => !w.TryGetTarget(out var t) || t == handler);
    // ^ removes DEAD entries as well as the matching one, so the
    //   list does not grow without bound.

    public void Raise(TSender sender, TArgs e)
    {
        // A DEAD SUBSCRIBER IS SKIPPED rather than crashing the
        // dispatcher, and each handler is invoked inside its own
        // try so one throwing does not stop the rest.
        foreach (var weak in _subs)
        {
            if (!weak.TryGetTarget(out var handler)) continue;
            try { handler(sender, e); }
            catch (Exception ex) { Log(ex); }
        }
    }
}
{{-- ^ the publisher holds the handler WEAKLY, so a short-lived
     subscriber can be collected, and the dispatcher re-establishes
     the subscription from the subscriber's own lifetime. This is
     the WPF and WinForms pattern, and it is the right answer
     whenever a singleton raises an event that a request-scoped
     object subscribes to. --}}

8.7 IEquatable, equality and GetHashCode

Equality has three layers in .NET: the == operator, Equals, and GetHashCode. Collections use the last two, never the operator. Implement IEquatable<T> and the two methods together, or use a record, which does it correctly for you.

// The correct manual implementation
public readonly record struct Version(int Major, int Minor) : IComparable<Version>
{
    // record generates Equals/GetHashCode/== for you.
    // For a plain class you would write all three yourself:
    public bool Equals(Version? other) => other is not null && Major == other.Major && Minor == other.Minor;
    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Major, Minor);
    // public static bool operator ==(Version? a, Version? b) => Equals(a, b);
    // public static bool operator !=(Version? a, Version? b) => !Equals(a, b);

    public int CompareTo(Version? other)
        => other is null ? 1 : (Major, Minor).CompareTo((other.Major, other.Minor));
}

// GetHashCode.Combine gives a well-mixed hash from multiple fields
Console.WriteLine(HashCode.Combine("a", 1, true));

// Equality is used by: Distinct, GroupBy, Contains, IndexOf,
// dictionary keys, HashSet members, List.Contains, SequenceEqual
var unique = new[] { new Version(1, 0), new Version(1, 0 }
    .Distinct().Count();   // 1

// string equality: always specify the comparison
Console.WriteLine("a".Equals("A"));                          // False (ordinal)
Console.WriteLine("a".Equals("A", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));   // True

// Reference equality: ReferenceEquals and object.ReferenceEquals
var a = new List<int>();
var b = a;
Console.WriteLine(ReferenceEquals(a, b));   // True

The rule that catches people: if you override Equals, you must override GetHashCode in the same commit. Objects that are equal but hash differently land in different buckets, and Distinct and HashSet return duplicates.

Two more rules: GetHashCode must not change while the object is in a hash-based collection, and it must be consistent with Equals across an entire process run. A hash derived from a mutable field or from DateTime.Now violates both.

Exercises 8

  1. Write a static counter and build three lambdas that increment it. Show the per-call allocation difference between a capturing and a non-capturing lambda.
  2. Implement a type with == but no Equals override, put two instances in a HashSet, and explain the result.
  3. Write a foreach loop that adds lambdas capturing the item, and fix the classic bug with a local copy. Prove the fix with output.
  4. Build a tiny event source with custom add/remove accessors, count subscribers, and raise the event to all of them.
  5. Create a publisher with three subscribers, show with a WeakReference that unsubscribing allows collection, then repeat with a weak event manager.
  6. Write a LINQ query that captures a mutable threshold, change the threshold after building the query, and observe the deferred-execution effect. Then fix it.

{{-- THE CONTRACT, and it has THREE parts that must agree: --}}
public sealed class Money : IEquatable<Money>
{
    public required decimal Amount   { get; init; }
    public required string  Currency { get; init; }

    // 1. Equals(T). The TYPE-SAFE form: no boxing, and it is what
    //    the == operator calls, so overriding it makes == correct.
    public bool Equals(Money? other)
        => other is not null
        && Amount == other.Amount
        && Currency == other.Currency;   // ^ the comparer is part of
                                        //   the equality, exactly
                                        //   as it is part of a
                                        //   dictionary key
}

{{-- 2. GetHashCode MUST AGREE with Equals, and this is the rule
     that gets broken: --}}
public sealed class CaseInsensitiveKey : IEquatable<CaseInsensitiveKey>
{
    public required string Value { get; init; }

    public bool Equals(CaseInsensitiveKey? other)
        => other is not null
        && string.Equals(Value, other.Value, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

    public override int GetHashCode()
        => StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.GetHashCode(Value);
        // ^ THE SAME COMPARER. If Equals ignores case and
        //   GetHashCode does not, then a HashSet holds BOTH forms as
        //   separate entries and Contains says false for a key that
        //   Equals says is the same object. Every collection lookup
        //   uses the hash first, so the symptom is "the object is in
        //   the set but it cannot be found".
}

public sealed class Broken
{
    public required string Value { get; init; }

    public bool Equals(Broken? other)
        => other is not null
        && string.Equals(Value, other.Value, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

    public override int GetHashCode() => Value.GetHashCode();
        // ^ ORDINAL, while Equals IGNORES CASE. Two objects the
        //   operator calls equal can hash to different buckets, so
        //   the HashSet's Contains returns false for one of them.
        //   Nothing warns, and the failure is intermittent.
}

{{-- 3. THE == OPERATOR AND object.Equals, which are DIFFERENT from
     each other and from the typed Equals: --}}
public static void ThreeEqualMethods()
{
    var a = new Money { Amount = 100, Currency = "GBP" };
    var b = new Money { Amount = 100, Currency = "GBP" };

    a.Equals(b);              // the TYPED one: no boxing, and what
                              // the operator calls
    a.Equals((object)b);      // object.Equals, which DISPATCHES BACK
                              // to the typed one — so this is right
                              // by accident rather than by design
    a == b;                   // THE OPERATOR, which you must also
                              // define or it uses reference equality
                              // and says FALSE for two identical
                              // values
}
{{-- ^ THE THREE MUST AGREE. A type that implements the typed Equals
     and defines == but does not override object.Equals works
     through the typed path and fails through a reference-typed
     variable — which is why the defect appears only after somebody
     has typed a variable as object or as a collection element. --}}

{{-- AND WHERE IT IS NOT WORTH WRITING BY HAND: --}}
// valueT HAS THE GENERATED Equals AND GetHashCode, already correct,
// AND the operator, all three consistent.
var x = new MoneyValue(100, "GBP");
var y = new MoneyValue(100, "GBP");
// x == y                      true, with no code written
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE VERSION TO REACH FOR: a record or a record
     struct generates all three consistently, so a hand-written
     triple can only ever introduce the disagreement the record
     version does not have. --}}
public sealed record MoneyValue(decimal Amount, string Currency);

9 · Exceptions & Error Handling

9.1 try, catch, finally9.2 Exception filters9.3 Custom exception types9.4 Inner exceptions and AggregateException9.5 The Result pattern9.6 Practices and anti-patterns

Chapter nine covers what happens when things go wrong. Exceptions are the mechanism for the exceptional, and they are expensive: a throw costs microseconds and a stack trace. That single fact explains the whole design philosophy of this chapter — exceptions for the genuinely exceptional, and a result type for the expected failures.

9.1 try, catch, finally

The shape is always try / any number of catch clauses, most specific first / optional finally. A catch without a type catches everything, which is almost never what you want outside of a top-level handler.

A try block wraps code that can fail, a catch handles it, and a finally runs either way. Three things about the arrangement matter more than the syntax: a catch that rethrows loses the original stack trace if it constructs a new exception, a finally that throws hides the exception that was already propagating, and a bare catch catches everything including the ones nobody can recover from.

What each part is for

The try block should be as small as the operation that can fail. A large block that wraps a whole request means that an exception from an unrelated line is handled by whatever catches it, and the handler cannot tell which operation failed. The catch should handle only what it can do something about, and the finally should only release resources — anything else in a finally runs on the exception path, where an exception of its own replaces the one that was propagating.

Exception filters

A filter on a catch runs before the handler is chosen, and an exception that the filter rejects propagates to an outer handler without unwinding the stack. That makes a filter the right place for a condition that is expensive or that produces a diagnostic, because it happens without having entered the handler.

// try/catch/finally: the canonical shape
try
{
    string content = File.ReadAllText(path);
    Console.WriteLine(content.Length);
}
catch (FileNotFoundException ex)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"Missing: {ex.FileName}");
}
catch (UnauthorizedAccessException ex)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine("Permission denied.");
    return default;
}
catch (IOException ex) when (ex.Message.Contains("disk"))
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine("Transient: retry later.");
}
finally
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine("always runs");
}

// try/finally without catch: cleanup without handling
try { DoWork(); }
finally { Cleanup(); }

// Rethrow, preserving the original stack trace
try { Risky(); }
catch (FormatException ex)
{
    throw new ParseException("bad input", ex);   // inner exception kept
}

// The single most common exception-handling bug
// catch (Exception) { }   -- empty catch swallows EVERYTHING, including
// OutOfMemoryException and StackOverflowException, and hides real bugs.

// throw; re-throws the same exception with the original trace intact
// throw ex;  RESETS the trace to this line -- never do this

// Unwinding order: inner finally, then inner catch, then outer catch/finally

Use throw; to re-throw the current exception and throw ex; never: the second form resets the stack trace to the line of the re-throw and destroys the information you need to debug.

Catching Exception and returning a default value silently converts a bug into wrong data. That is far more expensive to diagnose later than a crash at the point of failure. If you must catch broadly, log at warning level with the full exception and re-throw, or translate it deliberately.


{{-- THREE THINGS THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE SYNTAX: --}}
static void SmallTry(string path)
{
    // THE try BLOCK AS SMALL AS THE FAILING OPERATION. A block
    // wrapping a whole request means an exception from an
    // UNRELATED line is handled by whatever catches it, and the
    // handler cannot tell which operation failed.
    try
    {
        string json = File.ReadAllText(path);
        Save(json);                     // ^ if THIS throws, a
    }                                  //   catch around the whole
    catch (IOException ex)             //   method will treat it as
    {                                  //   a file problem
        Log(ex);
    }
}

{{-- AND A RETHROW THAT LOSES THE STACK TRACE, which is the defect
     this area is most often blamed for: --}}
try
{
    Load();
}
catch (InvalidOperationException ex)
{
    // WRONG: a NEW exception with the old one as inner. The stack
    // trace now starts HERE, and the frames where it actually
    // happened are only reachable through the InnerException —
    // which a log aggregator rarely walks.
    throw new ApplicationException("could not load", ex);
}

catch (InvalidOperationException)
{
    // RIGHT: a bare rethrow preserves the ORIGINAL exception, its
    // type and its stack trace exactly.
    throw;
}
{{-- ^ which means: to ADD context, catch-and-wrap, but to ADD A
     LOG and continue, catch-and-log. Wrapping to add a message
     that nobody reads costs the one thing the exception was for. --}}

{{-- A BARE catch CATCHES EVERYTHING, including the ones nobody can
     recover from: --}}
try { Run(); }
catch { Restart(); }
{{-- WRONG: this catches OutOfMemoryException, StackOverflowException
     (where it can be caught at all), AccessViolationException and
     ThreadAbortException. Restarting after a stack overflow does
     not help, and catching it means the process continues in a
     state the runtime cannot describe. --}}

catch (Exception ex) when (IsRecoverable(ex))
{
    // ^ AN EXCEPTION FILTER: it runs BEFORE the handler is chosen,
    //   and an exception the filter rejects propagates to an outer
    //   handler WITHOUT UNWINDING THE STACK. That is why it is the
    //   right place for an expensive check or for a diagnostic:
    //   the stack is still intact when it runs.
}

catch (Exception ex) { Report(ex); throw; }

{{-- AND A finally THAT THROWS HIDES THE ORIGINAL: --}}
try { Run(); }
finally { Cleanup(); }        {{-- if Cleanup throws while an
                                    exception is PROPAGATING, the
                                    new exception REPLACES it and
                                    the original is LOST, along
                                    with the only stack trace
                                    anybody had --}}

{{-- SO A finally RELEASES AND DOES NOTHING ELSE: --}}
public static async Task ReadAsync(string path)
{
    await using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
    try
    {
        Process(stream);            // the only thing that can
    }                              // legitimately throw
    finally
    {
        // Nothing that can fail. Releasing is handled by the
        // using declaration above, which runs its dispose AFTER
        // this finally and reports its own failure separately.
    }
}

9.2 Exception filters

The when clause (C# 6) decides whether a catch applies without entering the block. A filter that throws is treated as false and the original exception continues unwinding, and a filter does not clear the "already handled" state, so catch order between filtered clauses matters less than you would expect.

A filter is a predicate on an exception, evaluated before any handler is entered. Two properties make it different from catching and rethrowing: the stack has not been unwrapped when it runs, so it can inspect the whole call chain, and an exception it rejects continues to the next handler without having been caught at all.

The second property is the one people miss

Catching, inspecting and rethrowing is almost the same thing and is not: the rethrowing form resets the exception's own information in some logging setups, and it means the exception has been caught by a handler that could have side effects. With a filter, an exception that does not match is invisible to that handler — it never became its exception.

When a filter is worth the cost

When the predicate is cheap and precise, always. When it is expensive — a stack walk, a database query — the cost is paid once per handler that filters, so a stack of six handlers each walking the stack walks it six times. The remedy is to filter once at the outermost handler rather than at each level.

// A filter that examines the exception before committing to the handler
try
{
    await client.SendAsync(request, ct);
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests)
{
    await Task.Delay(delay, ct);
    // retry
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode is >= 500)
{
    // server error: fail over
}
catch (HttpRequestException)
{
    // 4xx: do not retry
    throw;
}

// Filters can call logging without risking an exception inside the handler
catch (Exception ex) when (LogIfInteresting(ex)) { throw; }

// A retry helper built on filters and exception predicates
static async Task WithRetry<T>(
    Func<Task<T>> operation, int attempts, CancellationToken ct)
{
    for (int attempt = 1 ; ; attempt++)
    {
        try { return await operation(); }
        catch (Exception ex) when (attempt < attempts && IsTransient(ex))
        {
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(50 * attempt), ct);
        }
    }
}

// Why filters beat if-checks inside the catch:
//   1. The filter runs BEFORE the finally blocks of intervening frames, so the
//      stack is still intact and a debugger can step through it.
//   2. If the filter returns false the exception keeps unwinding, so filters
//      compose: several handlers can each decline.

Exception filters are the framework’s own mechanism. Task.Wait uses one to unwrap an AggregateException; ASP.NET Core uses them to decide whether a middleware should handle an error or let it continue up the pipeline.

For retries, classify rather than blanket-catch. Transient errors (timeouts, 429, 503) deserve a retry with backoff; a 400 or a NullReferenceException does not, and retrying it just delays the inevitable while multiplying the load.


{{-- A FILTER RUNS BEFORE ANY HANDLER IS ENTERED, and two properties
     follow: --}}
static void Filter(IOException ex)
{
    // 1. THE STACK HAS NOT BEEN UNWOUND, so the filter can inspect
    //    the whole call chain with a stack trace that is still the
    //    original.
    // 2. AN EXCEPTION IT REJECTS CONTINUES TO THE NEXT HANDLER
    //    WITHOUT HAVING BEEN CAUGHT AT ALL.
}

{{-- 2 IS THE PROPERTY PEOPLE MISS. Catching, inspecting and
     RETHROWING is almost the same thing and IS NOT: --}}
try
{
    Run();
}
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is TimeoutException && Attempts() > 2)
{
    throw new ServiceUnavailableException(ex.Message, ex);
}
{{-- ^ with a filter, a TimeoutException on the FIRST two attempts
     was NEVER caught by this handler — it propagated to an outer
     one, and this handler's catch block has no side effects that
     ran. The catch-inspect-rethrow form would have run them. --}}

{{-- WHERE FILTERS SHINE, and it is the diagnostic cases: --}}
static void Diagnostics()
{
    try { Run(); }

    catch (Exception ex) when (LogFirstAndRethrow(ex, "outer"))
    { }

    catch (Exception ex) when (LogFirstAndRethrow(ex, "inner"))
    { }
}

static bool LogFirstAndRethrow(Exception ex, string where)
{
    // ^ LOGS AND RETURNS FALSE, so the exception is NOT caught here
    //   and the NEXT handler logs it. With catch-inspect-rethrow
    //   both log entries appear and the second is a duplicate.
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"{where}: {ex.GetType().Name}");
    return false;
}

{{-- AND THE COST, which is worth knowing before adding filters to
     a deep stack: --}}
static void Expensive()
{
    try { Run(); }

    catch (Exception ex) when (NeedsStackWalk(ex))    // 1 walk
    { }

    catch (Exception ex) when (NeedsStackWalk(ex))    // ANOTHER walk
    { }

    catch (Exception ex) when (NeedsStackWalk(ex))    // AND ANOTHER
    { }
}
{{-- ^ THE PREDICATE IS PAID ONCE PER HANDLER THAT FILTERS. Six
     handlers each walking the stack walk it six times, on the
     failure path, which is exactly when nobody wants to spend
     time. THE REMEDY: filter ONCE, at the outermost handler, and
     let the rest catch broadly. --}}

{{-- AND THE STANDARD FILTER, which is the pattern worth copying: --}}
public sealed class TransientFailureException(string message) : Exception(message)
{
    public int Attempt { get; init; }
}

static async Task WithRetries(Func<Task> operation)
{
    for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++)
    {
        try
        {
            await operation();
            return;
        }
        catch (Exception ex) when (ex is TransientFailureException
                                   && attempt < 5)
        {
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(attempt));
            // ^ the DELAY IS INSIDE THE HANDLER, which is only
            //   correct because the filter proved the attempt limit
            //   has not been reached. Move the delay outside and the
            //   filter no longer controls it.
        }
    }
}

9.3 Custom exception types

A custom exception should carry structured data that a caller can act on, serialise cleanly, and read well in a log. Derive from Exception for unexpected errors, and add the three standard constructors so the type works with every serialiser and every framework convention.

A custom exception type exists so a handler can distinguish one failure from another without inspecting a message string. That single purpose implies everything else about its design: it needs a serialisation constructor if it crosses an application boundary, and it should add data the caller can branch on rather than only a sentence a human reads.

The three constructors, and why all three

A parameterless constructor is required by conventions that reflect over types and instantiate them. A message constructor is what a caller uses. A message-and-inner constructor is what a wrapper uses, and it is the one that preserves the original stack trace when a failure crosses a layer that has to add context.

What a custom exception should carry

Not just the message. The identifiers a handler would otherwise have to parse out of it — an order number, a status code, a retry-after — because a handler that parses a message is a handler that breaks when the message is reworded for a log. This is the single most valuable thing a custom exception does, and it is the reason the pattern exists.

[Serializable]
public sealed class PaymentFailedException : Exception
{
    // The three constructors every serialisable exception needs
    public PaymentFailedException() { }
    public PaymentFailedException(string message) : base(message) { }
    public PaymentFailedException(string message, Exception inner) : base(message, inner) { }

    // Protected: for derived types only. Sealed above, so optional.

    // Structured, actionable data
    public string TransactionId { get; }
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    public PaymentError Reason { get; }

    public PaymentFailedException(string txn, decimal amount, PaymentError reason)
        : base($"Payment {txn} for {amount} failed: {reason}")
    {
        TransactionId = txn; Amount = amount; Reason = reason;
    }
}

public enum PaymentError { InsufficientFunds, ExpiredCard, NetworkTimeout }

// Callers can now branch on data, not on message text
try { await charge(); }
catch (PaymentFailedException ex) when (ex.Reason == PaymentError.InsufficientFunds)
{
    ShowDecline(ex.Amount);
}

// ApplicationException is the base class for application-level errors,
// but it is not sealed and adds nothing: derive from Exception directly.

// Exception naming convention: end in "Exception"
// Exception.Message must be readable, Exception.Data for extras
// Exception.HResult and .Source are set by the base class

Because the message is a constructor argument, a custom exception can carry everything needed to diagnose it. An exception that only says "operation failed" forces every investigation back to the log for context that should have travelled with the exception.

Do not catch ApplicationException and do not throw it. It was intended as a marker for "this is an application error, not a system error", but nothing enforces that and modern guidance is to derive from Exception directly.


{{-- A CUSTOM EXCEPTION EXISTS SO A HANDLER CAN DISTINGUISH FAILURES
     WITHOUT PARSING A MESSAGE STRING. --}}
[Serializable]
public class OrderNotFoundException : Exception
{
    // 1. A PARAMETERLESS CONSTRUCTOR, required by conventions that
    //    reflect over exception types and instantiate them.
    public OrderNotFoundException() { }

    // 2. A MESSAGE CONSTRUCTOR, which is what a caller uses.
    public OrderNotFoundException(string message) : base(message) { }

    // 3. A MESSAGE-AND-INNER CONSTRUCTOR, which is what a WRAPPER
    //    uses — and it is the one that preserves the original stack
    //    trace when a failure crosses a layer that must add
    //    context.
    public OrderNotFoundException(string message, Exception inner)
        : base(message, inner) { }

    [Obsolete("the serialisation constructor is required by BinaryFormatter")]
    protected OrderNotFoundException(
        System.Runtime.Serialization.SerializationInfo info,
        System.Runtime.Serialization.StreamingContext context)
        : base(info, context) { }

    // WHAT IT SHOULD CARRY, and this is the whole point: not just
    // the message. The identifiers a handler would otherwise have
    // to PARSE OUT OF IT.
    public required string OrderReference { get; init; }
    public int? RetryAfterSeconds { get; init; }
}
{{-- ^ OrderNotFoundException("could not find ORD-" + reference) and
     a handler doing reference.Split('-')[1] is the defect this
     prevents: the handler breaks the moment somebody rewords the
     message for a log. --}}

{{-- AND A SEALED DERIVED TYPE, which is worth writing when the
     difference is behavioural rather than informational: --}}
[Serializable]
public sealed class PaymentDeclinedException : OrderNotFoundException
{
    public PaymentDeclinedException(string message) : base(message) { }

    public required string DeclineCode { get; init; }
    public decimal? AttemptedAmount { get; init; }
}

// WHICH MAKES THIS THE RIGHT SHAPE:
static async Task Handle(Order order)
{
    try
    {
        await ChargeAsync(order);
    }
    catch (PaymentDeclinedException ex) when (ex.DeclineCode == "insufficient_funds")
    {
        // A SPECIFIC branch on DATA, not on a message substring.
        await NotifyCustomer(order, "insufficient funds");
    }
    catch (PaymentDeclinedException ex)
    {
        await NotifyCustomer(order, "payment declined");
    }
}
{{-- ^ adding a new decline code is a new catch clause rather than
     an edit to a message comparison, and the compiler finds every
     site that handles the base type. --}}

{{-- AND WHERE A CUSTOM TYPE IS A MISTAKE: --}}
// WRONG: a type per message. This produces a hundred exception
// types, none of which anyone can catch usefully, and a handler
// that has to list them all.
public class OrderNotFoundBecauseItWasArchivedException : Exception { }

// RIGHT: ONE type per CALLER-VISIBLE DISTINCTION, with the detail
// carried as data. Six decline codes is six properties or one
// string property, not six types.

9.4 Inner exceptions and AggregateException

An InnerException chains a lower-level failure into a higher-level one, preserving the full cause. AggregateException carries several exceptions at once, which is what Task.WhenAll and Parallel.ForEach throw when more than one operation failed.

When a failure crosses a layer that cannot describe it in the caller's terms, the lower layer's exception becomes the inner exception of a higher one. The chain is preserved and each link adds what that layer knew, which is the whole purpose — and the trap is that a chain six deep is unreadable unless something walks it.

Aggregate exceptions, and the parallel case

An aggregate exception holds several, and it exists for two unrelated reasons: a parallel operation where several failures happened, and a bulk operation where the caller asked for everything to be attempted. The second is a design decision with a cost — a bulk operation that validates everything before failing is more useful and slower, and a bulk operation that stops at the first error is faster and reports less.

The unwrap decision

A handler that catches a wrapper and inspects the inner exception is coupling itself to a layer's internal structure. Where the wrapper is an implementation detail, unwrapping in the handler is the wrong place; where the inner type is part of the contract — a database timeout, a cancellation — unwrapping is correct and the alternative is losing the distinction.

// Inner exception: wrap, never discard
try
{
    return await Parse(raw);
}
catch (FormatException ex)
{
    throw new ConfigurationException($"Could not read '{raw}'", ex);
}

// Walking the chain when diagnosing
static void PrintChain(Exception ex, int depth = 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{new string(' ', depth * 2)}{ex.GetType().Name}: {ex.Message}");
    if (ex.InnerException is not null) PrintChain(ex.InnerException, depth + 1);
}

// AggregateException: multiple failures in one
var t1 = Task.Run(() => Work("a"));
var t2 = Task.Run(() => Work("b"));

try { await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2); }
catch (AggregateException agg)
{
    foreach (Exception e in agg.InnerExceptions) Console.WriteLine(e.Message);
}

// The await rule: awaiting a single Task unwraps automatically, so
// `await Task.WhenAll(...)` throws the FIRST exception, not an AggregateException.
// To see all of them, do not await inside the try, or use:
//   try { await Task.WhenAll(tasks); } catch { /* tasks is complete; inspect each */ }
//   foreach (var t in tasks) if (t.Exception is not null) Report(t.Exception);

// Creating and flattening
var agg = new AggregateException("2 of 5 failed", e1, e2);
var flat = agg.Flatten();          // flattens nested aggregates
Console.WriteLine(flat.InnerExceptions.Count);   // 2

The "await unwraps" rule surprises everyone once. Task.WhenAll throws an AggregateException only when you call .Wait() or .Result. Inside an async method, await re-throws the first inner exception directly, and the remaining failures are available on each task’s Exception property.

Never read Task.Result or Task.Wait() in an async method. It blocks a thread-pool thread and can deadlock. The moment you feel the urge to call .Result, the answer is await.


{{-- A FAILURE CROSSING A LAYER BECOMES THE INNER EXCEPTION, and the
     chain is what makes the failure readable. --}}
public sealed class CheckoutService
{
    public async Task<Order> PlaceAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        try
        {
            return await _repository.SaveAsync(order, ct);
        }
        catch (DbUpdateException ex)
        {
            // ^ THE LAYER THAT CANNOT DESCRIBE IT IN THE CALLER'S
            //   TERMS. It knows about a constraint violation and
            //   nothing about checkout, so it adds that.
            throw new CheckoutFailedException(
                $"Could not place {order.Reference}", ex);
        }
    }
}

static async Task Unwrap()
{
    try { await Checkout(); }
    catch (CheckoutFailedException ex)
    {
        // THE CHAIN, and it is only useful if something WALKS it:
        for (Exception? e = ex; e is not null; e = e.InnerException)
            Console.Error.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name}: {e.Message}");
        // CheckoutFailedException: Could not place ORD-1
        //   DbUpdateException: duplicate key value violates unique
        //     constraint "IX_Orders_Reference"

        // OR, the one line that matters:
        if (ex.GetBaseException() is TimeoutException)
            Retry();
        // ^ GetBaseException walks to the ROOT. Correct when the
        //   root is a well-known type every layer passes through —
        //   a cancellation, a timeout — and wrong when the root is
        //   an implementation detail, because then the handler is
        //   coupled to a layer it should not know about.
    }
}

{{-- AGGREGATE EXCEPTIONS, for two unrelated reasons: --}}
static async Task InParallel()
{
    // (1) A PARALLEL OPERATION where several failures happened. The
    //     caller wants all of them, not the first.
    var results = await Task.WhenAll(
        ChargeAsync("card"), ChargeAsync("wallet"), ChargeAsync("credit"));

    // Task.WhenAll THROWS THE FIRST and stores the rest. So:
    try
    {
        await Task.WhenAll(ChargeAsync("card"), ChargeAsync("wallet"));
    }
    catch (Exception first)
    {
        // The other failures are here, not lost:
        if (first is AggregateException agg)
            foreach (var e in agg.InnerExceptions) Report(e);
    }
}

public sealed class BulkResult
{
    public required IReadOnlyList<Order> Succeeded { get; init; }
    public required IReadOnlyList<Rejected> Failed { get; init; }
}

static async Task<BulkResult> ValidateAllAsync(IEnumerable<Order> orders)
{
    var ok = new List<Order>();
    var bad = new List<Rejected>();

    // (2) A BULK OPERATION where the CALLER ASKED FOR EVERYTHING TO
    //     BE ATTEMPTED — and this is a DESIGN DECISION with a cost:
    //     validate-everything is more useful and slower; stop-at-
    //     first-error is faster and reports less. The caller has to
    //     choose, and the signature is how it says so.
    foreach (var order in orders)
    {
        var verdict = await ValidateAsync(order);
        if (verdict.Ok) ok.Add(order); else bad.Add(verdict.Rejected);
    }

    // ^ ONE RETURN, never a throw for a rejected item: a throw
    //   loses the other 99 results, which is the entire reason the
    //   bulk operation exists.
    return new BulkResult { Succeeded = ok, Failed = bad };
}

9.5 The Result pattern

A Result<T> moves expected failures out of the exception channel and into the return value. Callers must handle the failure case, the compiler enforces it, and a failed parse costs nanoseconds instead of microseconds. This matters enormously in hot paths, in parsers and in bulk data processing.

The result type makes a failure a value rather than an exception. It buys three things exceptions cannot: the compiler forces a caller to consider the failure, the failure carries typed data, and there is no cost on the success path for the unwinding machinery the exception model implies.

What it costs, and where the cost lands

Every call site that could fail needs a check, and a method that calls five such methods needs five branches or a combinator. That is the real cost: it is paid at every call site, and it is why a result type adopted wholesale into a codebase with a million call sites is a rewrite rather than a change. The version that works is a boundary — the layer where failure becomes a return value, while the layers above and below still use exceptions.

When it is and is not worth it

It is worth it where failure is expected and frequent — parsing user input, calling an unreliable service, validating a batch — because an exception per bad row is both slow and log-noisy. It is not worth it where failure is genuinely exceptional, because the check at every call site is cost paid for a case that almost never happens.

// A minimal discriminated union: three states, no exceptions
public enum ResultState { Success, NotFound, Invalid }

public readonly record struct Result<T>
{
    public bool IsSuccess { get; }
    public T? Value { get; }
    public string? Error { get; }

    private Result(bool ok, T? value, string? error)
    {
        IsSuccess = ok; Value = value; Error = error;
    }

    public static Result<T> Ok(T value) => new(true, value, null);
    public static Result<T> Err(string error) => new(false, default, error);

    // Fold: collapse a Result<Result<T>> into a Result<T>
    public Result<TNext> Bind<TNext>(Func<T, Result<TNext>> next) =>
        IsSuccess ? next(Value!) : Result<TNext>.Err(Error!);

    // Map: transform the success value, keep the failure
    public Result<TNext> Map<TNext>(Func<T, TNext> f) =>
        IsSuccess ? Result<TNext>.Ok(f(Value!)) : Result<TNext>.Err(Error!);
}

// Use: the failure is in the signature, so it cannot be forgotten
static Result<int> ParseId(string text)
    => int.TryParse(text, out int id)
        ? Result<int>.Ok(id)
        : Result<int>.Err($"'{text}' is not an id");

static Result<string> Load(int id)
    => id < 1 ? Result<string>.Err("no such id") : Result<string>.Ok($"row-{id}");

// Chain without a try/catch anywhere
var result = ParseId("abc").Bind(Load);
Console.WriteLine(result.IsSuccess);   // false
Console.WriteLine(result.Error);        // 'abc' is not an id

// And an async version that never throws for expected failures
// ValueTask<Result<T>>, or OneOf<T, Error> as a named alternative

The rule that keeps this pattern from being noise: use Result for failures the caller is expected to handle (validation, not-found, conflict) and exceptions for failures nobody can handle (out of memory, a broken invariant, a null you promised would never be null).

Two library options if you do not want to write your own: OneOf<T0, T1>, which is a proper discriminated union with exhaustive Switch, and Argu, which is a source generator for results. Both are NuGet packages and both are worth it once the pattern appears in more than one project.


{{-- A RESULT TYPE MAKES FAILURE A VALUE, and buys three things an
     exception cannot: a compiler-ENFORCED check at every call site,
     TYPED data on the failure, and no unwinding cost on success. --}}
public readonly struct Result<T, TError>
{
    private readonly T? _value;
    private readonly TError? _error;

    private Result(T value)       { _value = value; _error = default; }
    private Result(TError error)  { _value = default; _error = error; }

    public bool IsSuccess => _error is null;
    public bool IsFailure => _error is not null;

    public T Value => _value ?? throw new InvalidOperationException(
        "A failed result has no value. Check IsSuccess, or use Match.");
    public TError Error => _error ?? throw new InvalidOperationException(
        "A successful result has no error.");

    public static Result<T, TError> Ok(T value)   => new(value);
    public static Result<T, TError> Fail(TError e) => new(e);

    // MATCH, which is what removes the branch from the CALL SITE and
    // is the reason the type pays for itself.
    public R Match<R>(Func<T, R> onSuccess, Func<TError, R> onFailure)
        => IsSuccess ? onSuccess(_value!) : onFailure(_error!);
}

{{-- WHAT IT COSTS, and the cost lands AT EVERY CALL SITE: --}}
static async Task ProcessAsync(Order order)
{
    // Without combinators, FIVE branches for five calls:
    var customer = await LoadCustomerAsync(order.CustomerId);
    if (customer.IsFailure) { Report(customer.Error); return; }

    var priced = Price(order, customer.Value);
    if (priced.IsFailure) { Report(priced.Error); return; }

    var tax = Tax(priced.Value, customer.Value.Region);
    if (tax.IsFailure) { Report(tax.Error); return; }

    var saved = await SaveAsync(tax.Value);
    if (saved.IsFailure) { Report(saved.Error); return; }
    {{-- ^ WHICH IS THE REAL COST. It is paid at every call site, and
         it is why adopting a result type WHOLESALE is a rewrite
         rather than a change. --}}
}

{{-- THE VERSION THAT WORKS: combinators, so the CALL SITE is one
     LINQ CHAIN and the branches disappear into Match: --}}
static readonly Result<Order, DomainError> Validate(Order order) =>
    from c    in LoadCustomer(order.CustomerId)
    from p    in Price(order, c)
    from t    in Tax(p, c.Region)
    select Save(t);

static async Task Show(Order order)
{
    // AND THE CALLER HANDLES ONE THING:
    var outcome = await Validate(order);
    if (outcome.IsFailure) Report(outcome.Error);
    else Confirm(outcome.Value);
}

{{-- WHERE IT IS AND IS NOT WORTH IT, which is the actual rule: --}}
static async Task<BulkResult> ImportAsync(IEnumerable<string> rows)
{
    var ok = new List<object>();
    var bad = new List<ParseError>();

    foreach (string row in rows)
    {
        // WORTH IT HERE: failure is EXPECTED and FREQUENT. An
        // exception per bad row is both slow (a throw costs
        // microseconds against a nanosecond return) and log-noisy:
        // 40,000 exceptions in an import is 40,000 stack traces a
        // monitoring system has to be told to ignore.
        if (!TryParse(row, out var value, out var error)) { bad.Add(error); continue; }
        ok.Add(value);
    }

    // NOT WORTH IT where failure is genuinely EXCEPTIONAL, because
    // the check at every call site is cost paid for a case that
    // almost never happens.
    return new BulkResult { Succeeded = ok, Failed = bad };
}

9.6 Practices and anti-patterns

A short list of rules that separate exception handling that helps from exception handling that hides bugs. Each of these has a cost when ignored, and the cost always shows up later, in production, in the one code path you did not test.

// 1. Do not catch what you cannot handle. Catch the specific type you act on.
//    catch (Exception) { }   swallows NullReferenceException, OutOfMemoryException,
//                           ThreadAbortException and your own bugs alike.

// 2. Do not use exceptions for control flow. A throw costs microseconds
//    and a stack trace; a Result costs a struct copy and a branch.

// 3. Never lose the inner exception when wrapping.
//    catch (Exception ex) { throw new MyException("failed"); }   // ex is GONE
//    catch (Exception ex) { throw new MyException("failed", ex); }  // kept

// 4. throw; not throw ex;  -- the first preserves the stack trace
//    catch (IOException) { logger.LogWarning(ex, "retrying"); throw; }

// 5. Make Dispose idempotent, and prefer using declarations
//    using var conn = new Connection();   // exception-safe, whole scope

// 6. Validate at the boundary, not throughout the middle
public static int ParsePositive(string input)
{
    // Argument guards are for programmer errors: they throw immediately,
    // at the call site, with the parameter name attached.
    ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(input);
    ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative(1);
    // .NET 8 added these ThrowIf* helpers; on older targets write the if+throw.

    return int.Parse(input);   // may throw FormatException: that is fine here
}

// 7. Aggregate errors instead of failing on the first one, when the caller
//    would rather fix everything in one pass
var errors = new List<string>();
foreach (var line in lines) if (!Validate(line, out string? why)) errors.Add(why);
// if (errors.Count > 0) return Result<T>.Err(string.Join("\n", errors));

// 8. Log the exception object, not just ex.Message -- the stack trace matters
// logger.LogError(ex, "could not load {Id}", id);     correct
// logger.LogError("could not load {Id}: {Message}", id, ex.Message);  lossy

// 9. Cancellation is not an error: it deserves its own log level, or none
// catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
//     { return; }   // normal shutdown, do not log as a warning

The test for whether an exception is the right tool: could a reasonable caller have done something different to avoid it? If yes, it is a control-flow case and belongs in the return value. If no, and the only response is to fail, throw.

Never return null to signal failure. string? Parse(string s) forces every caller into a null check with no explanation, and a genuine null result from a legitimate computation is indistinguishable. Return a Result, or an empty value with a documented meaning.

Nullable reference types and exceptions solve different problems and are not alternatives. NRT stops the compiler letting you forget a check on a value that is already null. Exceptions handle the case where an operation genuinely failed. You need both, and you need them for different reasons.

Exercises 9

  1. Write a parser that throws on bad input, then time 100,000 bad parses. Rewrite it with a Result and time it again. Record the difference.
  2. Build a Result<T> with Bind and Map, and compose a four-step validation chain with no try block anywhere.
  3. Create a custom exception with structured properties, throw it with an inner exception, and print the whole chain with your diagnostic walker.
  4. Run two failing tasks through Task.WhenAll and demonstrate the difference between await (first exception) and Task.Wait() (aggregate).
  5. Implement a retry helper using an exception filter and prove that a non-transient exception is not retried.
