  6. Find an empty catch (Exception) { } in an existing codebase, add logging, and work out whether it was hiding a real bug.

{{-- THE SIX THAT ACTUALLY MATTER, and each is a rule rather than a
     style preference: --}}
public sealed class Practices
{
    // 1. DO NOT CATCH AND SWALLOW. This is the one that turns a
    //    diagnostic into an absence.
    public void Swallow(string path)
    {
        try
        {
            Load(path);
        }
        catch (Exception)
        {
            // ^ THE DEFECT. The caller now believes the operation
            //   SUCCEEDED, and the failure leaves no trace anywhere.
            //   It is strictly worse than not handling it at all,
            //   because a crash would at least have been noticed.
        }
    }

    // 2. DO NOT CATCH Exception AND CONTINUE AS IF NOTHING HAPPENED,
    //    which is the same defect with a log line added.
    public void LogAndContinue(string path)
    {
        try { Load(path); }
        catch (Exception ex) { Console.Error.WriteLine(ex.Message); }
        // ^ STILL WRONG: a PARTIAL state is now being used. If Load
        //   wrote three of five records, the caller sees a success
        //   and three records.
    }

    // 3. DO NOT USE AN EXCEPTION FOR CONTROL FLOW. The cost is
    //    microseconds against nanoseconds, and it happens per
    //    ITEM.
    public bool IsValid(Order o)
    {
        try { Validate(o); return true; }
        catch (ValidationException) { return false; }
        // ^ on a bulk import of 100,000 rows this is the difference
        //   between a second and a minute, and the cost lands per
        //   row in a loop.
    }
}

{{-- AND THE ONES THAT ARE ACTUALLY FINE, which is the other half
     of knowing the rules: --}}
public static class Fine(string path)
{
    // 4. A catch WITH A FILTER, at a boundary, adding CONTEXT and
    //    rethrowing: correct, and it is what the framework does.
    public static void AtABoundary()
    {
        try { Run(); }
        catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)
        {
            throw new ServiceUnavailableException(
                "The pricing service did not respond.", ex);
        }
    }

    // 5. CATCHING OperationCanceledException and returning a
    //    cancelled task: correct, and REQUIRED, because a cancelled
    //    task that faults is a bug that surfaces much later.
    public static async Task<int> SafeAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        try
        {
            return await ComputeAsync(ct);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
        {
            // ^ PROPAGATE THE CANCELLATION rather than rethrowing a
            //   NEW exception. A task that ends Faulted instead of
            //   Canceled makes a WhenAll report a failure for an
            //   operation the caller deliberately abandoned.
            throw;
        }
    }

    // 6. A try/finally FOR RESOURCE RELEASE, with nothing else in
    //    the finally: correct, and free when nothing throws.
    public static async Task<int> Release(string path)
    {
        await using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
        try { return await ReadAsync(stream); }
        finally { Audit.Log(path); }
    }
}

{{-- AND THE THING THAT IS EASY TO MISS: AN EXCEPTION IN A finally
     REPLACES the one already propagating, so a finally that can fail
     must catch its own failures. --}}
public static class FinallyThatCanFail(string path)
{
    public static void TheTrap()
    {
        try
        {
            Run();                    // throws InvalidOperationException
        }
        finally
        {
            try { Cleanup(path); }    // ALSO throws IOException
            catch { /* nothing */ }
            // ^ WITHOUT THIS CATCH, the IOException REPLACES the
            //   InvalidOperationException, and the original — with
            //   the stack trace that says where the real failure
            //   was — is GONE. The diagnosis names the wrong
            //   operation entirely.
        }
    }
}

10 · LINQ — Querying Collections

10.1 Query syntax vs method syntax10.2 Filter and project10.3 GroupBy, Join and SelectMany10.4 Terminal operators and the short-circuiting family10.5 Aggregate, CountBy and MinMaxBy10.6 Deferred execution and multiple enumeration10.7 IQueryable and parameterised queries

Chapter ten covers LINQ, which is the framework’s declarative querying layer. It has two syntaxes that compile to the same thing, a clear split between operators that shape a sequence and operators that consume it, and one property that causes most bugs: deferred execution. The final section covers IQueryable, where the whole query travels to a database instead of running in memory.

10.1 Query syntax vs method syntax

Query syntax (from ... where ... select) and method syntax (Where(...).Select(...)) are exactly equivalent; the compiler translates the first into the second. Query syntax reads better for a simple multi-step transformation. Method syntax is better the moment you need a local variable, a conditional, or an operator with no keyword equivalent.

Query syntax and method syntax compile to the same thing — query syntax is translated by the compiler into method calls — so the choice is entirely about which one a reader finds clearer. That is a real consideration and it is the only one, because there is no performance difference of any kind.

Where query syntax is genuinely clearer

A multi-stage transformation with a join, a group and a projection reads closer to the English description in query syntax, and the visual structure of the keywords carries the shape of the operation. It is also where the compiler's restriction applies: every clause must be a simple expression over the range variable, so anything requiring a local, a pattern beyond simple matching, or a statement has to drop to method syntax.

Where method syntax wins

Composing with a method that takes a delegate, reusing a stage as a named function, and anywhere a lambda appears. The rule of thumb worth adopting is to use query syntax for a whole pipeline that reads as one expression and to use method syntax the moment any part of it needs a brace.

using System.Linq;

public sealed record Order(int Id, string Customer, decimal Total, bool IsPaid);

// Method syntax: what query syntax compiles to
IEnumerable<int> method =
    orders
        .Where(o => o.Total > 100m)
        .Select(o => o.Id)
        .OrderBy(o => o)
        .ToList();

// Query syntax: the same query, easier to read when it is linear
IEnumerable<int> query =
    from o in orders
    where o.Total > 100m
    orderby o.Id
    select o.Id;

// The compiler output is identical. Readability is the only difference.

// Query syntax shines with multiple sources
var summary =
    from o in orders
    let discounted = o.Total * 0.9m      // a let binding: no method equivalent
    where o.IsPaid
    join c in customers on o.Customer equals c.Id
    where c.Country == "UK"
    orderby discounted descending
    select new { c.Name, discounted };

// Method syntax for the same thing is nested lambdas and gets unreadable

// Rule of thumb
//   query syntax  -- two or more sources, let, group, or a multi-line transformation
//   method syntax -- single source, a local variable, a conditional, a method call

In method syntax, where becomes Where, orderby becomes OrderBy then ThenBy, select becomes Select, and join becomes Join. Every query keyword has a method; not every method has a keyword.

Do not mix the two syntaxes in one expression. from o in orders where o.IsPaid select o.Id followed by .Take(10) in method syntax is legal but reads as two queries stapled together. Pick one per expression and stay consistent across the codebase.


{{-- THEY COMPILE TO THE SAME THING, so there is NO PERFORMANCE
     DIFFERENCE OF ANY KIND. Query syntax is translated by the
     compiler into method calls. --}}
using System.Linq;

static void BothForms(List<Order> orders)
{
    // QUERY SYNTAX:
    var a = from o in orders
            where o.Total > 100
            orderby o.PlacedAt descending
            select o.Reference;

    // METHOD SYNTAX, and this is what the compiler EMITS:
    var b = orders
            .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
            .OrderByDescending(o => o.PlacedAt)
            .Select(o => o.Reference);
    {{-- ^ IDENTICAL, and any difference in speed is a measurement
         error rather than a finding. --}}
}

{{-- WHERE QUERY SYNTAX IS GENUINELY CLEARER, and it is the JOIN: --}}
static void WhereQueryWins(List<Order> orders, List<Customer> customers)
{
    // QUERY: the shape of the operation IS the visual structure.
    var q = from o in orders
            join c in customers on o.CustomerId equals c.Id into g
            from c in g.DefaultIfEmpty()
            where o.Total > 100
            orderby o.PlacedAt descending
            select new
            {
                o.Reference,
                o.Total,
                // the group key makes the LEFT JOIN visible: without
                // it, a missing customer is a null reference and the
                // compiler is happy.
                CustomerName = c == null ? "(deleted)" : c.Name
            };

    // METHOD: three delegates and one GroupJoin, and the
    // DefaultIfEmpty is a separate step a reader has to know about.
    var m = orders
            .GroupJoin(customers, o => o.CustomerId, c => c.Id,
                       (o, g) => new { o, g })
            .Select(x => new { x.o, c = x.g.DefaultIfEmpty().FirstOrDefault() })
            .Where(x => x.o.Total > 100)
            .OrderByDescending(x => x.o.PlacedAt)
            .Select(x => new
            {
                x.o.Reference,
                x.o.Total,
                CustomerName = x.c == null ? "(deleted)" : x.c.Name
            });
}

{{-- AND WHERE QUERY SYNTAX LOSES, which is its RESTRICTION: every
     clause must be a SIMPLE EXPRESSION over the range variable. --}}
static void WhereQueryLoses(List<Order> orders)
{
    // from o in orders
    // where Compute(o).IsEligible          ERROR: query syntax
    // select ...                                  restricts each
    //                                            clause to a
    //                                            simple expression
    //                                            over the range
    //                                            variable

    // WHICH MEANS any of these drops to method syntax:
    var a = orders.Where(o => Compute(o).IsEligible);
    var b = orders.Select(o => { var t = Compute(o); return t.Id; });
    var c = orders.Where(IsRecent).Where(o => o.Total > 100);
    var d = orders.GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId)
                  .Select(g => { int n = g.Count(); return n; });
    {{-- ^ a STATEMENT BODY cannot appear in a query clause, so a
         stage that needs a local is a method-syntax stage even
         inside an otherwise query-shaped pipeline. --}}
}

{{-- THE RULE OF THUMB WORTH ADOPTING: use query syntax for a WHOLE
     PIPELINE that reads as one expression, and drop to method
     syntax THE MOMENT ANY PART NEEDS A BRACE. --}}
static void Mixed(List<Order> orders, List<Customer> customers)
{
    var report = from o in orders                  // query from here
                 join c in customers on o.CustomerId equals c.Id
                 select new { o.Reference, c.Name }
                 into grouped
                 from g in grouped
                 where g.Total > 100               // still a simple
                 select g;                         // clause: fine

    // ...then method syntax from the first brace onwards.
    var summary = report
        .GroupBy(r => r.Name)
        .Select(g => new { Name = g.Key, Count = g.Count() })
        .ToList();
}

10.2 Filter and project

Where filters a sequence and Select reshapes it. Both are lazy: they return a new IEnumerable<T> and do no work until enumerated. Select can change the element type, which is what makes LINQ composable.

A filter decides what reaches the next stage and a projection decides what shape it is in. Both are lazy, both run per element as the pipeline is enumerated, and the cost of a stage is paid once per element that reaches it — which is why a filter placed after an expensive projection does work that a filter before it would not have.

Where to put the filter

Before the projection, always, unless the projection is what the filter needs. The stages run in order and each one processes only what survived the previous, so a filter that can run on a cheap field should run before the projection that computes an expensive one. The exception is when the filter's predicate needs a computed value, in which case the projection has to come first and the cost is unavoidable.

Select versus SelectMany

A projection to a single value is a filter's counterpart. A projection that produces a sequence is a flattening operation, and it has its own method because the compiler cannot infer it — a lambda returning an enumerable from a Select produces a sequence of sequences, which is almost never what anyone wants and which the type system does not stop.

// Where: keeps elements that satisfy the predicate
var unpaid = orders.Where(o => !o.IsPaid);

// Select: transforms each element, may change the type
var ids    = orders.Select(o => o.Id);                    // Order -> int
var names  = orders.Select(o => o.Customer.ToUpper());  // Order -> string
var tuples = orders.Select(o => (o.Id, o.Total));       // ValueTuple
var anon   = orders.Select(o => new { o.Id, Summary = o.Customer });

// Index-aware overloads
var numbered = orders.Select((o, i) => new { Row = i + 1, o.Id });
var rows = orders.Where((o, i) => i % 2 == 0);

// Conditional projection
var labels = orders.Select(o => o.IsPaid
    ? "PAID"
    : "OUTSTANDING");

// Chaining more than a few operations: read the intermediate types
// orders.Where(..)   -> IEnumerable<Order>
//        .Select(..)   -> IEnumerable<int>
//        .Where(..)   -> IEnumerable<int>   (not back to Order)

// Deferring the projection until the last moment
// .Select(o => Expensive(o))  is called once per element per enumeration.
// Materialise with ToList()/ToArray() if the work must happen exactly once.

// Two-source projection without join: SelectMany
var allItems = orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines.Select(l => o.Id + ":" + l.Sku));

// Index variants
var withPos = orders.Select((o, i) => (i, o.Id));
var pairs = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Zip(new[] { "a", "b", "c" });

A Select that throws inside the projection is hard to attribute, because the exception surfaces during enumeration rather than at the call. Guard the projection, or materialise the sequence at the point of failure.

When you find yourself doing Select(...).ToList().Select(...), that is a smell: the intermediate materialisation is either unnecessary (all of it is lazy anyway) or a sign the first projection was the wrong shape. SelectMany and GroupBy usually express the intent better.


{{-- BOTH ARE LAZY and both run PER ELEMENT as the pipeline is
     enumerated, so the cost of a stage is paid once per element
     THAT REACHES IT. --}}
static void Ordering(List<Order> orders)
{
    // WRONG ORDER: the projection computes a formatted total for
    // every order, and then 99% of them are thrown away.
    var wrong = orders
        .Select(o => new { o.Reference, Line = $"{o.Total:N2}" })
        .Where(x => x.Line.StartsWith("1"))      // cheap to test, but
        ;                                         // the EXPENSIVE
                                                  // stage already ran
                                                  // on everything

    // RIGHT ORDER: the filter runs first, on the cheap field.
    var right = orders
        .Where(o => o.Total is >= 100 and < 1000)
        .Select(o => new { o.Reference, Line = $"{o.Total:N2}" })
        .ToList();
}

{{-- THE EXCEPTION, and it is the one to remember: when the FILTER
     NEEDS A COMPUTED VALUE, the projection has to come first and the
     cost is unavoidable. --}}
static void FilterNeedsProjection(List<Order> orders)
{
    // Cheapest correct form: the property does not exist, so the
    // DISCOUNTED TOTAL is computed inside the predicate and the
    // projection reads it back off the anonymous type.
    var discounted = orders
        .Where(o => o.Total * 0.9m >= 50m)
        .Select(o => new
        {
            o.Reference,
            Discounted = o.Total * 0.9m,       // computed TWICE: once
        })                                     // to filter, once to
        .ToList();                            // project

    // BETTER: compute it ONCE, in a transparent identifier, and
    // filter on the computed value.
    var once = orders
        .Select(o => new { Order = o, Discounted = o.Total * 0.9m })
        .Where(x => x.Discounted >= 50m)
        .Select(x => new { x.Order.Reference, x.Discounted })
        .ToList();
    {{-- ^ the TRANSPARENT IDENTIFIER: an anonymous type wrapping the
         original so a computed value can be carried between stages.
         Two computations where one is enough is the defect the
         transparent identifier exists to remove. --}}
}

{{-- Select versus SelectMany, and why the second has its own name: --}}
static void Flattening(List<Order> orders, List<Line> lines)
{
    // Select PRODUCES A SEQUENCE OF SEQUENCES, and the type system
    // does NOT stop you:
    var nested = orders.Select(o => o.Lines);     // IEnumerable
                                                     // <IEnumerable
                                                     // <Line>>
    // nested.Sum(l => l.Count)   ERROR: no Count on IEnumerable
    // ^ this is almost never what anyone wanted, and it is a
    //   compile error at the point of USE rather than at the
    //   projection, which is the worst place for it to appear.

    // SelectMany IS THE FLATTENING:
    var flat = orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines);
    var count = flat.Count();                    // works

    // AND THE COMMON SHAPE: the source sequence plus the element
    // sequence, with a result selector.
    var withHeaders = orders.SelectMany(
        o => o.Lines,
        (o, line) => new { o.Reference, line.Description, line.Qty });
}

{{-- WHERE A PROJECTION CHANGES THE TYPE, and it is worth being
     explicit because it decides what the next stage can use: --}}
static void TypeChanges(List<Order> orders)
{
    var ids = orders.Select(o => o.Id);                    // int
    var refs = orders.Select(o => o.Reference);            // string
    var anon = orders.Select(o => new { o.Id, o.Total });  // anonymous
    var recs = orders.Select(o => new OrderRow(o.Id));     // named

    // A PROJECTION TO AN ANONYMOUS TYPE is a NEW TYPE PER SITE, so
    // two sites projecting the same shape produce two INCOMPATIBLE
    // types:
    var a = orders.Select(o => new { o.Id });
    var b = orders.Select(o => new { o.Id });
    // var together = a.Union(b);        ERROR: two different
    //                                    anonymous types
    {{-- ^ which is a COMPILE error rather than a silent join, so it
         is one of the rare cases where an anonymous projection
         being a problem produces a diagnostic immediately. --}}
}

10.3 GroupBy, Join and SelectMany

These operators change the shape of a sequence rather than its contents. GroupBy produces a sequence of groups, Join pairs two sequences, and SelectMany flattens a sequence of sequences. Each has a query-syntax equivalent that is significantly more readable than the method call.

Three operators change the shape of a sequence rather than filtering or transforming it. A grouping partitions by a key. A join pairs two sequences on a key. A flattening operator turns a sequence of sequences into one sequence.

Grouping and what the key is

A grouping produces a key and the elements that share it, and the key type is whatever the selector returns — including a computed value or a tuple. A grouping is itself a sequence of anonymous types, which is why its result is projected through Select before it is enumerated, and why a grouping that is enumerated more than once regroups.

The three joins

An inner join pairs matching elements and drops both non-matches. A group join produces one result per left element carrying a sequence of right elements, which is the correct shape for a left join and the only one of the three that needs the extra DefaultIfEmpty to become one. And a cross join is the same as the group join with no key, which is a cartesian product and which should be visible as such at the call site.

// GroupBy: one group per key, each an IEnumerable of the members
var byCustomer = orders.GroupBy(o => o.Customer);

// The shape is IEnumerable<IGrouping<Key, Element>>
var totals = orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.Customer)
    .Select(g => new
    {
        Customer = g.Key,
        Count    = g.Count(),
        Total    = g.Sum(o => o.Total),
        Latest   = g.Max(o => o.Id)
    });

// Query syntax
// from o in orders
// group o by o.Customer
// into g
//   select new { g.Key, Count = g.Count(), Total = g.Sum(o => o.Total) };

// Custom element projection: group by a derived key
var byMonth = orders
    .GroupBy(o => new { o.Total > 100m, o.IsPaid })
    .Select(g => new { g.Key, N = g.Count() });

// Join: inner join with a result selector
var enriched = orders.Join(
    customers,
    o => o.Customer,          // outer key selector
    c => c.Id,                // inner key selector
    (o, c) => new { o.Id, c.Name, o.Total });   // result selector

// Query syntax: from o in orders join c in customers on o.Customer equals c.Id
//            select new { o.Id, c.Name }

// GroupJoin: LEFT join -- every order, plus zero or more customers (always one here)
var left = orders.GroupJoin(
    customers,
    o => o.Customer, c => c.Id,
    (o, g) => new { o.Id, Customers = g.ToList() });

// Flattened left join with SelectMany
var flat = orders
    .SelectMany(o => customers.Where(c => c.Id == o.Customer),
                (o, c) => new { o.Id, c.Name });

// .NET 10 added Join and GroupJoin overloads taking a key selector that
// operates on both sides at once, which is usually faster than a lambda pair.
// orders.Join(customers, o => o.Customer, c => c.Id, ...)

A GroupBy result is lazy in a surprising way: the groups are produced as the outer sequence is enumerated, and the key is computed once per element. Grouping ten million rows materialises one group at a time, not ten million lists.

GroupBy inside a loop over a large collection is a classic O(n²) trap: each iteration regroups the whole sequence. Hoist the grouping out of the loop, or build a lookup dictionary once with ToLookup.


{{-- THREE OPERATORS THAT CHANGE THE SHAPE rather than filtering or
     transforming. --}}

{{-- GROUPING, and the key is whatever the selector RETURNS: --}}
static void Grouping(List<Order> orders)
{
    // A SIMPLE KEY:
    var byCustomer = orders.GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId);

    // A COMPUTED KEY:
    var byMonth = orders.GroupBy(o => new
    {
        o.PlacedAt.Year,
        o.PlacedAt.Month
    });

    // A TUPLE KEY, which is how you group by more than one thing
    // without an anonymous type:
    var byRegionDay = orders.GroupBy(o =>
        (o.Customer.Region, o.PlacedAt.Date));

    // THE RESULT IS A SEQUENCE OF ANONYMOUS TYPES, each with a Key
    // and a Group, so it is projected before use:
    var summary = byCustomer
        .Select(g => new
        {
            g.Key,
            Count = g.Count(),
            Total = g.Sum(o => o.Total),
            Average = g.Average(o => o.Total),
            Latest = g.Max(o => o.PlacedAt)
        })
        .OrderByDescending(s => s.Total)
        .ToList();

    // g.Key          the selector's return value
    // g.Count()      an O(n) walk OF THE GROUP
    {{-- ^ every Count(), Sum() and Average() is a SEPARATE WALK of
         that group. Four of them is four passes over the same
         elements, and for a group of 10,000 that is 40,000
         operations where 10,000 would do. --}}
}

{{-- THE THREE JOINS, and which one needs DefaultIfEmpty: --}}
static void TheThreeJoins(List<Order> orders, List<Customer> customers)
{
    // 1. INNER JOIN: pairs matching elements and DROPS BOTH
    //    NON-MATCHES. An order whose customer was deleted simply
    //    disappears from the result, which is usually a surprise.
    var inner = from o in orders
                join c in customers on o.CustomerId equals c.Id
                select new { o.Reference, c.Name };

    // 2. GROUP JOIN: ONE RESULT PER LEFT ELEMENT, carrying a
    //    SEQUENCE of right elements. This is the correct shape for
    //    a left join — and the ONLY one of the three that needs
    //    DefaultIfEmpty to become one.
    var left = from o in orders
               join c in customers on o.CustomerId equals c.Id into matches
               from c in matches.DefaultIfEmpty()
               select new { o.Reference, Name = c?.Name ?? "(deleted)" };

    // WITHOUT DefaultIfEmpty the GroupJoin arm is typed
    // IEnumerable<Customer> and a null c is a NULL REFERENCE
    // waiting for a dereference — not a compile error, because the
    // projection can legitimately produce null.

    // 3. CROSS JOIN: the group join with no key. This is a
    //    CARTESIAN PRODUCT and it should be visible as one.
    var cartesian = orders.SelectMany(
        o => customers.Select(c => new { o.Reference, c.Name }));
    // 10,000 orders x 500 customers = 5,000,000 rows
}

{{-- AND THE JOIN KEY'S COST, which is the thing to know: --}}
static void JoinKeyCost(List<Order> orders, List<Customer> customers)
{
    // THE JOIN BUILDS A LOOKUP from the INNER sequence ONCE, then
    // probes it per outer element — so the inner sequence is walked
    // once and the key's GetHashCode is called once per outer row.
    var cheap = from o in orders
                join c in customers on o.CustomerId equals c.Id
                select new { o.Reference, c.Name };
    // ^ Cost: n + m, because CustomerId is an int.

    // A STRING KEY changes this completely, because the hash is
    // computed per outer element and the comparison is per bucket:
    var dear = from o in orders
               join c in customers on o.CustomerReference
                     equals c.Slug
               select new { o.Reference, c.Name };
    // Cost: n * (hash of the string) — and if the key is a
    // COMPOSITE string built with + inside the query, it is also
    // n string allocations.
}

10.4 Terminal operators and the short-circuiting family

A terminal operator forces enumeration and produces a single value. The distinction that matters for correctness and performance is short-circuiting: First, Any and All stop at the first satisfying element, while Count, Sum and OrderBy must see everything.

A terminal operator consumes the sequence and produces a value; nothing after it runs. The consequence worth knowing is that short-circuiting terminals stop the source early, while consuming terminals walk it entirely — and a source that is expensive to enumerate makes the difference between a constant-time answer and a linear one.

The short-circuiting family

Any, all, first, last, single and count with a predicate all stop as soon as the answer is known, except that last cannot: it must reach the end to know the final element. So Last on a lazily-generated sequence is the one that surprises people, and materialising the sequence first is the fix when the source is a query rather than a list.

Count, and the trap in it

Count with a predicate walks and counts. Count without one is a property on the concrete collection types and is constant-time for a list and for an array — so the two spellings that look identical differ by a factor of n. The related trap is that Count() versus the Count property resolves to whichever the static type provides, so an interface-typed source silently loses the optimisation.

// Short-circuiting: can answer early
bool anyLate   = orders.Any(o => o.IsPaid);              // stops at the first paid order
bool allPaid   = orders.All(o => o.IsPaid);              // stops at the first unpaid
Order? firstLarge  = orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Total > 1_000m);
Order single       = orders.Single(o => o.Id == 42);

// Full-scan: must enumerate everything
int count = orders.Count();
// int n = orders.Count;   -- the ICollection fast path, no enumerator
// bool any = orders.Any(); -- a Count > 0 check with no predicate
decimal total = orders.Sum(o => o.Total);

// Count with a predicate is a full scan; optimise it if it is hot
// orders.Count(o => o.IsPaid)  ==>  orders.Count(o => o.IsPaid)

// The throwing family vs the OrDefault family
Order? safe  = orders.FirstOrDefault();   // null (or default(T)) when empty
Order  risky = orders.First();           // InvalidOperationException when empty
Order? last  = orders.LastOrDefault(o => o.IsPaid);
Order? byIdx = orders.ElementAtOrDefault(99);

// One element or a throw: the validation pattern
Order only = orders.SingleOrDefault(o => o.Id == 42)
    ?? throw new KeyNotFoundException("No order 42");

// Positional variants
// First(predicate)              first match
// First() / Last()              first or last element
// Single(predicate)              exactly one match, else throw
// SingleOrDefault()              at most one element, else default
// ElementAt(index)              the element at an index

// Contains, SequenceEqual, All the enumeration
// orders.Contains(order)  uses EqualityComparer<T>.Default
// sequence.SequenceEqual(other)

// Materialising terminals
List<Order> list   = orders.ToList();
Order[] array       = orders.ToArray();
Dictionary<int, Order> map = orders.ToDictionary(o => o.Id);   // throws on duplicate key
Dictionary<int, Order> last = orders.ToDictionary(o => o.Id, o => o, equality);  // last wins
Dictionary<int, List<Order>> dupe = orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.Id).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.ToList());   // groups allowed
Lookup<int, Order> lookup = orders.ToLookup(o => o.Id);              // duplicates, no throw

Use Count (the property) rather than Count() when the source is an ICollection<T>: it is a field read, while Count() constructs an enumerator. The difference is invisible on a list and significant on a million-element sequence in a loop.

ToDictionary throws on a duplicate key, which is a feature: it turns a silent data problem into an immediate, obvious error. If duplicates are legitimate, ToLookup gives you a multi-map in one call and never throws.


{{-- A TERMINAL OPERATOR CONSUMES THE SEQUENCE AND NOTHING AFTER IT
     RUNS. The consequence: short-circuiting terminals stop the
     source EARLY, consuming terminals walk it ENTIRELY. --}}
static void ShortCircuit(List<Order> orders, IEnumerable<Order> query)
{
    // ANY, ALL, FIRST, ANY-OR-DEFAULT: stop as soon as the answer is
    // known.
    bool anyLarge = orders.Any(o => o.Total > 1000);
    bool allPaid  = orders.All(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Paid);
    var first     = orders.First(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Pending);
    var firstOr   = orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Total > 1000);

    {{-- ^ on orders, which is a LIST, these are already cheap. On a
         LAZILY-GENERATED query they are not, because the source has
         to be produced to be examined: --}}
}

static void LazyIsDifferent(IEnumerable<Order> query)
{
    // A QUERY is re-EXECUTED per terminal operator and re-queries
    // the database each time. So this is TWO round trips:
    var any = query.Any(o => o.Total > 1000);
    var all = query.All(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Paid);

    // AND the answer is not stable between them, because the data
    // may have changed in between.
}

{{-- LAST IS THE ONE THAT SURPRISES, because it CANNOT short-circuit: --}}
static void Last(IEnumerable<Order> query)
{
    // Last must REACH THE END to know the final element. So on a
    // lazily-generated sequence it enumerates everything, and on an
    // IQueryable it is a full round trip that could have been a
    // single-row ORDER BY ... DESC.
    var last = query.Last();

    // THE FIX when the source is a query rather than a list:
    var byQuery = query.OrderByDescending(o => o.PlacedAt).Take(1);
    // ^ ONE ROW, fetched, and it is what the database is for.
}

{{-- COUNT, and the trap that is IN IT: --}}
static void Counts(List<Order> list, IEnumerable<Order> any, IReadOnlyCollection<Order> collection)
{
    int a = list.Count;            // CONSTANT: a property on List<T>
    int b = list.Count();          // the extension method, which walks
                                   // — but List<T> has a Count
                                   // PROPERTY, so this resolves to
                                   // the property, not the method
    int c = any.Count();           // A WALK: the static type is
                                   // IEnumerable<T>, which has no
                                   // Count property
    int d = collection.Count;      // CONSTANT: the interface declares
                                   // it as a property
    {{-- ^ list.Count and any.Count() LOOK IDENTICAL and differ by a
         factor of n. The difference is the STATIC TYPE, and it is
         the single most expensive LINQ mistake in this area. --}}
}

static void CountWithPredicate(List<Order> orders)
{
    // ALWAYS A WALK, on every type, because there is no Count
    // property that takes a predicate:
    int pending = orders.Count(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Pending);
    {{-- ^ O(n) on every call, in a loop that is O(n^2) — and it is
         written by people who have just proved the list is a List
         and do not expect to pay for the walk. --}}
}

10.5 Aggregate, CountBy and MinMaxBy

Aggregate is the general fold: it threads an accumulator through a sequence with a function you supply. The other operators in this section are specialised folds that read better at the call site.

The aggregation operators collapse a sequence to one value, and each one states what it does about the empty case. That is the property worth knowing before reaching for one: some throw on empty, some return a default, and the difference decides whether a caller needs a guard.

Seed, accumulator and result

A seed-based aggregate takes a seed and an accumulator and produces a value, and it can fold over a type that is not numeric. A simple aggregate takes only an accumulator, seeds with the first element, and therefore throws on an empty sequence — which is the version that appears as a defect when a filter upstream returns nothing.

Selecting by an order

Min and max take a comparer, not a selector, so getting the element with the largest key means projecting and re-finding. The by-forms take a selector and are the correct answer, and they exist because the projection form does not compile when the key is not the element.

// Sum, Average, Min, Max -- with and without a selector
decimal revenue = orders.Sum(o => o.Total);
decimal biggest  = orders.Max(o => o.Total);
Order? latest    = orders.MaxBy(o => o.Id);          // the element, not the key
decimal? cheapest = orders.Min(o => o.Total);        // Nullable for reference types
Order? firstOrd   = orders.MinBy(o => o.Total);
double mean = orders.Average(o => o.Total);

// Aggregate: seed + accumulator function + (optional) result selector
int sum = numbers.Aggregate(0, (acc, n) => acc + n);
int max = numbers.Aggregate(0, (acc, n) => Math.Max(acc, n));
string path = parts.Aggregate("", (acc, p) => acc + "/" + p);

// The overload without a seed lets the first element be the seed
var running = numbers.Aggregate((a, b) => a + b);
// Warning: it THROWS on an empty sequence

// A practical use: building a lookup in one pass
var totals = orders.Aggregate(
    new Dictionary<string, decimal>(),
    (acc, o) =>
    {
        acc[o.Customer] = acc.GetValueOrDefault(o.Customer) + o.Total;
        return acc;
    });

// CountBy (added in .NET 9): frequency counting in one call
var counts = orders.CountBy(o => o.Customer);
// IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<string, int>>

// Index (added in .NET 9): first-occurrence position, or -1
int at = orders.Index(o => o.Id == 42);

// Repeat and Range: infinite or generated sequences
// Enumerable.Repeat("x", 5)  -> x x x x x
// Enumerable.Range(1, 5)     -> 1 2 3 4 5

// Distinct, Chunk, Order -- .NET 6 and later
// numbers.Chunk(100)      -> IEnumerable<int[]> in batches of 100
// numbers.Distinct()       -> removes duplicates using the default comparer
// orders.Order(o => o.Total) -> orders, sorted in place

// OrderBy / OrderDescending / ThenBy / ThenByDescending
var sorted = orders
    .OrderByDescending(o => o.Total)
    .ThenBy(o => o.Customer, StringComparer.Ordinal)
    .ThenBy(o => o.Id);

// Order is stable; OrderBy is also stable, so equal keys keep input order
// Always add a final ThenBy on a unique key if the order must be deterministic.

Aggregate is where a hand-written foreach becomes visible LINQ. It is genuinely useful for stateful folds, but for anything a named operator already covers, the named operator is clearer and usually faster.

Max on a reference type returns null for an empty sequence because the type is nullable, while Max on int throws because int is not. If you need the safe version on a value type, MaxOrDefault or MaxBy with a null check.


{{-- EACH COLLAPSES A SEQUENCE TO ONE VALUE, and EACH STATES WHAT IT
     DOES ABOUT THE EMPTY CASE — which decides whether a caller
     needs a guard. --}}
static void EmptyBehaviour(List<int> numbers, List<Order> orders)
{
    int a = numbers.Sum();                       // 0: empty is fine
    int b = numbers.Average();                   // INVALIDOPERATIONEXCEPTION
    int c = numbers.Min();                       // INVALIDOPERATIONEXCEPTION
    int d = numbers.Max();                       // INVALIDOPERATIONEXCEPTION
    int e = numbers.Count();                     // 0
    int f = numbers.Aggregate(0, (x, y) => x + y);   // 0: the seed
                                                   //   IS the answer
    {{-- ^ Sum and Count treat empty as zero; Min, Max and Average
         THROW. Nothing in the names says so, and the difference
         decides whether a caller needs a guard. --}}

    // Average AND Sum return DIFFERENT TYPES for the same empty
    // case, which is why a total is safe and an average is not:
    decimal total = orders.Sum(o => o.Total);          // 0
    decimal avg   = orders.Average(o => o.Total);      // throws
}

{{-- SEED, ACCUMULATOR AND RESULT — and it can fold over a type that
     is NOT NUMERIC, which is the whole reason it exists: --}}
static void Folding(List<Order> orders)
{
    // NUMERIC: the simple form, seeded with the FIRST ELEMENT, so
    // an empty sequence THROWS.
    var total = orders.Aggregate(0m, (sum, o) => sum + o.Total);

    // THE SEEDED FORM, which is the safe one and can fold over
    // anything:
    var running = orders.Aggregate(
        new RunningTotal(),                       // the SEED
        (acc, o) => acc.Add(o),                  // the ACCUMULATOR
        acc => acc.ToImmutable());               // the RESULT

    sealed class RunningTotal
    {
        public decimal Total { get; private set; }
        public int Count { get; private set; }
        public RunningTotal Add(Order o)
        {
            Total += o.Total;
            Count++;
            return this;                          // returns itself, so
        }                                         // the accumulator is
        public decimal Average => Total / Count;  // MUTABLE: which is
    }                                             // why the RESULT
                                                  // step exists, to
                                                  // freeze it before
                                                  // handing it on

    {{-- ^ THE MUTABLE ACCUMULATOR IS THE PATTERN for a fold over a
         non-numeric type, and the third step exists because the
         accumulator is a mutable object that callers must not be
         able to keep mutating. --}}
}

{{-- Min and max take a COMPARER, not a selector — so getting the
     element with the largest key means projecting and re-finding: --}}
static void MinMaxBy(List<Order> orders)
{
    var cheapest = orders.MinBy(o => o.Total);            // THE BY FORM
    var dearest  = orders.MaxBy(o => o.Total);
    var largest  = orders.MaxBy(o => o.Total, Comparer<decimal>.Default);
    // null on an empty sequence, rather than throwing

    // THE COMPARER FORM, which is what the plain Min/Max take — and
    // note what it means:
    var maxTotal = orders.Max(o => o.Total);              // a NUMBER
    // ^ Max with a selector returns the max OF THE SELECTED VALUES,
    //   not the element. So you have the largest total and not the
    //   order that has it.

    var firstOrder = orders.First(o => o.Total == maxTotal);  // a SECOND
                                                              // WALK
    {{-- ^ which is the trap: Max(o => o.Total) followed by
         First(o => o.Total == that) is TWO O(n) WALKS plus a
         comparison of DECIMALS for equality, when MaxBy does it in
         one. --}}
}

10.6 Deferred execution and multiple enumeration

Every operator except the terminal ones returns a recipe, not a result. Nothing runs until a terminal operator forces enumeration. This is what makes infinite sequences expressible (Enumerable.Range piped through a Take), and it is also the cause of the most common LINQ bug: enumerating a query twice re-executes it.

Every LINQ operator except a terminal one is deferred: it records a description of the work and returns an object that performs it when enumerated. That is what makes a query composable — a stage can be added after the fact and still be part of the plan — and it is also what makes enumerating a query twice run it twice.

The three costs of deferral

Captured variables are read at enumeration time rather than at construction time, so a loop variable that changes after the query is built changes what the query returns. Exceptions thrown by a selector happen at enumeration, often far from the code that caused them. And a query built inside a loop and enumerated inside the same loop re-executes the whole plan per iteration, which is the classic accidental n-squared.

Materialising, and when it is right

Calling ToList ends the deferral and runs the plan once. That is right when the source can change, when the sequence is enumerated more than once, and when the stages after the materialisation need random access. It is wrong to add it everywhere: it allocates a copy that the terminal operator would have produced anyway, and it defeats an execution strategy where the consumer would have handled the data differently.

// Deferred: the predicate runs at enumeration, not at Where()
var query = orders.Where(o => { Console.WriteLine("filtered"); return o.IsPaid; });
Console.WriteLine("nothing yet");       // no output from the predicate
foreach (var o in query) { }        // NOW it runs

// Infinite sequences are fine with a short-circuiting terminal
var naturals = Enumerable.Range(1, int.MaxValue)
    .Select(n => n * n)
    .Where(n => n % 2 == 1)
    .Take(5);                          // stops after 5

// The double-enumeration trap: work done twice, results possibly different
// foreach (var o in query) ...   // enumerates
// foreach (var o in query) ...   // enumerates AGAIN, from scratch

// Fix: materialise once
var materialised = query.ToList();
// foreach (var o in materialised) ...  // twice, but the source ran once

// In a nested loop this is O(n^2) work
// foreach (var a in orders)
//     foreach (var b in orders.Where(o => o.Id != a.Id)) { }  // re-filters every time
// Fix: build a lookup once
var byId = orders.ToLookup(o => o.Id);

// Captured variables are read at enumeration time -- see chapter 8
// Materialise when the query crosses a boundary (async, parallel, stored)

// LINQ is not free: every operator is a delegate call per element
// For hot inner loops, a plain for over an array with local variables
// is measurably faster than three chained LINQ operators.

Materialising is a correctness tool first and a performance tool second. The moment a query is enumerated in more than one place, or stored in a field, or crosses an await, call ToList() and be explicit about the trade.

Never expose an unmaterialised IEnumerable<T> across a thread boundary, return it from an iterator, or store it in a field. IEnumerable<T> is a promise to re-run the source later, and the source may be a closed file handle, a disposed connection or a modified collection.


{{-- EVERY OPERATOR EXCEPT A TERMINAL ONE IS DEFERRED: it records a
     DESCRIPTION of the work and returns an object that performs it
     when ENUMERATED. --}}
static void Deferral(List<Order> orders)
{
    IEnumerable<Order> q = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100);
    // ^ NOTHING HAS HAPPENED YET. No filter ran, no delegate was
    //   invoked. The object is a description.

    // The terminal operator is where it runs:
    var n = q.Count();      // NOW the filter runs, once per element

    // AND A SECOND TERMINAL RE-RUNS THE WHOLE PLAN:
    var m = q.Count();      // the filter runs AGAIN
    {{-- ^ on a List this is cheap. On an IQueryable it is a SECOND
         ROUND TRIP, and the data may have changed between them. --}}
}

{{-- COST 1: CAPTURED VARIABLES ARE READ AT ENUMERATION TIME. --}}
static void CapturedAtEnumerationTime(List<Order> orders)
{
    int threshold = 100;
    var q = orders.Where(o => o.Total > threshold);
    // ^ reads 'threshold' NOW, when enumerated.

    threshold = 1000;
    var n = q.Count();      // uses 1000, not 100
    {{-- ^ which is CORRECT and almost never intended: the query was
         "where total is over 100" when it was written, and it is
         "over 1000" when it runs. The fix is to capture into a
         local the query does not see, or to materialise. --}}
}

{{-- COST 2: EXCEPTIONS FROM A SELECTOR HAPPEN AT ENUMERATION, far
     from the code that caused them: --}}
static void ExceptionsAtEnumeration(List<Order> orders)
{
    var q = orders.Select(o => o.Total / o.Quantity);
    // ^ NO EXCEPTION HERE. DivideByZeroException cannot occur yet,
    //   because nothing has run.

    var results = q.ToList();   // THROWS HERE, several lines below
    //                                  the builder of the query
    {{-- ^ and the stack trace names the LINQ internals, not the
         caller. Which is why a query built in one place and
         enumerated in another produces a diagnostic that points at
         nothing the reader can change. --}}
}

{{-- COST 3: A QUERY BUILT AND ENUMERATED IN A LOOP IS n-squared: --}}
static void TheN2(List<Order> orders)
{
    foreach (var o in orders)
    {
        var q = orders.Where(x => x.CustomerId == o.CustomerId);  // BUILT
        var matches = q.Count();                                // and
        Report(o, matches);                                     // RE-RUN
    }
    {{-- ^ the plan is rebuilt and re-executed for every outer
         element. On a List this is arithmetic; on an IQueryable it
         is one database round trip per row, which is the shape of a
         report that times out. --}}

    // THE FIX: one query, grouped in the database.
    var byCustomer = orders
        .GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId)
        .Select(g => new { CustomerId = g.Key, Count = g.Count() })
        .ToList();
    foreach (var o in orders)
        Report(o, byCustomer.First(b => b.CustomerId == o.CustomerId));
    {{-- ^ one round trip, and a dictionary lookup in memory instead
         of a linear scan. --}}
}

{{-- MATERIALISING, and WHEN IT IS RIGHT: --}}
static void Materialising(List<Order> orders)
{
    // RIGHT: the sequence is enumerated more than once.
    var q = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100);
    var snapshot = q.ToList();
    var a = snapshot.Count;
    var b = snapshot.Count;     // ONE execution, because the plan is
                                // already complete

    // RIGHT: the source can change between stages.
    var consistent = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100).ToList();
    foreach (var o in consistent) { /* the source is stable here */ }

    // RIGHT: random access is needed afterwards.
    var indexed = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100).ToList();
    Console.WriteLine(indexed[0]);

    // WRONG TO ADD EVERYWHERE: it allocates a copy the terminal
    // operator would have produced anyway, and it defeats an
    // execution strategy where the consumer handles the data
    // differently.
    var wasted = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100).ToList().ToList();
    {{-- ^ the second ToList copies a list that is already a list. --}}
}

10.7 IQueryable and parameterised queries

IQueryable<T> extends IEnumerable<T> with the ability to translate the query into something else — SQL, a NoSQL filter, an OData expression tree. Instead of executing, it accumulates an expression tree that the provider turns into a query. This is how Entity Framework Core and every other ORM work.

// IQueryable defers TRANSLATION, not just execution
IQueryable<Order> q = dbContext.Orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100m);   // no SQL yet
Console.WriteLine(q.ToQueryString());          // SELECT ... WHERE Total > 100
await foreach (var o in q.AsAsyncEnumerable()) { }   // now it executes

// The provider translates what it can and client-evaluates the rest.
// Server-side: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, Join, Take, Skip, Any, Count
// Often client-side (a full fetch first): ToList on a complex projection,
//                         custom methods, non-translatable operators

// This is the N+1 problem: one query, then one per row
// foreach (var o in db.Orders)
//     Console.WriteLine(o.Customer.Name);   // a query per order
// Fix: eager load / project in one query
// var data = db.Orders.Select(o => new { o.Id, o.Customer.Name }).ToList();
// or db.Orders.Include(o => o.Customer).ToList();

// Composition: an in-memory filter over a queryable is a client filter
var expensiveOnly = db.Orders.Where(o => o.Total > 1000m);
// var r = expensiveOnly.Where(CheapFilter).ToList();
//   -- the DB returns everything > 1000, then CheapFilter runs in memory.

// Composition in the other order pushes the whole thing to the server
// var r = db.Orders.Where(CheapFilter).Where(o => o.Total > 1000m).ToList();

// AsQueryable: LINQ over anything, still client-side
var q2 = orders.AsQueryable().Where(o => o.IsPaid);

// Common providers and what they translate
//   Entity Framework Core   -> SQL, LINQ to Entities
//   MongoDB.Driver           -> BSON documents
//   Azure Data Tables        -> OData filters
//   Jint / expression evaluators -> dynamic languages

The rule that prevents most ORM performance bugs: put as much of the query on the server as possible and fetch as few rows and columns as possible. Anything that cannot be translated is a boundary — find it deliberately, and check ToQueryString() to see exactly what the database will receive.

For ASP.NET Core APIs, project to a DTO in the query itself (.Select(o => new OrderDto(...))). That keeps the query translatable, avoids loading columns nobody needs, and stops the database model from leaking into your public contract. The ASP.NET Core guide covers the API side in depth.

Exercises 10

  1. Write the same three-step query in both syntaxes and confirm with a decompiler (or a debugger breakpoint) that they compile to identical call chains.
  2. Build a nested loop over a Where query and measure the time, then replace it with a ToLookup and measure again.
  3. Write a GroupBy report with count, sum and average per customer, then do the same with CountBy and Aggregate. Compare readability.
  4. Demonstrate deferred execution: log inside a Select and show it runs once per enumeration, then materialise with ToList().
  5. Build an infinite generator with yield return and combine it with Take, Skip and First. Note which terminals short-circuit.
  6. Write a Result<T>-returning LINQ pipeline using Select and Where that validates an IEnumerable<string> of inputs and collects every failure.

{{-- IQueryable IS A DESCRIPTIVE OBJECT, and the provider translates
     it. The translation happens at ENUMERATION, which is why a query
     is parameterised when it runs rather than when it is built. --}}
public sealed class OrderQueries(AppDbContext db)
{
    public IQueryable<Order> UnpaidOlderThan(TimeSpan age) =>
        db.Orders
          .Where(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Pending)
          .Where(o => DateTimeOffset.UtcNow - o.PlacedAt > age);

    public async Task<List<Order>> GetAsync(CancellationToken ct) =>
        await UnpaidOlderThan(TimeSpan.FromDays(7)).ToListAsync(ct);
    {{-- ^ ToListAsync IS WHERE THE SQL HAPPENS. Everything before
         it is an EXPRESSION TREE being composed in memory, and a
         debugger stepping through it shows no database activity
         because there is none. --}}
}

{{-- AND THE PARAMETERISED PART, which is the point of the type: --}}
public async Task<List<Order>> ByStatusAsync(
    OrderStatus status, int limit, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // THE VALUE IS CAPTURED INTO A PARAMETER by the provider, not
    // pasted into the SQL text.
    return await db.Orders
        .Where(o => o.Status == status)     // @__status_0
        .Take(limit)                          // @__limit_1
        .ToListAsync(ct);

    // SELECT TOP (@__limit_1) ... WHERE [Status] = @__status_0
    {{-- ^ WHICH IS WHY THE PLAN CACHE WORKS and why a loop of 10,000
         iterations with 10,000 different statuses does NOT produce
         10,000 different plans. --}}
}

{{-- THE DEFECT THIS PREVENTS, and it is a REAL ONE rather than a
     theoretical one: --}}
public static void NeverInterpolate(IQueryable<Order> q, string reference)
{
    // WRONG: string interpolation produces a CONSTANT in the tree.
    var bad = q.Where(o => o.Reference == $"ORD-{reference}");
    // -> WHERE [Reference] = N'ORD-' + @__reference_0 ... evaluated
    //    by the DATABASE per row, so the index on Reference is NOT
    //    used and the query becomes a full scan.
    {{-- ^ WHICH IS WHY THE VALUE MUST BE A CAPTURED VARIABLE rather
         than an expression: the provider can only turn a CONSTANT
         into a parameter. An interpolated string is a constant the
         moment it is built. --}}

    // RIGHT: a captured variable, so the provider parameterises it.
    string prefix = $"ORD-{reference}";
    var good = q.Where(o => o.Reference == prefix);
    {{-- ^ note the LOCAL: 'prefix' is computed once in C#, and the
         provider sees a variable reference rather than a
         concatenation expression. --}}
}

{{-- AND WHAT YOU CANNOT EXPRESS IN A QUERY, which is where the
     provider throws rather than translating: --}}
public static async Task CannotExpress(AppDbContext db, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // string methods other than a few are not TRANSLATABLE:
    // db.Orders.Where(o => o.Reference.ToUpper() == "ORD-1")
    // -> InvalidOperationException: could not be translated

    // The SQL-side equivalents that ARE translatable:
    await db.Orders
        .Where(o => EF.Functions.Like(o.Reference, "ORD-%"))
        .Where(o => EF.Functions.DateDiffDay(o.PlacedAt, DateTimeOffset.UtcNow) > 7)
        .ToListAsync(ct);

    // A LOCAL FUNCTION IS EVALUATED IN MEMORY, so calling one in a
    // Where is not translatable either — which means the filter is
    // applied AFTER the rows are fetched, and a "query" that fetches
    // a million rows to discard 999,995 of them is worse than no
    // query at all.
    static bool IsOverdue(Order o) => DateTimeOffset.UtcNow - o.PlacedAt > TimeSpan.FromDays(7);
    // db.Orders.Where(IsOverdue)     throws at ENUMERATION, and the
    //                                 stack names ToListAsync rather
    //                                 than the Where, because that
    //                                 is where translation happens
}

11 · Async / Await & Concurrency

11.1 async and await11.2 Task vs ValueTask11.3 WhenAll, WhenAny and error handling11.4 CancellationToken11.5 IAsyncEnumerable and await foreach11.6 Parallel.ForEachAsync and TPL11.7 Task.Run and when not to use it11.8 Deadlocks, ConfigureAwait and SynchronizationContext11.9 Channels and producer/consumer

Chapter eleven covers the concurrency story in modern .NET. async/await lets you write concurrent code that reads sequentially, CancellationToken makes cancellation cooperative and clean, and Channel<T> replaces ad-hoc producer/consumer plumbing. The two mistakes that dominate real bugs are blocking on async code and hiding CPU work in Task.Run.

11.1 async and await

An async method returns a task instead of a result. await suspends the method at that point and resumes it on completion — without blocking a thread. The method runs synchronously until the first real suspension, which is why putting I/O first is a common and worthwhile optimisation.

An async method returns a task rather than a value, and the await keyword suspends it at that point and resumes it when the awaited operation completes. Two things follow that surprise people: nothing runs synchronously between the method's start and its first await — so code before the first await is a block that cannot be interrupted — and after an await the method continues on a different thread unless a synchronization context is present.

The rule that removes most of the difficulty

Only one thread ever runs the body of an async method at a time, and it does not matter which. That is why a continuation can safely touch a variable declared before the await: there is no concurrency within the method, so the compiler is free to lift that variable into a closure. What is not safe is assuming which thread you are on, and that assumption is what the synchronization-context rules are about.

Where the continuation runs

If the awaited task's continuation is captured from a synchronization context — a UI thread, or a request context in a server — the continuation is posted back to it. If there is no context, it runs on a thread-pool thread. Both are correct; the difference is whether a continuation can touch anything that belongs to the capturing thread.

static async Task<string> FetchAsync(string url, CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    using var client = new HttpClient();
    using var response = await client.GetAsync(url, ct);
    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    return await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(ct);
}

// Calling it: await, never .Result or .Wait()
string body = await FetchAsync("https://example.com", ct);

// sequential: total time = a + b
var a = await FetchAsync(urlA, ct);
var b = await FetchAsync(urlB, ct);

// concurrent: total time = max(a, b). Start BOTH before awaiting either.
var ta = FetchAsync(urlA, ct);     // starts now, runs until its first await
var tb = FetchAsync(urlB, ct);     // starts now
var a = await ta;                    // suspends until A is done
var b = await tb;                    // B was already running

// The mistake: the second call has not even started yet
// var a = await FetchAsync(urlA, ct);
// var b = await FetchAsync(urlB, ct);   // serialised -- no speedup at all

// Naming: methods returning Task should end in Async, to make the
// asynchrony visible at the call site.

async is not "make this parallel". It means "this operation completes later, and I would rather not block a thread while it does". Actual parallelism comes from overlapping I/O or from a scheduler. Naming the method Async keeps callers honest.

async void is only legitimate for event handlers and a handful of framework overrides. Everywhere else it returns Task and must be awaited, because a fire-and-forget async void silently swallows exceptions and crashes the process from a thread-pool callback.


{{-- async RETURNS A TASK, and await SUSPENDS the method and RESUMES
     it when the awaited operation completes. --}}
public sealed class OrderService(OrderRepository repo)
{
    // NOTHING RUNS SYNCHRONOUSLY BETWEEN THE START AND THE FIRST
    // AWAIT, so code before the first await is a BLOCK THAT CANNOT
    // BE INTERRUPTED:
    public async Task<Order> LoadAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("1. runs on the calling thread");
        Console.WriteLine("2. runs on the calling thread");
        Console.WriteLine("3. runs on the calling thread");

        await Task.Delay(10, ct);        // SUSPENDS here

        Console.WriteLine("4. runs on a POOL THREAD");
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct);
        Console.WriteLine("5. runs on a POOL THREAD");
        return order;
        // ^ after an await the method continues on a DIFFERENT
        //   THREAD unless a synchronization context is present — and
        //   which thread it is has never been something the code
        //   could rely on.
    }
}

{{-- THE RULE THAT REMOVES MOST OF THE DIFFICULTY: ONLY ONE THREAD
     EVER RUNS THE BODY AT A TIME, and it does not matter which. --}}
public async Task SafeAfterAwait(List<int> items)
{
    int total = 0;                  // DECLARED BEFORE the await
    foreach (int i in items)
    {
        await ProcessAsync(i);     // SUSPENDS, and other code runs
        total += i;                // ^ SAFE: there is no concurrency
    }                              //   WITHIN the method, so the
    return total;                  //   compiler lifts 'total' into
}                                  //   a closure
{{-- ^ WHICH IS WHY THE CONTEXT-LOSS BUG almost always appears in a
     method that SHARES state with something else — a field, a
     shared list, an outer variable also written by another path —
     and never in a purely local one. --}}

{{-- WHERE THE CONTINUATION RUNS, and both answers are correct: --}}
public sealed class Form
{
    public async Task RefreshAsync()
    {
        await Task.Delay(10);
        // ON A UI THREAD: the continuation is POSTED BACK to the UI
        //   thread, so touching controls is legal.
        statusLabel.Text = "done";

        await Task.Run(() => Compute());   // NO CONTEXT: the
        //                                    continuation runs on a
        //                                    POOL THREAD, and
        //                                    touching a control here
        //                                    THROWS.
    }

    public async Task ServerAsync()
    {
        await Db.ReadAsync();
        // IN ASP.NET CORE: there is NO synchronization context by
        //   default, so continuations run on the pool and nothing
        //   needs posting back — which is why ConfigureAwait(false)
        //   is a NO-OP there and why adding it is cargo cult.
    }
}

11.2 Task vs ValueTask

Task is a reference type and allocates. ValueTask<T> is a struct that wraps either a result or a pooled task, and it avoids the allocation when the result is already available synchronously. It is a hot-path optimisation with sharp edges, not a default.

A Task allocates and a ValueTask usually does not. That single difference produces a real performance gap on a hot path that awaits millions of times, and it also produces a large number of defects on paths where the result is awaited more than once.

The rule that decides whether a value task is safe

A value task may wrap a pooled buffer, and reading that buffer twice gives the wrong answer the second time. So it is safe only when the await happens exactly once, at the top level of the caller's method, and the result is never stored, never awaited again and never combined with WhenAll. Everywhere else it is a defect waiting for the second reader.

Where the win actually is

The saving is one small allocation per operation, so it matters when the operation is cheap relative to its allocation — a socket read already buffered, a cache hit, an arithmetic helper. It does not matter for a database call or an HTTP request, where the allocation is noise beside the network. Using it for those is the common mistake, because it converts a definite allocation into a constraint on every caller.

// ValueTask for a method that usually completes synchronously
public ValueTask<int> TryReadAsync(Stream s, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (s.CanRead && s is MemoryStream mem && mem.Position < mem.Length)
    {
        // synchronous fast path: no Task allocation at all
        return new ValueTask<int>((int)mem.ReadByte());
    }
    // slow path: the struct wraps the in-flight Task
    return new ValueTask<int>(ReadSlowAsync(s, ct));
}

// Awaiting a ValueTask is syntactically identical to Task
int n = await TryReadAsync(stream, ct);

// The rules, which are the entire reason ValueTask is not the default
//   1. await it at most ONCE
//   2. store the result in a local, or await it immediately
//   3. never return the same ValueTask from two places
//   4. never call .Result or .Wait() on one (or on a Task)
//   5. do not box it into Task.Delay, WhenAll, or a collection

var vt = TryReadAsync(stream, ct);
// var x = await vt;  await vt;   -- reading a completed ValueTask twice is undefined

// When in doubt: use Task. It is one allocation per call and always safe.
// ValueTask earns its place in: parsers, hot protocol loops, pooled-buffer APIs,
// and framework internals that must not allocate.

A ValueTask<T> backed by an IValueTaskSource must be consumed exactly once. Reading it twice, or reading it after it has been boxed into a Task, gives undefined results that will not throw — they will simply be wrong, which is far worse.

A good middle ground is Task<T> that is cached: if a method returns the same completed task for the same input, callers pay nothing extra. But never return Task.FromResult from a hot path expecting the runtime to cache it — it does not, and each call allocates.


{{-- A Task ALLOCATES and a ValueTask USUALLY DOES NOT. One small
     allocation per operation. --}}
public ValueTask<int> CountAsync(string key, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (_cache.TryGetValue(key, out int cached))
    {
        // A CACHE HIT: the cheap operation relative to its
        // allocation. ONE ValueTask<int> STRUCT, no allocation —
        // which is the case the type exists for.
        return new ValueTask<int>(cached);
    }

    // A COLD MISS: an I/O-bound database call. The allocation is
    // NOISE BESIDE THE ROUND TRIP, and this is where people reach
    // for ValueTask anyway.
    return new ValueTask<int>(CountFromDatabaseAsync(key, ct));
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE COMMON MISTAKE: it converts a DEFINITE
     allocation into a CONSTRAINT ON EVERY CALLER, to save a saving
     nobody can measure against a network round trip. --}}

{{-- THE RULE: A VALUE TASK MAY WRAP A POOLED BUFFER, so reading it
     TWICE gives the wrong answer the second time. --}}
public ValueTask<int> CountAsync(string key, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // THE FAST PATH, which is the one that CAN wrap a pooled
    // buffer:
    if (_cache.TryGetValue(key, out int cached))
        return new ValueTask<int>(cached);

    // ...
}

static async Task Wrong(int key)
{
    var vt = svc.CountAsync(key, ct);

    // SAFE: awaited ONCE, at the top level of the method.
    int n = await vt;

    // UNSAFE 1: awaited AGAIN. The second await reads the pooled
    //            buffer AFTER it has been returned, so it returns
    //            whatever now occupies it — a plausible wrong
    //            number rather than an exception.
    // int again = await vt;

    // UNSAFE 2: STORED. The value task escapes the method, so the
    //            buffer's lifetime is no longer bounded here.
    // return await vt;

    // UNSAFE 3: COMBINED. WhenAll enumerates a task's identity
    //            more than once internally, and a value task does
    //            not support being enumerated.
    // await Task.WhenAll(vt, other);
}
{{-- ^ SO A VALUE TASK IS SAFE ONLY WHEN the await happens EXACTLY
     ONCE, at the top level of the caller's method, and the result
     is NEVER STORED, never awaited again, and never combined with
     WhenAll. Everywhere else it is a DEFECT WAITING FOR THE SECOND
     READER, and the second reader is usually a refactor six
     months away that changes one line. --}}

{{-- AND A Task<Result> IS NOT THE SAME TRADE: --}}
static async Task<Task<int>> Twice(int n)
{
    // A Task<Result> ALLOCATES TWO OBJECTS: the inner result and
    // the task wrapping it. It saves nothing over Task<int>, which
    // is why returning it from an async method is nearly always a
    // mistake.
    return await Task.FromResult(n * 2);
}

static async Task<int> Once(int n) => await Task.FromResult(n * 2);
// ^ ONE allocation. The double form exists only for a method that
//   must return a task synchronously, and even then Task.FromResult
//   wrapped once is the correct spelling.

11.3 WhenAll, WhenAny and error handling

Task.WhenAll waits for every task and returns an array of results. Task.WhenAny returns as soon as one completes, which is the basis for timeouts and for racing mirrors. The error semantics differ in one important way that catches everyone once.

The two combinators answer different questions. WhenAll completes when every task has completed and throws if any of them failed. WhenAny completes as soon as one does, which makes it a race — and a race that returns a task rather than a result has to unwrap the task to find out whether it succeeded.

The failures nobody expects

Only the first exception is thrown by WhenAll; the rest are swallowed unless the thrown one is an aggregate. And WhenAny does not throw at all: it throws only when the returned task is awaited, and if the first-completing task faulted while a second would have succeeded, the caller sees a failure for a race it won. Both behaviours are documented and neither is what a first reading suggests.

The shape worth writing

For a fan-out where partial failure is acceptable, the shape is: start everything, await WhenAll inside a try, and inspect each task's own status afterwards rather than relying on the aggregate. That gives per-item outcomes, which is what a batch job actually needs.

// WhenAll: all complete, results in argument order
var tasks = new[] { FetchAsync(urlA, ct), FetchAsync(urlB, ct) };
string[] results = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
Console.WriteLine(results[0]);       // corresponds to urlA, not to whoever finished first

// WhenAll with no result
await Task.WhenAll(tasks);          // Task, throws on the FIRST failure

// Error semantics: await unwraps, and the OTHER tasks still run to
// completion. Failures are not cancelled.
try { await Task.WhenAll(tasks); }
catch (HttpRequestException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);          // the first one that failed
    // ... but every other task is still running. Inspect each:
    foreach (var t in tasks.Where(t => t.IsFaulted))
        Console.WriteLine(t.Exception!.Message);
}

// WhenAny: the first to finish, whatever its state
Task finished = await Task.WhenAny(tasks);
Console.WriteLine(finished.Status);          // RanToCompletion, Faulted or Canceled

// A timeout, the correct way
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
try { await FetchAsync(url, cts.Token); }
catch (OperationCanceledException) { Console.WriteLine("timed out"); }

// WhenAny with a delay task: no CancellationTokenSource needed
Task winner = await Task.WhenAny(work, Task.Delay(5000));
if (winner == work) await work; else Console.WriteLine("timed out");

// WhenAll with a mix of Task and Task<T>: the result type unifies
await Task.WhenAll(Task.Delay(100), FetchAsync(url, ct));

// Common mistake: await inside a loop
// foreach (var url in urls) { results.Add(await FetchAsync(url, ct)); }  // serial
// var results = await Task.WhenAll(urls.Select(u => FetchAsync(u, ct)));    // parallel

Awaiting inside a loop is the single most common async performance mistake after blocking on .Result. It is invisible in a test with three items and catastrophic with three thousand. Task.WhenAll(urls.Select(...)) is a one-line fix.

Task.WhenAll does not cancel the remaining tasks when one fails, and in .NET 6 and earlier it also did not pass a token. If you need fail-fast behaviour, use WhenAny in a loop with a linked CancellationTokenSource that you cancel as soon as the first failure appears.


{{-- WHEN ALL: completes when EVERY task has completed, throws if ANY
     failed. WHEN ANY: completes as soon as ONE does — a RACE. --}}
static async Task Both(List<Task<Order>> jobs)
{
    // WhenAll THROWS the FIRST failure, and SWALLOWS THE REST unless
    // the thrown one is an aggregate.
    await Task.WhenAll(jobs);
    // -> AggregateException: the first, with the others as InnerExceptions
    // -> HttpRequestException: one, and the other four failures are
    //    GONE unless you look at each task yourself.

    // WHICH IS WHY THE PER-ITEM SHAPE IS WORTH WRITING for a batch:
    var outcomes = await Task.WhenAll(jobs.Select(Observe));

    // Observe WRAPS each task, so a failure becomes a RETURNED VALUE
    // and WhenAll has nothing to throw.
    static async Task<Outcome<Order>> Observe(Task<Order> job)
    {
        try { return Outcome<Order>.Ok(await job); }
        catch (Exception ex) { return Outcome<Order>.Fail(ex); }
    }
}

{{-- WHEN ANY: A RACE, and it does not throw — it throws only when
     the RETURNED task is awaited. --}}
static async Task<string?> FirstSuccessful(IEnumerable<Task<string>> probes)
{
    var all = probes.ToArray();

    // THE FIRST TO COMPLETE, whether it SUCCEEDED or FAILED:
    var winner = await Task.WhenAny(all);
    return await winner;      // -> THROWS if the winner faulted,
                              //    EVEN IF a second task would have
                              //    succeeded a millisecond later
    {{-- ^ WHICH IS THE BEHAVIOUR NOBODY EXPECTS. A caller racing
         three providers where the first to answer is down gets a
         failure, and the fix is to loop until one succeeds rather
         than to trust the race. --}}
}

static async Task<string?> LoopUntilSuccess(IEnumerable<Task<string>> probes)
{
    var pending = probes.ToList();
    var errors = new List<Exception>();

    while (pending.Count > 0)
    {
        var winner = await Task.WhenAny(pending);
        pending.Remove(winner);

        try { return await winner; }                  // SUCCEEDED
        catch (Exception ex) { errors.Add(ex); }      // try the next
    }

    throw new AggregateException("all probes failed", errors);
    {{-- ^ THE SHAPE WORTH WRITING: a race whose losers are RETRIED
         rather than reported, which is what "first available"
         actually means. --}}
}

{{-- AND WHEN ANY WITH A TIMEOUT, which is the version that appears
     in a request path: --}}
static async Task<Order> WithTimeout(Func<Task<Order>> fetch)
{
    var work = fetch();
    var completed = await Task.WhenAny(work, Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)));

    if (completed != work)
    {
        // CANCEL IT, or the work continues and holds a connection
        // that the caller has already given up on:
        _cts.Cancel();
        throw new TimeoutException("no response within 2s");
    }

    return await work;
    {{-- ^ note that a TIMEOUT IS NOT A CANCELLATION: the work is
         still running unless something cancels it, and a task that
         is abandoned still completes, still uses resources, and can
         still write to a database. --}}
}

11.4 CancellationToken

Cancellation in .NET is cooperative: you pass a token down the call chain and each operation checks it and throws OperationCanceledException when signalled. Nothing is aborted forcibly. That is why every long-running framework method takes a token as its last parameter.

A cancellation token is a signal, not a force. It says "stop if you can" and it carries no authority: a method that ignores it will run to completion regardless, and nothing warns about it. That is deliberate — an operation that is halfway through committing a transaction should finish the commit rather than abandon it — and it means the obligation to observe the token sits with every method that takes one.

Where to observe it

The pattern is to pass the token down rather than to check it locally, so the operation that actually blocks is the one that sees it. Checking in a caller and then calling a method that takes no token produces cooperative cancellation that stops before the work rather than during it.

The three sources

A token can come from the caller — a request, a console signal — from a timeout, or from a linked combination of the two. Linking exists because an operation with a deadline and an ambient cancellation needs both, and a token that represents "either" has to be built rather than chosen.

// Accept a token, check it, pass it on
static async Task ProcessAsync(IEnumerable<int> items, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await foreach (var item in items.ToAsyncEnumerable().WithCancellation(ct))
    {
        ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();      // the idiomatic check
        await HandleAsync(item, ct);
    }
}

// Creating and linking tokens
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();          // manual cancel
using var timed = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
using var manual = new CancellationTokenSource();
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(
    manual.Token, ct);                      // cancels if EITHER fires

linked.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));

// Reacting to a token rather than checking it
ct.Register(() => { connection.Close(); });

// The correct catch
try { await LongOperationAsync(ct); }
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    // expected: we asked for this
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    // a real failure -- do not swallow it as cancellation
    Report(ex);
}

// Disposing: call Dispose so the timer and registrations are released
// CTS instances register callbacks; leaking them leaks the callbacks.

The when (ct.IsCancellationRequested) filter on the catch is important: without it, a genuine timeout inside the operation is indistinguishable from your own cancellation and gets silently treated as success.

Only OperationCanceledException should be swallowed for cancellation. The framework throws TaskCanceledException and TimeoutException in different situations; a catch (Exception) around an awaited call will hide real errors along with the cancellation.


{{-- A TOKEN IS A SIGNAL, NOT A FORCE: it says "stop if you can" and
     carries NO AUTHORITY. --}}
public sealed class ExportService
{
    // WRONG: TAKES A TOKEN AND IGNORES IT. Nothing warns, and the
    //         caller's cancellation does nothing at all.
    public async Task<byte[]> ExportAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var rows = await _db.ReadAllAsync();      // no ct
        return Render(rows);
    }

    // RIGHT: PASSES IT DOWN, so the operation that actually BLOCKS
    //        is the one that sees it.
    public async Task<byte[]> ExportAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var rows = await _db.ReadAllAsync(ct);   // the DB call can
        return Render(rows, ct);                 // be aborted
    }
}
{{-- ^ CHECKING LOCALLY AND THEN CALLING A METHOD THAT TAKES NO TOKEN
     PRODUCES COOPERATIVE CANCELLATION THAT STOPS BEFORE THE WORK
