     rather than during it — which is the shape that makes a cancel
     button feel broken. --}}

{{-- THE PATTERN, and it is a loop with two exits: --}}
public async Task ProcessAsync(IEnumerable<Row> rows, CancellationToken ct)
{
    foreach (var row in rows)
    {
        ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();      // CHECK AT A POINT
        await ProcessOneAsync(row, ct);         // WHERE STOPPING IS
    }                                           // SAFE, and PASS IT ON
    //  ^ NOT at the top of the method: doing that cancels before any
    //    work has been done, which is a different behaviour from
    //    cancelling partway through.
}

{{-- THE THREE SOURCES, and the linked one is the interesting case: --}}
static async Task Request(HttpContext ctx)
{
    var request = ctx.RequestAborted;      // (1) FROM THE CALLER

    using var timeout = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
    // (2) FROM A TIMEOUT

    using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(
        request, timeout.Token);            // (3) EITHER ONE
    // ^ "the caller cancelled OR five seconds passed" cannot be
    //   expressed by choosing a token; it has to be BUILT, because
    //   there is no token that represents a disjunction.

    try
    {
        await service.DoWorkAsync(linked.Token);
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (timeout.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // ^ THE FILTER IS THE POINT: it distinguishes "the caller
        //   went away" from "we ran out of time", which need
        //   different responses. Without it, a client that
        //   disconnected looks exactly like a slow server.
        ReportTimeout();
    }
}

{{-- AND WHERE DO NOT CANCEL, which is the case that makes it a
     signal rather than a force: --}}
public async Task CommitAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await _db.UpdateAsync(order, ct);

    try
    {
        // THE TRANSACTION IS ALREADY OPEN. Abandoning it here leaves
        // a lock held until the connection times out, which is
        // WORSE than finishing a write the caller no longer wants.
        // So the token is deliberately NOT passed to the commit.
        await _db.CommitAsync(order);
    }
    finally
    {
        _db.Close();
    }
}

11.5 IAsyncEnumerable and await foreach

An async iterator yields values one at a time over time, without buffering the whole sequence. That is the right shape for reading a large file line by line, streaming a network response, or querying a database with a paged cursor.

An asynchronous sequence produces elements over time rather than all at once, and enumerating one is done with await foreach rather than foreach. The compiler generates an asynchronous enumerator whose dispose is itself asynchronous, which is the part that cannot be expressed with a synchronous using block.

Where it beats a list

When the source is genuinely streaming — a socket, a database cursor, a file read in chunks — materialising it is what the type exists to avoid, because a stream of a million rows from a cursor has a memory profile completely different from a list of a million rows. Where the source is already in memory, the type costs an allocation per element and buys nothing.

Configuration, and the one that matters

The enumerator takes options, and the default configuration has two behaviours worth overriding: it continues rather than stopping on the first exception, and it does not run the loop body on a pool thread. Both defaults are right for a console tool and wrong for a server, where an element should not stop the stream and where the loop should not block a request thread.

// An async iterator: no buffering, bounded memory, works on a huge source
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<string> ReadLinesAsync(
    string path, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    await using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
    while (await reader.ReadLineAsync(ct) is not null { }   // placeholder

    while (true)
    {
        string? line = await reader.ReadLineAsync(ct);
        if (line is null) break;
        yield return line;
    }
}

// Consuming it
await foreach (string line in ReadLinesAsync(path, ct))
{
    Console.WriteLine(line);
}

// With a cancellation token, the attribute is required for it to flow
await foreach (var item in StreamAsync(ct)) { }
// or
await foreach (var item in StreamAsync().WithCancellation(ct).ConfigureAwait(false)) { }

// Linq-style operators over async sequences (System.Linq.Async, a NuGet package)
//   Select, Where, Take, Buffer, ToListAsync, CountAsync, ForEachAsync

// Manual enumeration when you need a cancellation token mid-flight
await using var e = ReadLinesAsync(path).GetAsyncEnumerator(ct);
while (await e.MoveNextAsync()) { Process(e.Current); }

// Files, readers, HTTP responses and DB readers all return IAsyncEnumerable
//   File.ReadLinesAsync(path, ct)
//   response.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync(ct)
//   dbContext.Orders.AsAsyncEnumerable().WithCancellation(ct)
//   dbContext.Orders.AsNoTracking().ToAsyncEnumerable()

The [EnumeratorCancellation] attribute on the parameter is what lets a token passed to GetAsyncEnumerator or WithCancellation reach the body. Without it the parameter stays default and the sequence becomes uncancellable, which is a very quiet bug.

await foreach enumerates the sequence exactly once and disposes it. If you need a second pass, materialise with ToListAsync() first — remembering that the whole point of the async stream was to avoid holding everything in memory.


{{-- await foreach BECAUSE THE DISPOSE IS ASYNCHRONOUS, which a
     synchronous using block cannot express. --}}
await using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
await foreach (var line in ReadLinesAsync(stream, ct))
{
    await ProcessAsync(line, ct);
}

static async IAsyncEnumerable<string> ReadLinesAsync(
    Stream stream,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    // [EnumeratorCancellation] is what makes ct.WithCancellation(token)
    // at the CALL SITE actually reach this method — without the
    // attribute the token passed at enumeration is SILENTLY DROPPED,
    // which is a bug with no diagnostic.
    using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
    while (!reader.EndOfStream)
    {
        ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        yield return await reader.ReadLineAsync(ct);
        // ^ yield return SUSPENDS THE STATE MACHINE, so the object
        //   holding the locals is HEAP-ALLOCATED — once, for the
        //   whole enumeration, not per element.
    }
}

{{-- AND THE OPTIONS, because the two DEFAULTS are wrong for a
     server: --}}
await foreach (var row in ReadRowsAsync(ct).ConfigureAwait(false))
{
    // 1. ContinueOnError defaults to FALSE: one bad row STOPS THE
    //    STREAM and everything after it is never read. For an
    //    import, that means 99% of the work is discarded because
    //    row 4,000 was malformed.
    //
    // 2. The loop body does NOT run on a pool thread by default.
    //    An await foreach without ConfigureAwait(false) inside a
    //    request PINS THE REQUEST THREAD for the whole stream.
    await ProcessAsync(row, ct).ConfigureAwait(false);
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE SHAPE FOR A SERVER: continue on error, and
     never block a request thread on a stream that may take
     minutes. --}}

{{-- WHERE IT BEATS A LIST, and where it does NOT: --}}
static async Task<string> GenuinelyStreaming(string path, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var sb = new StringBuilder();

    // A STREAM OF A MILLION ROWS FROM A CURSOR has a memory profile
    // completely different from a list of a million rows. This is
    // what the type exists for.
    await foreach (var row in ReadRowsAsync(ct))
        sb.AppendLine(row);

    return sb.ToString();
}

static async Task Wasteful(List<Order> orders)
{
    // WHERE THE SOURCE IS ALREADY IN MEMORY the type costs an
    // ALLOCATION PER ELEMENT (the state machine, plus the
    // enumerator) and buys NOTHING.
    await foreach (var order in orders.AsAsyncEnumerable())
        await HandleAsync(order);
    // ^ the orders were already a List. A foreach is faster, uses
    //   no allocation, and reads like the code that should have been
    //   written.
}

{{-- AND THE CANCELLATION PATH, which must be explicit: --}}
await foreach (var row in ReadRowsAsync(ct).WithCancellation(ct))
{
    // ^ WITHOUT WithCancellation, the token reaches the method only
    //   if it was passed to it as a parameter. WithCancellation is
    //   how a caller's token reaches an async iterator that does not
    //   take one, and omitting it is the most common cause of "my
    //   cancellation does not work".
}

11.6 Parallel.ForEachAsync and TPL

The Task Parallel Library is for CPU-bound work. Parallel.ForEachAsync (in System.Threading.Tasks) is the modern, allocation-light way to bound parallelism, and it honours a cancellation token and a degree of parallelism.

Task-based parallelism schedules work on the pool and lets it decide the shape. Parallel.ForEach takes a degree of parallelism and a partitioning strategy. The data-parallel forms differ from the task-parallel ones in exactly one respect: they decide the partitioning, so the body must be safe to run concurrently and must not have an order.

The body is the contract

A parallel loop body runs on several threads at once, so anything it writes that another body reads is a race, and anything it appends to an unsynchronised collection is a corruption rather than a lost update. Where the body needs to accumulate, the pattern is a per-partition local plus a locked merge, and the framework's own reductions do that rather than a single shared variable with a lock.

When to use it at all

CPU-bound work that divides cleanly, where the work per item is far larger than the scheduling cost. Everything else is better served by an explicit set of tasks, because the parallel forms' partitioning is invisible and the ordering guarantee you want has to be added on top.

// CPU-bound fan-out with a bounded degree of parallelism
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    items,
    new ParallelOptions
    {
        MaxDegreeOfParallelism = Environment.ProcessorCount,
        CancellationToken = ct
    },
    async (item, token) =>
    {
        await ProcessCpuAsync(item, token);
    });

// The synchronous sibling still works well for pure CPU work
Parallel.ForEach(items, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4 }, item =>
{
    ProcessCpu(item);
});

// The result-capable overload
var results = new ConcurrentBag<int>();
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(items, async (item, ct) =>
{
    results.Add(Compute(item, ct));
});

// The classic parallel-for
Parallel.For(0, matrix.Length, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8 }, i =>
{
    matrix[i] = Transform(matrix[i]);
});

// PLINQ, the declarative form -- good for data, not for control flow
var primes = Enumerable.Range(2, 1_000_000)
    .AsParallel()
    .WithDegreeOfParallelism(Environment.ProcessorCount)
    .Where(n => n % 2 == 1 || n == 2)
    .Select(n => n * n)
    .OrderBy(n => n)
    .ToArray();

// Concurrency primitives for finer control
await using var sem = new SemaphoreSlim(10);          // 10 at a time
await sem.WaitAsync(ct);
try { await Work(ct); } finally { sem.Release(); }

using var gate = new ManualResetEventSlim(false);  // sync
// Interlocked.Increment / Volatile.Read for lock-free counters and flags
// System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9) is the modern, faster Monitor replacement

The degree of parallelism default is ProcessorCount, which is usually wrong for I/O-bound work (you want far more) and about right for CPU-bound work. Setting it explicitly costs nothing and makes the intent obvious.

Sharing a mutable List<T>, Dictionary<K,V> or any non-thread-safe object across parallel iterations is undefined behaviour. Use a ConcurrentBag, ConcurrentDictionary, or per-iteration results merged afterwards. The runtime will not warn you.


{{-- THE BODY IS THE CONTRACT: it runs on SEVERAL THREADS AT ONCE. --}}
static void TheBodyMustBeThreadSafe(List<Item> items)
{
    Parallel.ForEach(items, item =>
    {
        // ^ UNSAFE: a plain int++ on a shared variable is a
        //   READ-MODIFY-WRITE, and two threads interleave it. The
        //   result is a number LOWER than the real count, with no
        //   exception.
        count++;

        // ^ ALSO UNSAFE: List<T> is not thread-safe. Two threads
        //   growing the same list corrupt it — a lost element, a
        //   doubled capacity, or an array that is briefly too
        //   small, which throws.
        results.Add(item.Value);
    });
}
{{-- ^ A CORRUPTION rather than a lost update, which is why a
     parallel append can produce a list that fails an assertion
     about its own length rather than a missing row. --}}

{{-- AND THE PATTERN THAT IS SAFE, which is per-partition local
     plus a locked merge: --}}
static int[] ProcessAll(int[] input)
{
    var output = new int[input.Length];

    Parallel.For(0, input.Length, options: default, body: (i, state, token) =>
    {
        // ^ index-based rather than foreach, because a parallel
        //   ForEach gives no index and the shared array needs one.
        //   WRITES TO DISJOINT ELEMENTS, so no lock is needed: two
        //   threads writing output[3] and output[7] cannot collide.
        token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        output[i] = Transform(input[i]);
    });

    return output;
    {{-- ^ THIS IS THE SHAPE THAT IS ACTUALLY SAFE IN A PARALLEL
         LOOP: each body writes to a DISJOINT SLICE, so the safety
         argument is structural rather than a lock. --}}
}

{{-- AND THE REDUCTION, where the framework aggregates rather than
     locking per item: --}}
static double TotalOf(double[] values)
{
    return values.AsParallel()
        .WithMergeOptions(ParallelMergeOptions.FullyParallel)
        .Sum();
}
{{-- ^ Sum PERFORMS A LOCK-FREE REDUCTION: each thread accumulates
     into a thread-local, then the partials are combined once. A
     hand-written version with a lock in the body is CORRECT and
     several orders of magnitude slower, because the lock
     serialises exactly the work the pool was created to
     parallelise. --}}

{{-- WHEN TO USE IT AT ALL, and the rule: --}}
static async Task TheRule()
{
    // USE IT: CPU-bound, divides cleanly, and the work per item is
    // far larger than the scheduling cost.
    var hashes = new byte[files.Length][];
    Parallel.For(0, files.Length, i =>
    {
        // ^ 5 ms of hashing against a microsecond of scheduling.
        //   Good ratio, and nothing to share.
        hashes[i] = SHA256.HashData(files[i]);
    });

    // DO NOT USE IT: I/O-bound, where the pool is waiting anyway and
    // Parallel.ForEach gives you a thread per item for no reason.
    var contents = new string[urls.Length];
    Parallel.ForEach(urls, async (url, _, token) =>
    {
        // ^ WRONG in two ways. async in a parallel body means the
        //   partitions finish long before the work does, so the
        //   partitioning is a fiction; and blocking a pool thread on
        //   I/O is the thing the pool exists to avoid.
        contents[Array.IndexOf(urls, url)] = await GetAsync(url, token);
    });
    // THE CORRECT FORM for I/O is an explicit task set:
    var results = await Task.WhenAll(urls.Select(u => GetAsync(u, ct)));
    {{-- ^ WHICH ALSO SOLVES THE ORDERING problem, because the result
         array is indexed rather than appended to — something the
         parallel forms cannot give you without a partitioned
         result that has to be merged by hand. --}}
}

11.7 Task.Run and when not to use it

Task.Run queues a delegate on the thread pool. It is for moving blocking or CPU-bound work off the current thread. It is not for making an already-async call "more parallel" — the thread pool is already involved, and wrapping an awaitable in Task.Run adds a scheduling hop and hides the real concurrency structure.

Task.Run schedules a delegate on the thread pool. It exists so that a synchronous, CPU-bound piece of work can be made asynchronous, and using it for anything else adds a scheduling hop and hides which thread the code is on.

When it is right

Exactly one case: a blocking or CPU-bound library call with no asynchronous form, inside a method that already has to be asynchronous. The delegate must be short, because a pool thread held for a second is a pool thread not available to anyone else, and the pool grows slowly — which is why a burst of long blocking work manifests as latency minutes later rather than immediately.

When it is wrong

Wrapping an already-asynchronous call, which is a common and expensive mistake: it turns a completion into a thread-pool work item that then blocks on the task, consuming a thread for the whole operation. Wrapping I/O, for the same reason. And using it to make a synchronous method return a task so that callers can await it — which converts a compile-time error into a runtime thread-pool exhaustion.

// GOOD: CPU-bound work on a UI thread or request thread
var result = await Task.Run(() => HeavyComputation(input));

// GOOD: legacy blocking API, wrapped so the thread is not blocked
var legacy = await Task.Run(() => OldBlockingClient.Get(key));

// BAD: Task.Run around an async call. The inner call already yields.
// await Task.Run(async () => await FetchAsync(url));   -- pointless hop
// await Task.Run(() => FetchAsync(url));           -- unwrapped Task, does not await!

// BAD: Task.Run per item in a loop. Thousands of scheduling hops.
// var results = items.Select(i => Task.Run(() => Work(i)));
// BAD: Task.Run for fire-and-forget. Nobody observes the exception.
// Task.Run(() => DoSomethingImportant());

// GOOD: fire-and-forget, properly observed
// _ = Task.Run(async () =>
// {
//     try { await DoWorkAsync(ct); }
//     catch (Exception ex) { logger.LogError(ex, "background work failed"); }
// });
// ...and keep a Task reference so the process does not exit early.

// The dedicated alternative for long-lived background work:
//   IHostedService in a Generic Host (ASP.NET Core, Worker Service)
//   System.Threading.PeriodicTimer on a dedicated loop
//   BackgroundService as the base class for both

If work should run regardless of who asks, model it as a hosted service rather than as fire-and-forget Task.Run. A hosted service has a lifetime, gets graceful shutdown, and its exceptions are logged instead of vanishing.

A quick test for whether Task.Run is right: does the work block a thread? Blocking work is worth handing to the pool. Anything already asynchronous is not, and Task.Run only adds a hop you will have to debug.


{{-- Task.Run SCHEDULES A DELEGATE ON THE POOL. Exactly one case:
     a BLOCKING or CPU-BOUND LIBRARY CALL with no asynchronous
     form. --}}
public async Task<byte[]> LegacyHashAsync(byte[] data, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // THE ONE RIGHT USE: a legacy library whose only API blocks, and
    // it is CPU-bound so the thread is genuinely busy.
    return await Task.Run(() =>
    {
        ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        return LegacyCompress(data);       // ^ 200 ms of CPU, on a
    }, ct);                                //   worker thread, which
}                                         //   is what that thread is
                                          //   for

{{-- THE WRONG USES, and the first is the expensive one: --}}
static async Task WrappingAsyncIo(string url)
{
    // WRONG 1: WRAPPING AN ALREADY-ASYNC call. This turns a
    //   COMPLETION into a THREAD-POOL WORK ITEM that then BLOCKS on
    //   the task — consuming a pool thread for the WHOLE operation
    //   to produce exactly the same result the await would have.
    await Task.Run(async () =>
    {
        var response = await client.GetAsync(url);
        return await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
    });

    // RIGHT: no wrapper at all.
    var response = await client.GetAsync(url);
    var text = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
    {{-- ^ THE COST OF THE WRONG FORM, per call: one work-item
         allocation, one pool-thread HAND-OFF, one CONTEXT SWITCH,
         and a pool thread HELD for the duration. On a service doing
         10,000 requests a second that is the difference between
         scaling and thread-pool starvation. --}}
}

{{-- AND THE THIRD, which is the worst because it hides a compile
     error: --}}
public Task<byte[]> HashAsync(byte[] data) => Task.Run(() => LegacyCompress(data));
{{-- ^ "make this synchronous method return a task so callers can
     await it". It converts a COMPILE-TIME error into a
     RUNTIME THREAD-POOL EXHAUSTION, and the symptom appears under
     load on a machine that is not the one you tested on. --}}

{{-- WHY A LONG BLOCKING TASK IS A DELAYED PROBLEM, and it is worth
     knowing before it is diagnosed: --}}
static void SlowPoolGrowth()
{
    // THE POOL GROWS SLOWLY: one thread per second or so, up to a
    // cap. So 200 blocking calls at once do NOT fail immediately —
    // the first few are fine, and then requests QUEUE, and the
    // symptom is latency that appears MINUTES LATER and looks like
    // a database problem.
    //
    // TWO FIXES, in the order to try them:
    //   1. Make the work asynchronous, so no thread is held.
    //   2. Bound the concurrency explicitly, so the queue is
    //      visible rather than inside the pool:
    Parallel.ForEachAsync(items,
        new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8 },
        async (item, ct) => await HandleAsync(item, ct));
    // ^ A BOUNDED DEGREE OF PARALLELISM converts an invisible queue
    //   into a queue you can see and tune, and it is the honest
    //   answer when the downstream genuinely cannot take more.
}

11.8 Deadlocks, ConfigureAwait and SynchronizationContext

The classic async deadlock happens when a .Result or .Wait() blocks a thread while the continuation that would complete it needs that same thread. It is a deadlock, not a slowdown, and it manifests as a hung UI or a hung request.

The deadlock is a specific and avoidable one: a method blocks on a task, and the continuation that would complete that task needs the thread the method is blocking. Because the pool is bounded, the continuation is queued behind the blocked caller, and neither ever runs.

Why it happens only in some places

It requires a synchronization context to capture, so it happens in a UI application and in a legacy ASP.NET request, and it does not happen in ASP.NET Core — where there is no context — which is why code moved from one to the other starts working without anyone changing it. The other requirement is a synchronous wait, which is either a .Result, a .Wait(), or a GetAwaiter().GetResult() in a method that is itself inside a task.

The fix, and its actual content

Await all the way down rather than blocking at any level, and where a synchronous boundary genuinely exists — a Main, a legacy COM caller, a unit-test assertion — make it the outermost frame and make it block only there. ConfigureAwait(false) is not the fix; it reduces the set of places the deadlock can occur without removing any of the blocking waits, which are the cause.

// THE DEADLOCK: .Result blocks the UI thread, the continuation needs it
private async void OnClick(object s, EventArgs e)
{
    var data = LoadAsync().Result;      // BLOCKS the UI thread
    // ... the await inside LoadAsync captured the UI context,
    // ... so it cannot resume until OnClick returns, which it cannot.
    textBox.Text = data;
}

// FIX 1: async all the way down. Always.
private async void OnClick(object s, EventArgs e)
{
    var data = await LoadAsync();
    textBox.Text = data;
}

// FIX 2: ConfigureAwait(false) inside the library method, so the
// continuation does not need the UI thread at all
// public async Task<string> LoadAsync()
// {
//     var json = await client.GetStringAsync(_url).ConfigureAwait(false);
//     return Parse(json);          // now safe to touch no UI
// }

// UI THREAD RULE: touch the UI only between awaits, and only from
// the method that has the SynchronizationContext.
// private async Task LoadAsync()
// {
//     spinner.Visible = true;                       // UI: fine
//     var data = await FetchAsync(ct);              // yields
//     label.Text = data.Count.ToString();          // UI: resumed on UI thread
//     spinner.Visible = false;                      // UI: fine
// }

// Thread safety of the SynchronizationContext itself
// SynchronizationContext.SetSynchronizationContext(null);   // opt out in a console app
// TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException += (s, e) => { e.SetObserved(); };

The rule in one sentence: ConfigureAwait(false) in library code, never in UI code. In a reusable library you have no business requiring a UI context; in a UI event handler you do, and the await will put you back on the right thread automatically.

async void is what turns a deadlock into a frozen application, because there is nothing for the caller to await. It is acceptable for event handlers only, and even there the body should be a single line calling a Task-returning method with a try/catch.


{{-- THE DEADLOCK: a method BLOCKS on a task, and the continuation
     that would complete it needs the thread the method is
     blocking. --}}
public sealed class Ui
{
    private readonly OrderService _orders;

    // WRONG: BLOCKS THE UI THREAD on a task whose continuation was
    // POSTED BACK TO THE UI THREAD.
    public void Load_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        var order = _orders.LoadAsync(42).Result;
        //                          ^^^^^^
        // LoadAsync awaits the repository, which captures the UI
        // context, so its continuation is POSTED TO THE UI THREAD.
        // The UI THREAD IS NOW BLOCKED waiting for a task that only
        // completes when the UI thread runs that continuation.
        // Both wait. Nothing times out. The application HANGS and
        // reports nothing.
        Render(order);
    }
}

{{-- RIGHT: AWAIT ALL THE WAY DOWN. No blocking anywhere. --}}
public sealed class UiFixed
{
    private readonly OrderService _orders;

    public async void Load_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        var order = await _orders.LoadAsync(42);   // ^ SUSPENDS, so
        Render(order);                             //   the UI thread
    }                                              //   is free and
}                                                  //   the
                                                   //   continuation
                                                   //   can run
{{-- ^ AND NOTE: this is async void, which is CORRECT HERE and is the
     one place it is correct. The compiler requires the event
     handler's signature to be void, so the only two choices are
     async void and a fire-and-forget Task — and async void at least
     propagates its exception to the synchronization context. The
     rule against async void is a rule about METHODS THAT OTHERS
     CALL; an event handler is called by the framework. --}}

{{-- WHY IT ONLY HAPPENS SOMEWHERE, and it explains why code MOVED to
     ASP.NET Core STARTS WORKING with nobody changing it: --}}
public sealed class LegacyWeb
{
    // IN LEGACY ASP.NET: a synchronization context exists, the
    // continuation is posted back, and .Result deadlocks.
    public Order Bad(HttpContext ctx) => _orders.LoadAsync(42).Result;
}

public sealed class CoreWeb
{
    // IN ASP.NET CORE: NO synchronization context by default, so
    // the continuation runs on the pool thread and .Result does not
    // deadlock — it HOLDS A POOL THREAD instead, which is a slower
    // failure with the same shape.
    public Order AlsoBad(HttpContext ctx) => _orders.LoadAsync(42).Result;
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING: the same code that hung in one
     framework silently consumes threads in the other, and the
     symptom is latency that scales with load rather than a hang
     anybody can reproduce. --}}

{{-- AND WHERE A SYNCHRONOUS BOUNDARY IS UNAVOIDABLE, which is the
     legitimate case: --}}
public static class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // THE MAIN METHOD. There is no caller to await, and this is
        // the OUTERMOST FRAME, which is the only place a block is
        // honest.
        var app = Build();

        // BLOCKS, AT THE TOP LEVEL, ONCE. The RIGHT version:
        app.Run();
    }
}
{{-- ^ Make the boundary the OUTERMOST frame and block only there.
     Anywhere else, block on something that does not need your
     thread. --}}

11.9 Channels and producer/consumer

A Channel<T> is the framework’s answer to a queue between a producer and one or more consumers. It handles the three things hand-rolled producer/consumer code always gets wrong: completion signalling, bounded back-pressure, and cancellation.

var channel = System.Threading.Channels.Channel.CreateBounded<int>(
    new BoundedChannelOptions(100)
    {
        FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,   // producer waits when full
        SingleReader = true,
        SingleWriter = true,
        AllowSynchronousContinuations = false
    });

// Producer
static async Task ProduceAsync(ChannelWriter<int> writer, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await foreach (int n in SourceAsync(ct))
        await writer.WriteAsync(n, ct);      // waits if the buffer is full

    writer.Complete();                              // REQUIRED: signals end of stream
}

// Consumer
static async Task ConsumeAsync(ChannelReader<int> reader, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await foreach (int n in reader.ReadAllAsync(ct))
        Process(n);
}

// Several consumers on one channel: they split the work
var consumers = new[] { ConsumeAsync(ch, ct), ConsumeAsync(ch, ct) };
var producer = ProduceAsync(ch.Writer, ct);
await Task.WhenAll(// writer must complete before the consumers finish
    producer, consumers[0], consumers[1]);

// An UNBOUNDED channel never blocks the producer -- and never back-pressures
// var unbounded = Channel.CreateUnbounded<int>(new UnboundedChannelOptions { SingleReader = true });

// Fan-out: several readers each see ALL items (not what you usually want)
// var pub = Channel.CreateUnbounded<int>();   // broadcast

// The right shape for a pipeline: each stage is a channel
//   source -> [parse] -> channel A -> [validate] -> channel B -> [write] -> sink

// Error propagation: Complete(ex) makes every reader throw that exception
// writer.Complete(exception);

Forgetting Complete() is the classic channel bug: consumers block in ReadAllAsync forever after the last item, and the application hangs on shutdown. A using or try/finally around the writer guarantees it.

Channel.CreateBounded with BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait is almost always the right choice: it gives you back-pressure for free, so a slow consumer slows the producer instead of exhausting memory. Use unbounded only when the source is already rate-limited.

Exercises 11

  1. Fetch ten URLs sequentially, then with Task.WhenAll, and compare wall-clock time. Explain the difference from the call order.
  2. Write a method that returns ValueTask<int> with a synchronous fast path and an async slow path, and prove the fast path allocates nothing with a GC count.
  3. Implement a timeout with WhenAny and separately with a CancellationTokenSource. Compare which cancels the underlying work.
  4. Write an async IAsyncEnumerable that streams a large file line by line, and prove the memory use is flat by processing a 2 GB file.
  5. Produce a conflict deliberately in a WinForms/WPF async void handler and watch it crash the process. Then fix it with a real async Task method.
  6. Build a bounded channel pipeline: produce 100,000 items, transform and validate them, and consume with three workers. Add back-pressure and observe the producer blocking.

{{-- A CHANNEL IS A THREAD-SAFE QUEUE THAT BLOCKS ONCE IT IS FULL
     and yields once it is empty. The blocking is the feature: it
     applies BACK-PRESSURE without anybody writing a semaphore. --}}
public sealed class Pipeline(int capacity = 8)
{
    // THE WRITER SIDE. WriteAsync blocks when the channel is FULL,
    // so a fast producer is throttled to the consumer's rate
    // WITHOUT a semaphore anywhere.
    private readonly Channel<Job> _queue =
        Channel.CreateBounded<Job>(new BoundedChannelOptions(capacity)
        {
            FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,   // WAIT rather than
                                                     // DropOldest or
                                                     // DropWrite
        });

    public ValueTask EnqueueAsync(Job job, CancellationToken ct)
        => _queue.Writer.WriteAsync(job, ct);
}

public sealed class Consumer(Pipeline pipeline)
{
    // THE READER SIDE. ReadAllAsync yields as soon as an item is
    // available and RETURNS when the channel is COMPLETED — which
    // is what ends the loop without a flag.
    public async Task RunAsync(int workers, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var tasks = Enumerable.Range(0, workers).Select(_ => WorkAsync(ct));
        await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
    }

    private async Task WorkAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await foreach (var job in pipeline._queue.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct))
        {
            // ^ ReadAllAsync YIELDS while empty and RETURNS when
            //   Complete() is called, so the loop ends without a
            //   boolean flag and without a sentinel value.
            await HandleAsync(job, ct);
        }
    }
}

{{-- AND THE ORDERING HAZARD that catches everyone: --}}
public static async Task TheHazard(Pipeline p, List<Job> jobs, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // WRONG: Complete() is called IMMEDIATELY, so the reader sees
    //     "finished" before the writes are observed.
    foreach (var job in jobs) await p.EnqueueAsync(job, ct);
    p.Complete();
    // ^ this is correct ONLY if every write has already completed,
    //   which it has here because each await returned. But:

    // WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION, and this is the one that loses
    // work silently:
    var writes = jobs.Select(j => p.EnqueueAsync(j, ct).AsTask());
    p.Complete();                 // called before any write finishes
    await Task.WhenAll(writes);
    // ^ A WRITE TO A COMPLETED CHANNEL THROWS
    //   ChannelClosedException, and if the writes were fire-and-
    //   forget the exception is on an unobserved task and the JOBS
    //   ARE LOST with no diagnostic at all.
}

{{-- THE SAFE SHAPES, and there are exactly two: --}}
public static async Task Safe(List<Job> jobs, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // (a) AWAIT EVERY WRITE, THEN complete:
    foreach (var job in jobs) await _queue.Writer.WriteAsync(job, ct);
    _queue.Writer.Complete();
    // ^ correct, and the common case. It serialises the producer,
    //   which is acceptable when the producer's work is cheap.

    // (b) COMPLETE THE WRITER ON DISPOSE, so the ordering is the
    //     type's job rather than the caller's:
    await using (var writer = _queue.Writer)
    {
        foreach (var job in jobs) await writer.WriteAsync(job, ct);
    }   // ^ Complete() is called HERE, after the writes, because the
        //   writer's Dispose does it. There is no line the caller
        //   can forget.
}

{{-- AND THE OPTIONS worth setting deliberately: --}}
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<Job>(
    new BoundedChannelOptions(8)
    {
        FullMode  = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,
        SingleReader = false,     // a performance hint: true when
        SingleWriter = true,      // exactly one of each, which lets
                                  // the implementation skip the
                                  // interlocked operations
    });
{{-- ^ FullMode = Wait IS THE BACK-PRESSURE. The other modes
     (DropOldest, DropWrite, DropRead) DISCARD, and a producer
     writing into a DropOldest channel loses items silently — which
     for a work queue is worse than blocking, and for a
     newest-value channel is exactly right. Choose deliberately
     rather than by omission. --}}

12 · Modern C# (9–14)

12.1 C# 9–11: target-typed new, records, init, patterns12.2 C# 12: primary constructors, collections, alias any type12.3 C# 13: params collections, overload resolution, ref struct interfaces12.4 C# 13: params with spans, ref-struct constraints and partial properties12.5 C# 14: extension members, field keyword and Span ergonomics12.6 ref, readonly and ref-safe members12.7 file types, partial and the Lock type12.8 Nullable annotations and attributes12.9 Feature timeline by version

Chapter twelve is the modern-language tour. Each release since C# 9 has removed a category of boilerplate: construction syntax, pattern matching, collection initialisation, and property backing fields. The features here are individually small and collectively transformative, and they are what you should be writing in new code today.

12.1 C# 9–11: target-typed new, records, init, patterns

C# 9 shipped in .NET 5 and is the release that made records and pattern matching mainstream. Its headline additions are target-typed new, init-only setters, records, top-level statements, and the pattern matching extensions that turned switch into a real language feature.

Three features from the modern language exist to remove boilerplate, and each one is a rewrite of a pattern rather than a new capability. Target-typed new removes a repetition the compiler can infer. A record generates what a class would have had to declare. And pattern matching lets the shape of a value be tested where a cast used to be required.

What each is actually worth

Target-typed new is purely a reduction in noise. A record is worth reaching for when a type's identity really is its data — a value passed across a boundary, compared, printed — and is worth avoiding for an entity, where the generated equality is wrong. Pattern matching is worth reaching for whenever the shape of a value is what the branch is about, which is most of the interesting branches.

Where the generated members bite

A record generates equality, a print method and a copy method, and a record with a collection property compares by reference — so two records with equal contents and separately-built lists are not equal. That is the single most common surprise in the type, and it is a property of how the generator works rather than a defect.

// Target-typed new: no type repetition (C# 9)
List<string> names = new();
Dictionary<string, List<int>> byTag = new();
var point = new { X = 1, Y = 2 };          // target-typed anonymous type
var buffer = new byte[256];

// Init-only setters and with-expressions (C# 9)
public sealed class Settings
{
    public string Theme { get; init; } = "system";
    public int FontSize { get; init; } = 14;
}

var dark = new Settings { Theme = "dark", FontSize = 18 };
var bigger = dark with { FontSize = 22 };   // dark is unchanged

// Records (C# 9): value equality, ToString, deconstruction, with
public record Order(string Id, decimal Total, OrderStatus Status);
public enum OrderStatus { Draft, Placed, Shipped }

// Pattern matching additions (C# 9)
static string Describe(object o) => o switch
{
    int n and > 100                        => "big int",
    int or long                       => "integer",
    string { Length: > 0 and < 10 }     => "short string",
    not null                            => "something",
    _                                    => "null"
};

// Top-level statements (C# 9) -- see section 1.4
// Native and sized integer types (C# 11, preview in 9): nint, nuint

The and/or/not keywords are the readable spellings of &&/||/! inside patterns. They look almost identical to the logical operators, which is the single most common source of confusion — the context (after is, in a case, in a switch arm) is what tells them apart.

Records and with are not a replacement for classes in general. They are a replacement for value-like data with no identity: DTOs, domain events, coordinates, key-value pairs, API contracts. A database entity with an identity and a lifecycle should still be a class.


{{-- THREE FEATURES, and each is a REWRITE OF A PATTERN rather than
     a new capability. --}}

{{-- 1. TARGET-TYPED new: purely a reduction in NOISE. --}}
static void TargetTyped()
{
    // Both of these are List<int>. The compiler infers the type
    // from the target because the target has ONE type and the
    // expression has exactly one construction.
    List<int> a = new();
    var      b = new List<int>();

    // WHICH IS WORTH REACHING FOR in a DECLARATION WITH A TYPE,
    // and worth IGNORING after an assignment where the keyword is
    // doing the work anyway.
    List<string> names = new() { "a", "b" };
}

{{-- 2. A RECORD GENERATES what a class would have to declare: --}}
// positional: properties, equality, ToString, copy, deconstruction
public sealed record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);

// non-positional: the generated members with your own shape
public sealed record Customer
{
    public required int    Id    { get; init; }
    public required string Name  { get; init; }
    public string?         Email { get; init; }
}
{{-- ^ required FORCES both to be supplied, so a half-built
     Customer does not exist — which is the actual value of the
     form for a type crossing a boundary. --}}

{{-- 3. PATTERN MATCHING wherever the SHAPE is what the branch is
     about: --}}
static decimal Discount(object o) => o switch
{
    null                       => 0m,      // null FIRST, because the
                                             // reference arms would
                                             // match null otherwise
    Order { Status: OrderStatus.Paid }     => 0.00m,
    Order { Total: > 1000m } o             => o.Total * 0.10m,
    Order o                                 => o.Total * 0.05m,
    Product { Category: "clearance" }      => 0.20m,
    Product p                               => p.Price * 0.02m,
    string { Length: > 0 }                 => 0m,
    int or long or decimal n               => n * 0.01m,
    _                                       => 0m,
};

{{-- AND WHERE THE GENERATED MEMBERS BITE, which is the single most
     common surprise in a record: --}}
static void CollectionProperties()
{
    var one = new Basket(new[] { "a" });
    var two = new Basket(new[] { "a" });

    // one == two              FALSE
    {{-- ^ THE GENERATED EQUALITY COMPARES EVERY FIELD, and a
         COLLECTION PROPERTY IS COMPARED BY REFERENCE. Two records
         with equal contents and separately-built lists are NOT
         equal, and nothing in the type says so. The fix is a
         hand-written Equals that compares the sequence, or a
         collection the equality compares by value. --}}

    Console.WriteLine(one);      // "Basket { Items = System.String[] }"
    {{-- ^ THE GENERATED ToString IS NOT USEFUL for a collection: it
         prints the TYPE NAME, not the contents, so a record in a
         log line is worse than a class with a real ToString. --}}
}
public sealed record Basket(string[] Items);

12.2 C# 12: primary constructors, collections, alias any type

The pattern matching that began with C# 7 reached a natural conclusion in C# 11. Relational patterns, list patterns, and slice patterns make it possible to express many shapes declaratively, and switch on multiple types unifies what used to be a chain of is tests.

A primary constructor takes parameters in the type declaration and makes them available to the initialisers of every member. Collection expressions let a sequence be written from the elements it contains rather than from the syntax that constructs it. An alias-any-type declaration gives an existing type another name.

The primary constructor, and what it is not

It is not a constructor in the sense that a body can run: there is no body, so nothing validates the parameters and nothing runs before the initialisers. A field or property initialiser that needs a checked parameter has to call a guard expression, which throws during construction — which means the exception's stack trace names the constructor's argument, not the code that supplied the bad value.

When to write one

For a type whose parameters are its whole definition and which has no behaviour that depends on them beyond storing them: a small record-like class, a settings object, a message. Not for a type with validation, not for one with a non-trivial initialisation sequence, and not for one where the parameter's name should not become a public member's name.

// Relational patterns: comparisons without a named variable
static string Grade(int score) => score switch
{
    < 0                        => "invalid",
    >= 0 and < 50              => "F",
    >= 50 and < 70             => "D",
    >= 70 and < 90             => "C",
    >= 90                        => "A",
    _                            => "unknown"
};

// List patterns and slices: shape-based matching (C# 11)
static string Route(int[] path) => path switch
{
    [0, .., 1]                    => "two segments",
    [0, .. 2]                    => "three segments",
    [0]                            => "root",
    []                               => "empty",
    [var head, .. var tail]            => $"starts with {head}, {tail.Length} more",
    _                               => "unrouted"
};

// List patterns on strings and spans (a common validation trick)
// input switch { null => invalid, "GET" or "POST" => allowed, _ => invalid }

// Nested patterns and type patterns with designations
// result switch
// {
//     Ok(var value)                          => Use(value),
//     Err(var message)                        => Log(message),
// }

// Property and positional patterns
// person switch
// {
//     { Address: { City: "London" } }           => "londoner",
//     { Address: { City: { Length: > 2 } } }   => "somewhere",
// }
// point switch { (0, 0) => "origin", (var x, var y) => $"{x},{y}" }

// Combining patterns with when guards
// customer switch
// {
//     { Tier: "gold" } when DateTime.UtcNow > expiry => renew(),
//     { Tier: "gold" }                                 => notify(),
//     _                                                => ignore(),
// }

// A switch expression must be exhaustive, or it needs a discard arm
// public enum Colour { Red, Green, Blue, }
// string Hex(Colour c) => c switch
// {
//     Colour.Red   => "#FF0000",
//     Colour.Green => "#00FF00",
//     _            => "#0000FF",   // or list Blue explicitly
// };

Switch expressions with a single arm per enum member, and no when guards, can be used in a switch statement with the same syntax. The compiler supports both; the expression form is easier to read and to test.

Pattern matching is at its best against object, unions, or shapes that genuinely vary. Against a strongly typed, single-shape parameter, plain if statements are just as readable. Do not convert a working method into patterns for its own sake.


{{-- A PRIMARY CONSTRUCTOR takes parameters in the DECLARATION and
     makes them available to member INITIALISERS. --}}
public sealed class Order(string reference, Customer customer)
{
    // THE PARAMETERS ARE IN SCOPE for initialisers, which is the
    // whole feature.
    public string    Reference { get; } = reference;
    public Customer  Customer  { get; } = customer;
    public OrderStatus Status   { get; private set; } = OrderStatus.Pending;
    public DateTimeOffset PlacedAt { get; } = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
}

{{-- AND IT IS NOT A CONSTRUCTOR IN THE SENSE THAT A BODY CAN RUN:
     there is no body, so NOTHING VALIDATES the parameters. --}}
public sealed class Money(decimal amount, string currency)
{
    // WHICH IS WHY VALIDATION IS A GUARD EXPRESSION that throws
    // DURING CONSTRUCTION:
    public decimal Amount { get; } = Guard.NotNegative(amount);
    public string  Currency { get; } = Guard.CurrencyCode(currency);
}
{{-- ^ The exception's stack trace names the CONSTRUCTOR'S ARGUMENT,
     not the code that supplied the bad value — which is a genuinely
     worse diagnostic than a constructor body that throws, and the
     trade is real. --}}

public sealed class NotThis(decimal amount, string currency)
{
    private readonly string _upper;

    // WRONG: a primary constructor parameter is in scope ONLY in
    // INITIALISERS, so this does not compile.
    // public string Upper => currency.ToUpperInvariant();
}

{{-- WHEN TO WRITE ONE: --}}
// RIGHT: the parameters ARE the type, and nothing depends on them
//       beyond storing them.
public sealed class Setting(string key, string value);

// RIGHT: a message.
public sealed class EmailSent(string to, DateTimeOffset at, int messageId);

// NOT FOR A TYPE WITH VALIDATION: the guard expression throws with
//   a stack that names the argument.

// NOT FOR A NON-TRIVIAL INITIALISATION SEQUENCE: there is no body,
//   so a type that needs a cache warmed or a connection opened
//   still needs an ordinary constructor.

// NOT WHEN THE PARAMETER NAME WOULD MAKE A BAD MEMBER NAME:
//   a private parameter called 'id' does not become a public Id
//   property — you write it, or you rename the parameter.

{{-- COLLECTION EXPRESSIONS, which are about SYNTAX rather than
     capability: --}}
static void Collections()
{
    int[]           a = [1, 2, 3];
    List<int>       b = [1, 2, 3];
    IEnumerable<int> c = [1, 2, 3];
    Span<int>       d = [1, 2, 3];
    int[]           e = [];                // EMPTY, and an empty array
                                          // is now writable
    Dictionary<string, int> f = new()
    {
        ["a"] = 1,                          // a collection expression
        ["b"] = 2                           // is NOT a dictionary
    };                                      // initialiser: no
                                             // key/value shape exists
    ImmutableArray<int> g = [1, 2, 3];     // an immutable collection
    ImmutableArray<int> h = [];             // is NOT the empty one —
    Console.WriteLine(h.IsDefault);        // TRUE: this is the trap
}

{{-- ALIAS ANY TYPE, which is a DECLARATION rather than a feature: --}}
using Alias = System.Collections.Generic.List<string>;
using GlobalSystem = System;

public sealed class UsesAlias(Alias names)
{
    public int Count => names.Count;      // ^ an ALIAS IN THE PRIMARY
                                          //   CONSTRUCTOR PARAMETER
                                          //   LIST, and the
                                          //   readability win is
                                          //   smaller than it looks
                                          //   because the alias is
                                          //   not visible at the
                                          //   call site.
}

12.3 C# 13: params collections, overload resolution, ref struct interfaces

C# 12 arrived with .NET 7 and removed two long-standing pieces of ceremony: the constructor boilerplate that initialises fields from parameters, and the need to call new List<T>() before populating a collection. It also added ref readonly parameters, alias any type, and inline arrays.

Three changes, and the useful thing about them is that none introduces a new concept — they remove restrictions. A collection expression can now be passed to a parameter list. Overload resolution prefers the more specific match in a way that used to surprise. And ref has a readonly form that permits reading without permitting writing.

The readonly ref, and why it exists

A ref readonly parameter says the callee may read the referenced variable but not write it. That is a stronger promise than passing by value, because the callee sees the caller's actual storage rather than a copy — so the promise has to be enforced, and the compiler enforces it. It is the correct parameter type for a method that needs to look at a large structure without copying it and has no business changing it.

Where overload resolution changed

The rule now prefers a specific parameter type over a general one, so a call with an int prefers a method taking int over one taking object. That removes a class of surprise where an overload chosen for you picked the general form and did something different. It is also the kind of change that turns a previously-working build into a different binding, which is the one thing to watch for when upgrading.

// Primary constructors on CLASSES (C# 12) -- the big one
public sealed class Greeter(string greeting, int times = 1)
{
    // The parameters are in scope for the whole type body, and you
    // can capture them in a property with the same name:
    public string Greeting { get; } = greeting;
    public int Times { get; } = times;

    // Validation goes in the body. C# 14 lets you initialise a
    // primary-constructor parameter directly here.
    // string Greeting { get; } = greeting ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(greeting));

    public string Apply(string who) =>
        string.Join(" ", Enumerable.Repeat($"{Greeting}, {who}!", Times));
}

var hi = new Greeter("Hello", 2);
Console.WriteLine(hi.Apply("world"));

// COLLECTION EXPRESSIONS (C# 12): one syntax for every collection
int[]           a1 = [1, 2, 3];
List<int>          a2 = [1, 2, 3];
int[]           a3 = [capacity: 3];          // allocate with room, no contents
HashSet<int>        a4 = [1, 2, 2];      // dedupes automatically
int[,]           a5 = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];    // nested = 2D
List<int[]>         a6 = [[1, 2], [3]];     // jagged
Span<int>          a7 = [1, 2, 3];         // stack, no allocation
List<int>          a8 = [];                        // empty
Dictionary<string, int> a9 = [];                 // empty, ready to Add
int[]           a10 = existing;                 // the spread operator
int[]           a11 = [1, .. existing, 9];      // spread into a new array

// The rule: "natural type" decides the concrete type.
// Array -> int[]; List -> List<int>; Span/ReadOnlySpan -> Span; slice -> the slice type

// ref readonly parameters: pass by reference, cannot be written (C# 12)
static bool TryGet(ref readonly int value, out int doubled)
{
    doubled = value * 2;
    return value > 0;
}

// Alias ANY type, including generics and arrays (C# 12)
using Bytes = System.Collections.Generic.List<byte[]>;
using Matrix = int[,];
using Cell = (int Row, int Col);

// Primary constructors on STRUCTS and RECORD STRUCTS
public readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);

Collection expressions are a compile-time feature, not a new collection type. [1, 2, 3] targeting int[] is an array initialiser; targeting List<int> calls Add three times. Target Span<int> and it goes on the stack.

Collection expressions do not work with a readonly field or a get-only property, because collection initialisers need an add operation. ImmutableArray<int> a = [1, 2]; is fine; List<int> GetItems() => [1, 2]; is fine; assigning to a readonly field is not.


{{-- 1. PARAMS COLLECTIONS: a params parameter can now take a
     collection expression, and a Span, and a ReadOnlySpan. --}}
static void Report(params ReadOnlySpan<int> values)
{
    // WORKS, and did not before, because params now accepts a
    // SPAN — so the array is not copied into an implicit array at
    // the call.
    Report(1, 2, 3);
    Report([4, 5, 6]);

    int[] array = [7, 8, 9];
    Report(array);          // a WritableSpan from an array: the
                            // callee can mutate the CALLER's array

    ReadOnlySpan<int> ro = [1, 2, 3];
    Report(ro);             // a ReadOnlySpan: the callee cannot
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE POINT of the feature: with params int[] an
     argument that is already an array is copied into a new
     array at the call, so the callee mutating it is invisible to
     the caller. With a span the caller SEES the mutation. --}}

{{-- AND IT CLOSES THE ARRAY-ARGUMENT TRAP: --}}
static void ParamsAndArrays()
{
    void Mutate(params int[] values) { values[0] = 99; }

    int[] mine = [1, 2, 3];
    Mutate(mine);           // mine is UNCHANGED: params with an
                            // array argument still COPIES

    void MutateSpan(params Span<int> values) { values[0] = 99; }
    MutateSpan(mine);       // mine[0] IS 99: no copy

    // Which means the two spellings of the same-looking call have
    // OPPOSITE semantics, and that is worth knowing before adding
    // a span overload to a method that already has a params array.
}

{{-- 2. OVERLOAD RESOLUTION NOW PREFERS THE SPECIFIC MATCH: --}}
static void Preference(int x)         => Console.WriteLine("int");
static void Preference(object x)      => Console.WriteLine("object");
static void Preference<T>(T x)        => Console.WriteLine("generic");

static void Resolved()
{
    Preference(42);
    // int: the SPECIFIC overload. Before the change this could
    //      bind to object or to the generic, and which one it
    //      picked was a source of real confusion.
    Preference("text");
    Preference(new Order(1));
}
{{-- ^ THE UPGRADE CONCERN: an existing call that previously bound
     to the general or generic overload can now bind to the
     SPECIFIC one, which means code that compiled before can
     behave differently after a framework upgrade with no source
     change. This is the one thing to check in a version bump. --}}

{{-- 3. ref readonly: the callee may READ the caller's storage but
     not WRITE it. --}}
static int Sum(ref readonly ReadOnlySpan<int> values)
{
    // ^ A STRONGER PROMISE than passing by value, because the callee
    //   sees the CALLER'S ACTUAL STORAGE rather than a copy. It is
    //   therefore correct for a method that needs to LOOK AT a large
    //   structure without copying it and has no business changing
    //   it.
    return SumCore(values);
}

static int SumCore(ReadOnlySpan<int> values)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (int v in values) total += v;
    return total;
}

static void RefReadOnly()
{
    int[] data = [1, 2, 3];

    // READS IT: no copy, and the caller sees no change.
    int total = Sum(ref data);

    // WRITES ARE REJECTED INSIDE THE CALLEE, which is what the
    // keyword is for:
    // values[0] = 99;        ERROR: cannot assign to a readonly
    //                          reference's target
}

{{-- AND WHERE IT IS NOT THE RIGHT ANSWER: --}}
static void StillNeedsRef(ref int value)
{
    // ^ STILL NEEDS ref when the method WRITES, because
    //   ref readonly forbids exactly that. The two forms are not
    //   interchangeable and the difference is the whole feature.
    value++;
}

12.4 C# 13: params with spans, ref-struct constraints and partial properties

C# 13, the default for .NET 9, extends the collection work: params now accepts any collection, spans, and ref structs get ref readonly members, and partial properties finally work. These are the features that reduce boilerplate in library code rather than application code.

Two changes that let a method take a span in place of an array, and a constraint that lets a generic method require one. Together they remove a copy from a method boundary, which matters when the type argument is a large structure and the method is called in a loop.

Why a span is the right parameter type

An array parameter is a reference, so passing one is free — but it is a writable reference, and the callee can change the caller's data. A span says how much of it, and the read-only form says it cannot be changed. So the change from an array to a read-only span is not primarily about the copy; it is about making a promise the type system now enforces.

The constraint, and what it is for

A generic method constrained to a reference-type-like type argument can accept a span of that argument without the compiler having to prove anything at run time. The constraint is what makes the conversion legal, and the reason it is needed is that a span of a type parameter is not something the compiler can verify on its own.

// params collections (C# 14): any collection type, not just arrays
static int SumAll(params ReadOnlySpan<int> values)      // zero allocation, no array
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (int v in values) total += v;
    return total;
}

Console.WriteLine(SumAll(1, 2, 3));              // 6
Console.WriteLine(SumAll(new int[3] { 4, 5, 6 }));    // 15
Console.WriteLine(SumAll([7, 8]));                        // 15, collection expression

// A params List<T> overload
static void LogAll(params List<string> lines) { }

// Ref readonly members on ref structs (C# 14)
public ref struct Number
{
    private readonly int _value;
    public ref readonly int Value => ref _value;   // no copy on access
    public ref readonly int Doubled => ref GetDoubled();

    // The ref-safe anti-pattern that makes this worthwhile
    // A method returning a wider type than it received can smuggle out
    // a reference into a shorter-lived buffer. ref readonly forbids that.
    private readonly ref int GetDoubled() => throw new NotSupportedException();
}

// Escape sequences \e and \x (C# 14)
string escape = "\e[0m";      // ESC, for terminal control codes
string hex    = "\x41";      // 'A'

// Non-destructive span extensions (C# 14): Take, Skip, Index, Length
// ReadOnlySpan<char> head = raw.AsSpan().Take(4);
// ReadOnlySpan<char> rest = raw.AsSpan().Skip(4);
// int width = buffer.Length;   // on a Span<T> with a known element size
// int third = buffer.Index(2);

// ref struct interfaces (from .NET 9)
// public ref struct IBufferSource { ReadOnlySpan<byte> GetSpan(); }

// The \e escape is not the only way to get ESC
// Console.Write("\u001b[2J\u001b[H");   // clear screen and home

params ReadOnlySpan<T> is the feature to reach for. The old params int[] allocated an array on every call; the span version allocates nothing and the JIT handles the fixed arguments efficiently. It is a small change that removes an allocation from every call site.

C# 13 also added allows ref struct constraints, so a generic method can accept a Span<T> type argument. Combined with params ReadOnlySpan<T>, you can write generic buffer APIs that are both zero-allocation and type-safe.


{{-- WHY A SPAN IS THE RIGHT PARAMETER TYPE: an array parameter is
     a WRITABLE reference, so the callee can change the caller's
     data. A span says how MUCH, and the read-only form says it
     cannot be changed. --}}
static int Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int> values)
{
    // THE CALL: an array argument is COPIED into an implicit array,
    // because params int[] and ReadOnlySpan<int> are not the same
    // conversion.
    int[] data = [1, 2, 3];
    int a = Sum(data);            // a COPY is made at the call

    int b = Sum(1, 2, 3);         // fine: no array exists
    int c = Sum([4, 5, 6]);       // a collection expression is
                                   // passed as a SPAN: no copy
    {{-- ^ WHICH IS THE POINT of the feature: with params int[] a
         caller's array is COPIED at the call, so a callee mutating
         it is INVISIBLE. With a span the caller SEES the
         mutation — which is why the two spellings of the same-looking
         call have OPPOSITE semantics. --}}
}

{{-- AND A WritableSpan FROM AN ARRAY IS THE SAME STORAGE: --}}
static void Fill(params Span<int> values)
{
    values[0] = 99;               // MUTATES THE CALLER'S ARRAY
}

static void VisibleMutation()
{
    int[] mine = [1, 2, 3];
    Fill(mine);                   // mine[0] is NOW 99
    // ^ WHICH IS CORRECT and worth knowing: a params span overload
    //   on a method that already has a params array CHANGES THE
    //   SEMANTICS of every existing call site from "caller's data is
    //   copied" to "caller's data is mutated", with no compile
    //   error anywhere.
}

{{-- THE REF-STRUCT CONSTRAINT, which is what makes a span of a type
     parameter legal at all: --}}
static int Measure<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T> values) where T : unmanaged
{
    // ^ THE CONSTRAINT IS WHAT MAKES IT LEGAL. The compiler cannot
    //   verify that a span of a type parameter points at valid
    //   memory, so it requires proof that T is unmanaged — and an
    //   unmanaged type CANNOT contain a reference, which is exactly
    //   the property that makes the span valid.
    return System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.SizeOf<T>() * values.Length;
}
{{-- ^ unmanaged is STRICTER than struct: a struct containing a
     string or an array is a struct but NOT unmanaged, so the
     constraint is doing real work rather than repeating the struct
     one. --}}

{{-- AND WHERE IT IS NOT THE RIGHT ANSWER, which is a case worth
     stating because the temptation is universal: --}}
static void NotThis<T>(T[] values) where T : unmanaged
{
    // ^ NEITHER BETTER NOR WORSE for an unmanaged T, because the
    //   array ALREADY exists and passing it copies nothing. The
    //   span form is for a boundary where a SPAN would otherwise
    //   be CONSTRUCTED — a slice of a larger buffer, a stackalloc,
    //   a rented array — not for a method that is handed a finished
    //   array and has no reason to care how much of it to look at.
}

12.5 C# 14: extension members, field keyword and Span ergonomics

C# 14 is the language version that ships with .NET 10. Its headline feature is extension members, which generalise extension methods to properties and static members. It also adds the field keyword, removing the backing-field boilerplate from auto-properties, and gives Span<T> first-class language support. Applies to .NET 10 or later; a C# 14 target framework is required.

Extension members allow an extension property and an extension block that contains static members, and the field keyword allows a type to expose a reference the compiler generates the storage for. Together they cover the cases that previously required a wrapper type or a copy.

What an extension property is for

A property on a type you do not own, computed without allocating a wrapper and without an extension method that takes a lambda. The canonical case is the span of a slice — a length, an emptiness check, a sub-range — where an extension method returning a value works but a property reads like the member it is standing in for. The constraint is that it must be read-only, because there is no place to store the backing state.

The field keyword, and its limitation

A field with a keyword generates the storage and the accessors rather than requiring them to be declared, which removes the primary-constructor-plus-property pattern. The limitation is real and worth knowing: the field must be of a type the generator can name, and it cannot participate in anything that needs the field's storage to be laid out by the caller.

// C# 14: extension members. Extension methods were always allowed; C# 14 adds
// extension PROPERTIES and static extension blocks, so an entire type can
// be extended without leaving methods behind.
public static class StringExtensions
{
    // an extension property - reads like a real property at the call site
    public static string Slugified(this string value) =>
        value.ToLowerInvariant().Replace(" ", "-");

    // a static extension block - new STATIC members on an existing type
    public static int WordCount(this string value) =>
        value.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Length;
}

var title = "Hello World Guide";
var slug  = title.Slugified;      // "hello-world-guide"
var words = title.WordCount();     // 3

// C# 14: the field keyword removes the backing-field boilerplate.
public sealed class Temperature
{
    // Before C# 14 you had to declare '_celsius' by hand.
    private decimal _celsius;
    public decimal Celsius
    {
        get => field;                    // 'field' is the compiler's storage
        set
        {
            if (value < -273.15m)
                throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(value));
            field = value;
        }
    }
    public decimal Fahrenheit => field * 9m / 5m + 32m;  // read the same field
}

// C# 14: null-conditional assignment.
Customer? customer = Find(id);
customer?.Email = "new@example.com";   // no-op when customer is null

// C# 14: first-class Span<T> - implicit conversions reduce noise.
public static int CountVowels(this ReadOnlySpan<char> text)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (var ch in text)                       // no string allocation
        if ("aeiou".Contains(ch)) total++;
    return total;
}
int n = "sequence".CountVowels();   // string converts implicitly

C# 14 in three parts: extension properties and static extension blocks, the field keyword so an auto-property can validate without a hand-written backing field, and implicit Span conversions so a string can be passed to a span-based method without allocating.

Extension members require a C# 14 language version and a .NET 10 target framework. The compiler enforces the pairing: using C# 14 syntax on a .NET 9 target is an error, not a warning.


{{-- AN EXTENSION PROPERTY, which is READ-ONLY because there is no
     place to store the backing state. --}}
public static class SpanExtensions
{
    extension(ReadOnlySpan<T> span)      // the EXTENSION BLOCK
    {
        // ^ READ-ONLY, and the canonical case is a span of a slice:
        //   computing these WITHOUT a wrapper type and WITHOUT an
        //   extension method that takes a lambda.
        public bool IsEmpty => span.IsEmpty;
        public int Length => span.Length;
        public ReadOnlySpan<T> Reversed => span.Reverse();

        // AN EXTENSION PROPERTY RATHER THAN A METHOD, because these
        // READ LIKE the members a Span already has, and calling
        // span.IsEmpty() instead of span.IsEmpty would be a second
        // way to write the same thing.
    }

    extension<T>(T[] array) where T : unmanaged
    {
        public ReadOnlySpan<T> AsReadOnly => array;
        // ^ THE SPAN OF AN ARRAY IS FREE, so a method that only
        //   needs to look at part of it should take this rather than
        //   a ReadOnlySpan<T> constructed by the caller. It reads as
        //   a member and it does not copy.
    }
}

static void Using()
{
    int[] data = [1, 2, 3];

    // READS LIKE A MEMBER, COPIES NOTHING, and — unlike an extension
    // method — CANNOT BE CALLED ON NULL without a warning, because
    // the compiler knows the receiver is a span.
    ReadOnlySpan<int> view = data.AsReadOnly;
    if (view.Length == 0) { /* ... */ }

    // WHICH AN EXTENSION METHOD ALSO ALLOWS, and cannot do as well:
    // bool IsEmpty(this ReadOnlySpan<int> s) => s.IsEmpty;
    // view.IsEmpty()      fine, but a METHOD CALL on what reads as
    //                     a value, and on a nullable span the
    //                     compiler cannot warn because the
    //                     receiver type is not part of the
    //                     signature's nullability story.
}

{{-- THE field KEYWORD, which GENERATES THE STORAGE rather than
     requiring it to be declared: --}}
public sealed class Measurement(string unit, double value)
{
    // THE OLD SHAPE: the parameter becomes a private field
    // implicitly and a property is written by hand.
    // public string Unit { get; } = unit;
    // public double Value { get; } = value;

    // THE NEW SHAPE: the field keyword generates the backing storage
    // and the accessor pair, so the primary-constructor-plus-property
    // pattern is not needed.
    public string Unit  { get; } = unit;
    public double Value { get; } = value;

    // WHICH REMOVES THE REPETITION, and it is a real reduction: the
    //   declaration above is the only place the property is named.
}

{{-- AND THE LIMITATION, which is worth knowing before reaching for
     it: --}}
// THE FIELD MUST BE OF A TYPE THE GENERATOR CAN NAME, and it cannot
// participate in anything that needs the field's STORAGE TO BE LAID
// OUT BY THE CALLER — so a field type that is itself a ref struct
// cannot be a field, and a field on a generic type cannot be a
// generic field of the containing type's parameter.
//
// THE VERSION WORTH REACHING FOR: a type whose parameters ARE its
// definition and which has no behaviour beyond storing them.
public sealed class Span2D(int width, int height)
{
    public readonly ref struct Slice
    {
        // ^ a ref struct NESTED in a class: it cannot be a FIELD of
        //   the class, and it cannot be boxed, and it cannot cross
        //   an async boundary. The compiler refuses all three
        //   rather than letting them fail at run time.
    }
}

12.6 ref, readonly and ref-safe members

C# gives you four ways to pass a value: by value (a copy), by ref (a writable alias), by in / ref readonly (a read-only alias, no copy), and by out (a write-only alias). The in-parameters are the ones beginners miss and performance-minded library authors use constantly.

Three parameter-passing forms exist and each says something different about whether the callee may keep the reference. A value is a copy. A ref is a reference the callee may both read and write, and it cannot be null. A ref readonly is a reference the callee may read but not write. And an in parameter is a reference that must be assigned before the call — which is how a method asks its caller to initialise something rather than passing an uninitialised value.

The ref-safe context, and why it exists

By default a method may not store a reference parameter in a field, because the method's caller could have passed a local that stops existing the moment the call returns. The escape analysis that makes this safe is conservative: it rejects a case that is provably fine and accepts nothing it cannot prove. Marking a member scoped relaxes it for exactly one scenario — an instance member that stores the parameter alongside its own receiver, so the reference cannot outlive it.

The in parameter

An in parameter must be assigned before the call, and the compiler enforces that the method does not assign to it. That is the useful property: it is how a method asks the caller to guarantee something has been set, rather than the method checking and the caller ignoring the check.

// The four passing modes, with a 40-byte struct to make the cost visible
readonly record struct Big(long A, long B, long C, long D, long E);

static void ByValue(Big b)    { }   // 40-byte copy
static void ByRef(ref Big b)   { b = b; }   // 8-byte pointer, writable
static void ByIn(in Big b)    { }   // 8-byte pointer, read-only
static void ByRefReadOnly(ref readonly Big b) { }   // C# 12, clearest

// A readonly method on a class is passed 'in' implicitly, with no
// 'in' keyword at the call site -- but declare it for discoverability.
public readonly int Magnitude() => new[] { A, B, C, D, E }.Max();

// 'in' in signatures: a promise about the contract, not just performance
public static bool TryNormalise(ref readonly Vector v, out Vector unit)
{
    double len = Math.Sqrt(v.X * v.X + v.Y * v.Y);
    // v cannot be assigned or passed to an 'out' parameter: no silent copies
    unit = len == 0 ? new Vector(0, 0) : new Vector(v.X / len, v.Y / len);
    return len > 0;
}

// ref returns: return a reference to existing storage, not a copy
public ref int Largest(ref int a, ref int b)
{
    ref int r = ref a > b ? ref a : ref b;   // the ternary keeps the ref
    return ref r;
}

ref int slot = ref Largest(ref a, ref b);
slot = 100;                     // writes through to a or b

// A Span<T> element reference, the everyday case
static ref T MaxOf(ref T a, ref T b) => ref (a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? ref a : ref b);

Use in or ref readonly for large readonly structs in hot paths, and add [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)] to the small accessors that return them, because a 40-byte copy hides inside the call overhead.

A ref return keeps the referenced object alive only as long as the ref itself. Storing a ref to an element of a collection and then mutating that collection invalidates the reference, and the compiler cannot stop you. Treat ref returns as a local, short-lived facility.


{{-- FOUR FORMS, and each says something about WHETHER THE CALLEE
     MAY KEEP THE REFERENCE. --}}
public sealed class Passing
{
    // 1. BY VALUE: a copy. The callee may change its own copy and
    //    the caller sees nothing.
    static void ByValue(int x) { x = 99; }

    // 2. ref: A REFERENCE the callee may READ and WRITE, and it
    //    CANNOT BE NULL — so the callee needs no null check.
    static void ByRef(ref int x)
    {
        x = 99;                 // ^ WRITE-THROUGH to the caller
        // x = null;            ERROR: a ref parameter cannot be
        //                        null, which is why it is different
        //                        from a normal reference argument
    }

    // 3. ref readonly: a reference the callee may READ but not
    //    WRITE — a STRONGER PROMISE than by value, because the
    //    callee sees the caller's actual storage rather than a
    //    copy.
    static long Sum(ref readonly long[] values)
    {
        // values[0] = 1;        ERROR: cannot assign through a
        //                        readonly reference
        long total = 0;
        foreach (long v in values) total += v;
        return total;
    }

    // 4. in: A REFERENCE THAT MUST BE ASSIGNED BEFORE THE CALL, and
    //    the method may not assign it. This is how a method asks
    //    its CALLER to guarantee something, rather than the method
    //    checking and the caller ignoring the check.
    static void MustBeSet(in DateTime cutoff)
    {
        // cutoff = DateTime.Now;   ERROR: an in parameter is
        //                           readonly, so the method cannot
        //                           repair it either
        Use(cutoff);
    }
}

{{-- AND WHY ref readonly IS THE CORRECT PARAMETER TYPE WHERE IT
     IS USED, rather than a micro-optimisation: --}}
public static void TheArgumentForRefReadonly(long[] values)
{
    // BY VALUE: COPIES the array REFERENCE, which is free — so
    //   there is no allocation argument for ref readonly here.
    long a = Sum(values);

    // ref readonly: the promise is that Sum cannot WRITE to the
    //   caller's array. Sum is also passed a REFERENCE TO THE
    //   CALLER'S STORAGE, so it sees the live array and not a
    //   snapshot — which matters when the array is mutated
    //   concurrently and a by-value parameter would have frozen
    //   the reference at call time rather than the contents.
    long b = Sum(ref values);
}

{{-- THE REF-SAFE CONTEXT, and the escape analysis is CONSERVATIVE:
     it rejects a case that is provably fine and accepts nothing it
     cannot prove. --}}
public sealed class Buffer(Span<byte> initial)
{
    private readonly Span<byte> _data = initial;    // ^ LEGAL: an
    //   instance member initialiser assigning a ref parameter to a
    //   field, because the reference cannot outlive the object.

    // public Span<byte> Field;      ERROR: cannot store a ref
    //                               parameter in a field

    // public static Span<byte> Static;   ERROR: a static field
    //   outlives every caller, so the parameter definitely can
    //   outlive its storage
}

{{-- AND scoped, which relaxes the analysis for EXACTLY ONE case: an
     instance member that stores the parameter alongside its OWN
     RECEIVER, so the reference cannot outlive it. --}}
public ref struct ScopedHolder<T>(ref T value)
{
    // scoped SAYS: this field's lifetime is TIED to the method's
    // parameter's lifetime. It is a PROMISE THE COMPILER CHECKS,
    // not an optimisation, and getting the promise wrong is a
    // use-after-free.
