    public scoped ref T Field => ref value;

    // THE COMPILER REFUSES scoped ON AN ARRAY FIELD:
    // public scoped T[] Array;    ERROR: a scoped reference cannot
    //                              be stored in a heap field,
    //                              because the array could keep
    //                              the reference alive past the
    //                              scope it belongs to
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE LIMITATION worth remembering: scoped works for
     a ref struct's own fields, and it does NOT work for anything
     that could be placed in an array, because an array's elements
     have no lifetime tied to the containing object. --}}

12.7 file types, partial and the Lock type

C# 11 added the file access modifier, a type a single file can see. C# 9 and 13 made partial far more useful. And System.Threading.Lock (new in .NET 9) is a modern, faster, ref-struct-based replacement for locking on an object.

Three features that changed how a type's members are declared rather than what they do. The file keyword spreads one type across several files, which is what a large implementation needs. Partial members make a member's declaration and its implementation separate, which is what a source generator needs. And the lock type exists so that a lock statement cannot be written against something that was not meant to be a lock.

The lock type, and what it prevents

A lock statement takes an expression and any reference type satisfies it — including this, a boxed value, or a string literal. All three are defects: locking on this exposes the lock to every caller holding a reference, and locking on a string literal locks a reference the runtime may intern, so two unrelated places can share a lock by accident. The dedicated type makes all three compile errors.

File types, and the trade

A file type puts a type's declaration in one file and its members in others, which is genuinely useful for a large implementation. The cost is that finding a member now requires searching, and that a partial type's members can be declared in an order that makes the file read badly. The rule worth adopting is that the file holding the public surface holds the primary constructors and the properties, and the others hold private helpers.

// file types: visible only inside this one file. Perfect for
// small helpers, test fixtures, and generated code.
file sealed class InternalMetrics
{
    // Intentionally invisible to the rest of the assembly
    public int Calls;
}

// Partial properties (C# 14): a real property, split across files
// -- one file --
// public partial class Order { public partial string Reference { get; set; } }
// -- another file --
public partial class Order
{
    private string? _reference;
    public partial string Reference
    {
        get => _reference ??= Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N").Substring(0, 8);
        set => _reference = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value) ? throw new ArgumentException() : value;
    }
}

// Partial members already existed: declarations with no body,
// implemented optionally. Used by source generators.
public partial class Generated
{
    // [GeneratedCode] partial void OnBuild();
    //   ^ a partial method with no implementation is erased by the compiler,
    //     and the CALL to it is removed too. Zero cost when unimplemented.
}

// System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9): the modern lock object
private readonly Lock _gate = new();

public void Update(Action action)
{
    lock (_gate) { action(); }        // same syntax, faster and safer
}

// Why it is better than lock(object)
//   - ~2-4x faster uncontended (it knows the size and alignment)
//   - Cannot be boxed, so it is safe inside async and generic code
//   - The compiler will not let you lock a string, ValueType or anything
//     whose equality is overloaded (a real bug with lock(object))
//   - EnterScope() for the Monitor-style API

// The field keyword (C# 14) removes property boilerplate entirely
public sealed class Counter
{
    private int _hits;
    public int Hits { get => _hits; set => _hits = value >= 0 ? value : _hits; }
}

System.Threading.Lock is a ref struct, which is exactly why it is safe: it cannot be boxed, cannot escape, and the compiler prevents locking on a value whose Equals is overloaded — the classic bug where two different lock statements on the same boxed string take different locks.

Use file-scoped types for test helpers and generated code rather than marking everything internal and adding InternalsVisibleTo. It keeps the visibility exactly as narrow as it needs to be and the compiler enforces it.


{{-- FILE TYPES: the declaration in one file, the members in
     others. Useful for a large implementation, and the cost is that
     finding a member now requires searching. --}}
public sealed partial class Order
{
    // THE FILE THAT HOLDS THE PUBLIC SURFACE holds the primary
    //   constructor and the properties, so a reader has one place
    //   to look for the shape.
    public required string Reference { get; init; }
    public decimal Total { get; private set; }
    public void Add(Line line) => Total += line.Total;
}

public sealed partial class Order
{
    // THE OTHERS hold private helpers, and each can have its own
    // usings, its own fields and its own nested types.
    private static readonly decimal TaxRate = 0.2m;

    private void Recalculate() { /* ... */ }
}

public sealed partial class Order
{
    // AND A PARTIAL TYPE MAY DECLARE A NESTED TYPE, which is how a
    // large type keeps its private helper types beside it.
    private sealed class Line(decimal total) { public decimal Total = total; }
}

{{-- PARTIAL MEMBERS, which is what a SOURCE GENERATOR needs: the
     DECLARATION and the IMPLEMENTATION are separate, so generated
     code supplies a body for a member declared by hand. --}}
public sealed partial class Repository
{
    // THE DECLARATION, and a source generator will supply the body
    // at compile time. If no generator runs, this is a COMPILE
    // ERROR — which is correct, and is why the diagnostic names the
    // partial member rather than reporting a missing implementation.
    public partial Task<Order?> FindAsync(long id);
}

{{-- AND THE LOCK TYPE, and what it prevents: --}}
public sealed class Concurrency
{
    private readonly Lock _gate = new();
    private decimal _balance;

    // RIGHT: a DEDICATED synchronisation object, so nothing outside
    //   this class can take the lock by holding a reference to it.
    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        lock (_gate)                   // ^ the Lock TYPE. Only a
        {                               //   Lock or a compatible
            _balance += amount;        //   synchronisation object
        }                               //   satisfies it.
    }

    // WRONG, AND ALL THREE ARE COMPILE ERRORS NOW:
    public void Others(object other, string key)
    {
        lock (this) { }                // ERROR: locks on this, so
                                       //   every caller holding a
                                       //   reference to the object
                                       //   contends for it
        lock (other) { }               // ERROR: locks on somebody
                                       //   else's object, which is
                                       //   a design nobody can see
        lock (key) { }                 // ERROR: locks on a string,
                                       //   and the runtime may
                                       //   INTERN two equal strings,
                                       //   so two unrelated places
                                       //   can share a lock by
                                       //   accident
    }

    // AND IT FIXES THE RECURSIVE-ACQUISITION TRAP, which is the
    // version people hit: a method that takes the lock and then
    // calls another method that takes it. Monitor is re-entrant, so
    // it works; a hand-written spin lock is not, and the result is a
    // deadlock that appears only under contention.
    public void DepositTwice(decimal amount)
    {
        Deposit(amount);
        Deposit(amount);              // ^ SAFE: Monitor is
                                       //   RE-ENTRANT, and a
                                       //   hand-rolled semaphore
                                       //   here would deadlock
                                       //   against itself.
    }
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS WHY THE LOCK TYPE'S OTHER purpose is being the
     IDEAL THING TO WRITE BY HAND: a Lock's documentation tells the
     reader it is re-entrant, which a private object does not, and
     which is the property somebody relies on without knowing they
     relied on it. --}}

12.8 Nullable annotations and attributes

Nullable reference types is one feature with two halves: the ? annotation and the flow analysis, plus a set of attributes for expressing intent to tooling. The attributes are what let the compiler understand your framework, and they are how you document and enforce contracts.

Nullable reference types are a set of annotations plus a set of attributes, and the attributes are the part that is genuinely optional. An annotation is erased at compile time. An attribute changes what a tool does with a symbol, and a project can use all of them, some of them, or none.

What each attribute is for

AllowNull says a null input is permitted even though the type is non-nullable, which is what a validating wrapper needs. DisallowNull is the opposite and is what a callback needs. MaybeNull says the method may return null on one path, and NotNull says it does not even when the type says so. The last two matter because the compiler cannot always prove which a method returns, and an attribute is how a human states it.

The flow analysis, and what it cannot do

The compiler tracks whether a reference may be null and reports where it flows into a place that cannot accept it. What it cannot do is follow a value across an abstraction boundary: a field set by a deserialiser, a value returned through an interface whose implementation the compiler is not compiling, or anything reached by reflection. Those are the places a suppression belongs, and each one wants a comment saying why.

// The two annotations
string  notNull = "x";        // the compiler assumes non-null
string? maybeNull = null;       // may be null; must be checked
string? alsoFine = "x";     // '?' does not force a null value

// Flow analysis, in practice
public string Describe(string? input)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(input)) return "(empty)";   // state: maybe-null
    return input.ToUpper();                    // state: not-null, no warning
}

// The attributes that drive analysis and tooling
[AllowNull]        public string Api { get; set; }     // callers may pass null
[DisallowNull]     public string Cached { get; set; }   // callers may not pass null
[MaybeNull]        public string Try { get; set; }        // the getter may return null
[NotNull]          public string Checked { get; set; }  // the getter never returns null
[MemberNotNull]    public void Init() { }                   // after Init, field is not null
[NotNullWhen(true)]  public bool TryGet(out string? v)   // the contract for Try*
[DoesNotReturn]    public void Fail() => Environment.Exit(1);  // no return after this

// [NotNullWhen] makes the flow analysis work on Try patterns
[NotNullWhen(true)]
public static bool TryRead(out string? value)
{
    value = "x";
    return true;
}

// [MemberNotNull] documents a postcondition instead of returning a bool
[MemberNotNull("Name")]
public void EnsureInitialised() { _name ??= "default"; }

// Attributes for trimming and interop (from .NET 5+)
[DynamicallyAccessedMembers(DynamicallyAccessedMemberTypes.PublicMethods)]
Type _pluginType;

[UnconditionalSuppressMessage("Trimming", Justification = "type is preserved by the linker")]
[RequiresUnreferencedCode]      // the method uses reflection
[RequiresDynamicCode]            // the method generates code

// MemberNotNullWith (C# 14) extends this to generic code paths

The NotNullWhen and MaybeNullWhen attributes are the ones that pay for themselves immediately. Without them, every caller of a hand-written TryGet gets a nullable warning; with them, the flow analysis is precise and the warning disappears.

For a public API, prefer MaybeNullWhen(false) on an out parameter over out T?, because the former also covers the nullable value type case and gives better IntelliSense. The BCL uses these attributes consistently, and matching them makes your API feel native.


{{-- ANNOTATIONS ARE ERASED; ATTRIBUTES CHANGE WHAT A TOOL DOES. And
     an attribute is how a human states what the compiler cannot
     prove. --}}
public sealed class Attributes
{
    // AllowNull: a NULL INPUT IS PERMITTED even though the type is
    // non-nullable. This is what a VALIDATING WRAPPER needs — the
    // parameter may arrive null and the method's job is to handle
    // it, so requiring a caller to write ? defeats the purpose.
    public static string NameOf([AllowNull] string? raw) =>
        raw ?? "(unnamed)";
    {{-- ^ WITHOUT AllowNull the compiler emits CS8604 at every call
         site passing something nullable, and the caller is forced
         to add a suppression to satisfy a method that was written
         precisely to handle the null. --}}

    // DisallowNull: the OPPOSITE, and it is what a CALLBACK needs —
    // the delegate will never pass null, so the callee can rely on
    // it and does not have to check.
    public static void ForEach(Action<[DisallowNull] string> action)
    {
        // ^ THE CALLEE CAN ASSUME non-null, so a null check inside
        //   the callee is dead code the compiler can now flag as
        //   always-false rather than leaving it as untested
        //   defensive code that nobody will ever exercise.
    }

    // MaybeNull: THE METHOD MAY RETURN NULL ON ONE PATH, which the
    // compiler cannot prove when the analysis gives up — through an
    // interface, a generic constraint, or a helper it does not see.
    [return: MaybeNull]
    public static string? FindById(IReadOnlyList<User> users, string id)
    {
        // ^ THE ATTRIBUTE SAYS the return is not always non-null
        //   even though the declared type is string. Without it the
        //   compiler assumes the method honoured its annotation and
        //   emits NO warning at the caller — a warning that would
        //   have caught the real defect.
        foreach (var u in users)
            if (u.Id == id) return u.Name;
        return null;
    }

    // NotNull: the OPPOSITE, and it is the one that fixes a method
    // whose body the compiler believes returns null even though the
    // annotation says it cannot.
    [return: NotNull]
    public static string Always(string? raw) => raw ?? "";
}
{{-- ^ MAYBECONFUSION IS THE COMMON PAIR: MaybeNull says the method
     MAY return null; NotNullIfNotNull says it returns null only if
     the named parameter is null. The second is what makes a
     Chained API null-safe in the compiler's view rather than only
     in the reader's. --}}

{{-- THE FLOW ANALYSIS, and what it CANNOT do: --}}
public sealed class WhatItCannotFollow
{
    // IT CANNOT FOLLOW A VALUE ACROSS AN ABSTRACTION BOUNDARY.
    private User _user = null!;      // the null-forgiving operator,
                                     // which SUPPRESSES the warning
                                     // without any runtime effect

    public void D1() { _user.Name.ToUpper(); }   // no warning: the
    //   suppression is on the FIELD, and the analysis believes it

    // IT CANNOT SEE THROUGH REFLECTION:
    public void D2()
    {
        var value = typeof(User).GetProperty("Name")!.GetValue(_user);
        // ^ 'value' is object?, and the compiler says so honestly —
        //   it has no idea what the property is. The unboxing here
        //   can fail at RUN TIME, and nothing in the code says so.
        Console.WriteLine(value);
    }

    // IT CANNOT SEE A FRAMEWORK DESERIALISER:
    public User FromJson(string json) => JsonSerializer.Deserialize<User>(json)!;
    // ^ The '!' is REQUIRED because the compiler believes the
    //   annotation, and the deserialiser sets the property by name
    //   through reflection. A malformed payload produces a null
    //   where a non-null was declared, and the crash is at the
    //   NEXT dereference rather than here.
}

{{-- AND WHERE A SUPPRESSION BELONGS, which is the rule worth
     adopting: --}}
#nullable enable
#pragma warning disable CS8602
// ^ WRONG: a file-wide suppression turns the analysis into nothing
//   for that file, and it is the first thing anybody tries when the
//   build is red.
#pragma warning restore CS8602

var length = order.Customer.Name.Length;
#pragma warning disable CS8602 // Customer is non-null from the db
var alsoLength = order.Customer.Name.Length;
#pragma warning restore CS8602
{{-- ^ RIGHT: ONE MEMBER, ONE REASON, INLINE. A reviewer can check
     the reason in the time it takes to read one line, which is the
     only reason a suppression is ever defensible. --}}

12.9 Feature timeline by version

Here is the whole modern feature set on one page, with the version that introduced it. Use it to check what is available on your target framework, and to spot the moment a piece of code you are reading was written.

VersionRuntimeHeadline features
C# 9.NET 5Records, init-only setters, target-typed new, pattern matching additions, top-level statements, native integers, static lambdas
C# 10.NET 6File-scoped namespaces, record structs, global usings, record struct, lambda natural types, caller argument expressions
C# 11.NET 7required members, raw string literals, UTF-8 strings, u8, list patterns, static abstract interface members, generic maths (INumber<T>), ref fields, scoped
C# 12.NET 8Primary constructors on classes, collection expressions, ref readonly parameters, alias any type, default lambda parameters, inline arrays, [Experimental]
C# 13.NET 9params collections, \e and \x escapes, ref readonly members, partial properties, allows ref struct, MemberNotNullWith, lock object, ref struct interfaces
C# 14.NET 10Extension members, the field keyword, null-conditional assignment, ??= as an expression, first-class span types, field-backed properties everywhere

C# 14 is the current version on .NET 10 and is fully supported. The field keyword and extension members are the two that will change how you write properties and extension methods day to day.

Every feature above is a language feature, but some have runtime requirements. Raw string literals need only the compiler. required members emit RequiredMemberAttribute, so a library using them needs a matching runtime. static abstract members and generic maths need .NET 7. Check the feature table before using a new feature in a library with broad targets.

Turn on the compiler’s suggestion output to see what your code could gain: <AnalysisLevel>latest-all</AnalysisLevel> or the Suggestion diagnostic level in .editorconfig. It will flag every place you could use a newer idiom, which is the fastest way to modernise an existing codebase.

Exercises 12

  1. Rewrite a constructor-and-backing-field class using a primary constructor and the field keyword, and compare the line counts.
  2. Convert three new List<T>() { a, b, c } initialisers to collection expressions, including one targeting Span<int> and one targeting a dictionary.
  3. Write a params ReadOnlySpan<char> method, call it four ways, and confirm with a GC allocation count that the array call site allocates nothing.
  4. Convert a switch chain of five conditions into a switch expression with relational and and patterns, and delete every if.
  5. Add a file-scoped helper type to a class and prove that another file in the same assembly cannot see it.
  6. Enable nullable analysis on an existing file, then fix every warning by changing a signature rather than by suppressing it. Count how many signatures changed.

{{-- THE FEATURE LIST IS NOT THE STORY. Here is what each version
     BOUGHT rather than what it changed. --}}

// 8. FOUNDATIONAL. Nothing after this is safe without it.
#nullable enable
string? maybe = null;          // a SECOND TYPE for every reference
                              // type, and the compiler now warns
                              // where a null can reach a
                              // dereference

// 9. THE LANGUAGE BECAME EXPRESSIVE.
var point = new Point { X = 1 };            // target-typed new
var copy  = point with { X = 3 };          // copy-with, so a value
                                           // type gets a safe
                                           // "changed" copy
if (o is Order { Status: OrderStatus.Paid, Lines.Count: > 0 })
    { }                                    // patterns COMPOSE and
                                           // nest, which is what
                                           // replaced the type
                                           // test plus the cast
record Point(int X, int Y);                // generated value
                                           // semantics

// 10. BOILERPLATE AND FILE-LEVEL CONVENTIONS.
namespace App;                              // file-scoped: no
                                           // braces, no indentation
global using System.Linq;                   // one using per PROJECT
readonly record struct Key(int A, int B);   // a value-type record, so
                                           // a dictionary key needs
                                           // no IEquatable

// 11. SAFETY AND CORRECTNESS OF LITERALS.
public required string Name { get; init; }  // cannot be half-built
byte[] utf8 = System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("x");
                                          // THE UTF8 PROPERTY is the
                                          // real one: encoding
                                          // literals as UTF-16 and
                                          // converting at run time
                                          // was a silent corruption
                                          // source
var json = """
    { "name": "test" }                    // NO ESCAPING AT ALL: the
    """;                                  // COUNT of quotes around it
                                          // is the escape mechanism
Reference? r;                             // list patterns
switch (r)
{
    case [{ Kind: "a" }, .. var rest]:    // a SLICE pattern: at
                                          // least one 'a', then
                                          // whatever, and the
                                          // remaining elements bind
                                          // to a collection
        break;
}


// 12. THE BOILERPLATE REMOVED.
public sealed class Order(string reference)   // no constructor body,
{                                            // so validation is a
    public string Reference { get; } = reference;   // GUARD EXPRESSION
}                                                 // that throws during
                                                   // construction
List<int> nums = [1, 2, 3];                  // a COLLECTION EXPRESSION
                                             // works for any collection
                                             // type, and the target
                                             // decides which
using Alias = System.Collections.Generic.List<string>;

// 13. MEMORY AND THREAD SAFETY AT THE TYPE LEVEL.
void Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int> values) { }   // a SPAN as params: no
                                               // copy from an array
                                               // argument
static int Sum(ref readonly int v) => v;        // READ THE CALLER'S
                                               // STORAGE without
                                               // permission to write
lock (obj) { }                                 // the Lock TYPE: a
                                               // dedicated
                                               // synchronisation
                                               // object, so
                                               // 'lock (this)' and
                                               // 'lock ("text")' are
                                               // compile ERRORS rather
                                               // than a global
                                               // bottleneck nobody
                                               // can see

// 14. THE TYPE AND ITS CONSUMERS CLOSE TOGETHER.
public sealed class Point
{
    public int X { get; } = 1;              // the field KEYWORD
    public int Y { get; } = 2;              // generates the backing
}                                           // storage and the
                                             // accessors, removing
                                             // the primary-constructor
                                             // plus property pattern
public static class Ext
{
    extension(ReadOnlySpan<int> s)
    {
        public bool IsEmpty => s.IsEmpty;   // an EXTENSION PROPERTY:
        }                                    // read-only, because
                                             // there is no place to
                                             // store backing state
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE USEFUL READING. 8 moved EVERYTHING, and 9–11
     made the language expressive. 12–13 removed boilerplate and
     made the unsafe code safe. 14 closed the gap between a type
     and the code that uses it. The feature COUNT per version is a
     poor proxy for how much each one moved: 8 is one feature and it
     is the foundation for every nullability diagnostic anyone has
     ever wanted. --}}

{{-- AND EVERY VERSION ALSO REMOVED SOMETHING, which is what makes
     the additions safe to use: --}}
// The unsafe context restriction: every pointer operation must be
//   inside an unsafe block or a pointer-typed parameter.
// The requirement that an iterator's locals be definitely assigned
//   before the first yield return.
// The ability to dereference a possibly-null value without a
//   warning — removed in 8 and not restorable without opting out.
//   ^ THAT REMOVAL is the entire point of the feature, and it is
//     also the one people notice as pain rather than as safety: a
//     codebase that opts out per-file has given up the only
//     mechanical defence against a NullReferenceException.

Appendix A · Language Cheat Sheet

A.1 Keyword referenceA.2 Interfaces worth knowingA.3 BCL survival kitA.4 Naming and style conventionsA.5 Common compile errors and fixesA.6 Glossary

The appendix compresses the whole guide into lookup tables: every C# keyword by category, the interfaces the framework expects you to implement, the base class library types you will reach for daily, the naming conventions the .NET team actually follows, and a table of the compile errors that cost every C# developer the same afternoon.

A.1 Keyword reference

C# has 77 reserved keywords. These are the ones you will meet in real code, grouped by what they do, with a one-line note on each.

CategoryKeywordsNote
Typesbool byte char decimal double float int long object sbyte short string uint ulong ushort voidKeywords; nint and nuint are contextual
Custom typesclass struct record interface enum delegaterecord is contextual
Modifierspublic private protected internal abstract sealed static readonly const virtual override new partial async extern unsafe volatile required fileSeveral are contextual
Membersthis base get set init value field ref out in paramsfield is the C# 14 backing-field keyword
Control flowif else switch case default while do for foreach break continue return goto throw try catch finally when
Operatorstrue false null is as new sizeof typeof awaitThe rest are symbols
Expressionschecked unchecked nameof with
Namespacesusing global namespaceglobal using is C# 10
Accessprivate protected protected internalTwo access levels at once

The most useful contextual keywords, which do not need @ escaping and are only keywords in specific positions: var, async, await, yield, record, init, required, file, field, and, or, not, when, where, scoped, allows, with, let, select, from, join, into, orderby, group, by, ascending, descending, on, equals.

Most of the keywords are modifiers that decide visibility, lifetime and thread-safety rather than adding behaviour, and reading a declaration without knowing which category a word falls into is what makes a signature hard to parse. Four of them are contextual — ordinary identifiers that mean something special in one position — and three of them are genuinely misnamed, which is where the reading difficulty actually comes from.

The four contextual keywords

var, record, init and required are all identifiers you can legally use as a variable name, and the compiler reads them as keywords only in a position where a declaration would otherwise be. That is worth knowing because a method named Required compiles, and a class named Record compiles, and both confuse a reader rather than the compiler. A fifth — partial — is a real keyword but is regularly mistaken for one of the contextual ones, because it appears in a declaration position and is mistaken for a type modifier.

The three misnomers

static has nothing to do with static variables; it means "not per-instance", which is why a static method has no this and a static class can hold no instances. sealed on a class means "cannot be inherited" and on a member means "cannot be overridden" — two different restrictions sharing one word, and the one that matters more is that a sealed override lets the compiler skip a virtual dispatch. And partial does not mean "some" or "optional"; it means the declaration is split across files, and a partial type is still one type with one constructor set and one inheritance chain.

The one worth knowing precisely

volatile prevents a compiler reordering, not a hardware one. It does not make an increment atomic, which is what people assume when they put it on a counter, and the failure is a count lower than the real one with no exception and no way to reproduce it on a single thread. What it does prevent is a spin loop caching a field in a register forever — which is a real problem and a narrow one, and worth knowing precisely because the misuse is so much more common than the use.

What the category tells you

Reading a declaration left to right, the modifiers answer questions in a fixed order: visibility, then lifetime, then mutability, then threading. A signature is hard to parse when those four are interleaved, and the fix is not knowledge of any individual keyword but the habit of reading them as four separate questions.


{{-- THE FOUR CATEGORIES, and most of the keywords are MODIFIERS. --}}

// 1. DECLARATION KEYWORDS: introduce a type or a member.
class  struct  interface  enum  delegate  event  namespace
record  file  init  required
// ^ ^ ^   ^      ^
// THE CONTEXTUAL FOUR: they are ordinary identifiers with a special
// meaning in ONE POSITION, and every one of them can legally be used
// as a variable name. A method called Required() compiles; a class
// called Record compiles; both confuse a reader and neither
// confuses the compiler.

// 2. MODIFIERS. These are what a signature is actually about.
public  private  protected  internal
// ^ FOUR LEVELS and the default is INTERNAL: a type with no
//   modifier is visible to the whole assembly and to nothing else,
//   which is why a library's public surface is explicit.
static  // NOT "has static storage": it means NOT PER-INSTANCE.
        // A static method has no 'this'; a static field is one per
        // type; a static class holds no instances and no
        // inheritance.
const   // A COMPILE-TIME CONSTANT, SUBSTITUTED INTO THE CALLING
        // CODE. The value lives in the CALLER's assembly, so
        // changing it requires recompiling the caller — which is
        // exactly why a const in a public API is a compatibility
        // commitment rather than a default.
readonly// A FIELD, so it can be read in a readonly method or a
        // constructor without a defensive copy. Making a property
        // readonly instead is a DIFFERENT and weaker promise.
virtual sealed abstract override new
        // ^ THE FOUR INHERITANCE WORDS, not interchangeable:
        //     virtual   may be overridden
        //     abstract  is virtual with no body
        //     override  replaces one
        //     sealed    refuses overriding (member) OR further
        //               derivation (type) — two different
        //               restrictions in one word
        //     new       HIDES rather than replaces, and which one
        //               runs is decided by the STATIC TYPE
async   // Returns a Task and permits await. NOT A THREAD: nothing
        // runs on a new thread because of it.
partial // The DECLARATION IS SPLIT ACROSS FILES. A partial type is
        // still one type, with one constructor set and one
        // inheritance chain.


// 3. LIFETIME AND THREAD SAFETY — the two that are routinely
//    confused, and the conflation costs real time.
unsafe      // PERMITS POINTER OPERATIONS inside this member. It
             // does not make anything faster by itself; it removes
             // a restriction.
fixed       // PINS a managed object so a pointer into it does not
             // move when the collector relocates it.
stackalloc  // Allocates in the CURRENT FRAME. The size must be
             // known at the allocation, and the buffer dies when
             // the method returns.
volatile    // PREVENTS A COMPILER REORDERING, not a hardware one.

public sealed class VolatileThatIsNotAtomic
{
    private static volatile int _count;

    public static void Wrong()
    {
        // THE THEORY: volatile keeps the thread from caching the
        //   field in a register, so a reader sees the latest
        //   value. That part is TRUE and it is the only part.
        //
        // THE REALITY: ++ is a READ-MODIFY-WRITE. Two threads
        //   interleave it and one increment vanishes. volatile
        //   does not make it atomic, because atomicity is a
        //   HARDWARE PROPERTY and volatile is a COMPILER
        //   INSTRUCTION.
        _count++;
        // ^ THE COUNT COMES OUT LOWER THAN THE REAL ONE, with no
        //   exception, no diagnostic, and no way to reproduce it
        //   on one thread. This is the single most common misuse of
        //   volatile in production code.
    }

    public static void Right()
    {
        // Interlocked.Increment issues a LOCKED INSTRUCTION, so
        // the read-modify-write is atomic.
        Interlocked.Increment(ref _count);

        // And THIS is what volatile is actually FOR: a flag a
        // spinning thread polls, where the failure it prevents is
        // a loop reading a cached value forever.
        private static volatile bool _ready;
        while (!_ready) Thread.SpinWait(1);
    }
}

// 4. CONTROL FLOW.
while  do  for  foreach  switch  break  continue  return  goto
yield  throw  await  try  catch  finally  using  lock
checked  unchecked  fixed
// ^ 'checked' AND 'unchecked' ARE OPERATORS, not statements: they
//   change OVERFLOW BEHAVIOUR for a block or a single expression,
//   and unchecked is the default for arithmetic.
//
//   'using' IS A STATEMENT with a DISPOSE METHOD counterpart,
//   which is why any type can participate by implementing the right
//   interface with no registration anywhere — and why a type with a
//   constructor that throws still has its constructor run to
//   completion unless it explicitly disposes what it acquired.
//
//   'yield' RESTRICTS A METHOD to returning IEnumerable, IEnumerator
//   or one of their async forms, and the restriction IS THE FEATURE:
//   the compiler builds a state machine that holds the locals
//   across a suspension, which is exactly the bookkeeping a
//   hand-written enumerator gets wrong.

A.2 Interfaces worth knowing

These are the interfaces the framework calls on your types. Implementing the right ones is what makes your code work with LINQ, ASP.NET Core model binding, data binding, serialisation and unit tests.

InterfaceImplement it whenMembers
IEquatable<T>Always, on a value-like typeEquals(T?) — avoids boxing and is what dictionaries use
IComparable<T> / IComparableThe type has a natural orderCompareTo — required by Sort, OrderBy, SortedDictionary
IComparer<T>You supply the ordering, not the typeCompare — pass to List.Sort or OrderBy
IFormattableYou control formattingToString(format, provider)
IParsable<T>You control parsingTryParse and Parse — enables generic parse code
IDisposableAlways, for anything holding a resourceDispose
IAsyncDisposableCleanup needs to awaitDisposeAsync — enables await using
IEnumerable<T> / IEnumerator<T>Custom collection, or a lazy sequence with yieldOne method each
IReadOnlyList<T>Expose a list you will not mutateIndexer plus Count
INotifyPropertyChangedAny bound model type (WPF, WinForms, Avalonia)Raise PropertyChanged after a change
INotifyCollectionChangedAny bound collectionOr just use ObservableCollection<T>
INotifyDataErrorInfoBound forms with validationPer-property and cross-property errors
INumber<T> and friendsYour own numeric typeThe full maths algebra, since .NET 7
ISpanFormattableA type formatted into a spanLets your type participate in span interpolation

For a WPF or WinForms model type, IEquatable<T>, INotifyPropertyChanged and IDisposable are the three that matter. The desktop guide covers the binding side in full.

An interface is also the seam that lets a type be replaced

A method that takes an interface can be given a different implementation in a test without a mocking framework, provided the substitute satisfies the whole interface. That proviso is the reason a large interface is harder to fake than a small one: a three-member interface can be hand-written in a test in thirty seconds, a twenty-member one cannot, and the twenty is why the mocking framework exists at all.

The corollary is that the size of an interface is a cost paid in two places, and only one of them is visible. It is visible at every call site, because a twenty-member interface means every caller sees twenty names it does not use. It is invisible at the point of implementation, because a class implementing twenty members has a much larger blast radius when one of them changes — and the compiler finds that at build time rather than at run time, which is the one mercy in this area.

The trap in testing for the interface

Checking whether a value implements an interface before using it is a defect waiting to happen, because the check fails silently when the implementation changes. The symptom is not an error: it is that one implementation takes a path nobody expected, and the path is correct for what it supports and wrong for everything else.

The alternatives are worth knowing in order. Where a method can work either way, make it work either way — a null parameter meaning "no filtering" is usually better than a runtime type test. Where it genuinely cannot, make the consumer's requirement a constructor parameter, so the alternative is supplied at composition time rather than discovered at run time. Two implementations that differ in behaviour are two strategies, and a strategy is chosen when the object graph is built rather than when a call is made.

The interface to be careful with

IEnumerable deserves one more note, because it is the one that is almost always in the signature by accident. A method that takes IEnumerable<T> and calls Count() twice has declared that the source may be enumerated twice, which is a promise the caller cannot check and which many sources cannot honour. A method that takes IReadOnlyCollection<T> instead says the same thing more precisely, and the change is one type name.


{{-- THE ONES A LANGUAGE FEATURE IS EXPRESSED THROUGH. --}}

// IEnumerable<T>: WHAT foreach AND LINQ BOTH COMPILE TO.
public sealed class TheEnumerationContract
{
    public static void WhatItCosts()
    {
        var list = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };

        // OVER THE CONCRETE TYPE: the compiler specialises it, no
        // allocation, no dispatch.
        foreach (int i in list) { }

        // OVER IEnumerable<int>: THE ENUMERATOR IS BOXED, ONCE PER
        //   LOOP, and every iteration is an INTERFACE CALL.
        IEnumerable<int> asInterface = list;
        foreach (int i in asInterface) { }
        {{-- ^ WHICH IS WHY A GENERIC CONSTRAINT is the difference
             between a specialised loop and an interface one, and
             why a method taking IEnumerable<T> when it could take
             List<T> is a real cost rather than a style choice. The
             alternative is an overload with a constraint, which the
             compiler picks first. --}}
    }

    // IEquatable<T>: REMOVES BOXING from a comparison.
    public readonly struct Key(int a, int b) : IEquatable<Key>
    {
        public bool Equals(Key other) => a == other.a && b == other.b;
        // ^ NO BOXING, because T is a concrete type parameter rather
        //   than object. Without it, key.Equals((object)other) boxes
        //   BOTH operands — and a dictionary probes once per
        //   bucket examined, so a hot key lookup allocates two
        //   objects per probe and the number of probes is
        //   logarithmic in the count.
    }

    // IFormattable: WHAT INTERPOLATION CHECKS FIRST.
    public readonly struct Money(decimal amount) : IFormattable
    {
        public string ToString(string? format, IFormatProvider? provider)
            => amount.ToString(format, provider);
        // ^ PROVIDING THIS IS WHAT MAKES $"...{this}..." HONOUR THE
        //   FORMAT SPECIFIER AND THE PROVIDER. Without it, the
        //   interpolated string falls back to the general ToString
        //   and BOTH ARE IGNORED — which is why a record's
        //   generated ToString prints raw unformatted numbers into
        //   a log line.
    }
}


// THE ONES THAT NAME A CAPABILITY, and using the interface rather
// than testing for the concrete type is what makes the code
// extensible.

// IDisposable: WHAT 'using' REQUIRES. NO REGISTRATION ANYWHERE.
public sealed class TemporaryFile : IDisposable
{
    private readonly string _path = Path.GetTempFileName();

    public void Dispose()
    {
        if (File.Exists(_path)) File.Delete(_path);
    }
    // ^ ANY TYPE CAN PARTICIPATE, which is why disposal needs no
    //   framework involvement at all. And the PATTERN-BASED form —
    //   a protected virtual Dispose(bool) plus a finalizer — is what
    //   makes DELETION THROUGH A BASE REFERENCE SAFE, because the
    //   compiler checks the pattern against the interface rather
    //   than against a virtual method a derived type can forget to
    //   override.
}

// IAsyncDisposable: A SEPARATE INTERFACE, and the separation IS the
// point — the synchronous form CANNOT WAIT.
public sealed class Connection : IAsyncDisposable
{
    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        await FlushAsync();
        await _connection.CloseAsync();   // a genuine round trip
    }
}
public static async Task TheSeparation()
{
    var c = new Connection();

    // using (c) { }      DOES NOT COMPILE, and that is correct: a
    //                    synchronously disposed asynchronous
    //                    resource either blocks a thread or throws
    await using (c) { }  // the right spelling

    // WHICH IS WHY THE TWO INTERFACES ARE NOT ONE WITH A FLAG: a
    //   flag would have to be checked before disposing, and the
    //   synchronous path would have to know whether waiting was
    //   possible. Two interfaces let the compiler refuse the wrong
    //   one at the call.
}

// IComparable against IComparer: THE TYPE KNOWING HOW TO COMPARE
// ITSELF, versus A CALLER SUPPLYING the comparison.
public sealed record Case(string Text);     // knows NOTHING about
                                            // ordering: two cases
                                            // compare EQUAL
public sealed record LocaleCase(string Text, CultureInfo Culture);

public static void TheDifference()
{
    var cases = new List<Case> { new("beta"), new("Alpha") };
    cases.Sort();
    // ^ uses IComparable<Case>, WHICH THE RECORD GENERATES: field
    //   comparison, and "Alpha" sorts before "beta" because
    //   ORDINAL character comparison puts uppercase first. It does
    //   NOT know about case-insensitivity, and nothing asks it to.

    var localized = new List<LocaleCase>
        { new("beta", fr), new("Alpha", fr) };
    localized.Sort((a, b) => string.Compare(
        a.Text, b.Text, a.Culture, StringComparison.CurrentCulture));
    // ^ A COMPARER SUPPLIED BY THE CALLER, because ordering is a
    //   property of the USAGE rather than of the type. And THIS
    //   VERSION IS DIFFERENT ON EACH MACHINE — which is why a
    //   persisted order, a paged query or a LIMIT applied after a
    //   sort needs an ordinal comparer rather than a cultural one.
    //   A cultural sort means the LIMIT is applied at a different
    //   row on each server, so two pages of a result set can
    //   overlap and skip rows.
}

System.Text.JsonJSONSerialize, Deserialize, source-generated contexts for AOT
System.Globalization.CultureInfoLocaleInvariantCulture, GetCultureInfo
System.Collections.ImmutableImmutable dataImmutableArray, ImmutableDictionary, ImmutableQueue

More of this type-specific reference material lives in the companion guides: HTTP clients and servers in the ASP.NET guide, Windows UI and data binding in the desktop guide, and storage and queries in the databases guide.

The one diagnostic worth having

Most collection defects in this area are diagnosed by one measurement rather than by reading code: how many times was the enumerator allocated, and how many times was the source enumerated. A method that appears to do one thing and does it twice is invisible in the source and obvious in a count.

The measurement is cheap and it generalises. The allocation profiler answers "where did that object come from", the allocation rate answers "which loop is producing garbage faster than the collector reclaims it", and the pair of them distinguishes a genuine leak from a hot path. A rate that stays flat is throughput; a rate that climbs with uptime is a leak, and the difference between those two is the difference between tuning and investigating.

What to check before reaching for a newer type

Whether the current type can express the requirement at all. A frozen set and a concurrent dictionary solve different problems, and a list with a lock is neither. Most "we need a concurrent collection" cases are a need for a guarantee about the order of operations rather than about simultaneous access, and a lock on the existing type is the smaller change.

Knowing which problem you have is the whole of the advice, and the two have different fixes. Simultaneous access needs a type whose operations are atomic; ordering needs either a lock or a message queue with a single consumer. Substituting the first for the second gives a collection that is thread-safe and still produces the wrong answer, which is worse than the original because the code now looks correct.

What is deliberately absent

No general-purpose utility library, and no micro-optimisation advice. The libraries change and their contents are not what they were; the optimisations are measurable rather than arguable, and an unmeasured allocation claim is a preference wearing a measurement's clothes.


{{-- THE COLLECTION TYPES, where the differences are SEMANTIC
     rather than merely performance. --}}
public sealed class Collections
{
    // List<T>: O(1) INDEX, O(1) APPEND, O(n) INSERT AT AN INDEX.
    //   A LIST IS AN ARRAY WITH A LENGTH, which is why the index is
    //   free and the insert is a memmove. Setting the capacity
    //   when the final size is known removes the doubling
    //   reallocations entirely.
    public static void ListBehaviour()
    {
        var sized = new List<Order>(count: 1024);   // NO REALLOCATIONS
    }

    // Dictionary<K,V>: O(1) amortised, and THE COMPARER IS PART OF
    //   MEMBERSHIP — a map built with one comparer CANNOT BE READ
    //   with another. This is the most common dictionary defect in
    //   production code: the key is present and the lookup returns
    //   false, because two declarations in the same file disagree
    //   about case sensitivity.
    public static void ComparerIsTheKey()
    {
        var byEmail = new Dictionary<string, User>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        byEmail["Ada@Example.COM"] = user;      // FOUND: the same
                                               // comparer throughout
    }

    // HashSet<T>: the same comparer rule, which is why a set of
    //   user names with the DEFAULT COMPARER IS CASE-SENSITIVE —
    //   almost never what a person means, and always what the code
    //   does.
    public static void SetComparer()
    {
        var ids = new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    }

    // Queue<T> / Stack<T>: FIFO and LIFO, both O(1), both the right
    //   answer for "what has been waiting longest" and "what was
    //   most recent" respectively.
    // PriorityQueue<T,TP>: orders by PRIORITY, not by insertion —
    //   and THE TIE-BREAK IS UNSPECIFIED. Two equal-priority items
    //   come out in an order the implementation chooses, and that
    //   can change between framework versions — so a bug depending
    //   on the order of equal-priority items appears on an UPGRADE
    //   rather than on a deployment, which is the hardest thing to
    //   reproduce.
    public static void PriorityTie()
    {
        var q = new PriorityQueue<string, int>();
        q.Enqueue("first",  1);
        q.Enqueue("second", 1);            // SAME priority
        q.Dequeue();                       // order unspecified
    }

    // ImmutableList<T>: MODIFICATION RETURNS A NEW COLLECTION.
    //   Quadratic to build one item at a time, which is why AddRange
    //   exists, and free to share — it is also usable as a
    //   dictionary key, which a mutable collection cannot be.
    public static void ImmutableCost()
    {
        var built = ImmutableList<Order>.Empty;
        foreach (var o in orders)
            built = built.Add(o);           // O(n) PER ADD: quadratic
        // WHICH IS WHY AddRange EXISTS:
        var fast = ImmutableList.CreateRange(orders);
    }

    // FrozenSet<T> / FrozenDictionary<T>: OPTIMISED FOR READING AND
    //   NEVER MODIFIED. Same interfaces as the mutable versions, so
    //   it is a drop-in for a lookup table built once at start-up —
    //   and its Contains is measurably faster than a dictionary's,
    //   because the layout is chosen for the exact set of keys
    //   rather than for insertion order.
}


// STRINGS AND PARSING, which REPLACE string manipulation:
public sealed class Strings
{
    public static void TheReplacements()
    {
        // string.Join, NOT a loop that appends a separator between
        // items. ONE allocation, and the separator handling is
        // better — a loop that appends before every non-first item
        // has an off-by-one that produces a trailing comma, and
        // that comma is then a parse failure on the way back in.
        string a = string.Join(", ", names);

        // string.Split with options, not a manual parse:
        var parts = csv.Split(',', StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries
                                    | StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);

        // int.TryParse, NOT int.Parse inside a try. Parse THROWS, and
        //   a throw for a malformed field in a batch is a cost per
        //   row plus a stack trace nobody reads — and a monitoring
        //   system has to be told to ignore it.
        if (int.TryParse(s, NumberStyles.Integer,
                         CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out int n)) { }

        // StringBuilder, NOT += in a loop. THE + OPERATOR HAS NO WAY
        //   TO MUTATE, so the loop is O(n^2) IN ALLOCATIONS and
        //   shows up in a profile as an allocation rate rather than
        //   as a loop — which is why it is diagnosed late.
        var sb = new StringBuilder(capacity);
        sb.Append(value);

        // MemoryExtensions over ReadOnlySpan<T>: IndexOf, CopyTo,
        //   SequenceEqual and Split ALLOCATE NOTHING, where the
        //   string equivalents allocate a substring at every call.
        //   Four searches over a 40-character line is four
        //   allocations before any real work starts.
        ReadOnlySpan<char> line = raw.AsSpan();
        int colon = line.IndexOf(':');
    }
}

// CONCURRENCY, because a hand-rolled lock is worse in every case:
public sealed class Concurrency
{
    private long _count;
    private readonly SemaphoreSlim _gate = new(8);
    private readonly Lock _mutex = new();

    // Interlocked: ATOMIC READ-MODIFY-WRITE, and the only correct
    //   answer for a counter shared across threads. This is what
    //   volatile does NOT give you.
    public void Record() => Interlocked.Increment(ref _count);

    // A SemaphoreSlim LIMITS CONCURRENCY, which is how a bound
    //   becomes visible rather than leaving it inside the thread
    //   pool's opaque queue. 'wait' is the honest spelling for a
    //   service calling a rate-limited downstream.
    public async Task<bool> CallAsync(Func<Task> f)
    {
        if (!await _gate.WaitAsync(0)) return false;   // reject fast
        try { await f(); return true; }
        finally { _gate.Release(); }
    }

    // A Lock, so that locking on 'this' or on a string is a COMPILE
    //   ERROR rather than a global bottleneck.
    public void Update() { lock (_mutex) { } }

    // A ConcurrentDictionary, whose ENUMERATOR TAKES A SNAPSHOT
    //   rather than throwing on concurrent modification — which is
    //   both the convenience and the danger: the enumeration sees
    //   a consistent state as of some moment, so a read-modify-
    //   write built on it is still racy.
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, byte[]> _cache = new();
}

// LOGGING, because a hand-written line LOSES structure a sink
// could have indexed:
public static class Diagnostics
{
    public static void Structured()
    {
        // THE WRONG WAY: the message is a STRING, so a sink cannot
        // index it, group by it, or query it.
        Console.WriteLine($"Order {id} failed: {ex.Message}");

        // THE RIGHT WAY: TEMPLATED, so the message template is a
        //   FIELD the sink stores and the VALUES are separate
        //   properties. A log aggregator can then answer "how many
        //   failures for order 42" without a full-text search.
        Log.Error("Order {OrderId} failed: {Reason}", id, ex.Message);
        {{-- ^ WHICH MATTERS MOST IN PRODUCTION, where the difference
             between an indexed field and a substring in a message is
             the difference between a query and an outage. The
             interpolation is evaluated eagerly and formatted in the
             SERVER'S culture unless the message specifies
             otherwise — which is a second reason not to do it. --}}
    }
}

A.4 Naming and style conventions

These are the official .NET naming guidelines, condensed. They matter beyond style: a JSON serialiser, a DI container, a data binder and a source generator all infer behaviour from your names.

ElementConventionExample
NamespacePascalCase, dotted, company root firstAcme.Billing.Invoicing
Class, struct, record, interface, enum, delegatePascalCaseInvoiceProcessor, IPaymentGateway
Method, property, event, constant, enum memberPascalCaseCalculateTotal, MaxRetries, OrderStatus.Paid
Parameter, local, type parametercamelCaseinvoiceId, TEntity
Private field_camelCase (or camelCase with this.)_totalAmount
Interface prefixI + PascalCaseIDisposable
Abstract class prefixOptional Abstract or BaseAbstractRepository
Async methodSuffix AsyncSaveAsync
Type parametersT for one, descriptive for severalT, TKey, TValue, TCustomer
BooleanIs, Has, Can, Should or a verbIsActive, HasChanges, CanExecute
CollectionPlural nounCustomers, LineItems
Primary constructor parameterscamelCase, because they are localspublic sealed class Order(string customerId)

An Async suffix is not cosmetic: it is the signal to a caller that they must await. It is also the convention that CA1 1 and the default .editorconfig enforce.

Put the conventions in .editorconfig with dotnet_diagnostic.IDE1006.severity = warning and the naming rules, then run dotnet format in CI. From then on the style is enforced by the build, not by code review.

Conventions exist so that a reader who has seen one file can predict every other, and the ones worth adopting are the ones where a wrong guess costs real time. A missing Async suffix makes a call mean something different from what it looks like. A bare boolean parameter makes two overloads indistinguishable in intellisense and unreadable at the call site.

What is a convention and what is a decision

A private field prefix is style: it has no bearing on reading and no effect on the compiler. Sealing a type is a design decision with a performance consequence, because it lets the compiler devirtualise, and it closes the door on a subclass that violates an invariant nobody documented. Only three things are worth arguing about — the suffix, the boolean prefix, and whether a type is sealed — and the argument about a field prefix is resolvable by preference rather than by evidence.

The one that is genuinely a trap

An explicit interface implementation. Without it, a type's interface members are public members of the type, which puts the interface's shape into the type's own API. For a cache that is a real problem: a caller who can enumerate it and mutate its entries has made the internal representation part of the contract, and no later change to that representation is then safe. With an explicit implementation, the members are reachable only through the interface, do not appear in intellisense on the type, and the contract stays where it belongs.

Why this is worth a page rather than a paragraph

Every item here is a case where the wrong choice is invisible in a diff and visible only to the next person. There is no build error for a missing suffix, no diagnostic for a bare boolean, and no warning for a public interface member on a type that should not have one — which is why these are convention rather than rule, and why a convention nobody knows about is worth nothing.


{{-- NAMING, and the ONE whose absence genuinely costs time. --}}
public sealed class Naming
{
    // RIGHT: the suffix says the call returns a task, so a caller
    //   who does not know finds out AT THE CALL SITE rather than by
    //   getting a task where they expected a value.
    public Task<Order?> FindAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct);

    // WRONG: a caller who does not know writes:
    //   var order = repo.Find(42);     -> a Task<Order?>
    //   Console.WriteLine(order.Id);   -> a compiler error saying a
    //                                    task has no Id, which
    //                                    takes longer to diagnose
    //                                    than the suffix would have
    //                                    taken to write.
    public Task<Order?> Find(long id, CancellationToken ct);

    // A BOOLEAN PARAMETER is named with is/has/can, because a bare
    // boolean at a call site is unreadable AND it makes two
    // overloads indistinguishable in intellisense.
    public static void Write(string text, bool isAppend) { }
    public static void Write(string text, bool isOverwrite) { }

    // Write(text, true)             unreadable
    // Write(text, isAppend: true)   says which, and makes the two
    //                                overloads distinguishable

    // COLLECTION NAMES SAY WHAT THEY CONTAIN, because
    //   IEnumerable<T> says nothing about cardinality or order and
    //   everything about cost.
    public static IReadOnlyList<Order> RecentOrders() => [];
    public static IReadOnlySet<string> ActiveIds() => new HashSet<string>();
    // ^ IReadOnlyList says INDEXABLE and ORDERED; IReadOnlySet says
    //   MEMBERSHIP, and that Contains is the cheap operation. A
    //   method returning IEnumerable<T> with a name saying List
    //   makes a reader assume both, and pays for it when they
    //   discover the O(n) Contains inside a loop.
}


// THE DESIGN DECISIONS, which are NOT style:
public sealed class Decisions
{
    // SEALED BY DEFAULT. A type that cannot be derived lets the
    //   compiler DEVIRTUALISE its virtual members, and it closes the
    //   door on somebody adding a subclass that violates an
    //   invariant nobody documented.
    public sealed class Money(decimal amount) { public decimal Amount = amount; }

    // OPEN WHEN DERIVATION IS THE POINT: a framework extension
    //   point, a plugin contract, an abstract base.
    public abstract class Handler
    {
        public abstract Task HandleAsync(Message m, CancellationToken ct);
    }

    // AN EXPLICIT INTERFACE IMPLEMENTATION, which is the answer to
    //   "this type implements an interface but callers must not see
    //   it".
    public sealed class Cache : IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<string, byte[]>>
    {
        private readonly Dictionary<string, byte[]> _entries = new();

        public void Put(string key, byte[] value) => _entries[key] = value;

        IEnumerator<KeyValuePair<string, byte[]>> IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<string, byte[]>>
            .GetEnumerator() => _entries.GetEnumerator();
        IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() => _entries.GetEnumerator();

        // ^ EXPLICIT, so the member is reachable ONLY through the
        //   interface. intellisense on Cache does NOT show it, and a
        //   caller holding a Cache cannot reach it without a cast —
        //   which is the point. Without this, the cache's internal
        //   representation becomes part of its contract, and a
        //   caller can enumerate it and MUTATE its entries.
    }
}

{{-- WHAT IS NOT STYLE, restated, because these three get argued
     about as if they were: --}}
// 1. THE async SUFFIX: its absence makes a call site mean something
//    different from what it reads as.
// 2. A BOOLEAN PREFIX: without it two overloads are
//    indistinguishable and a call site is unreadable.
// 3. SEALED BY DEFAULT: it changes what the compiler can optimise
//    and what a future subclass may break.
//
// A private field prefix is STYLE. It has no bearing on reading and
// no effect on the compiler, and the argument about it is
// resolvable by preference rather than by evidence — which is worth
// saying out loud, because the argument is otherwise reopened by
// every new developer and settled by whoever reviews last.

A.5 Common compile errors and fixes

Every C# developer meets these. Knowing what each one actually means saves the hour of guessing, because the compiler’s phrasing is often misleading about the cause.

ErrorWhat it meansFix
CS0029: cannot implicitly convert type X to YNo conversion exists, or narrowing needs a castAdd an explicit cast, or change the target type; check for a lost float/decimal suffix
CS0266: cannot implicitly convert a null literal to a non-nullable reference typeNullable analysis is on and the target is not nullableMake the target T?, or initialise it, or use default for a value type
CS8602: dereference of a possibly null referenceFlow analysis could not prove non-nullNull check, ??, ?., or a better signature on the method you call
CS8618: non-nullable property must contain a non-null valueA property is uninitialisedInitialise it, use required, make it ?, or use field
CS0122: inaccessible due to its protection levelAccess modifier mismatchCheck internal versus private protected across assemblies
CS0117: does not contain a definition for XWrong type, or an extension namespace is not importedAdd the using; for LINQ, check using System.Linq;
CS0161: not all code paths return a valueThe compiler cannot prove exhaustivenessAdd a throw, or a discard arm in a switch expression
CS8124: a value of type A cannot be handled by a pattern of type BThe pattern is unreachable given earlier armsReorder the arms: put the specific pattern first
CS1656: cannot assign to X because it is a 'read-only variable'Assigning to an in parameter, a foreach variable, or a property without a setterUse a local, or add a setter
CS0136: a local named X cannot be declared in this scopeA local and a parameter share a name in an older scopeRename the local; the scoping rules forbid shadowing an enclosing local
CS0201: only a variable, not an expression, can be assigned toYou tried to assign to a property or method resultAssign to a local, then pass it; or use ref returns for real mutation
CS1061: does not contain a definition for X and no extension methodCommonest cause: calling an instance method on a struct copyTake a copy into a local first, or make the member readonly
CS8410 / CS0161 in a switchMissing exhaustivenessAdd _ => throw ... and mark it with a comment explaining the future value
CS8981: lower-cased type nameA local function or type name starts lowercasePascalCase it

The three that catch nearly everyone at least once: CS0029 (silent narrowing), CS8602 (possible null dereference), and CS1061 on a struct member. The third one is worth remembering by heart, because the compiler message does not hint at the copy semantics that cause it.

Almost every confusing build error has one of a small number of causes, and recognising the cause is faster than reading the message. They cluster into four groups: a wrong type, a nullability gap, an overload that does not match, and a nullable value type that was never checked. The nullability group dominates, because a project enabling the feature produces thousands at once and because the messages do not group themselves.

The two that consume the most time

The nullability errors, whose cause is nearly always one thing: a value the compiler cannot prove is non-null. The fix is either an assertion where the value is known or a guard at the point of use, and the second is better because it produces a meaningful exception rather than a bare null at some later line. The other time-consuming group is overload resolution, where a lambda's parameter types are the real problem and the message names a parameter type instead — which sends most people to annotate the wrong thing first.

The misleading ones

An async void method produces no warning when an exception escapes it, and the failure is a process termination with a stack trace naming the thread pool. A null conditional applied to a nullable value type yields a nullable rather than an error, and the wrong meaning compiles. And a compound assignment under checked behaves differently from the two-step form, which reads as a compiler bug and is specified.

Why these four groups and not a longer list

Because a longer list would be a list of messages, and messages change between versions while causes do not. Every diagnostic in the nullability family is the same assertion about the same thing — that a value is not null at a point where the type says it must not be — and every one of them is fixed by one of two moves.


{{-- THE NULLABILITY CLUSTER, and it dominates because a project
     enabling the feature produces thousands at once. --}}
public sealed class Nullability
{
    // CS8600: converting a possibly-null value to a non-nullable
    //   type.
    static string Wrong(GetMaybeName()) => GetMaybeName();

    // THE FIX AT THE POINT OF TRUTH — an ASSERTION, where you know:
    static string AtTruth(Db db, long id) => db.Find(id)!.Name;
    // ^ '!' SUPPRESSES THE DIAGNOSTIC WITH NO RUNTIME EFFECT. It is
    //   a CLAIM, and it is correct only if the row exists. A
    //   NullReferenceException here is the runtime saying the claim
    //   was false — which is better than a warning and worse than a
    //   guarantee.

    // THE FIX AT THE POINT OF USE — a GUARD, which is better because
    //   it produces a MEANINGFUL exception rather than a bare null.
    static string AtUse(Db db, long id) => db.Find(id)?.Name ?? "(unknown)";

    // CS8602: dereference of a possibly-null value. The compiler is
    //   RIGHT NOT TO KNOW, so the question is WHERE THE PROOF IS
    //   MISSING rather than whether to suppress.
    static int Wrong(Order order) => order.Customer.Name.Length;

    // THE SHAPE THAT WORKS, and it is a shape rather than a line
    // because it proves the thing ONCE:
    static decimal Total(Order? order) =>
        order?.Lines.Sum(l => l.Total) ?? 0m;
    // ^ THE ?. MAKES THE REST OF THE EXPRESSION NULLABLE, and ?? brings
    //   it back, so there is NO PLACE for a null to slip through
    //   unchecked. The compiler knows the result is non-null and
    //   stops reporting on this line — which is the difference
    //   between silencing one diagnostic and structuring the code so
    //   there is nothing to silence.
}


// THE OVERLOAD-RESOLUTION CLUSTER, where a LAMBDA is the problem
// and the message does not say so:
public static class Overloads
{
    static void Apply<T>(IEnumerable<T> xs, Func<T, bool> keep) { }
    static void Apply<T>(IEnumerable<T> xs, Predicate<T> keep) { }

    static void TheLambda()
    {
        // CS0411: the type of parameter 'n' cannot be inferred
        Apply(numbers, n => n > 3);
        // ^ TWO APPLICABLE DELEGATE OVERLOADS, and the compiler does
        //   not choose between them. The message names a PARAMETER
        //   TYPE, which reads as though the lambda were the only
        //   problem — and it is, but not in the way the message
        //   implies, so the first thing most people try is to
        //   annotate the wrong thing.

        // THE FIX: make the parameter type explicit, which resolves
        // it without naming the method's type argument.
        Apply(numbers, (int n) => n > 3);
    }
}

// THE MISLEADING ONES, where the message points somewhere other
// than the cause:
public static class Misleading
{
    // (a) async void PRODUCES NO WARNING when an exception escapes.
    public static async void FireAndForget()      // ^ NO WARNING.
    {
        await LoadAsync();
        // ^ AN EXCEPTION HERE CRASHES THE PROCESS, and the stack
        //   trace names Task, the thread pool and the
        //   synchronisation context — none of which is where the
        //   failure is. The compiler does not warn because the
        //   signature is LEGAL: it is required for an event
        //   handler, and the compiler cannot tell an event handler
        //   from an ordinary method at the signature.
    }

    // (b) A NULL CONDITIONAL ON A VALUE TYPE produces a NULLABLE
    //   rather than an error, and the failure surfaces later.
    static int? Wrong(int? x) => x?.ToString().Length;
    // ^ x?. on an int? gives int?; ToString() on a nullable gives a
    //   STRING; .Length on that is fine. So this COMPILES and means
    //   something different from what it reads as. The correct form
    //   for a count is x.HasValue ? 1 : 0.

    // (c) THE COMPOUND ASSIGNMENT UNDER checked, which reads as a
    //   compiler bug and is SPECIFIED.
    static void CompoundUnderChecked()
    {
        checked
        {
            int n = int.MaxValue;
            n++;                        // OverflowException
            int m = int.MaxValue;
            m = m + 1;                  // OverflowException TOO
            // ^ ...but the two forms are NOT symmetric in every
            //   context; see below.
        }
        unchecked
        {
            int u = int.MaxValue;
            u++;                        // wraps
            u = u + 1;                  // ALSO wraps
            // ^ THE SAME IN BOTH FORMS when unchecked. The
            //   asymmetry is only in the CHECKED context, and only
            //   because the compound form does not perform a
            //   checked conversion OF ITS RESULT — which is in the
            //   specification, and which is why the natural
            //   refactoring from two statements to one changes the
            //   overflow behaviour.
        }
    }
}

A.6 Glossary

The terms this guide relies on, defined once and briefly. Each is short enough to remember and precise enough to be useful in a design discussion.

TermDefinition
AssemblyA compiled .dll or .exe: the unit of loading, versioning and deployment
BCE / metadataThe table of types and members the runtime reads to resolve references
BoxingConverting a value type to object on the heap; unboxing is the reverse
CLRCommon Language Runtime: the execution engine, JIT, GC and type system
CTS / CancellationTokenSourceCreates and signals CancellationTokens
Defensive copyThe implicit struct copy the compiler makes so a method cannot mutate the caller’s value
Dynamic dispatchChoosing a method at run time via virtual/override; contrast with static dispatch
GCGarbage collector: generational, non-deterministic, non-compacting by default
IDisposableThe deterministic cleanup contract for anything holding an unmanaged resource
JIT / AOTJust-in-time compilation at run time; ahead-of-time compilation at publish time
MetadataAssembly information: types, members, attributes, versions, references
NRTNullable reference types: compile-time null-safety annotations and flow analysis
NuGetThe .NET package manager and its feed
Project vs solutionOne project compiles to one assembly; a solution groups projects and their references
RoslynThe C# compiler and language service; powers every .NET IDE
SDK-style projectThe modern single .csproj format with implicit defaults
SpanA stack-only view over contiguous memory: no allocation, free slicing
TaskA promise of a result later; the unit of async work in .NET
Trimming / AOTRemoving unreachable code at publish time; reflection and dynamic code must be declared
Value typeCopied on assignment, cannot be null (without Nullable<T>), always sealed

This guide covers the language. Its two .NET siblings cover the stacks you will build with it: ASP.NET Core 10 for APIs, MVC, Razor and Blazor, and WinForms & WPF for Windows desktop. All three share the same C# described here.

  1. Write a program from memory that declares a class, a struct, a record and a record struct, and prints the default ToString and equality behaviour of each.
  2. Implement IEquatable<T>, IComparable<T> and IFormattable on a single type, then use it as a dictionary key, in a Sort, and in a formatted string.
  3. Set up a .editorconfig with the naming rules from this appendix, run dotnet format, and count how many violations the analyser finds.
  4. Deliberately trigger CS0029, CS8602, CS8618 and CS1061, and write down the one-line diagnosis for each from the table above.
  5. Write an INotifyPropertyChanged model type, raise the event correctly, and confirm the setter does not raise it when the value is unchanged.

13 · Data Access: ADO.NET, Dapper & EF Core

13.1 The layer stack and the ADO.NET primitives13.2 Parameters, injection and batching13.3 Async ADO.NET, multiple results and resilience13.4 Dapper: mapping, multi-mapping and command definitions13.5 EF Core: DbContext, configuration and tracking13.6 Migrations, bulk operations and choosing a layer

Data access in .NET is a stack, not a choice. At the bottom is ADO.NET, a provider-neutral contract for connections, commands and readers. Above it sit two accessors with different objectives: Dapper, a micro-ORM that maps rows to objects and does nothing else, and Entity Framework Core, a full ORM with a change tracker, a query translator and a migration system. This chapter documents the whole stack, the failure modes of each layer, and the criteria that decide which layer a given query should live in.

Applies to: .NET 10 (LTS) with C# 14, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 6.x, Dapper 2.x, EF Core 10. Requirements: a SQL Server 2022 or Azure SQL instance for the samples in this chapter; PostgreSQL uses Npgsql 10, MySQL uses MySqlConnector. Caveats: the SQL dialect differs per provider even though the ADO.NET types do not. Where SQL is provider-specific it is marked.

13.1 The layer stack and the ADO.NET primitives

ADO.NET defines five abstract types that every provider implements: DbConnection, DbCommand, DbDataReader, DbDataAdapter and DbTransaction. Writing against the abstract types keeps the code portable; writing against the concrete SqlConnection lets you use the provider-specific surface. Enterprise code starts against the abstraction and drops down only where the abstraction cannot express what is needed.

The ADO.NET primitives are four objects and each one owns exactly one resource. A connection owns a socket. A command owns a statement and its parameters. A data reader owns a cursor over a result set. And a transaction owns a consistency boundary. Knowing which object owns which resource is what makes the disposal order right the first time rather than after a leak.

Disposal order, and why it is fixed

A reader must be closed before the connection can be returned to the pool, a command before the connection, and a transaction before the connection. The nesting in the using declarations reflects that order, and it is not a style preference: a connection returned to the pool with an open reader is a connection that the next caller receives holding a cursor, which is the single most common cause of a "the pool ran out under load" report.

The pool, and what it does not do

A pool exists to avoid paying for a TCP handshake and a TLS negotiation per operation, and it caches both. It does not make a connection concurrent, does not make a disposed reader valid, and does not protect a connection from being left in a transaction when it is returned — which is why a transaction must be committed or rolled back before the connection goes back.

// The portable core: five provider-neutral types, async from top to bottom
public sealed class OrderReader(string connectionString)
{
    private readonly string _connectionString = connectionString;

    public async Task<List<int>> GetOrderIdsAsync(int customerId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // await using calls DisposeAsync, so the pooled connection is returned
        // even when the query throws. A forgotten Dispose leaks a pool slot
        // and the next request blocks for the pool timeout.
        await using DbConnection connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
        await connection.OpenAsync(ct);

        await using DbCommand command = connection.CreateCommand();
        command.CommandText = "SELECT Id FROM dbo.Orders WHERE CustomerId = @customerId";
        command.CommandType = CommandType.Text;

        DbParameter p = command.CreateParameter();
        p.ParameterName = "@customerId";
        p.DbType = DbType.Int32;                    // explicit type, no inference
        p.Value = customerId;
        command.Parameters.Add(p);

        var ids = new List<int>();
        await using DbDataReader reader =
            await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(CommandBehavior.SingleRow, ct);

        while (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))
        {
            ids.Add(reader.GetInt32(0));
        }

        return ids;
    }
}

// Reading
