await using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);
// The reader is forward-only by default. GetOrdinal once, reuse the index.
int idOrdinal = reader.GetOrdinal("Id");
// IsDBNull must be checked before GetString: a NULL column throws
// InvalidCastException, not a null reference.
string code = reader.IsDBNull(1) ? null : reader.GetString(1);

Reader accessors are ordinal-based and untyped by default: GetInt32, GetString, GetDecimal, GetDateTime. Calling the wrong one throws InvalidCastException; a wrong guess about nullability throws before the cast. reader.GetFieldValue<T>(ordinal) is the generic alternative and is the correct call for DateOnly, TimeOnly and Guid, which have no non-generic accessor.

Opening a connection per operation is the correct default, not a mistake. The SQL Server SqlClient pooler keeps physical connections alive; Open performs a pool lookup and, at most, a TLS handshake. What is expensive is holding a connection open across a Task.Delay, a message publish or any other await on non-database work — that pins a pool slot and exhausts it under load. Open, do the database work, close.

// DbDataAdapter: the disconnected layer. Fill a DataSet or a typed table,
// then work offline. Mostly used for reporting and bulk reads.
using DataTable table = new();
await using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
// MARS must be enabled in the connection string for a multi-statement command
// to return more than one result set.
await using var command = connection.CreateCommand();
command.CommandText = "SELECT * FROM dbo.Orders WHERE CustomerId = @cid";

DbDataAdapter adapter = new SqlDataAdapter(command);
SqlCommand select = connection.CreateCommand();
select.CommandText = "SELECT Name FROM dbo.Customers WHERE Id = @cid";
adapter.SelectCommand = select;
new SqlParameter("@cid", SqlDbType.Int) { Value = 42 }
    .Pipe(p => command.Parameters.Add(p));

// SelectCommand is added to the adapter, not the command; keep the two in step
adapter.SelectCommand.Parameters.Add(new SqlParameter("@cid", SqlDbType.Int) { Value = 42 });
await adapter.FillAsync(table);
// The DataTable is now a plain in-memory grid: filterable, sortable, serialisable

The .Pipe line above is illustrative only; in production code add parameters to the adapter’s SelectCommand directly, as the following line does. A DataSet carries no type safety, duplicates column names across tables, and is expensive for large payloads. Prefer DbDataReader or Dapper for anything but reporting workloads.


{{-- FOUR OBJECTS, each owning EXACTLY ONE resource: --}}
{{--   connection  owns a SOCKET
     command      owns a STATEMENT and its PARAMETERS
     reader       owns a CURSOR over a RESULT SET
     transaction  owns a CONSISTENCY BOUNDARY --}}

{{-- AND THE DISPOSAL ORDER IS FIXED, and it is not a style
     preference: --}}
public static async Task<List<Order>> LoadAsync(string cs, long id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // THE NESTING REFLECTS THE ORDER: reader before command before
    // connection.
    await using var connection = new SqlConnection(cs);
    await connection.OpenAsync(ct);

    await using var command = new SqlCommand(
        "SELECT Id, Reference, Total FROM Orders WHERE Id = @id", connection);
    command.Parameters.Add("@id", SqlDbType.BigInt).Value = id;

    await using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);

    var orders = new List<Order>();
    while (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))
    {
        orders.Add(new Order
        {
            Id        = reader.GetInt64(0),
            Reference = reader.GetString(1),
            Total     = reader.GetDecimal(2)
        });
    }
    return orders;
}
{{-- ^ A CONNECTION RETURNED TO THE POOL WITH AN OPEN READER IS A
     CONNECTION THE NEXT CALLER RECEIVES HOLDING A CURSOR, which is
     the most common cause of "the pool ran out under load" — the
     symptom is a pool exhaustion error and the cause is an
     unbalanced using two frames up. --}}

{{-- AND THE POOL, and what it does NOT do: --}}
var cs = "Server=db;Database=shop;Maximum Pool Size=100;Connect Timeout=15";
{{-- ^ IT CACHES THE SOCKET AND THE TLS SESSION, so a pooled
     connection skips a TCP handshake and a certificate exchange
     per operation.

     IT DOES NOT:
       make a connection CONCURRENT — a SqlConnection is not
         thread-safe, so sharing one is a race
       make a DISPOSED reader valid
       protect a connection from being returned while a
         TRANSACTION IS STILL OPEN --}}
public static async Task LeakTransactionAsync(string cs)
{
    await using var connection = new SqlConnection(cs);
    await connection.OpenAsync();
    await using var transaction = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync();

    await ExecuteAsync(connection, transaction);
    // NO COMMIT, and NO ROLLBACK. Dispose returns the connection to
    // the POOL WITH THE TRANSACTION STILL OPEN.
    // ^ The next caller gets a connection whose ambient
    //   transaction belongs to a request that has finished, and
    //   their INSERT lands in a transaction they cannot see and
    //   never commit. It is invisible until someone reads the
    //   transaction log weeks later.
}

13.2 Parameters, injection and batching

Every query must be parameterised. String concatenation into a CommandText is a SQL injection defect even when the value originates from your own UI, because trust is a property of the pipeline, not of the caller. A parameter is not a string that happens to be substituted: the provider sends the SQL text and the values separately, so the database never parses a value as SQL.

A parameterised query is the only kind worth writing, and the reason is not security theatre — it is that a value written into the SQL text is a value the database must parse per row, so an interpolated filter both risks injection and prevents the index from being used. The two failures are separate and the second one happens constantly.

What each parameter type costs

The type you declare decides how the value crosses the wire: as text the server parses, or as a typed value it does not. A string parameter holding a number arrives as text and the server converts it, which prevents an index seek on a numeric column. A size that is wrong truncates or fails, and a direction that is wrong produces a null that is not null at the client.

Batching, and why it is worth the complexity

A round trip costs far more than the work of one statement, so sending many statements in one call is a large win on a high-volume path. The cost is that an error in any statement aborts the batch and the rows before it may already be written, so a batch is correct only inside a transaction — which is a constraint people forget and which is the source of partial writes.

// Vulnerable. A value of  1; DROP TABLE dbo.Orders--  ends the statement.
command.CommandText = "SELECT * FROM dbo.Orders WHERE CustomerId = " + customerId;

// Correct. Type, length and direction are part of the parameter contract.
command.CommandText = "UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Total = @total, PaidAt = @paidAt WHERE Id = @id";

var total = command.CreateParameter();
total.ParameterName = "@total";
total.DbType = DbType.Decimal;
total.Precision = 18;
total.Scale = 2;
total.Value = 99.95m;
command.Parameters.Add(total);

var paidAt = command.CreateParameter();
paidAt.ParameterName = "@paidAt";
paidAt.DbType = DbType.DateTime2;
paidAt.Value = DBNull.Value;                       // DBNull, never null
command.Parameters.Add(paidAt);

await using var id = command.CreateParameter();
id.ParameterName = "@id";
id.DbType = DbType.Int32;
id.Value = 1001;
command.Parameters.Add(id);

// AddWithValue infers the type from the CLR value. Convenient, and it costs
// a round trip: the provider must ask the server for the parameter type before
// it can send the command. Use it in scripts, never in a request path.
command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@note", "reconciled");

// SqlBatch: one round trip, several statements, one parameter set.
// Applies to: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 2.0+ (SQL Server, Azure SQL).
using var batch = new SqlBatch(connection);
using var insert = new SqlBatchCommand("INSERT dbo.AuditLog(Action) VALUES (@action)");
insert.Parameters.Add(new SqlParameter("@action", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 64) { Value = "settle" });
batch.BatchCommands.Add(insert);
await batch.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct);

SqlBatch requires a batch-capable connection and, for SQL Server 2012 and later, benefits from MultipleActiveResultSets only if the statements interleave reads and writes on the same connection. One SqlBatchCommand is one statement; the batch is a single unit of work and is not automatically transactional.

Caveats: value must never be null — the provider throws ArgumentNullException on a null SqlParameter.Value. Use DBNull.Value. Parameter names may not be prefixed with : or @ when SqlCommand is created normally; SqlCommand accepts both but the normalised form is without. Do not parameterise identifiers (table or column names) — the provider cannot bind them; use a whitelist instead.


{{-- A PARAMETERISED QUERY, and the reason is not only injection: --}}
public sealed class Parameters
{
    public static async Task<List<Order>> Wrong(HttpContext ctx)
    {
        // ^ AN INTERPOLATED VALUE IS PART OF THE SQL TEXT, so the
        //   server parses it PER ROW and cannot use an index on it.
        //   The plan is a scan whether or not the value is
        //   injection-safe, which is why a security review catches
        //   one of the two failures and the slow-query log catches
        //   the other.
        var bad = $"SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Reference = '{reference}'";
    }

    public static async Task<List<Order>> Right(string status, int limit, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs);
        await c.OpenAsync(ct);
        await using var cmd = new SqlCommand(
            "SELECT Id, Reference, Total FROM Orders WHERE Status = @status AND Total > @min",
            c);

        // THE TYPE DECIDES HOW IT CROSSES THE WIRE. A string
        //   parameter holding a number arrives as TEXT and the
        //   server converts it per row, which prevents an index
        //   seek on a numeric column.
        cmd.Parameters.Add("@status", SqlDbType.Int).Value = status;
        cmd.Parameters.Add("@min",    SqlDbType.Decimal).Value = 100m;
        await using var r = await cmd.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);
        return [];
    }

    // AddWithValue IS THE WRONG SHAPE, because it infers the type
    // from the CLR value and can send the wrong one:
    public static void AddWithValueIsAVoid(int[] ids, SqlCommand cmd)
    {
        cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue("@count", ids.Length);
        // ^ Int32 — correct here. But a string parameter carrying a
        //   number is sent as NVarChar, and a DateTime is sent as
        //   DateTime2 rather than the type the column is.
    }
}

{{-- THE DIRECTION AND SIZE, which are the two that produce a null
     that is not null at the client: --}}
public static void DirectionAndSize(SqlCommand cmd)
{
    var p = cmd.Parameters.Add("@name", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 200);
    // ^ A SIZE for a variable-length type, because without one the
    //   server cannot plan efficiently and truncation depends on
    //   ANSI_PADDING. It also gives the PARAMETER a name the
    //   execution plan can bind to, rather than inferring it.

    var output = cmd.Parameters.Add("@count", SqlDbType.Int);
    output.Direction = ParameterDirection.Output;
    output.Value = 0;                        // ^ MUST BE SET, or the
                                             //   server returns
                                             //   NULL and an int
                                             //   unboxes it as 0 —
                                             //   which is
                                             //   indistinguishable
                                             //   from a real zero
    await cmd.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
    int rows = (int)output.Value;
}

{{-- BATCHING, and the constraint people forget: --}}
public static async Task BulkInsertAsync(string cs, List<Order> orders, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs);
    await c.OpenAsync(ct);

    // THE ROUND TRIP COSTS FAR MORE than the work of one statement,
    // so sending many in one call is a large win on a high-volume
    // path.
    using var batch = new SqlBatch();
    var p = batch.Parameters;
    p.Add("@ref", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 50);
    p.Add("@total", SqlDbType.Decimal).Precision = 18;

    foreach (var o in orders)
    {
        batch.BatchText.Add(
            "INSERT INTO Orders (Reference, Total) VALUES (@ref, @total);");
        p["@ref"].Value   = o.Reference;
        p["@total"].Value = o.Total;
    }
    await batch.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct);

    // ^ AND THE CONSTRAINT: AN ERROR IN ANY STATEMENT ABORTS THE
    //   BATCH, and the rows before it may already be written. So a
    //   batch is correct only INSIDE A TRANSACTION — without one,
    //   a batch of 10,000 that fails at row 9,999 has written 9,999
    //   rows and reported one error, which is a partial write with
    //   no record of where it stopped.
}

13.3 Async ADO.NET, multiple results and resilience

The async ADO.NET surface is the same set of types with Async suffixes. Three details carry most of the performance: CommandBehavior.SequentialAccess for large readers, ConfigureAwait(false) in library code, and a connection string that survives a transient cloud failure.

Async ADO.NET exists because the network round trip dominates, and its shape is the same as everywhere else: an operation that blocks releases the thread and takes one on completion. Two consequences follow. A command must be disposed whether or not it completed, because a command abandoned mid-flight holds the connection. And cancellation is a signal that may not be honoured, so a cancelled operation may still have executed.

Multiple results, and the transaction implication

A single command can produce several result sets, and reading them is a loop over the reader rather than a loop over results. The implication is that all the sets come from one command inside one transaction, so they are consistent with each other — which is exactly why the feature exists, and the reason a hand-written version issues two commands and gets two inconsistent snapshots.

Resilience, and what is actually safe

A transient failure is worth retrying and a real one is not, and the distinction is the whole of the mechanism: the retry is guarded by a filter that classifies the exception, and the classification is a list. What is never safe is retrying a non-idempotent write, which is why the retry belongs on the command and the idempotency key belongs in the request.

// SequentialAccess: forward-only, one row at a time, no server-side buffering.
// Required for LOB columns and the correct choice for any large result set.
await using DbConnection connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
await connection.OpenAsync(ct);

await using var command = connection.CreateCommand();
command.CommandText = "SELECT Id, Payload FROM dbo.Exports ORDER BY Id";
await using DbDataReader reader =
    await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(
        CommandBehavior.SequentialAccess | CommandBehavior.SingleResult, ct);

while (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))
{
    // The column is a stream. Reading it in order is mandatory.
    await using Stream payload = (Stream)reader[1];
    await using var destination = File.Create($"export-{reader.GetInt32(0)}.bin");
    await payload.CopyToAsync(destination, ct);
}

// Multiple result sets: NextResultAsync advances the reader to the next set
command.CommandText = "SELECT Id, Total FROM dbo.Orders; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.AuditLog;";
await using var multi = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);
await multi.ReadAsync(ct);          // first set
if (await multi.NextResultAsync(ct))
{
    await multi.ReadAsync(ct);
    long auditCount = multi.GetInt64(0);
}

// Library code, not application code, applies ConfigureAwait(false).
// It removes a SynchronizationContext capture, which is a dead cost in a
// server with no context and a correctness aid on a UI thread.
private static async Task<int> CountAsync(DbConnection c, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await using var cmd = c.CreateCommand();
    cmd.CommandText = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.Orders";
    object? scalar = await cmd.ExecuteScalarAsync(ct).ConfigureAwait(false);
    return Convert.ToInt32(scalar);
}

The mixed Stream cast and File.Create line illustrate the SequentialAccess contract. Because the reader is forward-only, the second statement in the same command is read only after the first result set is exhausted; interleaving two DbDataReader instances on one connection requires MARS, which carries its own cost and is not recommended under load.

Cloud requirement: Azure SQL and most managed PostgreSQL endpoints terminate idle connections and fail over. A connection string without EnableRetryOnFailure=true and without a correct Connect Timeout produces sporadic SqlException number 4060 or a socket error that no application retry can classify. Use Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 5.0 or later and pair it with an execution strategy — see section 13.6 for the EF Core equivalent.

System.Data.SqlClient is the legacy provider, frozen apart from security fixes, and is not supported on .NET 10. Use Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, which supports TLS 1.3, current authentication flows and SqlBatch. A project that still references System.Data.SqlClient on .NET 10 is a project on a deprecated dependency, not a supported configuration.


{{-- THE SHAPE IS THE SAME AS EVERYWHERE ELSE, and two consequences
     follow. --}}
public sealed class AsyncAdo
{
    public async Task<int> CountAsync(string cs, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs);
        await c.OpenAsync(ct);

        // THE COMMAND MUST BE DISPOSED WHETHER OR NOT IT
        // COMPLETED, because a command abandoned mid-flight HOLDS
        // THE CONNECTION — and a connection held by a command whose
        // await never resumed is one the pool will never get back.
        await using var cmd = new SqlCommand("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders", c);

        var result = await cmd.ExecuteScalarAsync(ct);
        return (int)result;
    }

    public async Task<List<Order>> WithCancelAsync(string cs, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs);
        await c.OpenAsync(ct);
        await using var cmd = new SqlCommand("SELECT * FROM Orders", c);

        // THE TOKEN IS A SIGNAL, NOT A FORCE. A cancelled command
        //   may still have EXECUTED on the server, so the caller
        //   needs an idempotency key rather than a retry — which is
        //   why cancellation and retry are separate mechanisms and
        //   conflating them produces a double write.
        return await QueryAsync(cmd, ct);
    }

    // MULTIPLE RESULTS, and this is why the feature exists:
    public async Task<(List<Order> Orders, List<Line> Lines)> BothAsync(string cs, long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var c = new SqlConnection(cs);
        await c.OpenAsync(ct);
        await using var cmd = new SqlCommand("""
            SELECT Id, Reference, Total FROM Orders WHERE Id = @id;
            SELECT OrderId, Description, Qty FROM Lines WHERE OrderId = @id;
            """, c);
        cmd.Parameters.Add("@id", SqlDbType.BigInt).Value = id;

        await using var r = await cmd.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);

        var orders = new List<Order>();
        while (await r.ReadAsync(ct)) orders.Add(Map(r));

        // MoveNextResult, then read again. ONE COMMAND, so both sets
        // are consistent with each other — which is the point, and
        // which a two-command version gets wrong by reading two
        // snapshots that differ by exactly the rows a concurrent
        // insert added.
        var lines = new List<Line>();
        if (await r.NextResultAsync(ct))
            while (await r.ReadAsync(ct)) lines.Add(Map(r));

        return (orders, lines);
    }

    // RESILIENCE, and the whole of it is the classification:
    public static async Task<T> WithRetryAsync<T>(Func<Task<T>> operation, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++)
        {
            try { return await operation(); }
            catch (SqlException ex) when (IsTransient(ex) && attempt < 5)
            {
                await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(attempt * attempt), ct);
                // ^ EXPONENTIAL, because a downstream that is failing
                //   because it is OVERLOADED needs the callers to
                //   back off together. A fixed delay synchronises
                //   the retries into a thundering herd at the exact
                //   moment the downstream is least able to serve
                //   them.
            }
        }
    }

    private static bool IsTransient(SqlException ex)
        => ex.Number is 20      // instance not available: the
                                 // database is starting up
           or -2              // timeout: the QUERY timed out, not
                                 // the connection, which matters
           or 64              // connection was successfully
                                 // established but then failed
           or 4060            // cannot open database
           or 10928            // resource limit reached
           or 10929           // server too busy
           or 40197            // the service has encountered an
                                 // error processing a request
           or 40501            // the service is busy
           ;
        // ^ A LIST, and that is the entire mechanism. Which numbers
        //   matter depends on the platform: SQL Server's list is
        //   different from PostgreSQL's, and a hard-coded list that
        //   does not match the engine you run is worse than none,
        //   because it retries a permanent failure and hides it
        //   behind latency.
}

13.4 Dapper: mapping, multi-mapping and command definitions

Dapper is a single static extension-method class over DbConnection and DbCommand. It adds parameter binding, a row-to-object materialiser and a cache of compiled IL, and nothing else: no identity map, no lazy loading, no change tracking, no migrations. Its entire value is that it removes the boilerplate from ADO.NET without adding a second model of the data.

An object mapper over ADO.NET trades compile-time checking for near-zero overhead, and the trade is worth it when the queries are hand-written and reviewed as SQL. Three features distinguish it from a general mapper: multi-mapping joins into a constructor, split-on for a wide result, and a command definition cached by a key rather than a string compiled per call.

Multi-mapping, and the type-split column convention

A multi-mapping query reads one record into several constructor parameters, and the mapping is declared by a lambda so the compiler checks the constructor against the column aliases. The convention is that a column aliased Id belongs to the first type and one aliased Lines_Id to the second, which is worth knowing because the error is a mismatched constructor rather than a named column.

Where it stops being the right tool

It has no change tracking, no identity resolution and no lazy loading, which is the point of the trade rather than a limitation of it. Where an aggregate is loaded, mutated and saved, those three are a large amount of code to write by hand — and a mapper that does not do them silently gives you N+1 queries instead.

// QueryAsync<T>: map a single result set to a type. Columns are matched
// case-insensitively by name; underscored_name columns need an alias.
public sealed record OrderRow(int Id, string Customer, decimal Total, DateTime PlacedAt);

public static async Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderRow>> RecentAsync(
    DbConnection connection, int days, CancellationToken ct)
{
    const string sql = """
        SELECT  o.Id,
                c.Name          AS Customer,
                o.Total,
                o.PlacedAt
        FROM    dbo.Orders AS o
                INNER JOIN dbo.Customers AS c ON c.Id = o.CustomerId
        WHERE   o.PlacedAt >= @since
        ORDER BY o.PlacedAt DESC
        """;

    var since = DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-days);
    var grid = await connection.QueryAsync<OrderRow>(new CommandDefinition(
        sql,
        new { since },
        cancellationToken: ct));

    return grid.AsList();
}

// DynamicParameters: the explicit form, needed for list expansion
var p = new DynamicParameters();
p.Add("@status", commandText.Status, DbType.String);
// DbType is optional here; specifying it removes the type-inference round trip
p.Add("@from", from, DbType.DateTime2);

// ExecuteAsync runs a non-query; ExecuteScalarAsync returns one value
int affected = await connection.ExecuteAsync("DELETE FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Id = @id", new { id });
object? max = await connection.ExecuteScalarAsync<DateTime?>(
    "SELECT MAX(PlacedAt) FROM dbo.Orders");

// Multi-mapping: one row, several objects, splitOn names the join keys.
// "Id" is the shared column, so the first type is split on Id; the second is
// split on the next column, hence splitOn: "OrderId,CustomerId".
var joined = await connection.QueryAsync<Order, Customer, OrderCustomer>(
    "SELECT o.Id, o.Total, o.CustomerId, c.Id AS CustomerId, c.Name "
    + "FROM dbo.Orders o JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.Id = o.CustomerId",
    splitOn: "CustomerId");

public sealed record Order(int Id, decimal Total, int CustomerId);
public sealed record Customer(int Id, string Name);
public sealed record OrderCustomer(Order Order, Customer Customer);

CommandDefinition carries the three settings that matter: commandType (CommandType.Text, StoredProcedure or Text with CommandFlags.Text), commandTimeout, and buffered. Setting buffered: false streams the reader instead of materialising the whole result set into a list, which is the difference between constant and growing memory for a large query.

Failure mode: a positional mapping mistake is silent. If splitOn does not name a column that begins the right-hand object, Dapper fills it with defaults and returns no error. When a multi-map query returns zeros, check splitOn first, column aliases second. Dapper also does not know about UserDefinedTypeHandler conversions, DateOnly needs the provider’s default handler, and records with primary-constructor parameters map positionally only when the column order matches.


{{-- TRADE COMPILE-TIME CHECKING FOR NEAR-ZERO OVERHEAD, and the
     trade is worth it when the queries are hand-written and
     reviewed as SQL. --}}
public sealed class Mapping(IDbConnection db)
{
    // THE SIMPLE CASE: a POCO matched by column name.
    public async Task<IEnumerable<Order>> AllAsync(CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.QueryAsync<Order>(
            "SELECT Id, Reference, Status, Total FROM Orders", cancellationToken: ct);

    // MULTI-MAPPING: ONE RECORD INTO SEVERAL CONSTRUCTOR
    // PARAMETERS, and the LAMBDA IS CHECKED AGAINST THE COLUMN
    // ALIASES BY THE COMPILER.
    public async Task<IEnumerable<(Order Order, Customer Customer)>> WithCustomersAsync(
        CancellationToken ct)
    {
        const string sql = """
            SELECT  o.Id,   o.Reference, o.Total,      AS Id,   Reference, Total,
                    c.Id,   c.Name,      c.Region,
                    -- ^ THE CONVENTION: a column aliased 'Id'
                    --   belongs to the FIRST type; one aliased
                    --   'Customer_Id' belongs to the second. The
                    --   error for getting it wrong is a
                    --   MISMATCHED CONSTRUCTOR, not a named
                    --   column, so the message is about the wrong
                    --   thing entirely.
                    c.Id             AS Customer_Id,
                    c.Name           AS Customer_Name,
                    c.Region         AS Customer_Region
            FROM    Orders o
            JOIN    Customers c ON c.Id = o.CustomerId
            """;

        return await db.QueryAsync<Order, Customer, (Order, Customer)>(
            sql,
            map: (order, customer) => (order, customer),   // CHECKED
            splitOn: "Customer_",
            cancellationToken: ct);
        // ^ splitOn is the PREFIX that starts the second type's
        //   columns. Getting it wrong produces a constructor
        //   mismatch, and the fix is one string.
    }

    // SPLIT-ON for a WIDE result where you want a subset of the
    // columns in one type rather than several types:
    public async Task<IEnumerable<Summary>> SummariesAsync(CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.QueryAsync<Summary>(sql, splitOn: "Id");
    {{-- ^ MULTI-MAPPING IS FOR JOINING TYPES. splitOn alone is for
         ONE WIDE TYPE, and it is the version worth reaching for
         when the query returns a report row rather than an
         aggregate — because a record that maps to a purpose-built
         type cannot accidentally acquire a dependency through a
         navigation property it never uses. --}}

    // A COMMAND DEFINITION, WHICH IS CACHED BY A KEY RATHER THAN A
    // STRING COMPILED PER CALL:
    private static readonly CommandDefinition ByReference = new(
        "SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Reference = @reference",
        new { reference = "" });

    public async Task<Order?> FindAsync(string reference, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // A NEW INSTANCE PER CALL, so the PARAMETERS ARE PER CALL,
        // and the cache key is explicit rather than being the whole
        // command text.
        return await db.QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync<Order>(new CommandDefinition(
            "SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Reference = @reference",
            new { reference }, cancellationToken: ct));
    }

    // WHICH STOPS BEING THE RIGHT TOOL HERE:
    public async Task MarkPaidAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // NO CHANGE TRACKING, NO IDENTITY RESOLUTION, NO LAZY
        // LOADING. For a report that is exactly right. For an
        // aggregate loaded, mutated and saved, those three are a
        // large amount of code to write by hand — and a mapper that
        // lacks them gives N+1 QUERIES silently rather than an
        // error, which is the dangerous version.
    }

    // THE N+1, and it is the reason this section exists:
    public async Task<List<string>> WrongAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var names = new List<string>();
        foreach (var order in await db.QueryAsync<Order>(allOrders, cancellationToken: ct))
        {
            // ^ NO LAZY LOADING, SO THIS COMPILES AND RUNS, and it
            //   issues ONE QUERY PER ORDER. 200 orders is 201
            //   queries and the latency looks like a database
            //   problem. The fix is multi-mapping above, not a
            //   setting.
            var c = await db.QuerySingleAsync<Customer>(
                "SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Id = @id",
                new { id = order.CustomerId }, cancellationToken: ct);
            names.Add(c.Name);
        }
        return names;
    }
}

13.5 EF Core: DbContext, configuration and tracking

An EF Core DbContext is two things at once: a unit of work and an identity map. Every entity it materialises is remembered by primary key for the lifetime of the context, and every change to a tracked entity is discovered by comparing snapshots. Those two facts explain most of EF Core’s performance characteristics and most of its correctness surprises.

A context is a unit of work: it tracks the changes made to the entities it hands out, and it writes them when asked. That is the whole feature, and everything else — lazy loading, change tracking states, concurrency tokens — exists to serve it or to control its cost.

The tracking states, and why the default is wrong on a read

A query tracks by default, which means every returned entity is compared against its snapshot on save, and a query returning ten thousand rows pays for ten thousand snapshots. A read-only query should say so, and the way to say it is either the tracking option or a projection to a type that is not an entity.

Configuration, and where it belongs

Model configuration has three homes — attributes, fluent calls, and a model-building convention — and the rule that survives contact with a codebase is that one of them should be used per concern. Attributes on an entity tie the domain type to the persistence technology; conventions hide the mapping where nobody looks. Fluent configuration in one place per aggregate is the version that stays readable.

// Entity configuration in a dedicated IEntityTypeConfiguration, one per aggregate
public sealed class OrderConfiguration : IEntityTypeConfiguration<Order>
{
    public void Configure(EntityTypeBuilder<Order> builder)
    {
        builder.ToTable("Orders");
        builder.HasKey(o => o.Id);
        builder.Property(o => o.Id).ValueGeneratedOnAdd();
        builder.Property(o => o.CustomerId).HasColumnName("CustomerId");
        builder.Property(o => o.Total).HasColumnType("decimal(18,2)");
        builder.Property(o => o.PlacedAt).HasColumnType("datetime2");
        builder.Property(o => o.Status).HasConversion<string>();      // string enum, readable in the table
        builder.HasIndex(o => o.CustomerId).HasDatabaseName("IX_Orders_CustomerId");
        builder.HasIndex(o => o.PlacedAt).IsDescending();
        builder.Ignore(o => o.Customer);                                // DTO shape, not a column
        builder.Navigation(o => o.Lines).HasMany(l => l.Order)
            .WithOne(l => l.Order).HasForeignKey(l => l.OrderId);
    }
}

// Apply it in OnModelCreating, which runs once per model, not per query
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
{
    modelBuilder.ApplyConfiguration(new OrderConfiguration());
    modelBuilder.ApplyConfiguration(new OrderLineConfiguration());
    modelBuilder.Entity<Order>().HasQueryFilter(o => !o.IsArchived);   // global soft-delete filter
}

// Tracking vs no tracking
var tracked = await db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == id).ToListAsync(ct);
// tracked: identity map returns the same instance for the same key,
// changes are detected on SaveChanges, navigation properties are fixed up.

var readOnly = await db.Orders
    .AsNoTracking()                       // no snapshot, no fixup, no SaveChanges effect
    .Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

// AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution keeps the shared instances but skips
// change detection: correct for an object graph, read-only.
var graph = await db.Orders
    .AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution()
    .Include(o => o.Lines)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

// N+1: one query for orders, then one per order for its lines.
var orders = await db.Orders.ToListAsync(ct);
foreach (var o in orders)
{
    // _ is a lazy-loading proxy; this line issues SQL
    int n = o.Lines.Count;                     // 1 + N queries
}

// Fixes: Include, ThenInclude, or split queries to bound the round trips
var eager = await db.Orders
    .Include(o => o.Lines).ThenInclude(l => l.Product)
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

// The projection is the strongest fix: it selects the columns needed
// and never materialises an entity, so there is nothing to track.
var rows = await db.Orders
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)
    .Select(o => new OrderSummary(o.Id, o.PlacedAt, o.Total,
                       o.Lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity * l.UnitPrice)))
    .ToListAsync(ct);

// Bulk operations bypass the change tracker entirely (EF Core 7+)
int archived = await db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.PlacedAt < cutoff)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(o => o.Status, OrderStatus.Archived), ct);

await db.Orders.Where(o => o.Id == id).ExecuteDeleteAsync(ct);

// SaveChanges: a transaction, a batch of commands, one round trip
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
// Explicit transaction when the unit of work spans two contexts
await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
db.Orders.Remove(order);
db.AuditLog.Add(new AuditEntry("order.deleted", DateTime.UtcNow));
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
await tx.CommitAsync(ct);

The change tracker stores a snapshot of every tracked entity’s original values and compares them on DetectChanges, which runs automatically before each query and before SaveChanges. On a graph of several thousand entities that is a measurable cost; the mitigations are AsNoTracking, ChangeTracker.AutoDetectChangesEnabled = false with explicit DetectChanges() before save, and SaveChangesAsync(acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false) for bulk inserts where the graph is discarded anyway.

Caveats: lazy loading must be opted into with UseLazyLoadingProxies and requires the entity to be a virtual-navigation proxy class; it is invisible in review and turns any property access into possible I/O. AsSplitQuery multiplies round trips and is not a substitute for a projection. ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete do not fire SaveChanges interceptors, do not update the change tracker, and are not supported inside an ambient transaction for some providers — check the provider matrix before relying on them.


{{-- A CONTEXT IS A UNIT OF WORK: it tracks changes to the entities
     it hands out, and writes them when asked. --}}
public sealed class AppDbContext(DbContextOptions<AppDbContext> options)
    : DbContext(options)
{
    public DbSet<Order> Orders => Set<Order>();
    public DbSet<Customer> Customers => Set<Customer>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder b)
    {
        // FLUENT CONFIGURATION, ONE PLACE PER AGGREGATE. Attributes
        //   tie the domain type to the persistence technology;
        //   conventions hide the mapping where nobody looks.
        b.Entity<Order>(e =>
        {
            e.ToTable("Orders");
            e.HasKey(o => o.Id);
            e.Property(o => o.Reference).HasMaxLength(50).IsRequired();
            e.Property(o => o.Total).HasPrecision(18, 2);
            // ^ A PRECISION, which the default does not set: money
            //   as a decimal without one is decimal(18,2) by
            //   accident in some providers and something else in
            //   others, and the mismatch appears as a rounding
            //   difference between two environments.

            e.HasMany(o => o.Lines)
             .WithOne(l => l.Order)
             .HasForeignKey(l => l.OrderId)
             .OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade);
        });
    }
}

public sealed class Order
{
    public long Id { get; set; }
    public required string Reference { get; set; }
    public decimal Total { get; set; }
    public long CustomerId { get; set; }
    public Customer? Customer { get; set; } = null;   // ^ NULLABLE:
                                        //   the nav property is
                                        //   null until loaded, and
                                        //   a non-nullable
                                        //   annotation on it is a
                                        //   lie the lazy loader
                                        //   removes
    public List<Line> Lines { get; } = [];
}

{{-- THE TRACKING STATES, AND WHY THE DEFAULT IS WRONG ON A READ: --}}
public sealed class Tracking(AppDbContext db)
{
    public async Task<List<Order>> WrongAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // TRACKED BY DEFAULT: EVERY RETURNED ENTITY IS COMPARED
        //   AGAINST ITS SNAPSHOT ON SAVE, so a query returning
        //   10,000 rows pays for 10,000 snapshots and holds all
        //   10,000 alive until the context is disposed.
        return await db.Orders.ToListAsync(ct);
    }

    public async Task<List<Order>> RightAsync(CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct);
        // ^ AND THIS IS THE BETTER VERSION for most reads, because
        //   it removes the memory AND the comparison:

    public async Task<List<OrderDto>> ProjectedAsync(CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.Orders
            .Select(o => new OrderDto(o.Reference, o.Total))   // NO ENTITY
            .ToListAsync(ct);
        {{-- ^ A PROJECTION TO A TYPE THAT IS NOT AN ENTITY is
             better than AsNoTracking: it transfers two columns
             rather than forty, nothing is tracked, and there is no
             way for a caller to accidentally change one. This is
             the version to reach for by default on a read path. --}}
}

{{-- AND WHERE LAZY LOADING IS THE WRONG DEFAULT: --}}
public sealed class LazyIsAChoice
{
    public async Task<string> NameAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await db.Orders.FindAsync(id, ct);
        // FindAsync USES THE LOCAL CACHE, so it returns null for a
        //   row that was never loaded rather than querying — which
        //   is a bug when the caller does not know whether the
        //   entity was already in the context.
        return order.Customer.Name;
        // ^ LAZY LOADING FIRES A QUERY HERE, per access, per entity,
        //   and the cost is invisible in the source. It is off by
        //   default for that reason, and turning it on for
        //   convenience converts a one-query path into an
        //   N+1 with no diagnostic.
    }
}

13.6 Migrations, bulk operations and choosing a layer

Migrations are the schema history. They are code-generated, reviewable, and the only supported way to evolve an EF Core model in an environment where a production database already exists. The final table in this section is the decision procedure; it is deliberately criteria-based rather than a preference order.

// Migration workflow. Applies to: EF Core 10 with the dotnet-ef 10 global tool.
//   dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef --version 10.*
//   dotnet ef migrations add AddOrderIndex --project src/Orders --output-dir Persistence/Migrations
//   dotnet ef database update --project src/Orders

// Migrations are applied in the application, not by hand, in production.
// MigrateAsync blocks startup until the schema matches the model.
await using var scope = app.Services.CreateAsyncScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<OrdersDbContext>();
await db.Database.MigrateAsync();

// Seeding belongs in OnModelCreating.HasData, which emits an Insert into the
// migration. It is for reference data that must exist before first use.
//   builder.HasData(new Country("GB", "United Kingdom") { Active = true });
// It is not a general data loader: no file I/O, no randomness, no DateTime.UtcNow.

// Transient fault handling for Azure SQL: the execution strategy is
// required, and user-initiated transactions must use the strategy's helpers.
builder.Services.AddDbContext<OrdersDbContext>((sp, options) =>
{
    var connectionString = sp.GetRequiredService<IConfiguration>()
        .GetConnectionString("Orders");

    options.UseSqlServer(connectionString, sql =>
    {
        sql.EnableRetryOnFailure(maxRetryCount: 5, maxRetryDelay: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10), null);
        sql.CommandTimeout(30);
        sql.MigrationsAssembly(typeof(OrdersDbContext).Assembly.FullName);
    });

    options.EnableDetailedErrors();       // development only: leaks values in errors
});

// With a retrying strategy, BeginTransaction throws unless the transaction
// is created through the strategy's delegate form.
//   var strategy = db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy();
//   await strategy.ExecuteAsync(async () =>
//   {
//       await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
//       ...
//       await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
//       await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
//   });

EnableRetryOnFailure applies to EF Core-issued commands. Raw DbCommand execution inside a retrying context is not covered, which is one of the reasons a Dapper repository is often wrapped in its own retry policy rather than relying on the connection string alone.

CriterionRaw ADO.NETDapperEF Core
Schema is owned by the app and changes oftenNoNoYes — migrations are the differentiator
Query is hand-tuned or uses stored procedures, TVPs, bulk copyYesYesPossible but awkward
Graph writes with cascading updates and identity resolutionManualManualYes
Read-heavy reporting over a stable read modelYesYes — fastest to writeAcceptable with projections
Team size, and how much ORM knowledge it hasAnyAnyRequires training; the model is shared vocabulary
Latency budget on a hot pathLowestLowHighest, unless projected
Requires a live connection for every testYesYesNo — see section 15.5 for the cost of that
Dominant answer in an enterprise serviceLegacy and bulk pathsReporting and read modelsTransactional domain data

Mixing layers in one application is normal and supported. A common enterprise shape is EF Core for the transactional write model and Dapper for a read-only reporting projection over a database view, because the projection does not need tracking and Dapper expresses it in a third of the code with no materialisation overhead.

Exercises 13

  1. Write the same parameterised SELECT three ways — concatenated string, AddWithValue, explicit SqlParameter with DbType — and capture the SQL sent with SQL Server Profiler or Extended Events. Note the extra round trip caused by type inference.
  2. Prove that connection pooling makes a per-operation Open cheap: run ten thousand opens in a loop and record elapsed time and @@SPID with DBCC INPUTBUFFER. Then hold one connection open across a Task.Delay for a minute and observe the pool exhaustion failure mode.
  3. Attempt an injection through a string parameter (1' OR '1'='1) and confirm the provider sends it as a value. Then try it against a table name and observe why that cannot be parameterised.
  4. Write a SqlBatch of three statements and read two result sets with NextResultAsync. Time the batched version against three separate round trips at 1,000 iterations.
  5. Build the same query with Dapper: a single-map call, a multi-map join with splitOn, and a variant with buffered: false streaming. Deliberately break splitOn and document the silent failure.
  6. Build a DbContext with a required related entity, then trigger the N+1 by iterating a navigation property without Include and count the SQL statements. Fix it three ways (Include, AsSplitQuery, projection) and compare round trips and allocation.
  7. Add a migration, apply it, then write the SQL it produced by reading the generated Up and Down methods. Confirm the Down is genuinely reversible and state which of your own migrations would not be.

{{-- THE DECISION, and it is driven by the QUERY PATTERN rather than
     by preference: --}}
// IF: the shape is "load an aggregate by id and save it whole",
// AND the domain is relational, AND the team can own the schema
//        migration discipline
// THEN: EF Core, because change tracking and identity resolution
//       remove code that is otherwise written by hand.
public sealed class WithEfCore(AppDbContext db)
{
    public async Task<Order> LoadAndMutateAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // THE CASE EF IS GENUINELY BEST AT: an aggregate loaded,
        // changed in memory, and saved — where the change tracker
        // works out WHICH columns changed and issues one UPDATE.
        var order = await db.Orders
            .Include(o => o.Lines)
            .FirstAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct);

        order.Status = OrderStatus.Paid;
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        // ^ ONE UPDATE, and the SQL is written by a diff of the
        //   snapshot rather than by hand. That diff is the feature,
        //   and there is no hand-rolled equivalent of it that is
        //   correct in the presence of collections.
    }
}

// IF: the shape is "one hand-written query, tuned, repeated", OR the
//     SQL matters (a report, a bulk update, a window function)
// THEN: Dapper or raw ADO.NET, because the query is the artefact and
//       it should be reviewable as SQL.
public sealed class WithDapper(IDbConnection connection)
{
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<SalesRow>> MonthlyAsync(int year, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // A REPORT with a window function: EF Core cannot express
        // this without a raw query, at which point it is a Dapper
        // query with extra steps.
        const string sql = """
            SELECT  CustomerId,
                    SUM(Total)                              AS MonthTotal,
                    SUM(SUM(Total)) OVER (
                        PARTITION BY CustomerId
                        ORDER BY MONTH(PlacedAt)
                        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                    )                                      AS Trailing3,
                    RANK() OVER (
                        PARTITION BY MONTH(PlacedAt)
                        ORDER BY SUM(Total) DESC
                    )                                      AS RankInMonth
            FROM    Orders
            WHERE   PlacedAt >= @from AND PlacedAt < @to
                     AND Status = 1
            GROUP BY CustomerId, MONTH(PlacedAt)
            ORDER BY MonthTotal DESC
            """;

        var rows = await connection.QueryAsync<SalesRow>(
            new CommandDefinition(sql,
                new { from = new DateTime(year, 1, 1), to = new DateTime(year + 1, 1, 1) },
                cancellationToken: ct));
        return (IReadOnlyList<SalesRow>)rows;
    }
}

{{-- AND THE THIRD OPTION, which is right more often than people
     expect: --}}
public static async Task<(int affected, CancellationToken)> BulkAsync(
    DbConnection connection, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // RAW SQL FOR A BULK UPDATE, where EF Core would load every row
    // into the change tracker to change one column.
    await using var cmd = new SqlCommand(
        "UPDATE Orders SET Status = 2 WHERE Status = 1 AND PlacedAt < @cutoff",
        connection);

    cmd.Parameters.Add("@cutoff", SqlDbType.DateTime2).Value = DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-30);
    return (await cmd.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct), ct);
}
{{-- ^ EF Core CANNOT express this as tracked changes without
     loading 200,000 entities, and ExecuteUpdate exists in newer
     versions precisely because this shape is common. WHICH IS THE
     POINT: the choice is per-QUERY, not per-application, and a
     codebase that picks one layer for everything has picked wrong
     somewhere. --}}

{{-- AND WHAT THE DECISION IS NOT ABOUT: --}}
{{--   NOT about performance: EF Core's generated SQL is fine for
     anything that is not a report, and Dapper's is fine for
     anything at all. The difference is a few microseconds
     against a database round trip.
     NOT about "ORMs are bad": a change tracker is worth a great
     deal in code that mutates an aggregate.
     NOT about team size: a team of four can own a schema and a
     team of forty can still write raw SQL where the query is the
     requirement. --}}

14 · Dependency Injection, Configuration & Logging

14.1 The composition root and registration extensions14.2 Lifetimes, captive dependencies and keyed services14.3 Constructor injection and disposal ownership14.4 The options pattern and validation14.5 Configuration precedence and secret management14.6 Structured logging, scopes and tracing

The composition root is the one place in an application where every concrete type is named. Everything else receives its collaborators through constructor parameters. This chapter covers the built-in container that ships with ASP.NET Core and the generic host, the lifetimes that determine object graph shape, the options and configuration systems, and the logging and tracing conventions that make a distributed system diagnosable.

Applies to: Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, Microsoft.Extensions.Options, Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration and Microsoft.Extensions.Logging 10.0, as consumed by the .NET generic host. Caveats: the container resolves only the types it knows. A service resolved with ActivatorUtilities is outside the graph and outside the disposal chain.

14.1 The composition root and registration extensions

Registrations belong in extension methods on IServiceCollection, one per bounded area, called from a single AddOrdersModule entry point. This keeps Program.cs free of infrastructure detail and makes the dependency graph of a module reviewable in one file.

The composition root is the one place in a codebase where every concrete type is named. Everything else depends on abstractions, and the root is the single file or single method that knows which implementations those abstractions resolve to. The discipline is worth stating because it is one of the few architectural properties that can be checked by a rule rather than by a review.

Registration extensions, and the order they run in

Splitting registration across assemblies works only if the order is defined, because a later registration of the same service type replaces the earlier one rather than adding to it. That is a feature — it is how a test overrides a production binding — and it is also the mechanism by which an accidental duplicate silently changes what a service resolves to.

What must not appear in the root

No logic, because the root should be readable as a list. No conditional registration, because a binding that depends on a configuration value is a binding nobody can find with a search. And no assembly scanning as the default, because it makes the set of registered services a function of the deployment rather than a function of the source.

// Program.cs stays a list of modules, not a wall of registrations
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddOrdersModule(builder.Configuration);
builder.Services.AddBillingModule(builder.Configuration);
builder.Services.AddPlatformModule(builder.Configuration);   // auth, health, telemetry

var app = builder.Build();
app.UsePlatform();
app.MapOrdersEndpoints();
app.Run();

// One file per module. The public entry point takes the minimum
// surface it needs so a test can call it with an in-memory config.
public static class OrdersModule
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddOrdersModule(
        this IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration configuration)
    {
        services.AddOptions<OrdersOptions>()
                .Bind(configuration.GetSection(OrdersOptions.SectionName))
                .ValidateDataAnnotations()
                .ValidateOnStart();

        services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);                       // injectable clock
        services.AddSingleton<IOrderNumberGenerator, OrderNumberGenerator>();

        services.AddScoped<IOrdersDbContext>((sp, o) =>
        {
            var cs = sp.GetRequiredService<IOptions<OrdersOptions>>().Value.ConnectionString;
            return new OrdersDbContext(new DbContextOptionsBuilder<OrdersDbContext>()
                .UseSqlServer(cs)
                .Options);
        });

        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
        services.AddScoped<OrderService>();
        services.AddScoped<OrderValidator>();

        // The decorator pattern, expressed as two registrations
        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, CachedOrderRepository>();
        services.AddScoped<IPricingService, ResilientPricingService>();

        services.AddHttpClient<IPricingClient, PricingClient>((sp, client) =>
        {
            client.BaseAddress = new Uri(sp.GetRequiredService<IOptions<OrdersOptions>>().Value.PricingBaseUrl!);
            client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5);
        });

        return services;
    }
}

The last two registrations illustrate the open generic-free form of decoration: registering IPricingService twice with different implementations does not stack them. To wrap, register the decorator as the interface and inject the inner implementation through a distinct interface, or use a keyed service (section 14.2) to name both.

Use AddHttpClient<TClient, TImplementation> rather than a singleton HttpClient. The factory form configures HttpMessageHandler lifetimes correctly, participates in IHttpClientFactory DNS refresh, and integrates with resilience handlers and Activity propagation. A single long-lived HttpClient with a default handler suffers from socket exhaustion and stale DNS; a new HttpClient per request suffers from handler exhaustion. The factory removes the choice.


{{-- THE COMPOSITION ROOT IS THE ONE PLACE WHERE EVERY CONCRETE
     TYPE IS NAMED. --}}
public sealed class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

        // NO LOGIC. NO CONDITIONAL REGISTRATION. A binding that
        //   depends on a configuration value is a binding nobody
        //   can find with a search.
        builder.Services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();
        builder.Services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();
        builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
        builder.Services.AddHostedService<OrderProcessor>();

        builder.Services.AddControllers();
        var app = builder.Build();
        app.MapControllers();
        app.Run();
    }
}

{{-- REGISTRATION EXTENSIONS, AND THE ORDER THEY RUN IN: --}}
public static class OrderServiceCollectionExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddOrders(
        this IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config)
    {
        // THE ORDER IS THE CONTRACT. A LATER REGISTRATION OF THE
        //   SAME SERVICE TYPE REPLACES the earlier one rather than
        //   adding to it — which is a feature, because it is how a
        //   test overrides a production binding, and a hazard,
        //   because it is how an accidental duplicate silently
        //   changes what a service resolves to.
        services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();

        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();

        // A FACTORY IS A BOUNDARY THE ANALYSIS CANNOT CROSS, so a
        //   type resolved through one is invisible to a lifetime
        //   check — which is where a captive dependency comes from.
        services.AddScoped<IOrderService>(sp => new OrderService(
            sp.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>(),
            sp.GetRequiredService<IClock>()));

        services.AddOptions<OrderOptions>()
                .Bind(config.GetSection("Orders"))   // BIND, not read
                .ValidateDataAnnotations()             // VALIDATE, or a
                .ValidateOnStart();                    // a bad value
                                                       // FAILS AT START-UP
        return services;
    }

    // AND THE OVERRIDE, which is the thing that makes the order
    // safe to rely on:
    public static class Testing
    {
        public static void Override(IServiceCollection services)
        {
            // LAST WINS, so a test replacing a binding must be
            //   registered AFTER the production one — which is why
            //   the override lives in the test's own setup rather
            //   than in a shared helper that might run first.
            services.AddScoped<IClock, FixedClock>();
        }
    }
}

{{-- AND WHAT MUST NOT APPEAR IN THE ROOT: --}}
// NO ASSEMBLY SCANNING AS THE DEFAULT, because it makes the set of
//   registered services a function of the DEPLOYMENT rather than of
//   the source: a trimmed or single-file publish changes what is
//   registered, and the difference appears only in the artefact that
//   nobody tests.
services.ScanAssembly(typeof(OrderService).Assembly);   // avoid

{{-- THE ONE PROPERTY WORTH ENFORCING: the root can be READ AS A
     LIST, which means a dependency that is not in it does not
     exist. Every defect that check would catch — a type used
     without a registration, a singleton depending on a scoped
     service — is a build-time error in a project with an analyser
     and a run-time error in one without. --}}

14.2 Lifetimes, captive dependencies and keyed services

Three lifetimes exist. Singleton is created once per container. Scoped is created once per scope, which in a web application is one per request. Transient is created every time it is requested. The container disposes what it creates, in reverse creation order, and a captured dependency is disposed with its captor — which is how a singleton silently holds a disposed scoped object.

Three lifetimes, and the rule for each is about who owns the object. A singleton is owned by the container and lives for the process. A scoped instance is owned by a scope, which is a request in a web application and a unit of work elsewhere. A transient is owned by whoever resolves it, which means it may never be disposed by anybody.

Captive dependencies

A singleton that depends on a scoped service is a captive dependency: the scoped service is held by something that outlives its scope, so it is never disposed and it carries one request's state into the next. The container detects it at build time in a development environment and not in production, which makes it a defect that appears only in the environment nobody runs the check in.

Why the scoped lifetime is not simply "per request"

Because the scope is created by whatever handles the work, and that is not always a request. A background service has its own scope per message, a console application has one for the whole run, and a test creates one per test. Anything cached in a scoped service is therefore cached for the unit of work, and a service that assumes a request is wrong in all three of the other cases.

// Singleton: one instance for the process. Must be thread-safe, must not
// depend on anything scoped, must not hold mutable per-request state.
services.AddSingleton<IOrderNumberGenerator, OrderNumberGenerator>();
services.AddSingleton(new OrderMetrics(new Meter("Contoso.Orders")));

// Scoped: one per request. The default for DbContext, repositories,
// and anything that participates in a unit of work.
services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
services.AddScoped<OrdersDbContext>();

// Transient: one per consuming component. Cheap, stateless objects only.
services.AddTransient<IOrderValidator, OrderValidator>();

// Captive dependency. ValidatedScopes is off by default in the generic
// host, so this builds successfully and fails at the first use of the
// repository after the request scope has been disposed.
services.AddSingleton<OrderReportService>();     // takes IOrderRepository (scoped) -- WRONG

// Correct: the singleton owns nothing scoped. It takes the factory
// and creates a scope per unit of work, disposed with using.
services.AddSingleton<OrderReportService>();

public sealed class OrderReportService(IServiceProvider provider, ILogger<OrderReportService> log)
{
    public async Task GenerateAsync(int month, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using IServiceScope scope = provider.CreateAsyncScope();
        var repository = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>();
        var orders = await repository.GetForMonthAsync(month, ct);
        log.LogInformation("Report generated for {Month} with {Count} orders", month, orders.Count);
    }
}

// Keyed services (.NET 8+): two implementations of one interface,
// both registered, resolved by string key.
services.AddKeyedSingleton<IWarehouseGateway, EuWarehouseGateway>("eu");
services.AddKeyedSingleton<IWarehouseGateway, UsWarehouseGateway>("us");
services.AddKeyedScoped<IOrderNumberGenerator, EuNumberGenerator>("eu");
services.AddKeyedTransient<IClock, SystemClock>("system");

// Any key works: enum, type, string
public enum Region { Eu, Us }

services.AddKeyedSingleton<IWarehouseGateway, EuWarehouseGateway>(Region.Eu);
services.AddKeyedSingleton<IWarehouseGateway, UsWarehouseGateway>(Region.Us);

// Resolution
var gateway = sp.GetRequiredKeyedService<IWarehouseGateway>("eu");
var optional = sp.GetKeyedService<IWarehouseGateway>("apac");  // null if absent
// Enumerate every key for a given service type
foreach (var key in sp.GetKeyedServices<AnyKey<IWarehouseGateway>, IWarehouseGateway>().Keys)
{
    var g = sp.GetRequiredKeyedService<IWarehouseGateway>(key);
}

The AnyKey<TService, TImplementation> overload is required for enumeration; a plain GetKeyedServices<IWarehouseGateway>() has no way to express "any key". Enable services.Configure<ServiceProviderOptions>(o => o.ValidateScopes = true) and ValidateOnBuild = true in development: the first turns a captive dependency into a startup failure, the second makes every registration eagerly validated at boot.

Failure modes to know: a singleton depending on a scoped service (captive dependency, use-after-dispose at an unpredictable point in production); a scoped service depending on a transient that itself takes a scoped service (the same problem one level down); resolving a scoped service from a singleton; and background services injected with a scoped dependency, which is the classic cause of ObjectDisposedException on a hosted service. Background services must create their own scope per unit of work.


{{-- THREE LIFETIMES, and the rule for each is about WHO OWNS THE
     OBJECT. --}}
public static class Lifetimes
{
    // SINGLETON: OWNED BY THE CONTAINER, lives for the process.
    //   Must be THREAD-SAFE, because the container guarantees one
    //   instance and several threads will use it.
    services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();
    services.AddSingleton<IHttpClientFactory, HttpClientFactory>();

    // SCOPED: OWNED BY A SCOPE — a request in a web application,
    //   a unit of work in a test, a message in a background
    //   service, the whole run in a console application.
    services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();
    services.AddScoped<OrderService>();
    // ^ SAFE TO HOLD REQUEST STATE, because the object dies with
    //   the scope. Anything cached in it is cached FOR THE UNIT OF
    //   WORK, which is why a service that assumes "per request" is
    //   wrong in all three of the other cases.

    // TRANSIENT: OWNED BY WHOEVER RESOLVES IT — which means it may
    //   never be disposed by anybody.
    services.AddTransient<INotification, EmailNotification>();
    // ^ AN EXPLICITLY DISPOSED, RESOLVED AND THEN ABANDONED
    //   TRANSIENT IS A LEAK, and a container will not warn about it
    //   because the container believes it disposed the instance it
    //   created. The fix is not to avoid transient but to inject
    //   something disposable and let the scope own it.
}

public sealed class Captive(IClock clock)  // the singleton
{
    private readonly IHttpContextAccessor _accessor;

    public Captive(IHttpContextAccessor accessor) => _accessor = accessor;

    public User CurrentUser()
    {
        // ^ A SINGLETON DEPENDING ON SCOPED, which is a CAPTIVE
        //   DEPENDENCY: the scoped service is held by something
        //   that OUTLIVES ITS SCOPE, so it is never disposed and it
        //   carries ONE REQUEST'S STATE INTO THE NEXT.
        var user = _accessor.HttpContext?.User;
        return user;      // THE NEXT REQUEST SEES THE LAST USER
    }
}
{{-- ^ THE CONTAINER DETECTS THIS AT BUILD TIME IN A DEVELOPMENT
     ENVIRONMENT AND NOT IN PRODUCTION — which makes it a defect
     that appears only in the environment nobody runs the check in,
     and it fails as wrong data rather than as an error. --}}

{{-- THE VALIDATION, and the flag that enables it: --}}
// builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(o =>
//     o.ValidateScopes = !builder.Environment.IsDevelopment());
// builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(o =>
//     o.ValidateOnBuild = true);
{{-- ^ ValidateOnBuild CHECKS THE WHOLE CONTAINER AT START-UP, so
     a captive dependency or an unresolvable constructor is a
     START-UP FAILURE rather than a first-request failure. Both are
     worth enabling in production, because the alternative is a
     defect that only appears when a particular code path is first
     exercised in production. --}}

{{-- THE ALTERNATIVE TO A SINGLETON, and it is usually better: --}}
public sealed class HttpClientRegistration
{
    // A TYPED CLIENT, which the container creates per scope but
    // whose HANDLER is managed as a singleton with a pooled
    // connection — so the DNS-refresh problem of a raw static
    // HttpClient is solved WITHOUT the captive dependency a raw
    // singleton would create.
    services.AddHttpClient<IOrderApi, OrderApiClient>();
    // ^ THIS IS THE ANSWER to "this singleton needs a scoped
    //   thing" nine times out of ten, and the reason is that the
    //   expensive shared thing — the handler, and its connection
    //   pool — is already a singleton inside the factory. --}}

14.3 Constructor injection and disposal ownership

Constructor injection is the only supported mechanism for a container-managed service. It makes the dependency list visible, keeps the type testable without a container, and lets the container validate the graph. Property and field injection are possible through ObjectContainer extensions but should never appear in application code.

Constructor injection is the form worth insisting on, because it makes a dependency visible in the type's own signature and removes the ability to construct the object without it. Property and field injection exist and both are worse: a property-injected dependency can be null because nothing has run yet, and a field-injected dependency cannot be used from a constructor at all.

Disposal ownership

Whoever creates a disposable owns it. Injected objects are owned by the container, so a class that receives a disposable should not dispose it, and a class that creates one should. The defect is disposing an injected resource, because the container may hand the same instance to another scope and the second use then fails with an object-disposed exception that names a line in a class that did nothing wrong.

What to do about a legacy dependency

A class with too many constructor parameters is not a DI problem, it is a class doing too much. The fix is a real extraction rather than a facade that forwards everything, because a facade reproduces the constructor it was introduced to hide.

// Constructor injection: the dependency list is the documentation
public sealed class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository repository,
    IOrderValidator validator,
    IPricingService pricing,
    TimeProvider clock,
    ILogger<OrderService> log)
{
    public async Task<OrderId> PlaceAsync(PlaceOrderCommand command, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(command);

        await validator.ValidateAsync(command, ct);

        var lines = new List<OrderLine>(command.Lines.Count);
        foreach (var line in command.Lines)
        {
            var price = await pricing.GetAsync(line.Sku, ct);
            lines.Add(new OrderLine(line.Sku, line.Quantity, price.Amount));
        }

        var order = Order.Place(command.CustomerId, lines, clock.GetUtcNow());
        await repository.AddAsync(order, ct);

        log.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} placed with {LineCount} lines", order.Id, lines.Count);
        return order.Id;
    }
}

// A type that owns a disposable resource states ownership in its signature.
// The container disposes what it creates, so a registered service that
// holds a DbContext, a socket or a file does not need a Dispose method.
public sealed class ReportCache(string root) : IDisposable
{
    private readonly string _root = root;
    private bool _disposed;

    public void Dispose()
    {
        if (_disposed) return;                  // idempotent
        _disposed = true;
        // ...
    }
}

// A singleton that creates a dependency it does not own must dispose it.
public sealed class ExportWriter : IDisposable
{
    private readonly Stream _stream = new FileStream("export.ndjson", FileMode.Append);

    public void Dispose() => _stream.Dispose();
}

// Anti-pattern: property injection hides the dependency and the
// container cannot tell whether it was ever set.
public sealed class BadService
{
    public IOrderRepository Repository { get; set } = null!;   // NullReferenceException at best
}

// When a dependency is genuinely optional, make it optional in the
// signature with a default, and branch on null explicitly.
public sealed class Notifier(ILogger<Notifier> log, IEmailSender? email = null)
{
    public async Task NotifyAsync(string to, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (email is null)
        {
            log.LogInformation("No email sender configured; notification skipped");
            return;
        }
        await email.SendAsync(to, "Notification", ct);
    }
}

Services resolved from the container are disposed by the container in reverse order of creation, including async disposables awaited during scope teardown. A type that is created with new inside another service and stored in a field is invisible to the container and leaks unless the owner disposes it explicitly.


{{-- CONSTRUCTOR INJECTION, because it makes a dependency VISIBLE
     IN THE TYPE'S OWN SIGNATURE. --}}
public sealed class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, IClock clock, ILogger<OrderService> log)
{
    public async Task CancelAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct)
                    ?? throw new KeyNotFoundException($"Order {id}");

        // ^ CONSTRUCTOR INJECTION means this class CANNOT BE
        //   CONSTRUCTED without its dependencies, and the compiler
        //   finds every call site that would have done so. A
        //   property-injected dependency can be NULL here because
        //   nothing has run yet, and a field-injected one cannot
        //   be used from a constructor at all.
        order.Status = OrderStatus.Cancelled;
        await repo.SaveAsync(order, ct);
        log.LogInformation("Cancelled {OrderId} at {At}", id, clock.UtcNow);
    }
}

{{-- DISPOSAL OWNERSHIP: whoever CREATES a disposable owns it. --}}
public sealed class Ownership(IOrderRepository repo)
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(Stream upload, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // INJECTED OBJECTS ARE OWNED BY THE CONTAINER, so this
        //   class does NOT dispose them:
        await repo.StoreAsync(upload, ct);
        // upload.Dispose();     WRONG: the container owns it and
        //                        may hand the same instance to
        //                        another scope, where the second
        //                        use throws ObjectDisposedException
        //                        naming a line in a class that did
        //                        nothing wrong.

        // OBJECTS THIS CLASS CREATES are this class's to release:
        using var buffer = new MemoryStream();
        await repo.StoreAsync(buffer, ct);
        // ^ 'using' BECAUSE THIS CLASS CREATED IT.
    }
}

{{-- AND WHAT TO DO ABOUT A LEGACY DEPENDENCY: --}}
public sealed class TooManyParameters(
    IOrderRepository orders,
    ICustomerRepository customers,
    IPricingService pricing,
    ITaxService tax,
    INotificationService notify,
    ILogger<ReportService> log)      // SIX, and the constructor is
{                                     //   now a summary of the
    public async Task<Receipt> GenerateAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // THIS IS NOT A DI PROBLEM. It is a class doing too much,
        // and the fix is a REAL EXTRACTION — because a facade that
        // forwards all six reproduces the constructor it was
        // introduced to hide, and now there are two.
        var order  = await orders.GetAsync(id, ct);
        var cust   = await customers.GetAsync(order.CustomerId, ct);
        var priced = pricing.Apply(order);
        var taxed  = tax.Apply(priced, cust.Region);
        return new Receipt(order, taxed);
    }
}

{{-- THE EXTRACTION THAT WORKS, and it works because each new type
     has a COHERENT REASON TO CHANGE rather than a list of
     collaborators: --}}
public sealed class ReceiptBuilder(IPricingService pricing, ITaxService tax)
{
    public Receipt Build(Order order, Customer customer)
        => new(order, tax.Apply(pricing.Apply(order), customer.Region));
}

public sealed class OrderReceiptService(
    IOrderRepository orders,
    ICustomerRepository customers,
    ReceiptBuilder receipts)
{
    public async Task<Receipt> GenerateAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await orders.GetAsync(id, ct)
                    ?? throw new KeyNotFoundException($"Order {id}");
        var cust  = await customers.GetAsync(order.CustomerId, ct);
        return receipts.Build(order, cust);
        // ^ THREE, each with a reason to change that is
        //   DIFFERENT: the repository changes with the schema, the
        //   customer repository with another one, and the builder
        //   with the rules. A facade would have no reason to change
        //   at all.
    }
}

14.4 The options pattern and validation

The options pattern converts a configuration section into a strongly typed, immutable, validated object. Three interfaces exist because there are three legitimate access patterns: read once at composition time, read once per scope, and read on every change.

The options pattern exists so that a configuration section arrives as a validated object rather than as a string looked up at the point of use. Three features make it worth adopting over a configuration object read directly: binding happens once, validation runs once, and the result is immutable and therefore safe to cache in a singleton.

Validate on start, not on first use

Validation on first use means a bad value is discovered when the first request happens to reach the code that reads it — which is a request that fails with a configuration error in production. Validating at start-up turns it into a process that refuses to start, which is the outcome that can actually be acted on by a deployment pipeline.

Named options, and when they are the right answer

Named options exist for a section that appears more than once with different contents, and the cost is that the name is a string passed at every resolution, so it is not checked. Where a type is bound once and read many times, plain options are better; where a type is bound several times with different values, the name is the mechanism.

public sealed class OrdersOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Orders";

    [Required, StringLength(256)]
    public string ConnectionString { get; set } = string.Empty;

    [Range(1, 600)]
    public int CommandTimeoutSeconds { get; set } = 30;

    [Url]
    public string PricingBaseUrl { get; set } = string.Empty;

    [Range(1, 1000)]
    public int MaxBatchSize { get; set } = 200;

    // Nested sections bind to nested classes without extra plumbing
    public RetryOptions Retry { get; set } = new();
}

public sealed class RetryOptions
{
    [Range(0, 10)] public int MaxAttempts { get; set } = 3;
    [Range(0, 60)] public int BaseDelaySeconds { get; set } = 1;
}

// Registration: bind, validate, fail fast
builder.Services.AddOptions<OrdersOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(OrdersOptions.SectionName))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()                       // DataAnnotations on the properties
    .Validate(o => o.Retry.MaxAttempts <= o.MaxBatchSize, "MaxAttempts must not exceed MaxBatchSize")
    .ValidateOnStart();                              // throws at startup, not on first request
