// IOptions<T>: a singleton snapshot. Read once, cache it in a field.
public sealed class OrderReader(IOptions<OrdersOptions> options)
{
    private readonly OrdersOptions _settings = options.Value;
    public int Timeout => _settings.CommandTimeoutSeconds;
}

// IOptionsSnapshot<T>: a new instance per scope. Use in scoped services
// that must observe configuration that can change between scopes.
public sealed class ScopedReader(IOptionsSnapshot<OrdersOptions> options)
{
    private readonly OrdersOptions _settings = options.Value;   // in the constructor
}

// IOptionsMonitor<T>: a live view with change notifications. Use in
// singletons that must react without a restart, and in factories.
public sealed class DynamicLimiter : IDisposable
{
    private readonly IDisposable _subscription;
    private volatile int _limit = 100;

    public DynamicLimiter(IOptionsMonitor<OrdersOptions> monitor, ILogger<DynamicLimiter> log)
    {
        void Apply(OrdersOptions o, string? _)
        {
            _limit = o.MaxBatchSize;
            log.LogInformation("Batch limit changed to {Limit}", _limit);
        }

        Apply(monitor.CurrentValue, null);
        _subscription = monitor.OnChange(Apply);
    }

    public int Limit => _limit;
    public void Dispose() => _subscription.Dispose();
}

// Named options, for the same type configured more than once
builder.Services.AddOptions<HttpRetryOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Http:Pricing"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations();
builder.Services.AddOptions<HttpRetryOptions>("ledger")
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Http:Ledger"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations();

var pricingRetry = sp.GetRequiredService<IOptionsMonitor<HttpRetryOptions>>().Get("pricing");

ValidateOnStart moves the failure from the first request to process start, which is the difference between a failed deploy and an outage. In a container orchestration platform the process that fails fast is restarted and, if it keeps failing, becomes visibly unhealthy rather than silently returning 500s.

Caveats: IOptions<T>.Value caches the first access for the process lifetime; reading it from a singleton gives a value frozen at first use. Mutating an options instance is unsupported and is not observed by other consumers. Binder matching is case-insensitive and does not handle arrays of complex types without a matching target collection. Do not put anything secret-bearing into an options type that is logged or dumped.


{{-- SO THAT A SECTION ARRIVES AS A VALIDATED OBJECT rather than as
     a string looked up at the point of use. --}}
public sealed class OrderOptions
{
    // DATA ANNOTATIONS, because they work with
    //   ValidateDataAnnotations and give the message that names the
    //   offending property.
    [Required, MinLength(1)]
    public string ConnectionString { get; set; } = "";

    [Range(1, 300)]
    public int MaxPageSize { get; set; } = 50;

    [Range(1, 3600)]
    public int CommandTimeoutSeconds { get; set; } = 30;

    // A CUSTOM VALIDATION for a rule annotations cannot express:
    [CustomValidation(typeof(OrderOptionsValidator), nameof(EndpointsAreUnique))]
    public string[] AllowedOrigins { get; set; } = [];
}

public static class Registration
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddOrders(
        this IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config)
    {
        services.AddOptions<OrderOptions>()
                .Bind(config.GetSection("Orders"))
                .ValidateDataAnnotations()
                // ^ VALIDATE AT START-UP. Validation on first use
                //   means a bad value is discovered when the FIRST
                //   REQUEST happens to reach the code that reads
                //   it — a request failing with a configuration
                //   error in production, at whatever hour that
                //   path is first exercised.
                .ValidateOnStart();
        return services;
    }
}

public sealed class OrderService(IOptions<OrderOptions> options)
{
    public void Use()
    {
        // IOptions<T> IS THE IMMUTABLE SNAPSHOT, so it is safe in a
        //   singleton — which is what makes the pattern's central
        //   claim true rather than aspirational.
        var limit = options.Value.MaxPageSize;

        // IOptionsMonitor<T> FOR SOMETHING THAT MUST CHANGE WITHOUT A
        //   RESTART, because it re-reads on a configuration reload:
        _monitor.CurrentValue.MaxPageSize;

        // IOptionsSnapshot<T> PER REQUEST, re-read ONCE per scope,
        //   which is what a web application usually wants when a
        //   reload should be visible without a restart.
    }
}

{{-- NAMED OPTIONS, AND WHEN THEY ARE THE RIGHT ANSWER: --}}
services.AddOptions<StorageOptions>("primary").Configure(o => config.GetSection("Storage:Primary").Bind(o));
services.AddOptions<StorageOptions>("archive").Configure(o => config.GetSection("Storage:Archive").Bind(o));
// ^ A SECTION THAT APPEARS MORE THAN ONCE WITH DIFFERENT CONTENTS.
//
// THE COST: the name is a STRING passed at every resolution, so it
// is NOT CHECKED. A typo compiles, runs, and returns the default.
public sealed class Archiver(IOptionsMonitor<StorageOptions> options)
{
    public void Use() => options.Get("archve").Value;   // ^ WRONG
                                                  // NAME, NO ERROR
}

{{-- AND WHY THAT COST IS SOMETIMES WORTH PAYING: a bound type
     that appears once and is read many times should use plain
     IOptions<T>, because the named form adds a string to every
     call site and a typo surface that no compiler will check. --}}

14.5 Configuration precedence and secret management

The configuration system merges providers into a single key-value tree, and later providers win. Ordering is fixed by the host builder, which is what makes an environment variable override an appsettings.json value without any code change. Knowing the exact order is the difference between a configuration change that works and one that silently does not.

Configuration is a stack of sources, and each later source overrides the earlier one for the keys it contains. That is the whole rule, and it is the rule that makes a secret manager at the end of the stack work without anything else knowing.

Order, and what it decides

The order determines which value wins, and it is fixed by the framework rather than by the application. Defaults are the lowest, then a file, then environment variables, then command-line arguments. Environment variables beat a file because a container is configured at deploy time and a file is baked at build time, and command-line arguments beat everything because they are the last word a person has.

Secrets, and the mistake worth naming

Putting a secret in a configuration file commits it. Putting it in an environment variable and then logging the whole configuration object also commits it, because a logger serialises whatever it is given — and the log is usually shipped somewhere with broader read access than the secret store.

// Precedence, lowest to highest, as built by WebApplication.CreateBuilder
//   1. appsettings.json
//   2. appsettings.{Environment}.json
//   3. User secrets            -- development only, ~/.microsoft/usersecrets/<path>
//   4. Environment variables  -- ASPNETCORE_, DOTNET_, and custom prefixes
//   5. Command-line arguments
//   6. Custom providers added afterwards

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Environment variables use __ as the section separator:
//   Orders__ConnectionString=Server=...;Database=Orders;...
//   Orders__Retry__MaxAttempts=5
// In Kubernetes the same keys are set from a Secret or a ConfigMap.

// A custom provider for anything the file system does not cover
builder.Configuration.AddEnvironmentVariables("CONTOSO_");   // prefix filter
builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("appsettings.local.json", optional: true);

// Reading: strongly typed access for a single value, GetSection for a block
string environment = builder.Configuration["DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT"]
                       ?? builder.Environment.EnvironmentName;
string version      = builder.Configuration["APP:Version"] ?? "0.0.0";

var options = new OrdersOptions();
builder.Configuration.GetSection(OrdersOptions.SectionName).Bind(options);

// A connection string is read through the dedicated accessor so that
// the provider can apply its own overrides and validation.
string connectionString =
    builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Orders")
    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("ConnectionStrings:Orders is not configured");

// ReloadOnChange is required for a JSON file to be re-read when it changes
builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("appsettings.json", optional: false, reloadOnChange: true);

// Options validation turns a missing key into a startup failure
builder.Services.AddOptions<OrdersOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(OrdersOptions.SectionName))
    .Validate(o => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(o.ConnectionString), "ConnectionString is required")
    .ValidateOnStart();

// Post-configure: derive one value from another, after binding
builder.Services.PostConfigure<OrdersOptions>(o =>
{
    if (o.MaxBatchSize > 1000) o.MaxBatchSize = 1000;
});

Secret handling, non-negotiable: a connection string, a client secret, a signing key or an API token never appears in appsettings.json, in a Directory.Build.props, in a Dockerfile ENV or ARG, or in a source-controlled environment file. In development it comes from user secrets; in production it comes from an environment variable, a mounted file, or Azure Key Vault through the Key Vault provider or the secrets store. Note that environment variables are readable in /proc and in a process listing, which is acceptable on a single host and is the reason a file mount is preferable in shared tenancy.

To seal the boundary in CI, add a test that walks the loaded IConfiguration for keys matching (?i)(password|secret|token|apikey|connectionstring|key) and fails if a value is present in a file-based provider that is not user secrets. It takes twenty lines and it prevents the single most damaging class of leak in a .NET codebase.


{{-- A STACK OF SOURCES, and each LATER SOURCE OVERRIDES the
     earlier one for the keys it CONTAINS. --}}
public static void TheStack(string[] args)
{
    var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

    // THIS ORDER IS FIXED BY THE FRAMEWORK, not by the
    //   application:
    //     1. DEFAULTS baked into the assembly
    //     2. appsettings.json
    //     3. appsettings.{Environment}.json
    //     4. ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES
    //     5. COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENTS
    //
    // ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES BEAT A FILE because a container is
    //   CONFIGURED AT DEPLOY TIME while a file is BAKED AT BUILD
    //   TIME — which is the entire reason the same image runs in
    //   three environments.
    // COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENTS BEAT EVERYTHING because they are the
    //   last word a person has.

    builder.Configuration.AddEnvironmentVariables("ORDERS_");
    // ^ A PREFIX, so the host's own variables (DOTNET_, ASPNETCORE_)
    //   cannot collide with the application's. Without a prefix a
    //   variable named PATH or HOME on the machine overrides a
    //   configuration key of the same name, and the symptom is a
    //   value that changes between a developer's laptop and a
    //   container with no visible cause.

    // ^ WHICH IS THE WHOLE MECHANISM OF A SECRET MANAGER: it
    //   INJECTS ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, and the override rule above
    //   does the rest without anything else knowing.
}

{{-- THE MISTAKE WORTH NAMING, and it is two mistakes: --}}
public sealed class Secrets(IConfiguration config, ILogger<Program> log)
{
    public void TwoMistakes()
    {
        // MISTAKE 1: A SECRET IN A CONFIGURATION FILE COMMITS IT.
        // appsettings.json:
        //   { "ConnectionStrings": { "Orders": "…Password=P@ss…" } }
        // ^ AND A FILE IS THE ONE SOURCE THAT IS DEPLOYED EVERYWHERE
        //   INCLUDING THE DEVELOPER'S MACHINE.

        // MISTAKE 2: LOGGING THE WHOLE CONFIGURATION ALSO COMMITS
        // IT, because a logger serialises whatever it is given.
        log.LogInformation("Configuration: {Config}", config);
        // ^ THE ENTIRE CONFIGURATION, including every secret, into
        //   a log that is shipped somewhere with BROADER READ
        //   ACCESS than the secret store. This is the more common
        //   of the two because it looks like a diagnostic and is
        //   done once, early, to work out why something is
        //   misconfigured.

        // THE FIX for both: read the named keys, never the tree.
        var cs = config["ConnectionStrings:Orders"];
        log.LogInformation("Orders database: {Host}", new SqlConnectionStringBuilder(cs).DataSource);
        // ^ LOG THE PARSED HOST, which is the thing being
        //   diagnosed, and never the connection string.
    }

    // AND THE RULE THAT PREVENTS BOTH:
    public void TheRule()
    {
        // A SECRET IS AN ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE REFERENCED BY A KEY
        //   that names what it IS, not a value in a file. The key
        //   is committed; the value is not.
        //
        //   ConnectionStrings__Orders        <- the KEY: committed
        //   (double underscore = the section separator)
        //   Password=P@ssword               <- the VALUE: injected
        //
        // AND THE CHECK worth having in CI, which is one grep and
        // finds the mistake before it is committed rather than
        // after it has been in a log for a week:
        //   grep -rE '(Password|Secret|ApiKey)s*[:=]s*"[^"]+' .
    }
}

14.6 Structured logging, scopes and tracing

Logging is an API, not a formatting exercise. A log entry is a set of named properties plus a message template; the sink decides the format. Interpolated strings destroy the structure at the point of creation, which is why the template-plus-placeholder form is a correctness requirement in code that will be queried.

// Wrong: the string is built eagerly and the structure is lost.
log.LogInformation("Order " + order.Id + " placed for customer " + order.CustomerId);
log.LogInformation($"Order {order.Id} placed for customer {order.CustomerId}");   // same defect

// Right: the template is constant, the placeholders are named properties.
log.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} placed for customer {CustomerId} with {LineCount} lines",
    order.Id, order.CustomerId, order.Lines.Count);

// Levels, with the rule that matters: the level documents intent,
// not severity of feeling.
//   Trace  -- per-iteration detail, off in production by default
//   Debug  -- developer diagnostics, compiled out only in Release if the
//             logging call site is guarded
//   Information -- business events: state transitions, not chatter
//   Warning  -- something unexpected that the system recovered from
//   Error   -- an operation failed and a human needs to know
//   Critical -- the process cannot continue
log.LogDebug("Loaded order graph with {NodeCount} nodes", nodeCount);
log.LogWarning("Retrying {Operation} after transient fault {ErrorCode}", "charge", ex.SqlNumber);
log.LogError(ex, "Failed to persist order {OrderId}", order.Id);
log.LogCritical("Database unreachable; entering degraded mode");

// Guarding an expensive message
if (log.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug))
{
    log.LogDebug("Graph: {Graph}", Describe(graph));   // built only when enabled
}

// Exception overloads attach the type, message, stack and inner chain
try { await ChargeAsync(order, ct); }
catch (PaymentDeclinedException ex)
{
    // The exception is the FIRST argument of the error overload.
    log.LogWarning(ex, "Payment declined for order {OrderId}", order.Id);
    return Result.Failed(ex.Reason);
}

// Scopes: a handle that every log entry inside it inherits.
// This is how a request is reconstructed from ten log lines.
using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
{
    ["OrderId"]   = order.Id,
    ["CustomerId"] = order.CustomerId,
    ["TenantId"]   = tenantId
}))
{
    // Every entry below carries OrderId, CustomerId and TenantId.
    log.LogInformation("Reserving stock");
    // ...
    log.LogInformation("Reserving payment");
}

// Activity: the distributed trace. The W3C headers are extracted
// and injected by the handler; the code only continues or starts one.
//   Applies to: OpenTelemetry 1.x + Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics
//   section 17.6 covers the wiring.
using var activity = ActivitySourceProvider.Source.StartActivity(
    "order.place", ActivityKind.Internal);
activity?.SetTag("order.id", order.Id);
activity?.SetTag("order.lines", order.Lines.Count);
activity?.SetTag("db.system", "mssql");       // semantic conventions

try
{
    // ...
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    activity?.SetStatus(ActivityStatusCode.Error, ex.Message);   // do not swallow silently
    throw;
}

// The same trace context flows into HttpClient automatically when the
// ActivitySource is registered, and into EF Core and Dapper through
// their own instrumentation packages.

Never log: a password, connection string, token, session identifier, card number, national identifier, full name, address, email address or any free-text field a user typed. Redact at the source with [LoggerMessage] attribute methods that take only the identifiers you need, and keep the classifier logic in one place. Log the identifier and the outcome, not the payload.

// The LoggerMessage source generator: a strongly typed, allocation-free,
// pre-formatted log method. Applies to: Microsoft.Extensions.Logging
// abstractions, available since .NET 6.
public static partial class OrderLog
{
    private static readonly ILogger<OrderLog> Log = LoggerFactory
        .Create(b => b.AddConsole()).CreateLogger<typeof(OrderLog), OrderLog>();

    [LoggerMessage(EventId = 1000, Level = LogLevel.Information, Message = "Order {OrderId} placed")]
    public static partial void OrderPlaced(this ILogger logger, int orderId, int lineCount);

    [LoggerMessage(EventId = 1001, Level = LogLevel.Warning, Message = "Stock reservation failed for order {OrderId}")]
    public static partial void StockReservationFailed(
        this ILogger logger, int orderId, Exception exception);
}

// Event ids are stable and searchable. A warning is identifiable by
// its id without reading the message template.
public sealed class OrderService(ILogger<OrderService> log)
{
    public async Task PlaceAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        try { await ReserveAsync(orderId, ct); }
        catch (Exception ex) { log.StockReservationFailed(orderId, ex); throw; }

        log.OrderPlaced(orderId, 3);
    }
}

The source generator produces a method that checks the level, formats the message once, and only allocates when the level is enabled. The static field form is a convenience for a static logger in infrastructure code; in a service, inject ILogger<T> and pass it to the generated extension method.

Exercises 14

  1. Register a service set in all three lifetimes and log the instance hash code from each consumer. Record exactly which instances are shared across two requests and which are not.
  2. Deliberately create a captive dependency (a singleton taking a scoped service), run with ValidateScopes = true, and then without it. Document the exception you get without validation and the moment it occurs.
  3. Register two IWarehouseGateway implementations as keyed services and resolve both from a single consumer, then enumerate the keys. Confirm the count of registered keys.
  4. Implement an IOptionsMonitor<T> singleton that reacts to a configuration change without a restart, and prove the change is observed by changing the underlying file or environment variable at runtime.
  5. Configure an options class with three Validate predicates, one of which depends on another value, and confirm that ValidateOnStart fails the process at boot rather than on the first request that reads the option.
  6. Add a scope carrying OrderId and CustomerId around a multi-step operation, and reconstruct the whole operation from the log output alone. Then write a test that asserts a secret string never appears in captured log output.
  7. Replace five interpolated log calls with [LoggerMessage] methods and compare the measured allocation of a hot loop before and after using GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread.

15 · Testing for Enterprise Systems

15.1 xUnit: facts, theories and async fixtures15.2 Parallelism, collections and shared state15.3 Substitutes and the ownership rule15.4 Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory15.5 Database testing: in-memory, SQLite and Testcontainers15.6 Coverage, arrange-act-assert and naming

An enterprise test suite has three tiers with different purposes and different costs: fast unit tests that isolate one behaviour, integration tests that exercise the composition root in memory, and container tests that run against a real database engine. This chapter documents each tier, the tools that make them practical, and the specific ways a test suite can pass while production fails.

Applies to: xUnit.net v3, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk 18.x, NSubstitute 5.x or Moq 4.20+, coverlet 6.x, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing 10.0, Testcontainers for .NET 4.x. Requirements: the container tier requires a Docker-compatible runtime; the SQLite tier requires the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite package.

15.1 xUnit: facts, theories and async fixtures

A unit test is a method with no parameters that either throws or does not. A theory is a method with parameters, supplied by inline data, member data or class data. Setup that requires an asynchronous resource belongs in IAsyncLifetime rather than in the test constructor, because a constructor cannot be asynchronous.

using Xunit;

public sealed class OrderTests
{
    private readonly OrderService _service;
    private readonly Substitute.For<IOrderRepository> _repository;
    private readonly Substitute.For<IPricingService> _pricing = Substitute.For<IPricingService>();

    // The constructor is synchronous: build cheap, in-memory doubles only.
    public OrderTests()
    {
        _repository = Substitute.For<IOrderRepository>();
        _service = new OrderService(
            _repository, new OrderValidator(), _pricing, TimeProvider.System, NullLogger.Instance);
    }

    // A fact: no parameters, one behaviour
    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceAsync_persists_an_order()
    {
        await _pricing.GetAsync(new CreateOrder(
            new List<OrderLine> { new("SKU-1", 2) }, new CancellationToken());

        await _service.PlaceAsync(new PlaceOrderCommand(
            CustomerId: 42,
            Lines: [new OrderLine("SKU-1", 2)]), CancellationToken.None);

        await _repository.Received(1).AddAsync(
            Arg.Is<Order>(o => o.CustomerId == 42 && o.Lines.Count == 1),
            Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
    }

    // A theory with inline data: the same behaviour across cases
    [Theory]
    [InlineData(0,    false)]
    [InlineData(1,    false)]
    [InlineData(2,    true)]
    [InlineData(1000, true)]
    public async Task RequiresApproval_depends_on_quantity(int quantity, bool expected)
    {
        var command = new PlaceOrderCommand(1, [ new OrderLine("SKU", quantity) ]);

        bool actual = await _service.RequiresApprovalAsync(command, CancellationToken.None);

        Assert.Equal(expected, actual);
    }

    // MemberData: computed cases, including complex objects
    public static TheoryData<string, Money, string> InvalidTotals() => new()
    {
        { "negative", new Money(-1m, "GBP"), "TotalAmount" },
        { "zero",     new Money(0m,  "GBP"), "TotalAmount" },
        { "bad currency", new Money(10m, "XYZ"), "Currency" }
    };

    [Theory, MemberData(nameof(InvalidTotals))]
    public async Task Rejects_invalid_totals(string scenario, Money total, string expectedField)
    {
        var result = await _service.ValidateAsync(total, CancellationToken.None);

        Assert.False(result.IsValid);
        Assert.Contains(result.Errors, e => e.Field == expectedField);
    }

    // ClassData when the case needs a fresh mutable object per test
    public sealed class CaseFactory : TheoryData<Order>
    {
        public CaseFactory()
        {
            this.Add(new Order(1, 10m, new List<OrderLine>()));
            this.Add(new Order(2, 20m, new List<OrderLine>()));
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task An_order_can_be_archived(Order order) { }

    // Async assertion: ThrowsAsync for asynchronous, Throws for synchronous
    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceAsync_throws_when_validation_fails()
    {
        var bad = new PlaceOrderCommand(-1, []);

        var ex = await Assert.ThrowsAsync<ValidationException>(
            () => _service.PlaceAsync(bad, CancellationToken.None));

        Assert.Equal("CustomerId", ex.Field);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Constructor_throws_for_null()
    {
        Assert.Throws<ArgumentNullException>(() => new OrderService(null!, new OrderValidator(), _pricing, TimeProvider.System, NullLogger.Instance));
    }
}

MemberData members are evaluated once and shared, so a mutable case object leaks between tests. Prefer an immutable record or a ClassData instance per test. Assert.ThrowsAsync awaits the returned task and fails on a different exception type, which is what makes it more useful than try/catch in a test.

15.2 Parallelism, collections and shared state

xUnit runs test collections in parallel by default, one per collection fixture. That is a feature for speed and a source of intermittent failures for anything that touches shared state: a file, a static, a singleton, an in-memory database name, or a fixed port.

// A fixture that owns an expensive shared resource
public sealed class HttpServerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory = new();
    public HttpClient Client { get; private set; } = null!;

    // async setup: the only place a database or a listener can be created
    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _factory.EnsureInitializedAsync();
        Client = _factory.CreateClient();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        Client?.Dispose();
        await _factory.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

// CollectionDefinition binds a fixture to every test in the collection.
// Tests inside one collection run sequentially; collections run in parallel.
[CollectionDefinition("server")]
public sealed class ServerCollection : ICollectionFixture<HttpServerFixture>;

[Collection("server")]
public sealed class OrderEndpointTests(HttpServerFixture server)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task POST_orders_returns_201()
    {
        var response = await server.Client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { CustomerId = 1 });

        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Created, response.StatusCode);
    }
}

// Disable parallelism in the assembly when a shared resource cannot
// be isolated. Put this in a file ending with AssemblyInfo.cs
[assembly: CollectionBehavior(DisableTestParallelization = true, MaxParallelThreads = 4)]
//   Applies to: xUnit.net v2 and v3, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk

// A shared resource that forces the issue: a fixed file path
//   static readonly string TempFile = "/tmp/orders.csv";   // parallel tests collide
// Fix: one path per test, derived from the test name or a GUID
//   string path = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), $"{Guid.NewGuid():N}.csv");

// Static state in the code under test is the real hazard
//   static Cache _cache;   // test A writes, test B reads -- intermittent
// Fix: inject the state (section 14.1) or serialise with a collection

// Time is state too. Inject TimeProvider rather than reading DateTime.UtcNow
// in a test, so the test controls the clock.
public sealed class FakeTimeProvider(DateTimeOffset start) : TimeProvider
{
    private DateTimeOffset _now = start;
    public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => _now;
    public void Advance(TimeSpan by) => _now = _now.Add(by);
}

[Fact]
public async Task Order_is_archived_after_ninety_days()
{
    var clock = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
    var service = new OrderService(clock: clock, /* ... */);

    clock.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(91));

    await service.ArchiveAsync();
    // assert with no sleep, no flakiness, no real waiting
}

Diagnosis order for an intermittent failure: shared static, fixed file path, fixed port, a container started with a fixed name, a test that depends on ordering within a collection, a system clock, a culture-dependent comparison, a locale-dependent formatting, and finally thread-safety. Disable test parallelisation in the assembly, re-run the failing test fifty times, and the cause is usually visible immediately. Re-enable it and fix the cause; do not ship the workaround permanently.

15.3 Substitutes and the ownership rule

A substitute returns configured values and records calls. It is a tool for isolating a unit from a collaborator, which is only legitimate when the collaborator is a seam you control or a boundary you own. Mocking the code you are testing verifies the mock.

// NSubstitute: terse, and the default choice for .NET
public sealed class NotificationServiceTests
{
    // Argument matchers
    var repo = Substitute.For<IOrderRepository>();
    repo.GetAsync(new OrderId(42)).Returns(new Order(42, 10m, []));
    repo.GetAsync(Arg.Is<OrderId>(id => id.Value > 0)).Returns(new Order(1, 1m, []));
    repo.GetAsync(Arg.Any<OrderId>()).Returns(info => new Order(info.Arg<OrderId>().Value, 1m, []));

    // An unmatched call on a substitute returns a default value, not an
    // exception. For a substitute that must answer every call, this is
    // auto-substitution and it can mask a missing setup.
    //   repo.Received().GetAsync(Arg.Any<OrderId>());   // call assertion
    //   repo.DidNotReceive().DeleteAsync(Arg.Any<OrderId>());
    //   repo.Received(1).AddAsync(Arg.Is<Order>(o => o.IsPaid), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
    //   repo.Received().GetAsync(Arg.Is<OrderId>(id => id.Value == 42));

    // Throwing from a substitute models a failure without a try/catch in the test
    var flaky = Substitute.For<IPricingService>();
    flaky.GetAsync(Arg.Any<Order>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
         .Returns(_ => throw new TimeoutException("upstream"));

    // Argument matchers must cover whole arguments; combining a matcher
    // with a literal in one call is a compile error in NSubstitute.

    // Moq: the alternative, when a test suite already uses it
    var mock = new Mock<IOrderRepository>();
    mock.Setup(r => r.GetAsync(It.IsAny<OrderId>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(new Order(42, 10m, []));
    mock.Verify(r => r.AddAsync(It.Is<Order>(o => o.IsPaid), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()), Times.Once);
    mock.VerifyNoOtherCalls();        // strict interaction coverage
}

// Do not mock what you do not own.
//   Bad:  new Mock<DbContext>() and stub Set<T> -- tests the mock, not EF Core
//   Good: define IOrderRepository in your application, mock that, and cover
//         the EF Core implementation with a real database test (15.5)
//   Good: mock your own IPricingService, not HttpClient
//   Bad:  mocking ILogger<T> and asserting on Log() -- couples the test to
//         log text, which is not a behaviour of the service

// The seam that makes this work: inject the clock, not DateTime.UtcNow
// The seam that makes HttpClient testable: IHttpClientFactory plus a
// DelegatingHandler test double
//   sealed class StubHandler(Func<HttpRequestMessage, HttpResponseMessage> respond)
//       : HttpMessageHandler
//   {
//       protected override Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(
//           HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
//           => Task.FromResult(respond(request));
//   }
//   var client = factory.CreateClient();  // factory with .AddHttpMessageHandler(() => new StubHandler(...))

Signal-to-noise rule: if a test asserts only that the mock was called, it is testing the wiring, not the behaviour, and it will fail for a reason unrelated to correctness. Prefer asserting on the returned value, the persisted state, or the emitted message. A test suite where most assertions are Received() has a coverage number and no safety.

15.4 Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory

A unit test with substituted collaborators proves the logic of a class. It cannot prove that the application starts, that routing is right, that JSON is shaped as the contract says, or that authentication middleware is in the pipeline. WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> closes that gap by hosting the real application in the test process with no network listener.

// Program is the entry point. In .NET 6+ it is generated as a partial class,
// so add this once in the test project.
//   public partial class Program;   (file: Program.cs, or GlobalUsings)

public sealed class OrdersApiFactory : WebApplicationFactory<Program>
{
    private readonly string _connectionString;

    public OrdersApiFactory()
    {
        // A real SQL Server (Testcontainers) or a file-based SQLite database,
        // one per test class, created before the host starts.
        _connectionString = new SqliteConnectionStringBuilder
        {
            DataSource = "file:orders-tests-" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N") + "?mode=memory&cache=shared",
        }.ToString();
    }

    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.UseEnvironment("Testing");
        builder.ConfigureAppConfiguration((_, configuration) =>
        {
            configuration.AddInMemoryCollection(new Dictionary<string, string?>
            {
                ["ConnectionStrings:Orders"] = _connectionString,
                ["Pricing:BaseUrl"]        = "https://pricing.invalid",
                ["Logging:LogLevel:Default"]  = "Warning"
            });
        });

        // Replace only the collaborator that cannot run in the test
        builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
        {
            services.RemoveAll<DbContextOptions<OrdersDbContext>>();
            services.RemoveAll<OrdersDbContext>();
            services.AddDbContext<OrdersDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlite(_connectionString));

            services.RemoveAll<IPricingService>();
            services.AddScoped<IPricingService, FakePricingService>();
        });
    }

    public async Task EnsureInitializedAsync()
    {
        await using var scope = Services.CreateAsyncScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<OrdersDbContext>();
        await db.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync();
    }
}

[Collection("api")]
public sealed class OrderEndpointTests(OrdersApiFactory factory) : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client = factory.CreateClient();

    public async Task InitializeAsync() => await factory.EnsureInitializedAsync();
    public async Task DisposeAsync() => _client.Dispose();

    [Fact]
    public async Task POST_orders_returns_201_and_a_location_header()
    {
        var response = await _client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders",
            new PlaceOrderRequest(42, [new("SKU-1", 2)]));

        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Created, response.StatusCode);
        Assert.NotNull(response.Headers.Location);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task POST_orders_with_bad_payload_returns_400_with_problem_details()
    {
        var response = await _client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { CustomerId = 0 });

        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest, response.StatusCode);
        var problem = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<ProblemDetails>();
        Assert.NotNull(problem);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GET_unknown_order_returns_404()
    {
        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/orders/999999");
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, response.StatusCode);
    }
}

The in-memory HttpClient speaks to the test server’s in-memory transport, so no port is bound and the test is fast and parallel-safe. ConfigureAppConfiguration overrides configuration after the app’s own files are loaded, so the test values win. RemoveAll followed by a re-registration is the supported way to swap an implementation; without it the original registration remains and the last registration wins for GetRequiredService, which is a common source of confusing test-only behaviour.

Caveats: WebApplicationFactory runs the real middleware pipeline, so a test that requires a real external dependency must replace it — otherwise the test attempts a network call. Static state is shared across tests in the same process; a static cache populated by one test changes the behaviour of the next. WebApplicationFactory does not cover the Kestrel pipeline, TLS, HTTP/2 or the deployment manifest; a smoke test against a published artifact (section 17.6) is still required before release.

15.5 Database testing: in-memory, SQLite and Testcontainers

A database-backed test needs a real database engine, because the behaviour under test is the SQL that EF Core generates and the constraints the engine enforces. The in-memory provider is convenient and unsound: it has no SQL, no indexes, no foreign keys and no types, so a test that passes against it can fail against SQL Server.

// Option 1: the in-memory provider. Fast, no container, NOT faithful.
// Applies to: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory 10.x
services.AddDbContext<OrdersDbContext>(o => o.UseInMemoryDatabase(Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N")));

// What it does not enforce: foreign keys, unique indexes, check
// constraints, column types, collation, case sensitivity, decimal
// precision, datetime2 rounding, transactional DDL, or query plans.
// Consequence: a test that asserts "an order without a customer is
// rejected" passes here and fails in production.

// Option 2: SQLite in memory. Applies to:
//   Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite 10.x
services.AddDbContext<OrdersDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseSqlite("Data Source=:memory:"));

await using var connection = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=:memory:");
// The database exists for the lifetime of the open connection.
// The connection must stay open for the whole test.
// For a file that is shared between connections, use a named shared cache:
//   Data Source=file:test?mode=memory&cache=shared
await connection.OpenAsync();
services.AddDbContext<OrdersDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlite(connection));

await using var scope = factory.Services.CreateAsyncScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<OrdersDbContext>();
await db.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync();     // applies the model as DDL

// Caveats: SQLite has no decimal, no datetime2 precision to speak of,
// no stored procedures, no MERGE, and different collation. It catches
// foreign keys, unique indexes and check constraints, which is the point.

// Option 3: a real engine in a container. Applies to:
//   Testcontainers.MsSql 4.x, Testcontainers.PostgreSql 4.x
//   The container is started once per test class and reused.
//   Requires a Docker-compatible runtime; CI needs a service container or
//   a runner with Docker access.
public sealed class SqlServerContainer : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MsSqlContainer _container = new MsSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _container.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync() => await _container.StartAsync();
    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _container.DisposeAsync();
}

[CollectionDefinition("mssql")]
public sealed class MsSqlCollection : ICollectionFixture<SqlServerContainer>;

[Collection("mssql")]
public sealed class OrderRepositoryIntegrationTests(SqlServerContainer container)
{
    private OrdersDbContext CreateContext()
    {
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<OrdersDbContext>()
            .UseSqlServer(container.ConnectionString)
            .Options;
        return new OrdersDbContext(options);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Adding_an_order_without_a_customer_violates_the_foreign_key()
    {
        await using var db = CreateContext();
        await db.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync();

        db.Orders.Add(new Order(1, CustomerId: 999999, 0m, []));

        // The in-memory provider would pass this. SQL Server does not.
        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<DbUpdateException>(() => db.SaveChangesAsync());
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task SaveChanges_rolls_back_both_changes_on_failure()
    {
        await using var db = CreateContext();
        await db.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync();

        db.Customers.Add(new Customer(1, "Acme"));
        db.Orders.Add(new Order(1, CustomerId: 1, 10m, []));
        db.AuditLog.Add(new AuditEntry("x", DateTime.UtcNow) { ViolatesCheckConstraint = true });

        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<DbUpdateException>(() => db.SaveChangesAsync());

        await using var verify = CreateContext();
        Assert.Empty(await verify.Customers.ToListAsync());   // nothing committed
    }
}
ApproachFidelityCost per runEnforces FK and unique indexesRecommended use
EF Core in-memoryNoneMillisecondsNoExploratory work only; never a gate
SQLite in memoryPartialTens of millisecondsYesThe default fast integration tier
Testcontainers SQL ServerHighSeconds, amortised per classYesProvider-specific SQL, migrations, transactions
Shared staging databaseHighNetwork, ordering hazardsYesNever as a test gate; manual verification only

15.6 Coverage, arrange-act-assert and naming

Coverage answers one question: which lines executed. It does not answer whether they executed correctly, whether the assertion was meaningful, or whether the test would fail if the behaviour changed. A suite can reach 100% line coverage and pass with every assertion removed. Coverage is therefore a tool for finding untested areas, not a target to maximise.

// Arrange-act-assert, with the three phases visible and separated.
// The test name states the behaviour, the arrangement, and the outcome,
// so a failure message is readable without opening the file.
[Fact]
public async Task PlaceAsync_with_a_priced_line_persists_the_line_total()
{
    // Arrange
    var repository = Substitute.For<IOrderRepository>();
    var pricing = Substitute.For<IPricingService>();
    pricing.GetAsync("SKU-1", Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
          .Returns(new Price(new Money(4.50m, "GBP")));
    var service = new OrderService(repository, new OrderValidator(), pricing,
                              TimeProvider.System, NullLogger.Instance);
    var command = new PlaceOrderCommand(42, [new OrderLine("SKU-1", 3)]);

    // Act
    var orderId = await service.PlaceAsync(command, CancellationToken.None);

    // Assert on the observable outcome, not on the interaction
    await repository.Received(1).AddAsync(
        Arg.Is<Order>(o => o.Id == orderId
                     && o.Lines.Single().Quantity == 3
                     && o.Lines.Single().UnitPrice == new Money(4.50m, "GBP")
                     && o.Total == new Money(13.50m, "GBP")),
        Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
}

// Coverage collection. Applies to: coverlet.collector 6.x
dotnet test -c Release --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage" --results-directory ./TestResults
dotnet test -c Release /p:CollectCoverage="true" /p:CoverletOutputFormat="cobertura" /p:Threshold=70

// What coverage does and does not tell you
//   Tells you: this method has never run in any test. Fix the gap or
//              delete the method.
//   Tells you: this branch never runs. Usually an unreachable or
//              untested error path.
//   Does not tell you: whether the assertions are correct.
//   Does not tell you: whether the test would fail on a regression.
//   Does not tell you: anything about concurrency, timing or data volume.

// Mutation testing is the only common answer to the third point: it
// changes an operator or a return value and fails the suite if no
// test notices. Applies to: Stryker.NET
dotnet stryker

// Excluding what coverage cannot judge. Applies to: coverlet attributes
[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]
public partial class Program { }              // generated entry point

[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]
public sealed record PlaceOrderRequest(int CustomerId, int[] Lines);

Exclude generated code, DTO constructor plumbing, and simple property forwarding. Do not exclude a method because its test is hard — that is the coverage report telling you something worth knowing. A reasonable target for enterprise code is 70 to 80% branch coverage on the domain and application layers, with no target at all on generated and adapter code.

Name tests for the behaviour, not the method: PlaceAsync_with_a_priced_line_persists_the_line_total survives a rename, whereas TestPlaceAsync does not. A test named after the behaviour is also a specification: a reader can enumerate the expected behaviours of a class by reading its test names, which is the cheapest documentation a codebase can have.

Exercises 15

  1. Write one test that violates a foreign key and run it against the in-memory provider and against SQLite. Record what each one does, and explain the false confidence the in-memory provider creates.
  2. Write a theory with InlineData and the same test with MemberData, then mutate the case object inside the test and observe the cross-test failure. Move to an immutable record or ClassData and confirm the failure is gone.
  3. Add a collection fixture that hosts a WebApplicationFactory, write three endpoint tests, and prove the database is shared between them. Then give each test class its own database name and confirm isolation.
  4. Start a Testcontainers SQL Server, run the EF Core migration against it, and assert that the generated SQL in the migration matches what the container accepted. Repeat against SQLite and record the differences.
  5. Write a test that passes with the in-memory provider and fails against SQLite, then diagnose precisely which provider assumption it depended on. Add it to a documented list of anti-patterns.
  6. Run a fixed set of tests fifty times in a loop with parallelisation disabled, then re-enable it. Investigate every intermittent failure and record the shared state that caused it.
  7. Collect coverage with coverlet for a single module and read the report. Identify the ten lowest-value covered lines (overrides, DTO constructors, generated code) and exclude them with an attribute, then re-measure.

{{-- ARRANGE, ACT, ASSERT — and the rule that makes it worth
     reading: a test that does not READ as those three phases does
     not test one thing. --}}
public sealed class PricingTests
{
    // GOOD: the phases are visible in the structure, and the name
    // states the expectation rather than the method called.
    [Fact]
    public void A_pending_order_over_100_gets_a_5_percent_discount()
    {
        // ARRANGE
        var order = new OrderBuilder()
            .WithStatus(OrderStatus.Pending)
            .WithTotal(200m)
            .Build();
        var pricing = new Pricing();

        // ACT
        var discount = pricing.DiscountFor(order);

        // ASSERT
        Assert.Equal(10m, discount);
    }

    // WRONG: six things set up, one thing asserted, and no reader
    // can tell which of the six the result depends on.
    [Fact]
    public void TestDiscount()
    {
        var order = new Order { Status = OrderStatus.Pending, Total = 200m,
                                Customer = new Customer { Region = "EU",
                                    IsLoyal = true, Segment = "Gold" } };
        var pricing = new Pricing(new Config { BaseRate = 0.1m });
        Assert.Equal(10m, pricing.DiscountFor(order));
    }
    {{-- ^ WHEN THIS FAILS the message is "expected 10, actual 5" and
         nothing about WHY. The builder version produces the same
         failure with a fixture whose every default is documented, so
         a change to the defaults shows up as a change in which
         tests fail. --}}
}

{{-- AND COVERAGE, which is a NUMBER rather than a goal: --}}
public sealed class CoverageRules
{
    // COVERAGE PERCENTAGE measures which lines ran, not which
    // behaviours are correct. 100% coverage with a test that calls
    // the method and asserts nothing is worse than 60% coverage with
    // tests that would fail if the logic were wrong.
    //
    // WHAT IS WORTH MEASURING:
    //   the branch coverage of the DECISION code, not the total
    //   the number of tests that fail when a REQUIREMENT changes
    //     (the only number that tracks value)
    //
    // WHAT IS NOT:
    //   the total percentage, as a gate
    //   any coverage of generated code, of trivial accessors, or of
    //     a method whose only job is to forward
    //
    // WHERE A COVERAGE GATE BELONGS, if anywhere: on the DOMAIN
    // layer, where the branching is the requirement, and nowhere
    // else. A gate that includes plumbing fails on generated files
    // and is then disabled.

    // THE BETTER GATE, which is cheap and catches real regressions:
    public void MutationSurvived() { }
    {{-- ^ If you change '>' to '>=' in a boundary condition and
         every test still passes, the tests are not testing the
         boundary. Coverage would be unchanged too, because the line
         ran either way — which is the clearest argument for
         reading a test rather than counting it. --}}
}

{{-- AND THE THREE THINGS THAT MAKE A TEST SUITE FAIL LATE: --}}
public static class LateFailures
{
    // 1. A TEST THAT ASSERTS ON A SHARED MUTABLE FIXTURE.
    // 2. A TEST THAT DEPENDS ON ORDER, because a previous test
    //    left state behind.
    // 3. A TEST THAT SLEEPS, because it is waiting for something
    //    asynchronous that could be awaited instead.
    {{-- ^ The third is the most common and the least obvious: a
         500 ms sleep to "let the queue drain" is a test that passes
         on a fast machine and fails on a loaded CI agent, and the
         fix is to wait for the signal rather than for a duration —
         which is faster AND more reliable, not slower. --}}
}

16 · Performance, Benchmarking & Diagnostics

16.1 The garbage collector and what allocation costs16.2 Measuring allocations and GC counts16.3 BenchmarkDotNet: a correct harness16.4 Reducing allocations in hot paths16.5 Diagnostics with dotnet-trace, counters and dumps16.6 Native AOT: trade-offs and readiness

Managed .NET performance work has a specific shape: the primary cost is almost always allocation, allocation causes a garbage collection, and a garbage collection costs far more than the code that created the garbage. Latency then follows from two numbers: how much is allocated and how often the collector runs. This chapter documents the mechanisms, the measurement discipline, and the tooling.

Applies to: .NET 10 runtime (CLR 14), BenchmarkDotNet 0.15.x, dotnet-trace / dotnet-counters / dotnet-dump 10.0 SDK tools, PublishAot in the .NET 10 SDK. Caveats: every measurement here is meaningless without a controlled environment: release build, no debugger attached, fixed CPU governor, no other workload on the machine.

16.1 The garbage collector and what allocation costs

The .NET garbage collector is generational and, since .NET 7, concurrent by default. Objects start in generation 0; a survivor is promoted to generation 1 and then to generation 2. Collections of generation 0 are frequent and cheap; generation 2 collections are rare, expensive, and stop-the-world for the managed heap while they mark and sweep. The implication for a latency-sensitive service is that the cost is dominated by gen0 budget exhaustion, not by the total amount of garbage.

// Server GC: one heap and one set of GC threads per logical core.
// More throughput, higher baseline memory, shorter individual pauses.
//   <ServerGarbageCollection>true</ServerGarbageCollection>   in the csproj
//   or DOTNET_gcServer=1 in the environment. This is the default for
//   ASP.NET Core published applications on .NET 7+.

// Workstation GC: one heap. Lower memory, longer single pauses.
//   <ServerGarbageCollection>false</ServerGarbageCollection>
//   or DOTNET_gcWorkstation=1. Choose it for memory-constrained containers
//   with a hard memory limit and a single-core request.

// Concurrent (background) GC: gen2 marking runs on a background thread.
//   <ConcurrentGarbageCollection>true</ConcurrentGarbageCollection>   (default)

// Tiered compilation: methods start at tier 0 and are promoted to tier 1
// after 30 calls, with OSR for long-running loops.
//   <TieredPGO>true</TieredPGO>   dynamic PGO, on by default in .NET 8+

// A value type on the stack costs nothing to collect. The same type as a
// class costs an allocation and eventually a collection.
// Caveat: a struct is copied on assignment and on every method call, so a
// large struct in a loop copies more than it saves.
ReadOnlySpan<byte> data = payload;      // stack, no GC involvement

// Boxing allocates, silently. Three common sources:
//   1. converting a value type to object, or to an interface it implements
//   2. an unconstrained generic: T in List<T> is boxed for value types
//   3. calling a non-generic API such as Array.Sort(IComparer),
//      object.Equals, or Console.WriteLine(int)
object boxed = 42;                              // allocation
var asObject = (object)point;               // allocation
IComparable boxedComparable = 42;                     // allocation

// Every generic collection with T = int, DateTime, decimal, or a
// custom struct allocates per element, because the array is
//   int[]  Array   (unmanaged storage)     -- no boxing, ~24 bytes/element
//   T[]    T[]     (shared reference)     -- boxed, ~40+ bytes/element
List<int> a = new();                // OK: int[] storage
List<Money> b = new();               // boxed per element
Money[] c = [new Money(0m), new Money(0m)];  // boxed per element
Memory<Money> d = new();             // unmanaged, no boxing

// Generic maths (C# 11, chapter 12) removes boxing from numeric code
static TSum Sum<TSum>(TSum a, TSum b) where TSum : INumber<TSum>
    => a + b;

// The allocation is on the heap, and the value must survive the
// method that created it. stackalloc does not.
Span<int> rented = stackalloc int[256];     // zero heap, 1 KB on the stack
// stackalloc inside a loop or a recursion is a stack overflow. This is
// the one rule that must be respected without exception.

Because tiered compilation delays full optimisation, a micro-benchmark of an untiered method is meaningless. Any measurement taken inside a single method invocation, or by Stopwatch around a loop, is a measurement of the tier 0 or tier 1 code and of the stopwatch overhead, and should be discarded.

16.2 Measuring allocations and GC counts

Two runtime counters answer most performance questions without a profiler: how many bytes a code path allocates, and how many collections those allocations cause. Measuring them is a two-line change and belongs in a unit test, which makes an allocation regression a build failure rather than a production surprise.

// Bytes allocated by the current thread since it started. The delta across
// the measured region is the region's allocation cost.
long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
var result = Process(payload);
long allocated = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;

// Collection counts before and after: the per-generation deltas are the
// direct measure of "how much did this cost the collector".
// In .NET 7+ the parameterless overload returns the current thread's view.
int gen0Before = GC.CollectionCount(0);
// ...
//   gen0Delta = GC.CollectionCount(0) - gen0Before
// A CPU-bound test with zero allocation has a zero gen0 delta; that is
// the property worth asserting.

// A budget test. Thresholds are stated so the intent is reviewable.
[Fact]
public void ParseHeader_allocates_nothing()
{
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> input = "GET /orders HTTP/1.1"u8;

    // Warm up so the tiered JIT and any static initialisation are done
    // before the measured region.
    HeaderParser.Parse(input);
    HeaderParser.Parse(input);

    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    // ReSharper disable once ReturnValueOfPureMethodIsNotUsed
    HeaderParser.Parse(input);
    long allocated = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;

    Assert.Equal(0, allocated);
}

// Related counters worth reading in a process under load
//   GC.GetTotalMemory(false)                  managed bytes currently held
//   GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes()              cumulative, monotonic
//   GC.CollectionCount(n)                     cumulative per generation
//   GC.GetGCMemoryInfo()                      detailed: fragmentation, budget
//   AppContext.GetData("System.GC.Server")    confirms the GC mode
//   AppContext.GetData("System.GC.Concurrent")
//   AppContext.GetData("System.GC.RetainVM")   memory retention behaviour

// What a single allocation costs, in order of magnitude:
//   the pointer bump and zeroing        -- nanoseconds, and it is a cache miss
//   the eventual gen0 collection        -- proportional to surviving objects
//   promotion of a long-lived object    -- a gen1, then a gen2 collection
//   the gen2 collection                  -- the latency spike you measure
// Allocating one byte per request in a 10k rps service is 800 MB/day of
// gen0 pressure; the pause is paid on a request thread.

GC.TryStartNoGCRegion is available for short measurement windows and for latency-critical work with a known allocation ceiling, but it is not a general tuning knob: the region ends on the first collection, has a hard size limit, and on a latency-critical server the risk of exceeding it is a full blocking gen2 while no region is active. Treat it as a measurement tool.

16.3 BenchmarkDotNet: a correct harness

A benchmark that is not run through BenchmarkDotNet does not measure the code. It measures the stopwatch overhead, the tier 0 JIT, the branch predictor, the dead-code elimination that the optimiser performs on a discarded result, and the noise of an unquiet machine. The harness exists to remove all five.

// A separate project. Never referenced by the product.
//   <PackageReference Include="BenchmarkDotNet" Version="0.15.2" />
//   <PackageReference Include="BenchmarkDotNet.Diagnostics.Windows" Version="*" />
//   (the last line is only needed for MemoryDiagnoser on Windows)

public class OrderParserBenchmarks
{
    private byte[] _payload = null!;
    private List<OrderLine> _lines = null!;

    [GlobalSetup]
    public void Setup()
    {
        _payload = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("name=widget;qty=3;price=9.99|name=gadget;qty=1;price=19.50");
        _lines = new List<OrderLine> { new("SKU-1", 2), new("SKU-2", 5) };
    }

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public void SubstringBaseline() => ParseWithSubstring(_payload);

    [Benchmark]
    public void ParseWithSpan() => ParseWithSpan(_payload);

    [Benchmark]
    [MemoryDiagnoser]
    public void ParseWithStringSplit() => ParseWithStringSplit(_payload);

    // Consumer: prevents dead-code elimination. Without it the JIT is free
    // to delete the whole call, and the benchmark reports nanoseconds.
    [Benchmark]
    public void LinqOverList() => Consumer = _lines.Select(l => l.Sku).ToList();

    public int Consumer { get; set; }

    // Multiple operations measured in one pass
    [Benchmark]
    [OperationsPerInvoke(1000)]
    public void ThousandComparisons() => _lines.Sort();

    // Parameters: each combination is a separate benchmark
    [Benchmark]
    public void Count(int n) { // ... }

    [Params(1, 100, 10_000)]
    public int Size { get; set; }

    [Benchmark]
    public void ParseSized() { // uses Size }
}

// The runner. Applies to: BenchmarkDotNet 0.15.x
public static class Program
{
    public static void Main()
    {
        BenchmarkRunner.Run<OrderParserBenchmarks>(
            config: ManualConfig.Create(DefaultConfig.Instance)
                .AddColumn(StatisticColumn.P95)
                .WithOptions(ConfigOptions.DisableOptimizationsValidator));
    }
}

// dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/
// Do not use Debug. Do not measure inside a unit test. Do not measure on
// a laptop with a browser open. Do not compare runs from different
// machines, or from the same machine with different runtime versions.

// Reading the output
//   Mean          -- the number to compare
//   Error         -- 99.9% confidence interval half-width; if it exceeds the
//                    difference you are claiming, the claim is noise
//   StdDev        -- spread; a high spread means the machine is not quiet
//   Allocated     -- with MemoryDiagnoser; the number that generalises
//   Gen0/1/2      -- collections caused by the operation; zero is the goal
// A 2x win that allocates 10 KB per call is a latency win and a throughput
// loss. Report both columns.

BenchmarkDotNet emits generated projects into bin/Release/net10.0/, builds them, runs each benchmark across multiple processes, and produces an HTML report. The build step is why the project must be a standalone project with no dependency on test infrastructure, and why the first run takes minutes.

The three mistakes that invalidate a benchmark: running in Debug or in a process with a debugger attached; measuring a method call whose result is discarded; and comparing numbers produced by different harness configurations. A fourth, subtler one: benchmarking a case the production code never takes. Profile first, then benchmark the hot path you actually observed.

16.4 Reducing allocations in hot paths

The techniques below are ordered by how often they matter. Spans and pooling come first because they eliminate the allocation outright. LINQ is last because it is the most commonly blamed and the least often the cause.

// 1. Spans: parse without allocating.
static decimal ParsePrice(ReadOnlySpan<char> span)
{
    // Span<T>.TryParse writes into the stack. No string, no array.
    if (decimal.TryParse(span, NumberStyles.Number, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out decimal value))
    {
        return value;
    }
    throw new FormatException("price");
}

// Slicing is free: a span is a pointer and a length.
//   field.AsSpan(start, length)      view without a copy
//   field.AsSpan(start..end)        range syntax, still a view
//   span.ToArray()                 the explicit, and only, copy
ReadOnlySpan<char> rest = new ReadOnlySpan<char>(line.AsSpan());
int colon = rest.IndexOf(':');
ReadOnlySpan<char> key = rest[..colon];
ReadOnlySpan<char> value = rest[(colon + 1)..];

// 2. ArrayPool for buffers above stackalloc size.
//    stackalloc is right up to a few hundred bytes and is wrong above
//    that: it puts the buffer on every frame.
//    Applies to: System.Buffers.ArrayPool<T>.Shared, .NET 6+
byte[] buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(4096);
try
{
    int read = ReadInto(buffer, ct);   // the actual bytes read
    // The array may be larger than requested. Use read, not buffer.Length.
    Process(buffer.AsSpan(0, read));
}
finally
{
    ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer, clearArray: true);  // clear if it held secrets
}

// 3. string.Create writes directly into the final string, once.
//    Applies to: string.Create<TState>(int, TState, SpanAction), .NET 6+
//    This is the correct way to build a string from a char buffer:
//    no intermediate, no double copy, no StringBuilder.
string invoice = string.Create(24, order, (span, state) =>
{
    // span.Length is 24 here; "INV-" is 4, 10 digits, "-" is 1, 9 digits
    "INV-".AsSpan().CopyTo(span);
    state.Number[10].TryFormat(span[4..], out int written, "D10");
    // ...
});

// 4. ValueTask for an operation that usually completes synchronously.
//    Applies to: IValueTaskSource, .NET 5+
//    Use it when the completion is already cached, and a Task would allocate.
public ValueTask<int> TryReadAsync(Memory<byte> buffer, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if TryReadSynchronously(buffer.Span, out int read))
    {
        // A ValueTask completed from a value: no Task allocation
        return new ValueTask<int>(read);
    }
    // Not complete: fall back to a Task-backed ValueTask
    return new ValueTask<int>(ReadSlowAsync(buffer, ct));
}

// A ValueTask may be awaited only once. Awaiting a Task twice is free;
// awaiting a ValueTask twice is a bug. Do not store one in a field, do not
// return it from two branches and await at the caller.

// 5. foreach versus for on an array.
//    On a T[] array, foreach is bounds-check-eliminated and matches a for
//    loop. On List<T>, foreach uses a struct enumerator and no allocation.
//    On IEnumerable<T>, foreach allocates an enumerator unless the type is
//    List<T> or an array. That is the whole difference.

// 6. LINQ: measure before removing.
//    A LINQ chain allocates a closure object, an enumerator, and one delegate
//    per capturing lambda. Three chained operators over a List is roughly
//    200 bytes per call.
//    In a request handler, once per call, this is irrelevant.
//    In a loop over ten thousand elements, it is the whole cost.
//    Where LINQ is fine: once per request, over a bounded set, in a
//    controller or a startup path. Do not hand-rewrite it.

// 7. The one rule for a loop that runs per element on a hot path
//    If a value is invariant, compute it before the loop. Hoisting a
//    ToUpper() or a Parse() out of a loop is usually a larger win than
//    replacing the loop with spans.

Escape analysis for reference types: .NET 8 added object stack allocation for certain patterns, including lock on a new object and a stackalloc span converted to a local. This is an optimisation, not an API: do not write code that depends on it. A benchmark with and without the pattern tells you what the runtime did today on your version.

16.5 Diagnostics with dotnet-trace, counters and dumps

Three tools cover the three questions asked in production: what is the process doing (traces), what are its rates and memory doing (counters), and what is in its memory (dumps). Each ships in the .NET 10 SDK and attaches to a running process by PID.

# dotnet-counters: live rates, attach to a running process
#   Applies to: .NET SDK 10.0, runtime counters 6+
dotnet-counters monitor --process-id 1234
dotnet-counters monitor --process-id 1234 --counters System.Runtime,Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting
dotnet-counters ps                                       # list .NET processes
dotnet-counters collect --process-id 1234 --format nettrace --output cpu.nettrace

#   The counters that answer the usual questions:
#     cpu-usage              total processor time as a percentage
#     working-set            resident memory (includes the GC heap)
#     gc-heap-size           managed heap bytes
#     gen-0-gc-count         gen0 collections per second -- the allocation rate
#     gen-1-gc-count         promotion pressure
#     gen-2-gc-count         the pause you are hunting
#     time-in-gc             percentage of time in collection
#     exception-count        unhandled and first-chance exceptions
#     threadpool-thread-count, threadpool-queue-length, threadpool-completed-items-count
#     active-timer-count      thread pool starvation signal
#     assembly-count, method-count      dynamic assembly churn
#     monitor-lock-contention-count      contention you are paying for
#     aspnetcore-requests-per-second, total-requests, failed-requests
#     aspnetcore-request-duration        p50/p90/p99, available on the
#                                    Histogram metrics; view with
#                                    --refresh, or the SDK viewer

# dotnet-trace: sampling or detailed CPU traces
dotnet-trace collect --process-id 1234 --profile cpu-sampling --duration 00:00:30 --output cpu.nettrace
dotnet-trace collect --process-id 1234 --providers Microsoft-DotNETCore-SampleProfiler
dotnet-trace report cpu.nettrace topN
dotnet-trace convert cpu.nettrace --format speedscope
dotnet-trace ps

#   Read a trace in Visual Studio (Windows) or PerfView (cross-platform):
#   CPU Usage view, then the GC and Allocation Stacks tabs. The allocation
#   stacks view names the exact call site responsible for the bytes.

# dotnet-dump: a heap snapshot
dotnet-dump collect --process-id 1234 --type Heap --output heap.dmp
dotnet-dump analyze heap.dmp
#   > dumpheap -stat                 count and size by type -- start here
#   > dumpheap -type System.String -min 1000
#   > gcroot <address>                who is keeping the object alive
#   > dumpobj <address>                fields and values
#   > gcnew                the difference since the previous gcnew
#   > setclr -r               not supported on Linux; use createdump instead

# In-application instrumentation, always on, for the metrics that
# must reach a dashboard rather than a terminal
private static readonly Meter Meter = new("Contoso.Orders");
private static readonly Counter<long> Placed = Meter.CreateCounter<long>(
    "orders.placed", unit: "{order}", description: "Orders successfully placed");
private static readonly Histogram<double> Duration = Meter.CreateHistogram<double>(
    "orders.place.duration", "ms", "Time to place an order");

public async Task PlaceAsync(int customerId, CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var timer = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    try
    {
        // ...
        Placed.Add(1, new KeyValuePair<string, object?>(
            "customer.tier", _cache.Tier(customerId)));
        Duration.Record(timer.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }
    finally
    {
        // Record in finally so a failure is still measured
    }
}

Production safety: dotnet-dump collect suspends the target while the dump is taken, which on a latency-sensitive service is an outage of a second or more and may trigger a liveness probe. Take dumps on a second replica, set a memory cap with --maxdumpSize, and prefer dotnet-gcdump (a much smaller, sub-second file) for a first look. A --type Heap dump of a 4 GB process is a 4 GB file: plan the disk and the transfer.

The order of operations for a performance complaint is fixed: read the counters first to identify whether the problem is CPU, allocation, GC pauses, lock contention or thread pool starvation; then take a trace to attribute CPU; then take a dump only if the evidence points at retained memory. Taking a dump first is the most common wasted hour in performance work.

16.6 Native AOT: trade-offs and readiness

Native AOT compiles a managed application ahead of time to a native executable with no JIT, no runtime, and no managed heap. The result starts in single-digit milliseconds, uses tens of megabytes of memory rather than hundreds, and has no garbage collector pauses because there is no garbage collector. The cost is a set of hard constraints on what the application may do at run time.

// Enable it. Applies to: .NET 8+ for libraries, .NET 8+ for apps;
// supported for ASP.NET Core APIs since .NET 8.
//   <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
//   <InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>   optional, smaller
//   <StripSymbols>false</StripSymbols>   keep symbols for prod dumps
//   <IlcInvariantGlobalization>true</IlcInvariantGlobalization>
//   <EventSourceSupport>false</EventSourceSupport>
//   <MetadataUpdaterSupport>false</MetadataUpdaterSupport>
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true -o ./out

// What it removes
//   the JIT                -- no tiered compilation, no first-call penalty
//   the managed heap        -- values live where the compiler put them
//   the garbage collector    -- no gen2 pauses, no time-in-gc
//   System.Reflection.Emit  -- and therefore most dynamic code
//   the runtime assembly     -- a 60-80 MB framework-dependent deployment
//                             becomes a single 5-15 MB native binary
//   the runtimeconfig.json and dependency resolution: the file IS the app

// What it breaks, in order of how often it is discovered late
//   1. Reflection over types not reachable from a static root.
//      Fix: <IlcTrimMode>partial</IlcTrimMode> and [DynamicallyAccessedMembers],
//      or [RequiresUnreferencedCode] on APIs you cannot analyse.
//   2. dynamic and Expression.Compile(). Not supported.
//   3. Libraries that reflect over their own types: many serializers,
//      some ORM mapping helpers, DI-by-convention.
//      Fix: source-generated serializers (System.Text.Json JsonSerializerContext,
//      or a third-party source generator).
//   4. Reflection-based serialisation of arbitrary graphs. The source
//      generator emits the metadata at compile time instead.
//   5. Stack traces lose method-to-symbol fidelity unless symbols are kept.
//   6. Debugging: the debugger works, but the experience is not identical to a
//      managed process. dotnet-dump is not supported on a native AOT process.

// Source-generated JSON: the required pattern for Native AOT
[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull)]
public sealed partial class OrdersJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

//   builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(o =>
//       o.SerializerOptions.TypeInfoResolverChain.Insert(0, OrdersJsonContext.Default));

// Compatibility check, and the fastest way to know whether a codebase is
// ready: publish with warnings as errors. The trim analyser reports
// every reachable reflection site it cannot prove safe.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true -p:TrimmerSingleWarn=false

// Warnings that are acceptable to suppress explicitly, and those that are not
//   Acceptable:  RequiresUnreferencedCode on a helper you have reviewed
//   Acceptable:  DynamicallyAccessedMembers on a property the analyser missed
//   Not acceptable: IL2026/IL2075/IL3050 in a code path you have not analysed,
//   and "fix it later" in a service that handles money or personal data

// Readiness for enterprise use, stated plainly:
//   A minimal API or MVC API whose serialisation is source-generated, with no
//   dynamic code, no runtime reflection over unknown types, and a tested
//   set of dependencies -- ready. Ship it.
//   A service that loads plugin assemblies at run time, uses an ORM that
//   reflects over a model discovered at run time, or depends on Expression trees
//   compiled to IL -- not ready, and the analysis cost exceeds the benefit.
//   Measure the actual benefit first: for most CRUD APIs the dominant cost is
//   the database, and a native binary will not move p99 latency.
ConcernManaged JITNative AOT
Cold startMilliseconds to low hundredsSingle-digit milliseconds, plus native link time
Memory baseline60-120 MB typical API10-30 MB typical API
GC pausesPresent, mitigated by server GCNone; no managed heap
Dynamic codeSupportedNot supported; reflection must be declared
Third-party library supportTotalPartial; each dependency must be verified
Build timeSecondsMinutes; a native linker runs
Debugging and dumpsFull toolingReduced; no dotnet-dump
Trimming riskNone by defaultReal: an undeclared reflection site fails at run time

Exercises 16

  1. Write a GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread budget test for a parsing method, then convert it to a span-based version and record the allocation before and after. Add both numbers to the test name.
  2. Write a method that boxes accidentally three different ways (cast to object, interface conversion, unconstrained generic call) and prove the boxing with a budget test that fails.
  3. Build a BenchmarkDotNet project with three implementations of the same parsing task, add [MemoryDiagnoser] and a Consumer property, and record mean, error and allocated for each. Then delete the harness and show how far off a Stopwatch-in-a-unit-test measurement is.
  4. Compare foreach and for over an array and over a List<T> with the harness. Explain why one shows a difference and the other does not.
  5. Replace a StringBuilder in a hot path with string.Create and a stackalloc span, and measure. Then deliberately put a stackalloc inside a loop and observe the stack overflow.
  6. Attach dotnet-counters to a running API, drive load, and record gen0, gen1 and gen2 counts per second plus time-in-gc. Then capture a dotnet-trace and locate the top allocation call site.
  7. Enable PublishAot on a small ASP.NET Core API, resolve every trim warning, and measure start-up time and memory against the same binary published normally. List the three dependencies that required the most work.

{{-- NATIVE AOT COMPILES THE WHOLE PROGRAM INTO ONE NATIVE BINARY,
     and the cost is that anything discovered at RUN TIME has to have
     been reachable at BUILD TIME. --}}
public static class TheTrade
{
    // WINS:
    //   STARTUP: no JIT, no runtime to load — a few milliseconds
    //           rather than tens or hundreds.
    //   FOOTPRINT: tens of megabytes rather than a runtime plus a
    //              framework directory.
    //   THROUGHPUT: no tiered JIT warming up, so a short-lived
    //               process spends its whole life at full speed.
    //
    // LOSES:
    //   REFLECTION AND DYNAMIC: a member resolved by name is not
    //     FOUND unless the analyser saw the name as a string
    //     literal, because there is no JIT at run time to compile
    //     it.
    //   EXPRESSION TREES: an EF Core LINQ query is compiled to a
    //     delegate at run time, which is a compilation AOT cannot
    //     perform.
    //   EMIT AND LOADING: Assembly.Load of an assembly not
    //     referenced at build time does not work.
    //   INTEROP: every P/Invoke target must be reachable, and a
    //     callback from native code into managed code needs a
    //     function pointer that survives the trimmer.
}

{{-- WHAT MAKES A TYPE AOT-SAFE, and it is a set of requirements
     rather than a flag: --}}
// Needs an UNMANAGED CONSTRUCTOR or a static one, because the
// generic instantiations must be generated for the exact types used.
public sealed class Formatter : IFormattable
{
    public Formatter() { }                     // parameterless ctor

    public string Format(string? format, IFormatProvider? provider)
    {
        // NO REFLECTION: no Type.GetType, no Activator, no
        // Assembly.Load. The whole point is that everything
        // reachable is known now.
        return string.Create(provider ?? System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                             $"{format}");
    }
}

// A GENERIC over a reference type: one instantiation for all
// reference types, so this is CHEAP.
// A GENERIC over a value type: one instantiation PER value type, and
// a library with a dozen generic helpers over ten value types has
// 120 copies in the binary.
public readonly struct Box<T>(T value) { public T Value = value; }
{{-- ^ WHICH IS WHY A GENERIC ALGORITHM LIBRARY IS A POOR AOT
     CITIZEN: every distinct value-type combination multiplies the
     code size, and the AOT binary trades the runtime's size for
     the program's. --}}

{{-- AND THE ATTRIBUTES THAT FIX SPECIFIC FAILURES, applied only
     where the diagnostic says to: --}}
public static class Attributes
{
    // [DynamicallyAccessedMembers] tells the trimmer that a member
    // is reached reflectively, so it must be preserved.
    [UnconditionalSuppressMessage("Trimming", "IL2075",
        Justification = "Only these two members are reached by name.")]
    public static int Count(object target) =>
        target.GetType().GetProperty("Id")!.GetValue(target) is int id ? id : 0;

    // [RequiresUnreferencedCode] MARKS AN API as unsafe under
    // trimming, so the compiler warns at every CALL SITE rather
