    // than the failure appearing at run time.
    [RequiresUnreferencedCode("Loads a plugin by name.")]
    public static object LoadPlugin(string assemblyName) =>
        System.Reflection.Assembly.Load(assemblyName);
}
{{-- ^ THE ATTRIBUTES ARE NOT EXCEPTIONS TO WRITE. Each one says
     "the trimmer cannot see this, and I am telling you where". A
     trimmer warning silenced without an attribute reappears as a
     NullReferenceException on a machine you do not control. --}}

{{-- AND THE READINESS CHECKLIST, which is short: --}}
public static async Task<bool> IsReady(WebApplication app)
{
    // 1. NO REFLECTION in the request path. If you need a plugin
    //    system, AOT is the wrong deployment model.
    // 2. NO EXPRESSION-TREE-ONLY LIBRARY: EF Core is NOT AOT-
    //    ready for its LINQ path. (Compile-time-generated models
    //    are a different story and are documented separately.)
    // 3. EVERYTHING REGISTERED IS REACHABLE: a dependency-
    //    injection registration by type is analysed; one by a
    //    factory lambda is a boundary the trimmer cannot cross.
    // 4. THE PUBLISH IS SELF-CONTAINED by definition, so the size
    //    number is not comparable with the framework-dependent one.

    await Task.CompletedTask;
    return true;
}
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE HONEST SUMMARY: AOT IS RIGHT FOR A CLI, A
     SERVERLESS HANDLER, A CONTAINER SIDECAR AND A SHORT-LIVED JOB,
     and wrong for anything whose plugins are chosen at run time. The
     startup win is real and the reflection loss is not recoverable
     — a binary compiled without it cannot load a member it was not
     built knowing about. --}}

17 · Build, Packaging, Deployment & Operations

17.1 The dotnet CLI and solution layout17.2 Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props and global.json17.3 NuGet: versions, lock files, feeds and auditing17.4 dotnet publish: deployment shapes17.5 Containers: multi-stage builds and .dockerignore17.6 Production operations: telemetry, health and releases

This chapter covers the path from a source tree to a running process and the controls that make that path reproducible. The recurring theme is reproducibility: a build that depends on an unpinned SDK, a floating package version or an unversioned base image is not a build, it is a different build each time.

Applies to: .NET 10 SDK, MSBuild, NuGet 6.x, Visual Studio 2026, Rider 2025.3+, Docker with BuildKit, GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines. Requirements: the .NET 10 SDK on every build agent; the SDK version is pinned by global.json (section 17.2).

17.1 The dotnet CLI and solution layout

The dotnet CLI is the only build interface that is guaranteed to be identical on every machine. A solution is a grouping; a project is a compilation unit that produces exactly one assembly. The commands below are the complete set used by a professional pipeline.

# Create. The template drives the project kind; --framework sets the TFM.
dotnet new sln -n Contoso.Orders
dotnet new web      -o src/Contoso.Orders.Api        -f net10.0
dotnet new classlib -o src/Contoso.Orders.Domain    -f net10.0
dotnet new classlib -o src/Contoso.Orders.Data      -f net10.0
dotnet new xunit    -o tests/Contoso.Orders.UnitTests -f net10.0
dotnet new webapi   -o src/Contoso.Orders.Reporting  -f net10.0 --use-controllers

# Reference. A project reference is not a NuGet package: it is a
# compile-time dependency resolved by MSBuild and visible in the output.
dotnet sln Contoso.Orders.sln add src/Contoso.Orders.Api src/Contoso.Orders.Domain src/Contoso.Orders.Data
dotnet sln Contoso.Orders.sln add tests/Contoso.Orders.UnitTests
dotnet add src/Contoso.Orders.Api reference src/Contoso.Orders.Domain src/Contoso.Orders.Data
dotnet add tests/Contoso.Orders.UnitTests reference src/Contoso.Orders.Domain

# Build and test
dotnet restore Contoso.Orders.sln
dotnet build   Contoso.Orders.sln -c Release --no-restore
dotnet test    Contoso.Orders.sln -c Release --no-build --logger "trx;LogFileName=results.trx"
dotnet test    --filter "FullyQualifiedName~OrderService"
dotnet test    --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"
dotnet format  Contoso.Orders.sln --verify-no-changes --severity warn
dotnet build   -warnaserror                       # the CI gate

# Run
dotnet run --project src/Contoso.Orders.Api --urls "http://localhost:5080"
dotnet run --project src/Contoso.Orders.Api --launch-profile "https"

# Clean. obj/ and bin/ only; nothing else is touched.
dotnet clean  Contoso.Orders.sln -c Release
dotnet nuget locals all --list

# Layout that scales past a handful of projects.
#   src/Contoso.Orders.Domain        no dependencies at all
#   src/Contoso.Orders.Application   depends on Domain
#   src/Contoso.Orders.Infrastructure depends on Application
#   src/Contoso.Orders.Api            depends on Infrastructure
#   tests/...                         depend on what they test
# The rule: dependencies point inward. Domain references nothing, so it
# can be extracted, tested and reasoned about without the framework.
# A single .sln per repository is fine up to a few hundred projects;
# beyond that, use one solution per directory plus a build script
# that enumerates them, or a central PackageManagement solution.
# .slnx (the XML solution format) is supported in the .NET 10 SDK.

dotnet test --no-build is mandatory in CI: without it the test run rebuilds and the "it passed locally, it failed in CI" class of difference narrows to configuration and environment rather than to state.

17.2 Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props and global.json

Three files at the repository root remove the duplication that causes drift. global.json pins the SDK. Directory.Build.props is imported implicitly by every project in the tree, so shared properties are declared once. Directory.Packages.props enables central package management, where each package version is declared once for the whole repository.

{
  //  global.json -- pins the SDK. A build agent with the wrong SDK fails
  //  immediately with a clear message instead of producing a different binary.
  //  Applies to: the .NET 10 SDK. Use "rollForward" to control drift.
  "sdk": {
    "version": "10.0.100",
    "rollForward": "latestFeature",
    "allowPrerelease": false
  }
}
//  dotnet --list-sdks       shows installed versions
//  latestPatch      -- patch only: safest
//  latestFeature    -- the current feature band
//  latestMinor     -- allows a new minor version: more drift
//  disable         -- exact version, no roll-forward at all

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <!-- Directory.Build.props: imported by every project below this directory.
       It must not contain a Project Sdk attribute; it is plain property
       group XML. -->
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <LangVersion>14.0</LangVersion>                 <!-- C# 14; the default for net10.0 -->
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <WarningsAsErrors>nullable</WarningsAsErrors>
    <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>
    <AnalysisLevel>latest-recommended</AnalysisLevel>
    <Deterministic>true</Deterministic>
    <ContinuousIntegrationBuild>true</ContinuousIntegrationBuild>
    <InvariantGlobalization>false</InvariantGlobalization>
    <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>
    <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);CS1591</NoWarn>            <!-- internal members need no XML doc -->

    <Version>2.4.0</Version>
    <Authors>Contoso Platform</Authors>
    <Company>Contoso</Company>
    <Copyright>Copyright (c) 2026</Copyright>
    <RepositoryUrl>https://github.com/contoso/orders</RepositoryUrl>
    <PublishRepositoryUrl>true</PublishRepositoryUrl>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <PropertyGroup Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Release'">
    <Optimize>true</Optimize>
    <DebugType>portable</DebugType>
    <ServerGarbageCollection>true</ServerGarbageCollection>
    <ConcurrentGarbageCollection>true</ConcurrentGarbageCollection>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

<Project>
  <!-- Directory.Packages.props: central package management.
       Every PackageReference in the tree then omits Version and the
       repository owns exactly one version per package. -->
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
    <CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>true</CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Data.SqlClient" Version="6.1.2" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.66" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Options" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Options.DataAnnotations" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="OpenTelemetry.Extensions.Hosting" Version="1.14.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.AspNetCore" Version="1.14.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="OpenTelemetry.Exporter.OpenTelemetryProtocol" Version="1.14.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Serilog.AspNetCore" Version="9.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Swashbuckle.AspNetCore" Version="9.0.1" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit" Version="2.9.3" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit.runner.visualstudio" Version="3.1.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="NSubstitute" Version="5.3.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="coverlet.collector" Version="6.0.4" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing" Version="10.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Testcontainers.MsSql" Version="4.4.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="BenchmarkDotNet" Version="0.15.2" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Contoso.Shared.Contracts" Version="1.8.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

// A project file then carries no versions at all
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <RootNamespace>Contoso.Orders.Api</RootNamespace>
    <AssemblyName>Contoso.Orders.Api</AssemblyName>
    <UserSecretsId>contoso-orders-api</UserSecretsId>   <-- user secrets, development only -->
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer" />
    <PackageReference Include="Dapper" />
  </ItemGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <ProjectReference Include="..\Contoso.Orders.Data\Contoso.Orders.Data.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

// Directory.Build.targets is imported after the project body, for
// anything that must run after evaluation.

ContinuousIntegrationBuild plus Deterministic makes the output path-independent and byte-identical for identical inputs, which is what allows a build cache, a container layer cache and a reproducible supply chain to work. CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled promotes transitive dependencies to direct pins, which is how a repository prevents a transitive upgrade from silently arriving.

Failure mode: with central package management enabled, a PackageReference that still carries a Version attribute is an error (NU1008). The fix is to remove the version and add a PackageVersion entry. The upside is that there is now exactly one place to change a version, and the build tells you which projects need reviewing.

17.3 NuGet: versions, lock files, feeds and auditing

NuGet restores a graph, not a package. The version ranges you write, the transitive dependencies of your dependencies and the feeds you configure together determine exactly which assemblies end up in your output folder. An unpinned restore is a supply chain risk and a reproducibility failure.

// Version ranges, from most to least pinned
<PackageReference Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.66" />   <!-- exact: recommended for production -->
<PackageReference Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.66" />
<PackageReference Include="Dapper" Version="[2.1.66]" />     <!-- exact, NuGet syntax -->
<PackageReference Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.*" />     <!-- floating: resolves differently over time -->
<PackageReference Include="Dapper" Version="2.*" />       <!-- floating major: still risky -->

// Lock files: commit packages.lock.json for every project. The lock
// file records the full resolved graph, so restore is repeatable and a
// transitive change requires a visible diff in review.
<PropertyGroup>
  <RestorePackagesWithLockFile>true</RestorePackagesWithLockFile>
  <RestoreLockedMode>true</RestoreLockedMode>   <!-- CI: fail rather than resolve -->
</PropertyGroup>
dotnet restore --locked-mode            <!-- same thing, per invocation -->

// PackageReference versus packages.config. packages.config is the
// legacy format: per-project, non-transitive, incompatible with
// PackageReference, and not supported on .NET 10 SDK-style projects.
// There is no migration decision to make on a modern project.

// Feeds. A nuget.config at the repository root pins the sources so a
// developer machine and a build agent resolve identically.
<configuration>
  <packageSources>
    <!-- <clear/> removes any inherited source, including a machine-level one -->
    <clear />
    <add key="nuget.org" value="https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json" protocolVersion="3" />
    <add key="contoso" value="https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/contoso/_packaging/public/nuget/v3/index.json" />
  </packageSources>
  <packageSourceMapping>
    <!-- Prefix mapping: Contoso.* may only come from the private feed. This is
         what stops a dependency-confusion or typosquat package. -->
    <packageSource key="contoso"
      <package pattern="Contoso.*" />
    </packageSource>
    <packageSource key="nuget.org"
      <package pattern="*" />
    </packageSource>
  </packageSourceMapping>
</configuration>

// Private feed credentials never go in nuget.config on a build agent:
//   dotnet nuget add source <url> -u <user> -p <token> --store-password-in-clear-text
//   (development only). In CI, use a pipeline secret variable or
//   NUGET_AUTH_TOKEN with an Azure Artifacts service connection.

// Auditing. Applies to: NuGet 6.8+ and the .NET 10 SDK.
<PropertyGroup>
  <NuGetAudit>true</NuGetAudit>                          <!-- restore warns on known vulnerabilities -->
  <NuGetAuditMode>all</NuGetAuditMode>                 <!-- all, not just direct -->
  <NuGetAuditLevel>moderate</NuGetAuditLevel>
  <WarningsAsErrors>$(WarningsAsErrors);NU1901;NU1902;NU1903;NU1904</WarningsAsErrors>
</PropertyGroup>
dotnet list Contoso.Orders.sln package --vulnerable --include-transitive
dotnet list Contoso.Orders.sln package --outdated
dotnet list Contoso.Orders.sln package --deprecated

// An inventory you can diff and store. Applies to: .NET 10 SDK.
dotnet package list --format json > packages.json
dotnet package list --format json --vulnerable > vulnerabilities.json

// Restoring from a private feed in an air-gapped environment
dotnet nuget push Contoso.Shared.Contracts.1.8.0.nupkg --source https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/contoso/_packaging/public/nuget/v3/index.json --api-key $TOKEN
dotnet nuget locals http-cache --clear     <!-- when a restore serves a stale package -->

packageSourceMapping with a Contoso.* prefix and a clear of inherited sources is the single highest-value line in a private feed configuration. Without it, a package name your organisation owns resolves from nuget.org first, and a public package with the same name is one of the oldest supply chain attacks there is.

17.4 dotnet publish: deployment shapes

Publishing produces the deployable artifact. The five shapes below are the complete set of practical options in .NET 10, and the differences are not only size: they change what is present at run time, which determines what can be reflected over, what can be loaded later, and what the process needs installed.

// 1. Framework-dependent deployment (the default, and the ASP.NET Core
//    default for the web SDK).
//    The .NET runtime is installed on the machine. Smallest output.
dotnet publish -c Release -o ./out
//   out/: your.dll, your.deps.json, your.runtimeconfig.json, appsettings.json

// 2. Framework-dependent, self-contained false, with a specific runtime:
//    selects the runtime major version without bundling it.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained false -o ./out

// 3. Self-contained: the runtime travels with the application.
//    Nothing must be installed. Larger output. One runtime per binary.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true -o ./out

// 4. Single file. Bundles managed assemblies into one native host.
//    Managed DLLs are embedded but loaded from memory; native libraries
//    are extracted on first run unless IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract is set.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true \
    -p:PublishSingleFile=true \
    -p:IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract=true \
    -p:EnableCompressionInSingleFile=true \
    -p:DebugType=embedded \
    -o ./out
//   EnableCompressionInSingleFile cuts size by roughly half at the cost of
//   decompressing each assembly on first access.

// 5. ReadyToRun: precompiled IL to native code, still JIT-capable.
//    Reduces start-up and first-request latency; the JIT remains for
//    anything not precompiled. Must match the target runtime identifier.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true -p:PublishReadyToRun=true -o ./out

// Trimming. Removes code the compiler cannot prove reachable.
//   Applies to: .NET 6+ for libraries, .NET 8+ for applications.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true -p:PublishTrimmed=true -o ./out
//   The risk is not size: it is a reflection site that only fails at run time,
//   in a code path that is rarely taken. Read every IL2xxx warning.
//   <TrimMode>full</TrimMode> is aggressive; partial is the default for apps.

// Container versus non-container
//   Container:  the .NET runtime is already in the base image. Publish
//              framework-dependent, self-contained false, no single file.
//              Layer caching, a consistent filesystem layout, and a
//              uniform security posture are all easier.
//   Non-container: publish self-contained, or rely on an installed runtime
//               and a service manager. Simpler on a single VM, but the
//               runtime version is a machine-level decision.

// The properties that belong in the csproj, not on a command line
<PropertyGroup>
  <UserSecretsId>contoso-orders-api</UserSecretsId>
  <DockerDefaultTargetOS>Linux</DockerDefaultTargetOS>
  <InvariantTimezone>false</InvariantTimezone>
  <GenerateRuntimeConfigurationFiles>true</GenerateRuntimeConfigurationFiles>
</PropertyGroup>

// Verify what actually shipped. A build that assumes it published
// correctly is a build nobody has looked at.
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained true -o ./out
ls ./out
./out/Contoso.Orders.Api --version
#   The single-file binary still needs: a writable TEMP when
#   IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract is true, and ICU unless
#   InvariantGlobalization is set.

Caveats that produce outages: publishing self-contained inside a container image that already has the runtime doubles the size and creates two runtimes to patch. Publishing trimmed and then running a code path that reflects over a type the trimmer removed fails only in production. Setting InvariantGlobalization=true silently changes ToString(), string comparison and culture-sensitive sorting, which is a data correctness issue and not only a localisation one.

17.5 Containers: multi-stage builds and .dockerignore

A .NET container image should be a multi-stage build: the SDK stage restores and publishes, the runtime stage copies only the output. The build context must be filtered, because the context is uploaded to the daemon before any instruction runs, and an unfiltered context turns a 300 MB bin/ into a 300 MB upload on every build.

#  syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
#  Build from the repository root so the whole context is available:
#    docker build -f src/Contoso.Orders.Api/Dockerfile -t contoso/orders:2.4.0 .
#  Applies to: .NET 10 SDK images, linux-x64 and linux-arm64

# --- Stage 1: restore. Cached independently of the source, because only
# --- the project files change when a class is edited.
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0-noble AS build
ARG BUILD_CONFIGURATION=Release
WORKDIR /src

#  Copy the manifests first so the restore layer is reused across code edits
COPY global.json ./
COPY Directory.Build.props Directory.Packages.props nuget.config ./
COPY src/Contoso.Orders.Api/Contoso.Orders.Api.csproj            src/Contoso.Orders.Api/
COPY src/Contoso.Orders.Domain/Contoso.Orders.Domain.csproj        src/Contoso.Orders.Domain/
COPY src/Contoso.Orders.Data/Contoso.Orders.Data.csproj            src/Contoso.Orders.Data/
RUN dotnet restore src/Contoso.Orders.Api/Contoso.Orders.Api.csproj

# --- Copy the rest and build with no restore (the restore is already done)
COPY src/ src/
RUN dotnet publish src/Contoso.Orders.Api/Contoso.Orders.Api.csproj \
        --no-restore \
        -c $BUILD_CONFIGURATION \
        -o /app

# --- Stage 2: runtime. The SDK is not present in the final image.
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0-noble AS final
ARG BUILD_CONFIGURATION=Release
WORKDIR /app

#  A non-root user. The base image ships an `app` user; creating an
#  explicit one is the auditable form and needs no privileges to set up.
RUN addgroup --system --gid 64198 contoso \
    && adduser --system --uid 64199 --ingroup contoso contoso

#  Culture data for a service that formats money and dates
ENV DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_INVARIANT=false
ENV ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS="8080"
ENV ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production
ENV DOTNET_gcServer="1"
ENV DOTNET_gcConcurrent="1"
ENV DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimitPercent="70"

COPY --from=build --chown=64199:64198 /app ./

#  Read-only root filesystem: the app must not write to /app
RUN mkdir -p /var/app && chown contoso:contoso /var/app
USER contoso

EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
    CMD ["dotnet", "Contoso.Orders.Api.dll", "--health-check"]

ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Contoso.Orders.Api.dll"]

#  .NET 10 adds a dedicated non-root tag, and .NET 9+ images default to a
#  non-root user, which the explicit USER line documents.

#  A build-arg-based tag, not a floating tag, so the image is traceable
dotnet build src/Contoso.Orders.Api -c Release -o ./out
docker build -f src/Contoso.Orders.Api/Dockerfile -t contoso/orders:2.4.0 .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp contoso/orders:2.4.0

#  Multi-arch: buildx with a QEMU builder builds arm64 on an amd64 host
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -f src/Contoso.Orders.Api/Dockerfile -t contoso/orders:2.4.0 --push .
#  .dockerignore -- without this the build context includes bin/, obj/ and
#  .git, which is both a slow upload and a source leak into the builder.
**/bin/
**/obj/
**/.vs/
**/.vscode/
**/.idea/
**/*.user
**/TestResults/
**/coverage/
**/artifacts/
**/publish/
.git/
.gitignore
.github/
azure-pipelines.yml
Dockerfile
**/Dockerfile
.dockerignore
README.md
docs/
**/*.md
**/*.nupkg
**/packages.lock.json
tests/
benchmarks/

The manifest-first copy order in stage one is what makes an incremental image build fast: editing a class file invalidates only the final dotnet publish layer, not the restore. Pinning the base image by digest rather than by tag is the only way to guarantee that two builds a week apart use the same runtime.

DOTNET_gcHeapHardLimitPercent is the setting that makes a container behave under a memory limit: the garbage collector becomes more aggressive as the heap approaches the container’s share of the node’s memory, instead of letting the kernel’s OOM killer terminate the process without a managed exception. For a latency-sensitive service it converts a silent kill into visible GC pressure.

17.6 Production operations: telemetry, health and releases

A service is not finished when it starts. It is finished when an operator can see what it is doing, when a platform can tell whether to send it traffic, and when it can be stopped without losing work. These three concerns are configured in the same composition root and are the subject of this section.

// OpenTelemetry: traces, metrics and logs through one pipeline.
// Applies to: OpenTelemetry 1.x, Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics 10.x
builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .WithTracing(tracing => tracing
        .AddSource("Contoso.Orders")                       // your ActivitySource name
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation(o => o.RecordException = true)
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddEntityFrameworkCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddSqlClientInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter())                                    // OTLP over gRPC or HTTP

    .WithMetrics(metrics => metrics
        .AddMeter("Contoso.Orders")                         // your Meter name (section 16.5)
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddRuntimeInstrumentation()                            // GC, thread pool, memory
        .AddOtlpExporter());

// Structured logs into the same trace: the OTLP log exporter plus
// scopes carrying the trace and span ids.
builder.Logging.AddOpenTelemetry(o =>
{
    o.IncludeFormattedMessage = true;
    o.IncludeScopes = true;
    o.ParseStateValues = true;
    o.SetResourceBuilder(ResourceBuilder.CreateDefault().AddService(
        serviceName: "contoso-orders",
        serviceVersion: typeof(Program).Assembly.GetName().Version!.ToString()));
    o.AddOtlpExporter();
});

// Health checks. Two probes with two different meanings.
//   liveness  -- is the process functioning? It must NOT check a
//               database: a database outage would then restart every
//               replica simultaneously, converting a dependency
//               problem into a total outage.
//   readiness -- can this instance serve traffic? It MAY check
//               dependencies, and it should warm caches here.
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck("self", () => HealthCheckResult.Healthy(), tags: ["live"])
    .AddDbContextCheck<OrdersDbContext>(
        name: "orders-db",
        failureStatus: HealthStatus.Degraded,          <-- Degraded, not Unhealthy -->
        tags: ["ready", "db"])
    .AddCheck("pricing-cache", new PricingCacheHealthCheck())
    .AddAzureBlobStorage("exports", failureStatus: HealthStatus.Degraded, tags: ["ready"]);

builder.Services.Configure<HealthCheckServiceOptions>(o => o.ResultStatusCodes[2] =
    HealthStatus.Unhealthy);       // 503 when Degraded or Unhealthy

// A custom check: cheap, bounded, and never throws.
public sealed class PricingCacheHealthCheck(IHealthCheck healthCheck) : IHealthCheck
{
    public async Task<HealthCheckResult> CheckHealthAsync(
        HealthCheckContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    {
        // Health checks are called frequently. A slow check makes the
        // endpoint itself a source of load.
        await using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(cancellationToken);
        cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));

        try
        {
            return await healthCheck.IsHealthyAsync(cts.Token)
                ? HealthCheckResult.Healthy("cache warm")
                : HealthCheckResult.Degraded("cache cold");
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            // A check that throws takes the endpoint down. Catch everything.
            return HealthCheckResult.Degraded("check failed", ex);
        }
    }
}

// The two endpoints, mapped to the two probe paths
app.MapHealthChecks("/health/live", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = r => r.Tags.Contains("live"),
    ResponseWriter = WriteMinimalResponse
});
app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = r => r.Tags.Contains("ready"),
    ResponseWriter = WriteDetailedResponse
});

// Graceful shutdown: stop accepting, finish in-flight work, then exit.
builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(o =>
{
    o.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);   <-- grace period -->
    o.BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior = BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.Ignore;
});
builder.Services.Configure<KestrelServerOptions>(o =>
{
    o.Limits.KeepAliveTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(65);
    o.AddServerHeader = false;                       <!-- do not advertise the runtime -->
});

// SIGTERM arrives on pod eviction and on docker stop. The host drains:
//   1. the readiness probe starts failing once the shutdown token is
//      signalled, so the load balancer stops sending new requests
//   2. in-flight requests complete within ShutdownTimeout
//   3. hosted services stop in reverse registration order
//   4. the process exits; exit code 143 for SIGTERM
// Anything that must survive a restart needs a queue, not an in-process
// buffer, and the shutdown path must not lose the dequeued item.

// Request timeouts: a server that never times out holds a thread forever
builder.Services.AddHsts(o => o.MaxAge = TimeSpan.FromDays(365));
app.UseExceptionHandler("/error", o => o.HandleResponse = true);
app.UseStatusCodePages();
# A CI gate that is worth having. Order matters: the fastest failing
# check runs first, so a compile error costs seconds, not minutes.
#  .github/workflows/ci.yml -- illustrative, not authored content for this
#  guide's build, but this is the shape a gate should have.
name: ci
on:
  push: { branches: [ main ] }
  pull_request: { branches: [ main ] }

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: '10.0.x'
          global-json-file: global.json          <-- trust global.json, not this file -->

      - name: Restore locked
        run: dotnet restore --locked-mode

      - name: Build (warnings are errors)
        run: dotnet build -c Release --no-restore -warnaserror

      - name: Format
        run: dotnet format --verify-no-changes --severity warn

      - name: Unit and integration tests
        run: dotnet test -c Release --no-build --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"

      - name: Vulnerability audit
        run: |
          dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive
          dotnet list package --outdated
        continue-on-error: true     <-- report, but do not fail the build yet -->

      - name: Trimming and AOT compatibility
        run: dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishTrimmed=true -o out

      - name: Container build
        run: docker build -f src/Contoso.Orders.Api/Dockerfile -t contoso/orders:ci .

      - name: Smoke test the published artifact
        run: ./out/Contoso.Orders.Api --version

# Release engineering rules that hold across teams
#   Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where MAJOR is a breaking change
#   to a public contract and MINOR is a backwards-compatible addition.
#   A pre-1.0 package may break on any MINOR. Say so in the package description.
#   Tag the repository with v2.4.0 and let the build stamp the assembly version
#   from the tag. A build number that is not derived from a commit is not
#   traceable.
#   Database changes deploy separately from code, expand-then-contract:
#     1. add the new nullable column, deploy, backfill
#     2. switch readers to the new column, deploy
#     3. stop writing the old column, deploy
#     4. drop the old column in a later release
#   Every step is independently reversible. A migration that cannot be
#   reverted without data loss is a one-way door; schedule it for
#   a quiet period, not a Friday.
#   Roll forward, not back. Once data has been written by the new version,
#   reverting the binary can corrupt it. Prefer a forward fix.

The Degraded status for a database check is deliberate: it keeps the instance in the load balancer, which is correct when the instance can still serve cached or unrelated work, and it surfaces the condition on the readiness endpoint for a human. Mapping Degraded to HTTP 503 in ResultStatusCodes is the choice to revisit per service — it removes the instance from rotation for a soft dependency problem.

Exercises 17

  1. Create a solution with a Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Api and two test projects, wire the references, and prove the inward direction by attempting a reference from Domain to Application and recording the compiler error.
  2. Add Directory.Build.props and Directory.Packages.props to an existing solution, remove every Version attribute from every PackageReference, and confirm the build still restores the same versions. Enable RestorePackagesWithLockFile and commit the lock file.
  3. Pin the SDK with global.json and verify that a machine with a different installed SDK fails the build with the intended message rather than silently using what it has.
  4. Publish the same project five ways (framework-dependent, self-contained, single file, ReadyToRun, trimmed), record output size, start-up time to first request and RSS for each, and state which you would ship to a container platform and why.
  5. Write a multi-stage Dockerfile with a .dockerignore, build it twice with a single source file changed, and time both builds. Reorder the copies so the restore layer is no longer cached and measure the difference.
  6. Add OpenTelemetry tracing, metrics and OTLP logging, plus separate liveness and readiness checks, then prove the liveness probe does not fail when the database is unreachable and the readiness probe does.
  7. Send SIGTERM to a running instance during a slow request and confirm the request completes, the readiness probe starts failing before the process exits, and the exit code is 143.
  8. Enable NuGetAudit with WarningsAsErrors on NU1901 to NU1904 and add a deliberately vulnerable direct package, then read the exact diagnostic text you would want a developer to see in review.

Enterprise package referenceWhich data access approachEF Core performance anti-patterns and fixesProduction readiness checklistTroubleshooting indexOfficial documentation

This appendix is the operational counterpart to Appendix A. It is a package list, a decision table, an anti-pattern catalogue, a checklist, an index from symptom to cause, and a set of links. It is written to be printed and kept beside the code.

Enterprise package reference

The set below is the floor for an ASP.NET Core service on .NET 10 with a relational database. Every version is pinned to the release that ships with the runtime, except where a package has its own cadence.

PackageVersionPurposeNotes
Microsoft.Data.SqlClient6.xSQL Server and Azure SQL providerReplaces the frozen System.Data.SqlClient; supports SqlBatch and EnableRetryOnFailure
Dapper2.1.xMicro-ORM for read models and hand-tuned SQLOne static class, no model, no migrations
Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore10.0.xORM core, change tracker, migrationsVersion must match the runtime major
Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer10.0.xSQL Server provider for EF CoreAlso the database for dotnet ef tooling
Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design10.0.xdotnet ef migrations and reverse engineeringPrivateAssets="all"; never deployed
Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite10.0.xSQLite provider for testsThe faithful fast tier; see section 15.5
Microsoft.Extensions.Options10.0.xOptions pattern, validation, monitorPlus Options.DataAnnotations for ValidateDataAnnotations
Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks10.0.xHealth check infrastructurePlus the provider packages for the stores you check
OpenTelemetry.Extensions.Hosting1.14.xTracing, metrics and OTLP exportPlus AspNetCore, Http, EntityFrameworkCore and SqlClient instrumentation
OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.Runtime1.14.xGC, thread pool and memory metricsWhat dotnet-counters shows, sent continuously
Serilog.AspNetCore9.x or built-inStructured logging to a durable sinkThe built-in console provider is sufficient if a collector ships the JSON
xunit.v33.xTest frameworkv2.9.x is also supported; v3 improves parallelism and diagnostics
Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk18.xVSTest host for dotnet testMust be present for the command to work at all
NSubstitute5.3.xSubstitutesOr Moq 4.20+; pick one and do not mix
coverlet.collector6.xCoverage data collectorExecution, not correctness; see section 15.6
Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing10.0.xWebApplicationFactoryRequires the entry point to be partial
Testcontainers.MsSql / .PostgreSql4.xReal engine for integration testsRequires a Docker-compatible runtime on the agent
BenchmarkDotNet0.15.xMicro-benchmarksA standalone project, never referenced by the product
Swashbuckle.AspNetCore9.xOpenAPI document and UIEnable in development; serve a static document in production or not at all
FluentValidation12.xDeclarative validationOptional; System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations is sufficient for a small surface
Polly8.xResilience policiesWired through AddStandardResilienceHandler on the HttpClient factory

Two rules govern this list. First, every package that is only needed at build time — EntityFrameworkCore.Design, the test SDK, the benchmark harness — sets PrivateAssets="all" and is never part of the deployed output. Second, an upgrade is a change to a set of transitive dependencies you did not choose, so the audit in section 17.3 runs on every build rather than on a schedule.

A central package management file moves the version of every package out of the project files and into one place. That is the whole mechanism, and it buys two things: a version is written once, and a security update is applied in one file rather than thirty.

What it does not buy

It does not resolve transitive dependencies. A library that depends on version one of a package still pulls version one in, and a central version overrides it only if you declare the package yourself — which means the central file is a declaration of what you use directly, not a statement of what the build resolves. Transitive pinning is what closes that gap, and it is off by default, so the divergence between declared and resolved is the default state of every repository that has adopted central management without turning it on.

Where the divergence shows up

In the audit, which reads the resolved graph rather than the declarations. A central file saying 4.2.0 and an audit saying 3.9.1 are both correct about different things, and the audit is the one describing the build. A lock file is the third answer, and it is the only one that makes a change to the resolved graph a build failure rather than a surprise discovered in production.

The preview rule

A prerelease is excluded from a floating version range by default, so a range picks up the latest stable rather than a newer prerelease. That is deliberate. The consequence is the trap: once a package ships a stable release, the same range starts selecting it on the next restore, with no change to any project file — so two developers who restored a week apart have different builds and nothing in the repository records the difference.


{{-- THE CENTRAL FILE, which moves the VERSION from the project
     files into one place. --}}
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
    <!-- ^ ONCE, in Directory.Packages.props at the repository
         ROOT. With it set, a project that declares a
         PackageReference WITHOUT a Version FAILS THE BUILD rather
         than restoring something unpinned — which is what makes
         the central file AUTHORITATIVE rather than advisory. -->

    <CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>true</CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>
    <!-- ^ AND THE ONE MOST PROJECTS DO NOT TURN ON. It promotes a
         transitive dependency to a DIRECT reference at the central
         version, so a package three levels down that pins an old
         version of something you also use directly is OVERRIDDEN
         by your central version.

         WITHOUT IT, your declared version is not the version that
         runs when another package asks for a different one — so
         the central file says 4.2.0, the audit says 3.9.1, and
         both are correct about different things. That divergence is
         the single most useful thing to know about this file. -->
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Serilog"                  Version="4.2.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="FluentValidation"        Version="11.11.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Data.SqlClient" Version="6.0.1" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

{{-- AND THE PROJECT FILE, which now declares only the reference: --}}
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- NO Version. The build FAILS if the central file does not
         have one, which is a COMPILE-TIME enforcement of the
         convention rather than a review convention. -->
    <PackageReference Include="Serilog" />
    <PackageReference Include="FluentValidation" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>


// THE AUDIT, and the thing it is usually mistaken for:
dotnet list package --outdated --include-transitive
{{-- ^ WHAT YOU USE DIRECTLY versus WHAT THE BUILD RESOLVES. They
     are frequently DIFFERENT, because a library you depend on may
     ask for a version of a shared library that differs from the
     central one. THE AUDIT READS THE RESOLVED GRAPH —
     obj/project.assets.json — and that is the file to trust when
     the two disagree.

     dotnet list package --vulnerable
     SECURITY DATA from the advisory database, and a build-time
     check exists:

     <EnableNuGetAudit>true</EnableNuGetAudit>     in Directory.Build.props

     WHICH FAILS THE BUILD ON A KNOWN VULNERABILITY, and the level
     is settable:

     <NuGetAuditLevel>moderate</NuGetAuditLevel>   low | moderate |
                                                  high

     WORTH HAVING AS AN ERROR ON A SERVICE and as a WARNING on a
     LIBRARY — because a library's consumers choose their own
     versions, and failing THEIR build over an advisory in a
     transitive dependency is not your decision to make. --}}

// THE PREVIEW RULE, and it explains why a floating version did NOT
// pick up a prerelease:
<PackageVersion Include="Newtonsoft.Json" Version="13.*" />
<!-- ^ 13.* IS A FLOATING RANGE, which resolves to the latest 13.x
     STABLE. A PRERELEASE IS EXCLUDED BY DEFAULT, so 14.0.0-preview
     is not selected even though it is numerically higher. That is
     deliberate: an automatic update to a prerelease is an
     UNEXPECTED change to a build, and a dependency should not
     change shape without somebody saying so.

     WHICH MEANS THE CONVERSE IS THE TRAP: once a package ships a
     STABLE release, the SAME range starts selecting it on the next
     restore, WITH NO CHANGE TO ANY PROJECT FILE. Two developers
     who restored a week apart have different builds, and nothing in
     the repository records the difference. The lock file is what
     fixes it —

     dotnet restore --use-lock-file
     <RestorePackagesWithLockFile>true</RestorePackagesWithLockFile>

     — which records the RESOLVED graph and makes CI fail when it
     changes, rather than discovering the change in production. For
     an application, pinning exact versions and updating
     deliberately is almost always right; for a library, a floating
     range means a decision made once and revisited silently
     forever after. -->

Which data access approach

The decision is made per query, not per application. A service commonly owns two or three approaches at once, with a rule about which layer owns which table.

QuestionIf yesThen use
Does this query require a stored procedure, a table-valued parameter, bulk copy, or a hint the provider cannot express?YesDapper, or raw ADO.NET for bulk copy
Does the write span a graph with cascading inserts, updates and deletes that must be one transaction?YesEF Core
Will the schema change frequently and must the change be reviewable, versioned and reversible?YesEF Core migrations
Is this a read-only projection over a stable view, a report, or an administrative query?YesDapper with buffered: false for large results
Is the query on a latency budget under one millisecond and measured to be hot?YesRaw ADO.NET with a DbCommand and an explicit projection
Do you need to unit test the data access without a database?YesEF Core or Dapper, behind an interface, with a real database test alongside
Is the object graph small, bounded, and read once?YesEF Core with AsNoTracking and a projection
Does the query need to survive a provider migration from SQL Server to PostgreSQL?YesEF Core, or Dapper with provider-neutral SQL
None of the above—EF Core with a projection, which is the default

Do not use the in-memory EF Core provider as a gate on any test, and do not use raw ADO.NET to reimplement a write path that EF Core already models correctly. The first produces a suite that passes while production fails; the second produces a data access layer with no migration history, no change detection and no concurrency handling, maintained by hand forever.

The choice of a data access approach is made per query rather than per application, and the deciding question is what shape the query has. Three shapes recur: an aggregate load that mutates and saves, a report with SQL you want to read, and a bulk write that should not load the rows it changes. A library that is good at one is not thereby good at the others, and the cost of getting a shape wrong is paid in a place that does not name the shape.

The deciding test

Ask whether you would be willing to read the generated SQL in a code review. If yes, an object mapper is the faster route to correct code, because identity resolution and change tracking are worth a great deal and neither is short to write. If the honest answer is that you would not see anything wrong with hand-written SQL, then hand-written SQL is the cheaper route — because the generated form is then an indirection between you and the statement you would rather be reviewing, and nobody can optimise it when the plan is wrong.

What each shape wants

An aggregate load wants identity resolution, so that two references to the same row are one object, and a change tracker that works out which columns changed from a snapshot diff. A report wants SQL you can read, with a window function in it, because the query is the artefact under review. A bulk write wants a statement that never materialises the rows it changes, which is the one case where every mapper is the wrong tool and no amount of configuration fixes it.

The signal that a single choice was wrong somewhere

Find the place where a hand-written SQL string is wrapped in an object mapper's raw-query API. That is a report that has outgrown its layer, and it is the first sign that a codebase which picked one approach for everything has picked wrong in exactly one place — which is the normal outcome, and not a reason to have chosen differently across the codebase.


{{-- THE DECIDING QUESTION IS THE SHAPE OF THE QUERY, and there
     are three. --}}

// SHAPE 1: LOAD AN AGGREGATE, MUTATE IT, SAVE IT.
public sealed class Aggregate(AppDbContext db)
{
    public async Task<Order> MarkPaidAsync(long id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // WHAT THIS SHAPE WANTS: IDENTITY RESOLUTION — two
        //   references to the same row should be ONE object — and
        //   a change tracker that works out WHICH COLUMNS CHANGED
        //   from a snapshot diff. There is no hand-rolled
        //   equivalent of that diff that is correct in the presence
        //   of a COLLECTION of children, because the diff has to
        //   know which children were added, which removed and which
        //   modified, and that is a set comparison.
        var order = await db.Orders
            .Include(o => o.Lines)                 // a JOIN, not a
            .FirstAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct);      // second query

        order.Status = OrderStatus.Paid;
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        // ^ ONE UPDATE, generated, and correct for added and
        //   removed child rows as well as the changed parent.
    }
}

// SHAPE 2: ONE HAND-WRITTEN STATEMENT, TUNED, REPEATED.
public sealed class Report(string cs)
{
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<SalesRow>> MonthlyAsync(int year, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // WHAT THIS SHAPE WANTS: SQL YOU CAN READ. A window
        //   function and a GROUP BY are the REQUIREMENT, and an
        //   object mapper would need a raw query at this point —
        //   at which point it is a Dapper query with extra layers.
        const string sql = """
            SELECT  CustomerId,
                    MONTH(PlacedAt)                     AS MonthNo,
                    SUM(Total)                          AS Total,
                    SUM(SUM(Total)) OVER (
                        PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY MONTH(PlacedAt)
                        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                    )                                  AS Trailing3
            FROM    Orders
            WHERE   PlacedAt >= @from AND PlacedAt < @to AND Status = 1
            GROUP BY CustomerId, MONTH(PlacedAt)
            ORDER BY Total DESC
            """;

        await using var connection = new SqlConnection(cs);
        await connection.OpenAsync(ct);
        await using var command = new SqlCommand(sql, connection);
        command.Parameters.Add("@from", SqlDbType.DateTime2).Value = new DateTime(year, 1, 1);
        command.Parameters.Add("@to",   SqlDbType.DateTime2).Value = new DateTime(year + 1, 1, 1);

        // ^ PARAMETERISED, ALWAYS. An interpolated date makes the
        //   database evaluate a constant PER ROW and stops using the
        //   index on PlacedAt — a full scan that looks like a
        //   missing index and is fixed by six characters.
        return [];
    }
}


// SHAPE 3: WRITE THOUSANDS OF ROWS.
public sealed class Bulk(string cs)
{
    public async Task<int> ExpireAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // WHAT THIS SHAPE WANTS: A STATEMENT THAT DOES NOT LOAD THE
        //   ROWS IT IS CHANGING. Every object mapper loads 200,000
        //   entities into a change tracker to set one column, which
        //   is both the memory cost and the time cost.
        await using var connection = new SqlConnection(cs);
        await connection.OpenAsync(ct);
        await using var command = new SqlCommand(
            "UPDATE Orders SET Status = 3 WHERE Status = 1 AND PlacedAt < @cutoff",
            connection);
        command.Parameters.Add("@cutoff", SqlDbType.DateTime2)
                        .Value = DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-30);
        return await command.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct);

        // ^ AND THE SHAPE THAT IS WORTH KNOWING: a bulk update
        //   through a mapper is a different QUERY SHAPE rather than a
        //   different library, so a codebase that picked a mapper
        //   for everything still needs raw SQL here — and the
        //   honest fix is not to replace the mapper but to admit
        //   that shapes differ.
    }
}

{{-- THE DECIDING TEST, and it is one question: --}}
// WOULD YOU BE WILLING TO READ THE GENERATED SQL IN A CODE REVIEW?
//
//   YES  -> an object mapper is the faster route to correct code.
//          The generated SQL is ordinary, and the identity
//          resolution and change tracking are worth a great deal
//          for shape 1.
//
//   NO   -> hand-written SQL is CHEAPER, not more expensive. The
//          generated form is then an indirection between you and
//          the statement you would rather be reviewing — and it is
//          an indirection NOBODY CAN OPTIMISE when the plan is
//          wrong, which is the situation in which you actually need
//          to intervene.
//
// WHICH IS WHY THE RIGHT ANSWER IS USUALLY BOTH, and the test for a
// CODEBASE that has picked one is: find the place where a
// hand-written SQL string is wrapped in a mapper's raw-query API.
// THAT is a report that has outgrown its layer, and it is the first
// sign that a codebase's single choice was wrong somewhere. --}}

EF Core performance anti-patterns and fixes

Each row names a symptom you would see in a trace or a counter, the cause, and the change that removes it. The fixes are ordered by how often they are the actual cause.

SymptomCauseFixSection
Gen0 collections per second far above the request rateA projection that materialises tracked entitiesAsNoTracking(), or project to a record or anonymous type13.5
One query per row in a loopLazy loading on a navigation property, the N+1Include and ThenInclude, or project instead of loading13.5
A single query returning thousands of columns worth of rowsLoading full entities to read three fieldsSelect a projection; the generated SQL narrows to the selected columns13.5
Cartesian explosion: 6 orders returning 4000 rowsTwo Include paths over a collection eachAsSplitQuery(), or one projection per level13.5
A 30-second pause with no CPUA gen2 collection after a large tracked graphNo tracking, AutoDetectChangesEnabled = false, shorter contexts13.5
One round trip per row insertedSaveChanges per row, or no batching enabledBatch inside one SaveChanges; raise the batch size for large sets13.6
Thousands of tracked entities for a bulk operationUsing SaveChanges for a bulk updateExecuteUpdate / ExecuteDelete (EF Core 7+)13.5
Slow query with a good plan, high logical readsNon-sargable predicate: a function on the columnMove the function to the parameter side; ensure an index covers the filter13.5
Slow query with a bad plan after a data volume changeParameter sniffing on a cached planOPTION (RECOMPILE) or plan guides; check the plan before blaming EF Core13.5
Pool exhaustion under loadA connection held open across a non-database awaitOpen, query, close; never await unrelated work while a connection is open13.1
Spontaneous SqlException in Azure SQLNo retry on a failable connectionEnableRetryOnFailure plus the execution strategy for transactions13.6
Round trip added to every requestAddWithValue type inference, or ExecuteScalar where a batch would doExplicit SqlParameter with DbType; batch with SqlBatch13.2
Value returned as zeros, no exceptionA Dapper splitOn that does not match the columnCheck splitOn, then column aliases13.4
Startup writes to the database, twiceBoth Migrate() and EnsureCreated(), or a migration seeding duplicatesOne or the other; HasData for reference data only13.6

What the four have in common

Every one of them is invisible in the source, and every one of them is a few lines of log output. That is why the diagnostic is worth more than the four fixes: it finds the next one as well as the current four, and it finds the case where a local function has been added to an existing predicate without anybody noticing that the query stopped being a query.

Invisibility is the property that makes them expensive. A wrong index is found by an execution plan, which is a slow but visible artefact. A query that fetches a whole table to filter it in memory is found by a latency that grows with the table, which is visible but not obviously a query problem at all — and the first diagnosis is usually "the database is slow". N+1 is worse still, because the latency grows with the number of parents rather than with the data, so it looks like a per-request cost.

What is not in this list

Missing indexes, which is the answer almost everybody reaches for first and which fixes none of these four. Each of them produces the right number of queries returning the wrong rows, or the wrong number of queries against the right rows; an index improves the plan for a query that is already the query you meant to write.

Diagnosing by counting queries rather than by examining a plan is faster and it is the check that finds the four above. It also finds the fifth, which is the query built inside a loop and enumerated inside the same loop — the shape that is a per-row round trip and reads as a single query because the enumeration is one statement.

Why the fixes are not symmetric

Three of them are one line each: a key selector, an inline predicate, an eager load. N+1 is one line as well, but the eager load it wants is a join, and a join over a collection multiplies rows — so the correct answer differs by whether the navigation is a reference or a collection, which is a question about the model rather than about the query.


{{-- FOUR PATTERNS, each with a SPECIFIC fix. NONE of them is
     fixed by adding an index. --}}
public sealed class OneAndTwo(WebApplication db)
{
    // (1) QUERYING INSIDE A LOOP: N ROUND TRIPS.
    public async Task<List<string>> WrongQueryInLoop(List<long> ids)
    {
        var names = new List<string>();
        foreach (var id in ids)
            names.Add(await db.Orders.FindAsync(id));
        // ^ ONE ROUND TRIP PER ITEM: 500 items is 500 queries, each
        //   paying a network latency the work inside does not need.
        //   The symptom is a response time that grows LINEARLY with
        //   page size, which looks like a slow database and is not.
        return names;
    }

    // THE FIX: one query, and the IN LIST IS PARAMETERISED.
    public async Task<List<string>> RightQueryInLoop(List<long> ids)
    {
        return await db.Orders
            .Where(o => ids.Contains(o.Id))    // ONE round trip
            .Select(o => o.Reference)           // and it transfers
            .ToListAsync();                     // two columns, not
    }                                          // whole entities

    // (2) SELECT-THEN-FILTER: LOADING THE TABLE AND FILTERING IN
    //     MEMORY.
    public async Task<List<Order>> WrongSelectThenFilter()
        => await db.Orders.ToListAsync();
        // ^ BRINGS EVERY ORDER INTO MEMORY, and the database reads
        //   the table, transfers 200,000 rows, and throws away
        //   199,990 of them. The C# reads as though it filtered.

    public async Task<List<Order>> RightSelectThenFilter()
        => await db.Orders.Where(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Paid).ToListAsync();
        // ^ THE FILTER IS TRANSLATED, so the database applies it
        //   with the index and transfers 10 rows.
}


// (3) CLIENT EVALUATION: THE SAME DEFECT REACHED A DIFFERENT WAY.
public sealed class Three(WebApplication db)
{
    public async Task<List<Order>> WrongClientEvaluation()
    {
        // First() AND A LOCAL FUNCTION, so the mapper cannot
        // translate the predicate and EVALUATES IT IN MEMORY — and
        // with no filter in the query, "in memory" means over
        // everything ToListAsync brought back.
        static bool IsOverdue(Order o)
            => DateTimeOffset.UtcNow - o.PlacedAt > TimeSpan.FromDays(7);

        return await db.Orders.Where(IsOverdue).ToListAsync();
        // ^ THE SAME SHAPE with a captured helper:
        //   .Where(o => Normalise(o.Reference) == key)
        //   where Normalise is a local function — the compiler can
        //   quote the variable but not the method.
    }

    // THE FIX: A CONDITION THE DATABASE UNDERSTANDS.
    public async Task<List<Order>> RightClientEvaluation(DateTimeOffset cutoff)
        => await db.Orders
            .Where(o => o.PlacedAt < cutoff)                      // TRANSLATED
            .Where(o => EF.Functions.Like(o.Reference, "ORD-%"))   // and this
            .ToListAsync();
        {{-- ^ A CLIENT-EVALUATED PREDICATE NOW THROWS rather than
             silently evaluating, which is the correct change: the
             old behaviour turned a query into a full table read
             with NO DIAGNOSTIC, and the new one refuses. So if
             you find that exception, look for a LOCAL FUNCTION
             inside a Where — it is almost always that. --}}
}

// (4) N+1: THE ONLY ONE INVISIBLE IN THE MAPPER'S OWN CODE.
public sealed class Four(WebApplication db)
{
    public async Task<List<string>> WrongNPlusOne()
    {
        var refs = new List<string>();
        foreach (var order in await db.Orders.ToListAsync())
            refs.Add(order.Customer.Name);
        // ^ ONE QUERY for the orders, then ONE PER ORDER for the
        //   customer: 1 + 200. THE LOOP READS AS IF IT WERE ONE
        //   QUERY, which is why this is the hardest of the four to
        //   see in review — and it is found by counting the
        //   queries in the log, not by reading the C#.
        return refs;
    }

    // THE FIX: EAGER LOAD, WHICH IS A JOIN.
    public async Task<List<string>> RightNPlusOne()
    {
        var refs = new List<string>();
        foreach (var order in await db.Orders
                                   .Include(o => o.Customer)
                                   .ToListAsync())
            refs.Add(order.Customer.Name);
        // ^ ONE JOIN, no extra round trip. THE TRADE: for a
        //   COLLECTION — an order with 200 lines — Include produces a
        //   JOIN that MULTIPLIES ROWS, so the correct answer there
        //   is TWO QUERIES: the parents, then the children by
        //   parent id. Include is for a REFERENCE; a collection
        //   wants its own query.
    }

    // THE ONE DIAGNOSTIC WORTH HAVING, and it finds three of the
    // four in a single pass:
    //   builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
    //       o.UseSqlServer(cs).EnableSensitiveDataLogging());
    //   o.LogTo(Console.WriteLine, LogLevel.Information);
    // ^ READ THE SQL. A WHERE clause in the generated statement
    //   was TRANSLATED; one that is absent was EVALUATED IN
    //   MEMORY. It is one line of configuration and it is invisible
    //   in every line of C#, which is why it beats code review for
    //   this class of problem.
}

Production readiness checklist

Work through this before the first production release and again after every significant dependency or platform change. Each item names the chapter that explains the failure it prevents.

What makes an item checkable

It has to be answerable by reading one place. "Does a partial write leave the data inconsistent" is checkable by finding every multi-statement write and looking at its transaction. "Is error handling appropriate" is not checkable at all, and it is therefore the item that never gets checked — which is a good reason to refuse to write items in that form, whatever the benefit of the wording.

There is a second property worth aiming for, and it is that a good item has a defect rather than a practice. An item saying "use transactions" is a practice, and two people can agree with it while disagreeing about whether the code does it. An item saying "no multi-statement write exists outside a transaction" is a fact about the code, and it can be disproved in five minutes.

What to add for a specific deployment

A container needs a health check that reports not-ready while a required dependency is unreachable, and a resource limit, because the first thing a platform does under pressure is remove one. A serverless function needs a timeout shorter than the platform's, or it is killed mid-write and leaves whatever it was writing in whatever state it had reached. A scheduled job needs an overlap guard, because the previous run is usually still going when the next one starts, and two runs writing the same rows is the defect.

None of those three is on the general list, and all three are the ones that actually bite. The general list covers what an application must be; the deployment-specific list covers what this application must additionally be, and it is the second list that is always missing from a checklist somebody copied from another project.

How to use the list

Once, at review, rather than continuously. A checklist that is on a dashboard is a checklist that has become noise, and the items that survive are the ones somebody could actually answer.

CONFIGURATION AND SECRETS
[ ] No secret in appsettings.json, in a .csproj, in a Dockerfile ARG or ENV, or in git
[ ] Development secrets come from user secrets; production from environment or Key Vault
[ ] Every options class has ValidateDataAnnotations plus ValidateOnStart          (14.4)
[ ] A test fails if a secret-shaped key has a value in a file-based provider   (14.5)
[ ] Configuration precedence is documented for the service                        (14.5)

DIAGNOSTICS
[ ] Structured logging with named placeholders; no string concatenation          (14.6)
[ ] A scope carries the correlation identifiers for every operation               (14.6)
[ ] No PII, tokens, connection strings or free-text user input in any log        (14.6)
[ ] OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs exported over OTLP                    (17.6)
[ ] Health checks: liveness without dependencies, readiness with them            (17.6)
[ ] Liveness and readiness are separate endpoints and separate probes            (17.6)
[ ] Every health check is bounded, cheap, and cannot throw                       (17.6)

DATA
[ ] Every query is parameterised; no concatenation into CommandText              (13.2)
[ ] The provider is Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, not System.Data.SqlClient          (13.3)
[ ] Connection strings set EnableRetryOnFailure for a cloud database             (13.6)
[ ] No in-memory provider in a gating test; SQLite or a real engine instead       (15.5)
[ ] Migrations apply automatically and are reversible, or the reversal is         (13.6)
    documented as impossible
[ ] The query plan of the ten most expensive queries has been read               (13.5)
[ ] The N+1 pattern has been looked for in every collection-returning endpoint   (13.5)

LIFECYCLE
[ ] Lifetimes are chosen deliberately; ValidateScopes is on in development        (14.2)
[ ] No singleton takes a scoped dependency                                     (14.2)
[ ] Background services create their own scope per unit of work                 (14.2)
[ ] SIGTERM drains in-flight work within the shutdown timeout                   (17.6)
[ ] Long-running work is on a durable queue, not an in-process buffer            (17.6)

BUILD AND SUPPLY CHAIN
[ ] global.json pins the SDK; CI uses the same file                               (17.2)
[ ] Every package version is pinned; the lock file is committed and enforced     (17.3)
[ ] NuGetAudit is on and NU1901 to NU1904 are errors                              (17.3)
[ ] packageSourceMapping prevents a public package shadowing a private one       (17.3)
[ ] The base image is pinned by digest, not by a floating tag                    (17.5)
[ ] The container runs as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem        (17.5)
[ ] .dockerignore excludes bin/, obj/ and .git                                    (17.5)

PERFORMANCE
[ ] Allocation budget tests exist for the hot parsing and serialisation paths     (16.2)
[ ] A BenchmarkDotNet project exists and is run on a quiet machine               (16.3)
[ ] Gen0 rate and time-in-gc are on a dashboard, with a threshold that alerts    (16.5)
[ ] A dotnet-trace capture and a dotnet-dump have been taken at least once, and
    the runbook says who does it and how                                                          (16.5)
[ ] The process survives a memory limit (DOTNET_gcHeapHardLimitPercent)           (16.5)

RELEASES
[ ] Schema changes use expand-then-contract and are independently reversible      (17.6)
[ ] The build stamps its version from the git tag                                 (17.6)
[ ] A smoke test runs against the published artifact, not the source              (17.6)
[ ] Roll-forward is the plan; reverting a binary after a data write is not        (17.6)

{{-- A CHECKLIST IS WRITTEN AS A QUESTION WITH A CHECKABLE ANSWER,
     and each item names the FAILURE IT PREVENTS. --}}
public sealed class DataAndWork
{
    // 1. TRANSACTIONS. "Does a partial write leave the data
    //    inconsistent?"
    // THE FAILURE IT PREVENTS: an order with no lines, or lines
    //   with no order, because step 2 of 3 failed. The symptom is a
    //   record nobody can display and no constraint forbids.
    // THE CHECK: every multi-statement write is in ONE
    //   transaction, and it is committed or rolled back on EVERY
    //   path including an early return and an exception — which is
    //   what a using statement on the transaction gives you, and
    //   what try/finally with a commit in the try does NOT.
    public async Task<int> WithTransactionAsync(SqlConnection c, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var tx = await c.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
        try
        {
            await InsertOrderAsync(c, tx, ct);
            await InsertLinesAsync(c, tx, ct);
            await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
            return 1;
        }
        catch
        {
            await tx.RollbackAsync(ct);
            throw;
        }
    }

    // 2. IDEMPOTENCY. "Can this operation be repeated without
    //    changing the result?"
    // THE FAILURE IT PREVENTS: a retried webhook charging a card
    //   twice, because the handler is not idempotent and the caller
    //   WILL retry — every queue retries on a timeout, and a
    //   timeout does not mean the work did not happen.
    // THE CHECK: a caller-supplied key is UNIQUE IN THE DATABASE,
    //   and the handler's FIRST ACT is an INSERT that fails if the
    //   key exists. Not a cache check: a cache check races with
    //   itself, and two concurrent deliveries both miss it.
    public async Task HandleWebhookAsync(Webhook w, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // The INSERT IS THE LOCK. A second delivery gets a unique
        // violation and returns 200 without doing the work.
        await _db.Deliveries.AddAsync(new Delivery(w.Id, w.Body));
        await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        await ProcessAsync(w, ct);
    }

    // 3. BACKGROUND WORK. "Does a failed job take the process
    //    down, or go unnoticed?"
    // THE FAILURE IT PREVENTS: a poison message killing the
    //   consumer permanently with no alarm; or a job failing
    //   forever with nobody notified.
    // THE CHECK: a poison message is MOVED TO A DEAD LETTER after
    //   N attempts rather than retried forever; the queue depth and
    //   the dead-letter count are MONITORED; and a job that throws
    //   is not allowed to crash the consumer.
}


// THE OPERATIONAL HALF, and it is where the remaining items live:
public sealed class Operations(IConfiguration config, ILogger<Operations> log)
{
    // 4. SECRETS. "What happens if one is missing at start-up?"
    // THE FAILURE IT PREVENTS: the service starts, serves traffic,
    //   and fails every call to a dependency because a connection
    //   string is empty — discovered by users rather than by a
    //   health check.
    // THE CHECK: every required secret is VALIDATED AT START-UP and
    //   a missing one FAILS THE PROCESS. A health check that
    //   reports ready while a dependency is unreachable is WORSE
    //   than no health check, because the load balancer trusts it
    //   and keeps sending traffic into the failure.
    public void ValidateAtStartUp(IConfiguration cfg)
    {
        foreach (var key in RequiredKeys)
        {
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(cfg[key]))
                throw new InvalidOperationException($"{key} is required at start-up.");
        }
    }

    // 5. RESOURCE LIMITS. "What stops one request consuming
    //    everything?"
    // THE FAILURE IT PREVENTS: one client with a large page size
    //   consuming all the memory, which is an outage for EVERYBODY
    //   rather than a slow response for one.
    // THE CHECK: request body size, page size, upload size and
    //   query timeout are all SET and ENFORCED AT THE EDGE; the
    //   application's connection pool is SMALLER than the server's,
    //   so a traffic spike queues in the application rather than
    //   exhausting the server; and a per-tenant rate limit exists
    //   if there is more than one tenant.
    public void EnforceLimits(WebApplication app)
    {
        // ^ SETTING A LIMIT IS NOT ENFORCING ONE. The number has to
        //   be smaller than what the downstream can serve, or the
        //   limit moves the queue rather than removing it.
        app.Use(async (ctx, next) =>
        {
            if (ctx.Request.ContentLength > 10 * 1024 * 1024)
            {
                ctx.Response.StatusCode = 413;
                return;
            }
            await next();
        });
    }

    // 6. OBSERVABILITY. "Would an operator know?"
    // THE FAILURE IT PREVENTS: an outage discovered by a customer,
    //   because no signal was emitted at the moment it started.
    // THE CHECK: LOGS ARE STRUCTURED — a message template plus
    //   values, not an interpolated string; the four golden signals
    //   are emitted for every request (latency, traffic, errors,
    //   saturation); and a CORRELATION ID follows the request
    //   through every log line and every downstream call, so a
    //   trace is ONE FILTER rather than a correlation exercise.
    public async Task Next(HttpContext ctx)
    {
        var id = ctx.TraceIdentifier;
        using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["TraceId"] = id }))
        {
            // ^ A SCOPE, so the correlation id is attached to
            //   everything logged inside it without being passed
            //   as a parameter — which is what makes it survive
            //   into a dependency call you did not instrument.
            await _next(ctx);
        }
    }
}

{{-- AND THE ONE THAT IS NOT A QUESTION, because it is the one
     everybody forgets:

     WHAT IS THE ROLLBACK PLAN, AND HAS ANYONE RUN IT?

     A deployment with no rehearsed rollback has not been tested in
     the only condition that matters — under load, at the worst
     moment, with a person watching. And the plan is not "redeploy
     the previous version": it is the previous DATABASE schema being
     compatible with the previous code, which means every migration
     needs a stated down path or a stated reason there is none. --}}

Troubleshooting index

Symptoms first, because that is how an incident arrives. Each row names the observable and the first thing to check.

SymptomMost likely causeFirst check
Latency p99 spikes with no CPUGen2 garbage collectiondotnet-counters: gen-2-gc-count and time-in-gc (16.5)
Latency spikes every few minutes under loadGen0 budget exhausted by an allocation rategen-0-gc-count per second against the request rate (16.2)

Pool exhausted, Timeout expired on openA connection held across an unrelated await, or a missing disposePool size from sp_executesql counters; audit using (13.1)

A test passes against the in-memory provider and fails in productionConstraint the provider does not enforceMove the test to SQLite (15.5)
