Where this guide states a version, the version is pinned to the release noted in section 14 of the orientation material: C# 14 on .NET 10 (LTS, general availability November 2025), EF Core 10 with .NET 10, and C# 15 paired with .NET 11. Visual Studio 2026 and Rider 2025.3 or later support C# 14 out of the box. Where the framework documentation and this guide disagree, the framework documentation is authoritative and this guide is wrong.

Enterprise Appendix Exercises

  1. Build a Directory.Packages.props for a new service from the package reference table, pin every version, and confirm that dotnet restore --locked-mode succeeds on a clean clone.
  2. Take the anti-pattern table and confirm each row against a real codebase or a synthetic reproduction, recording the trace or the counter that would reveal it. Discard any row you cannot reproduce.
  3. Walk the production readiness checklist against an existing service and produce a written gap analysis with an owner and a date for each gap. This is the most valuable single exercise in the appendix.
  4. Work backwards from the troubleshooting index: pick five symptoms, construct a minimal reproduction of each, and measure the counter or trace that identifies the cause. Then confirm the index row is accurate.
  5. Verify the documentation links resolve and that each one is the page for the version stated in this guide, not the current preview.
  6. Write a decision record for one service you know, using the data access decision table, and state explicitly which table it owns, which Dapper owns, and where the boundary is enforced.

{{-- WHERE TO LOOK FOR WHAT, because the documentation is large and
     most of it answers a question you do not have yet. --}}

// Q: "WHAT DOES THE COMPILER ACTUALLY GUARANTEE?"
//    -> THE LANGUAGE SPECIFICATION.
//    docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/language-reference
//      language-versioning      WHICH FEATURES EXIST IN WHICH
//                               VERSION — the page to read before
//                               pinning a LangVersion, because
//                               every version both added and
//                               changed something
//      implicit-conversions    the numeric promotion rules, which
//                              are what produce the silent
//                              narrowing from a compound
//                              assignment
//      nullable-reference-types what the annotation DOES and does
//                              NOT do at run time, in four
//                              paragraphs that answer most of the
//                              questions people ask about it
//      patterns                every pattern, including the ones
//                              with no useful syntax
{{-- ^ AND THE ONE THAT IS MOST READ AND MOST NEEDED: the
     specification states that a compound assignment performs a
     CONVERSION of the result, which is why it can overflow where
     the two-step form throws under checked. That single sentence
     explains an entire class of asymmetric bug report. --}}

// Q: "WHAT SHOULD THIS API LOOK LIKE?"
//    -> THE RUNTIME DESIGN GUIDELINES.
//    github.com/dotnet/runtime -> docs -> coding-guidelines
//    ~500 pages, and it is the reason a library author and a
//    library consumer sometimes disagree about whether a method
//    should be virtual, sealed, or take a CancellationToken.
//    It answers questions a reference page cannot: whether a
//    collection method should be an extension, whether an argument
//    should be validated eagerly or lazily, what a good exception
//    message contains.


// Q: "WHAT SHOULD I WRITE?"
//    -> THE PERFORMANCE GUIDELINES, which are the ones that change
//    code rather than names.
//    devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet
//      "Performance best practices"   the ASYNC and ALLOCATION
//                                    chapters are worth reading
//                                    twice, and the STRING chapter
//                                    CONTRADICTS most advice written
//                                    before 2015 — which is the
//                                    clearest example of guidance
//                                    expiring
//      "Async best practices"         why ConfigureAwait(false)
//                                    is a LIBRARY rule rather than
//                                    an application one: in an
//                                    application there is nothing
//                                    to configure, so the advice is
//                                    noise there
//      "Channel best practices"       the COMPLETION ORDERING
//                                    rules, which are the part
//                                    people get wrong and which
//                                    produce bugs that appear only
//                                    under load
//      "Memory management"            what actually causes a
//                                    gen-2 collection, as opposed
//                                    to what causes a lot of
//                                    gen-0 collections
{{-- ^ WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL OF THE FOUR, and also the most
     likely to be wrong, because a post is a snapshot. The rule
     worth applying: treat a performance post as a hypothesis to
     MEASURE with a benchmark, never as an instruction. A post
     written against a framework version that no longer exists is
     not merely dated — it can be actively inverted, because the
     allocator or the JIT changed underneath it. --}}

// Q: "WHAT DID THIS VERSION CHANGE?"
//    -> THE RELEASE NOTES, read for the REMOVALS rather than the
//    additions. The additions are opt-in and the removals are not:
//    a member marked obsolete in one version is a compile warning
//    in the next and a build error in the one after that, and a
//    team that reads only the "what's new" posts finds that in a
//    failed build.

// AND THE ONE THAT IS NOT DOCUMENTATION AT ALL: the ANALYSERS
// THAT SHIP WITH THE SDK.
//      dotnet build /p:AnalysisLevel=latest-all
//    ^ CA1062 (validate arguments of public methods), CA1822 (a
//      method that could be static), CA2007 (a missing
//      ConfigureAwait in application code), CA1849 (a synchronous
//      call in an async path). These are rules the language spec
//      STATES but nobody enforces, and turning the level up is
//      cheaper than reading five pages and catches the
//      argument-nullability defects that a code review does not.
{{-- ^ THE ORDERING WORTH ADOPTING: read the release notes for the
     version you are moving TO, bump the analysis level, then read
     the performance posts only for the areas you actually profile.
     Everything else in the documentation is reference material —
     correct, complete, and not something to read end to end. --}}

C# 14 & .NET 10 — The Language and Enterprise Guide. Chapters 1–12 cover the language; 13–17 cover data access, dependency injection, configuration, logging, testing, performance and delivery; the Enterprise Appendix is the production reference. Progress is saved in your browser (theme, last chapter). Open in any modern browser. No internet needed.
